q: You have a Microsoft Entra tenant. You invite an external partner as a B2B guest user and add them to a project security group. The partner wants to browse the directory to find other project members and view their profiles. By default, what can the guest see?
options: Only their own profile until an administrator assigns them the Directory Readers role
Limited properties and membership information of directory objects
Full details, but only for users in the same security group
Full profiles and group memberships for all users, identical to a member user
explain: By default, Entra ID applies guest user access restrictions, so guests see only limited properties and memberships of directory objects - they cannot enumerate the full directory like members can. Assigning Directory Readers would expand visibility, but it is not granted by default. Options C and D overstate default guest access, and B is wrong because guests can already see limited directory information without any extra role.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: You create a Microsoft Entra security group that uses dynamic membership with a rule adding users whose department attribute equals 'Finance'. A new employee joins the Finance department. Separately, a manager tries to manually add an external contractor to the same group. What is the result?
options: The contractor is added, but the new employee must wait for the next directory sync
Both additions are queued until an administrator approves the dynamic rule
The new employee is added automatically, and the contractor is added manually
The new employee is added automatically, but the manual addition of the contractor fails
explain: Dynamic membership groups evaluate their rule continuously, so the new Finance employee becomes a member automatically with no administrator action. Manual add or remove operations are not supported on dynamic groups - membership is rule-driven only. To include the contractor you would need a rule that matches them, or a separate group that uses assigned membership.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: You need to delegate management of Conditional Access policies to a security engineer. They must be able to create and modify the policies, but they must not manage users, reset passwords, or change other identity settings. Which built-in Microsoft Entra role provides this least-privilege access?
options: Global Administrator
Authentication Administrator
Security Administrator
Conditional Access Administrator
explain: Conditional Access Administrator can manage Conditional Access policies and nothing else, which matches the requirement exactly. Security Administrator is broader (security alerts, identity protection configuration), Authentication Administrator manages authentication methods and can require users to re-register MFA, and Global Administrator is full tenant access - all three violate least privilege.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: Your tenant synchronizes users from on-premises Active Directory with Microsoft Entra Connect. A synchronized user resets their password through self-service password reset (SSPR). The reset succeeds in the cloud, but the new password does not work when they sign in to their on-premises workstation. What is the most likely cause?
options: The user must wait 24 hours for the password to replicate
Password writeback is not enabled in Microsoft Entra Connect
SSPR requires Microsoft Entra ID P2 for synchronized users
The user needs to re-register their authentication methods
explain: SSPR writes the new password to Microsoft Entra ID only. For synchronized users, password writeback must be enabled in Microsoft Entra Connect so the change flows back to on-premises Active Directory. Without it, the on-premises password is unchanged and workstation sign-in keeps failing. There is no 24-hour replication delay, and re-registering authentication methods is unrelated to the on-premises mismatch.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: You enable self-service password reset (SSPR) for all users in the tenant. During the pilot, several users open the reset portal and are told they cannot reset their password yet. These users never completed any prior setup. What must they do before SSPR will work for them?
options: Ask an administrator to set their per-user MFA state to Enforced
Sign in once from a trusted office location
Wait for the next Microsoft Entra Connect synchronization cycle
Register authentication methods, such as the Authenticator app or a phone number
explain: SSPR can only verify identity using authentication methods the user registered in advance. With combined registration, a single setup flow registers the user for both MFA and SSPR. Per-user MFA state, directory synchronization, and sign-in location do not substitute for registered authentication information.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: You manage MFA using per-user MFA states. You set several administrators to Enforced, so they register at next sign-in. You then create a Conditional Access policy that requires MFA for all cloud apps. Which statement is true?
options: Both mechanisms work, but Microsoft recommends managing MFA through Conditional Access rather than per-user states
Per-user MFA in the Enforced state automatically exempts users from Conditional Access
The Conditional Access policy cannot evaluate users who are in the Enforced state
You must set the users back to Disabled before the Conditional Access policy applies
explain: Per-user MFA states (Disabled, Enabled, Enforced) still function, and Conditional Access policies evaluate normally for those users - neither mechanism blocks the other. However, per-user MFA is the legacy management path; Conditional Access is the recommended approach because it applies MFA based on signals like risk, location, and device instead of a static per-user flag.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: You have a Conditional Access policy that requires MFA for all users. Users complain about repeated MFA prompts when working from the corporate office, which uses a known public IP range. You want the office network excluded from the MFA requirement without weakening the policy elsewhere. What should you do?
options: Move office users into an exclusion group that bypasses all Conditional Access policies
Disable the Conditional Access policy during business hours
Add the office IP range to the trusted IPs list in the legacy per-user MFA settings
Create a named location for the office IP range and exclude it from the policy
explain: Named locations define trusted IP ranges or countries, and a Conditional Access policy can exclude them from its scope - so the MFA requirement stays enforced everywhere except the office. The legacy trusted-IPs list only affects per-user MFA, not Conditional Access. Disabling the policy or excluding users entirely removes protection far beyond the office network.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: Your security team wants to block legacy authentication protocols such as IMAP, POP3, and older Office clients, because they cannot perform MFA. Modern authentication must keep working. How should you scope the Conditional Access policy?
options: Use the User risk condition set to High
Use the Client apps condition to target legacy authentication clients
Use Session controls to enforce sign-in frequency
Use the Grant control to require MFA for all client apps
explain: The Client apps condition can target clients using legacy authentication, so the policy blocks exactly those protocols while modern authentication flows are unaffected. Requiring MFA in the grant control would not help, because legacy clients cannot complete MFA at all. Session controls and user risk do not distinguish authentication protocols.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: Microsoft Entra ID Protection flags a user as high user risk because their credentials appeared in a public breach. You configure a user risk policy with remediation. What happens the next time the user signs in?
options: The user is prompted for MFA once, and the risk is dismissed automatically
The user must complete a secure password change, which remediates the user risk
Nothing happens until an administrator manually resets the password
The user is blocked permanently until an administrator clears the risk
explain: A user risk policy can require a secure password change: the user changes their own password at sign-in, and ID Protection then remediates (closes) the user risk. This is separate from a sign-in risk policy, which evaluates each sign-in attempt and can require MFA or block access. MFA alone does not remediate leaked credentials, and no administrator action is required.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: You make a contractor eligible for the Contributor role on a subscription through Privileged Identity Management (PIM). The eligible assignment requires MFA, justification, and manager approval. The contractor opens the Azure portal and immediately tries to create a resource, but gets an access error. What must happen first?
options: The contractor must be assigned Global Administrator in Microsoft Entra ID
The contractor must activate the role: submit a justification, complete MFA, and obtain approval
An administrator must convert the eligible assignment into a permanent active assignment
Nothing; eligible assignments become active automatically within one hour
explain: Eligible is not active: PIM requires the user to activate the role, which triggers the configured checks - MFA, justification, and approval - and grants the role only for the configured time-limited duration. Converting to a permanent assignment or granting Global Administrator would bypass the just-in-time model that PIM exists to enforce.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: You configure quarterly access reviews in PIM for all eligible Azure resource role assignments. Auto-apply results is enabled. A reviewer denies one user's continued need for their eligible Contributor assignment. What happens to that assignment?
options: The assignment is converted to an active assignment for 30 days
The assignment stays until an administrator manually deletes it
The review only produces a report; assignments never change
The eligible assignment is removed automatically when the review ends
explain: With auto-apply enabled, PIM enforces reviewer decisions at the end of the review: denied access is removed automatically, so stale eligible assignments do not linger. Without auto-apply, an administrator would have to apply the results manually. Reviews never convert eligible assignments into active ones.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: A compliance analyst must grant Reader access to external auditors across your subscription. They must not be able to create, modify, or delete any resources. Which built-in Azure RBAC role gives this least-privilege access?
options: Reader
Owner
Contributor
User Access Administrator
explain: User Access Administrator can manage role assignments (granting Reader to the auditors) but cannot manage the resources themselves - exactly the split required. Owner and Contributor can both manage resources, which is excessive, and Reader cannot assign roles at all.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: A DevOps lead has Contributor on a resource group. They try to grant a teammate Contributor on the same resource group and receive an AuthorizationFailed error. Why did this fail, and what is the least-privilege fix?
options: Contributor cannot manage role assignments; additionally assign User Access Administrator
The lead must be assigned Owner, which is the only role that grants access to others
Contributor can only assign roles at the subscription scope, not the resource group scope
Only the Global Administrator can delegate Azure RBAC roles
explain: Contributor can manage everything about resources except access: assigning roles requires Microsoft.Authorization/roleAssignments/write, which only Owner and User Access Administrator hold. Adding User Access Administrator gives the lead delegation ability without the full power of Owner. Scope is irrelevant here - Contributor cannot assign roles at any scope.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: You need a custom Azure RBAC role that lets operators start, stop, and restart virtual machines, but not delete them or read disk encryption secrets. You plan to clone the Virtual Machine Contributor role. Which statement about the custom role definition is true?
options: DataActions cannot be restricted in a custom role
Custom role definitions can only be created at the tenant root scope
The role name must be globally unique across all of Azure
You remove the unwanted permissions with NotActions and limit where the role can be assigned with AssignableScopes
explain: A custom role is defined in JSON: Actions grants permissions, NotActions subtracts from them, and AssignableScopes controls the management group, subscription, or resource group scopes where the role may be assigned. Cloning Virtual Machine Contributor and trimming with NotActions is the standard pattern. Definitions can be created below the tenant root, DataActions and NotDataActions handle data-plane permissions, and names must be unique within the directory, not globally.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: You assign the Reader role to a security group at the subscription scope. One resource group in the subscription has no explicit role assignments. What access do group members have inside that resource group?
options: Contributor, because child scopes elevate read access
Owner, because subscription scope implies full control
No access until Reader is also assigned at the resource group scope
Reader, inherited from the subscription assignment
explain: Role assignments inherit down the management hierarchy: from subscription to resource groups to resources. Members get Reader on everything in the subscription unless a more specific assignment or a deny assignment changes it. Child scopes never elevate permissions on their own.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: You deploy a Deployment Stack to a production resource group with denySettings set to DenyDelete. An Owner of the subscription tries to delete a virtual machine in that resource group. What happens?
options: The deletion is blocked; deny assignments stop even Owners, and users cannot create deny assignments directly
The deletion succeeds after the Owner confirms a warning prompt
The deletion succeeds because Owner overrides all deny settings
The deletion is blocked only for Contributors, not for Owners
explain: DenySettings creates deny assignments, which take precedence over any allow-based role assignment - including Owner. Deny assignments are system-created (by Deployment Stacks or Blueprints); users cannot create them manually. This is how production resources are protected from accidental deletion regardless of who attempts it.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: You apply a CanNotDelete resource lock to a production storage account. Which action can still be performed against the storage account?
options: Deleting the storage account
Deleting a container in the account
Removing the lock with the Contributor role
Uploading blobs to a container in the account
explain: CanNotDelete blocks control-plane deletes (the account, its containers) but data-plane operations like uploading blobs continue to work. Removing a lock requires Microsoft.Authorization/locks/delete, which Contributor lacks - only Owner or User Access Administrator can delete the lock. Note this differs from a ReadOnly lock, which would also block data writes.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: You want to reorganize your environment by moving a virtual machine and its network interface from ResourceGroup-A to ResourceGroup-B. Both groups are in the same subscription. Which statement is true?
options: You can move the resources directly; renaming a resource group is not supported
You must deallocate the virtual machine before moving it
Resources cannot be moved between resource groups
The move works only if both resource groups are in different subscriptions
explain: Most resources can be moved between resource groups in the same subscription (and many across subscriptions) with no downtime - deallocation is not required. Azure does not support renaming a resource group, so moving resources into a correctly named group is the way to reorganize. A few resource types with dependencies cannot move, so you check move support per resource type.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: Finance needs cost reports grouped by a CostCenter tag. You apply the tag to each resource group, but the Cost Management report shows no CostCenter values on the resources. Why?
options: Tags applied to a resource group are not inherited by its resources
Tags take 30 days to appear in cost reports
Only subscription-level tags appear in cost reports
Cost Management cannot group or filter by tags
explain: There is no automatic tag inheritance in Azure: tagging a resource group does not tag the resources inside it. To propagate tags, use Azure Policy - for example a Modify or Append effect that inherits the tag from the resource group - or apply the tag to each resource directly. Cost Management groups and filters by resource tags normally once they exist on the resources.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: You assign a built-in Deny policy that blocks public network access on storage accounts at the subscription scope. One legacy application needs a temporary 30-day exception for a single storage account. What is the best approach?
options: Exclude the entire subscription from the policy assignment
Create an exemption scoped to the storage account with an expiration date
Assign a second policy that allows public access on that account
Change the policy effect from Deny to Audit for 30 days
explain: An exemption waives policy compliance for a specific scope (here, the storage account) and supports an expiration date - ideal for a time-bound exception. Excluding the subscription or switching to Audit would weaken protection everywhere. Exemptions are separate resources from assignment-scope exclusions and are the designed mechanism for temporary waivers.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: You assign a DeployIfNotExists policy definition that installs the Azure Monitor agent on virtual machines that lack it. New VMs get the agent automatically, but existing non-compliant VMs remain without it. What is required to remediate the existing VMs?
options: Change the policy effect to Deny
Create a remediation task for the policy assignment
Delete and recreate the non-compliant VMs
Reassign the policy individually to each virtual machine
explain: DeployIfNotExists evaluates when resources are created or updated, so it fixes new VMs automatically. Existing non-compliant resources need a remediation task, which executes the deployment for them. The assignment's managed identity must also hold sufficient RBAC (such as Contributor) on the target scope for the remediation deployment to succeed.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: You assign a regulatory compliance initiative to a management group that contains five subscriptions. Where do you review which subscriptions have non-compliant resources, and what does the management group scope achieve?
options: In Microsoft Entra ID audit logs; the assignment applies only to the first subscription
In Cost Management; initiatives only track spending compliance
On the Azure Policy compliance dashboard; the assignment cascades to all child subscriptions
You must assign the initiative separately to each subscription; management group scope is display-only
explain: An initiative is a collection of policy definitions assigned as one unit. Assigning it at the management group scope cascades to every subscription underneath, and the Policy compliance dashboard aggregates compliant versus non-compliant resources across all of them. Entra audit logs and Cost Management do not track policy compliance.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: Your organization has 15 subscriptions. You need the same set of Azure Policy assignments and RBAC role assignments applied to all of them, managed from a single place. What should you implement?
options: Use Azure Lighthouse to project the subscriptions into one view
Create a management group hierarchy, move the subscriptions under it, and assign policies and roles at the management group scope
Assign the policies and roles individually in each subscription
Place all resources in a single resource group shared across subscriptions
explain: Management groups form a hierarchy above subscriptions: assignments made at the management group scope inherit to all child subscriptions, so you manage policy and access once. Azure Lighthouse is for delegated management across tenants, not for unifying your own subscriptions, and resources cannot span subscriptions inside one resource group.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: You create a monthly Cost Management budget of $5,000 scoped to a resource group. You want email alerts when actual spending reaches 80% of the budget and when forecasted spending is projected to exceed 100%. Which statement is true?
options: Budget alerts can only trigger automation runbooks, not send email
Budgets can only be scoped to a subscription, not a resource group
You configure two alert conditions on the budget - one on actual cost at 80%, one on forecasted cost at 100% - with notification recipients
A budget supports only one alert threshold, so you must choose actual or forecasted
explain: Budgets support multiple alert rules combining actual and forecasted costs at different percentage thresholds, and each alert can notify email recipients and action groups. Budgets can be scoped to a subscription or a resource group, and email notification is a core capability - runbooks via action groups are optional, not the only output.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: Your platform team maintains an approved ARM template used by teams in ten subscriptions. You need versioning (teams must deploy exactly version 2.1) and RBAC-controlled access to the template itself. What should you use?
options: Email the template file to each team
Publish the template as a Template Spec with versions
Deploy the template with a Deployment Stack in each subscription
Store the template in a storage account and share the blob URL
explain: A Template Spec stores an ARM template as an Azure resource with multiple named versions, and standard RBAC controls who can read or deploy each version - so teams can target exactly version 2.1. A storage blob URL offers no versioning or RBAC, and Deployment Stacks manage resource lifecycle rather than template sharing.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: You have a storage account containing VM OS disks and a file share used by legacy applications. Management wants the account to survive a full datacenter outage within the same region without changing the public endpoint. You need the highest availability option available for this account. Which redundancy should you configure?
options: Locally redundant storage (LRS)
Geo-zone-redundant storage (GZRS)
Zone-redundant storage (ZRS)
Geo-redundant storage (GRS)
explain: ZRS synchronously replicates data across three availability zones in the primary region, so a full datacenter outage in-region is survivable while keeping the same endpoint. GRS/GZRS replicate to a secondary region but do not protect the primary endpoint in-region; the application would need to switch endpoints. ZRS is available for managed disks and Azure Files (Premium page blobs themselves are LRS-only). LRS offers no zone or region protection.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: You have a Standard general-purpose v2 storage account with the Hot tier. A compliance policy requires that monthly financial report blobs remain unread for at least 180 days and cost as little as possible during that time, but must be retrievable within minutes when auditors request them. What should you do?
options: Move the blobs to the Cold tier
Move the blobs to the Archive tier
Enable blob versioning on the account
Move the blobs to the Cool tier
explain: The Cold tier is priced for infrequently accessed data with long retention, and reads have millisecond-level latency just like Hot and Cool — no rehydration wait. Archive is cheaper still but rehydration takes hours, which fails the minutes requirement. Cool is optimized for short-term infrequent access (30-day minimum) and costs more than Cold for 180-day retention. Blob versioning adds protection, not cost optimization.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: You need to migrate 300 TB of backup files from an on-premises datacenter with no reliable WAN connection to Azure Blob storage. Shipping drives must be encrypted and the data must land in a storage account without traversing the public internet at your source site. Which service should you use?
options: AzCopy over the public internet
Azure Data Box
Storage Explorer upload
Azure File Sync
explain: Azure Data Box is the offline migration service: Microsoft ships you a ruggedized encrypted device, you copy data locally, ship it back, and Microsoft uploads it to your storage account. AzCopy, Storage Explorer, and File Sync all require network connectivity and are wrong for a no-WAN scenario. Data Box is specifically designed for this offline, large-scale seeding pattern.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: You create an Azure Files share for a line-of-business application and need it to accept NFSv4.1 connections from Linux VMs in an Azure VNet. The share must also support premium performance. Which storage configuration supports this?
options: A Standard general-purpose v2 account with the Cool tier
A Standard general-purpose v2 account with the Hot tier and SMB disabled
A Premium file shares (FileStorage) account with NFS enabled
A Premium block blobs account
explain: NFS 4.1 protocol support on Azure Files requires a Premium file shares (FileStorage) account. Standard GPv2 accounts only support SMB, not NFS. Premium block blobs accounts (BlockBlobStorage) hold blobs only, no file shares. Premium page blobs are for disks. The exam tests knowing that protocol choice (SMB vs NFS) is tied to the account kind and tier, not just a setting you flip.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: A partner organization must read files in one blob container for the next two weeks, but must never be able to list other containers or write anything. The security team requires that the credential be revocable without rotating the storage account keys. Which approach meets these requirements?
options: Create a service SAS on the container backed by a stored access policy
Generate an account SAS valid for two weeks and share the URL
Assign the partner the Storage Blob Data Reader role
Share the storage account key and rotate it after two weeks
explain: A service SAS scoped to a single container, backed by a stored access policy, can be revoked by changing or deleting the policy — no key rotation needed. An account SAS grants broader permissions than needed and cannot be revoked individually. Sharing account keys violates least privilege and revocation requires rotation. RBAC roles cannot easily expire on a schedule the way a SAS can.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: You have 2 PB of log data in the Archive tier. A small subset of logs from a security incident must be restored, and you need the data back within 24 hours. Rehydration cost is secondary to speed. Which rehydration priority should you select?
options: Standard priority rehydration
Move the blobs to the Cool tier first, then rehydrate
Bulk priority rehydration
High priority rehydration
explain: High priority rehydration completes in under one hour for blobs under 10 GB, versus up to 15 hours for standard priority — the right choice when speed matters and cost is secondary. There is no 'bulk' priority. You do not move to Cool first; rehydration IS the operation that copies the blob back to Hot or Cool. Standard priority would risk missing the 24-hour window at scale.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: Your company uses Azure File Sync with a cloud endpoint and three server endpoints at branch offices. A user accidentally deletes a critical folder on one server. The deletion has not yet synced. You need to prevent the deletion from propagating to Azure and the other servers. What is the fastest reliable action?
options: Restore the folder from an Azure Files snapshot in the portal
Delete and recreate the sync group
Pause the sync group, then recover the folder locally before resuming
Enable soft delete on the storage account
explain: Pausing (or taking the server offline from) the sync group stops the tombstone from propagating; you then restore the folder on the local server from its own backups or snapshots before resuming sync. Restoring a cloud snapshot only fixes the cloud copy after propagation. Recreating the sync group causes a full re-sync and risks data loss. Soft delete applies to blobs and Azure Files shares, but the immediate need is halting propagation, not point-in-time recovery.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: You create a storage account for a highly regulated workload. The account must be reachable only from a specific virtual network, and connections from that VNet must never traverse the public internet. What should you configure?
options: An SAS token with an IP restriction
A service endpoint on the subnet only
A service endpoint on the subnet and a storage firewall allow rule for the internet
A private endpoint for the storage account in the VNet
explain: A private endpoint assigns a private IP from the VNet to the storage account, so traffic stays on the Microsoft backbone/VNet and never touches the public internet. Service endpoints keep traffic off the public internet too, but the storage account still has a public endpoint address — with the strict 'never traverse' and 'only from the VNet' requirement, private endpoint is the precise answer. A firewall rule allowing the internet is wrong. SAS tokens authenticate, they do not control routing.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: You enable soft delete for blobs with a 30-day retention period. A user deletes a blob, then uploads a new blob with the same name two days later. What happens when you attempt to restore the soft-deleted blob?
options: The restore fails because a blob with the same name already exists
You must first delete the new blob, then undelete restores the original
The restore succeeds and overwrites the new blob automatically
Soft delete only applies to snapshots, so nothing can be restored
explain: Undelete restores the soft-deleted blob only if no active blob currently holds that name; with a name collision you must delete (or rename) the newer blob first, then the original can be restored within its 30-day retention window. The restore does not auto-overwrite. The name conflict causes the failure, not a missing feature. Soft delete protects base blobs (and optionally snapshots), not snapshots alone.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: A database team needs storage for SQL Server data files on Azure VMs with the lowest possible latency and consistent high IOPS. The workload issues 8 KB random writes. Which storage option should you recommend?
options: Azure Files on a Standard account with SMB
Standard HDD managed disks on a Standard GPv2 account
Standard SSD managed disks with the Cool tier
Premium SSD v2 managed disks
explain: Premium SSD v2 offers sub-millisecond latency and independently configurable IOPS and throughput, making it the right choice for latency-sensitive, high-IOPS database workloads. Premium SSD (v1) is capped per disk size; v2 decouples performance from size. Standard HDD and Standard SSD cannot match the latency or IOPS ceiling. Azure Files is not the recommended backing for SQL data files requiring lowest latency, and blob tiers do not apply to managed disks.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: You need to copy 50,000 small files from an on-premises file server to Azure Blob storage nightly, resuming automatically if the job is interrupted. The copy must preserve file timestamps as blob metadata and run unattended from a scheduled script. Which tool should you use?
options: AzCopy with the sync command
The Azure portal upload blade
Azure Data Box
Storage Explorer manual upload
explain: AzCopy sync compares source and destination and copies only changed/new files, supports resume, preserves timestamps, and is scriptable for unattended schedules. Storage Explorer and the portal are interactive GUI tools unsuitable for automation. Data Box is offline physical shipping, absurd for a nightly incremental job. The exam expects AzCopy for scripted bulk transfers and Data Box for offline migrations.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: Your security team mandates that all storage account encryption keys be managed by your organization, stored in Azure Key Vault, and automatically rotated every 90 days. Which configuration satisfies this mandate?
options: Customer-managed keys stored in Key Vault with auto-rotation enabled
Double encryption using two Microsoft-managed keys
An account SAS backed by a stored access policy
Microsoft-managed keys with infrastructure encryption enabled
explain: Customer-managed keys (CMK) in Azure Key Vault put key lifecycle — including automatic rotation — under your control, which is exactly what the mandate requires. Microsoft-managed keys are rotated by Microsoft, not your team, and do not satisfy 'managed by your organization.' Infrastructure encryption (double encryption) changes the encryption scope, not key ownership. SAS tokens control access delegation, not data-at-rest encryption.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: You have a lifecycle management policy on a storage account with two rules: Rule 1 moves blobs to the Cool tier after 30 days of no modification. Rule 2 deletes blobs 365 days after last modification. A blob is modified on day 40. When will it move to Cool and when will it be deleted?
options: Moves to Cool on day 30, deleted on day 365
Moves to Cool on day 70, deleted on day 365
Moves to Cool on day 70, deleted on day 405
Moves to Cool on day 40, deleted on day 365
explain: Lifecycle policies evaluate from the last-modified timestamp: modifying the blob on day 40 resets the clock, so Cool happens 30 days later (day 70) and deletion 365 days later (day 405). The policies do not use creation date. Day 30/365 would apply only if the blob were never touched after creation. This 'clock resets on modification' behavior is the classic exam trap for lifecycle questions.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: You deploy an application that writes large video files to blob storage and frequently overwrites the same blob names with new encodings. The team needs to keep every prior encoding for 14 days for rollback purposes, without creating separate blob names. Which feature should you enable?
options: Blob snapshots taken manually before each overwrite
Blob versioning with a lifecycle policy to delete prior versions after 14 days
Immutable storage with a time-based retention policy
Soft delete for blobs
explain: Blob versioning automatically creates a new version on every write to the same blob, keeping prior encodings under the same name; a lifecycle rule can then purge prior versions older than 14 days. Manual snapshots work but require the application to take them — not automatic. Soft delete only protects against deletions, not overwrites. Immutable storage would block the overwrites entirely, which breaks the workflow.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: A storage account holds backups replicated with read-access geo-redundant storage (RA-GRS). During a regional outage of the primary region, your runbook reads backup files directly from the secondary endpoint. Which statement about this scenario is true?
options: The secondary endpoint is readable because the account uses RA-GRS
RA-GRS makes the secondary writable during the outage
Reads from the secondary require a manual failover first
The secondary is only readable if GZRS is used instead
explain: RA-GRS (and RA-GZRS) expose the secondary copy for read access at all times via the -secondary endpoint, so the runbook can read backups during a primary outage without failing over. Plain GRS does not allow secondary reads. A failover (planned or unplanned) is only needed to make the secondary writable. GZRS adds zone redundancy to the primary, which is unrelated to secondary read access.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: You need to grant a data-science team access to blobs in a storage account. The team authenticates with Microsoft Entra ID and must use their existing identities — no shared keys or SAS tokens. Access must follow least privilege at the container level. What should you do?
options: Enable anonymous public read access on the containers
Distribute the storage account keys to the team
Assign the Storage Blob Data Contributor role on the specific containers to the team's Entra group
Create one account SAS and email it to the team
explain: Azure RBAC data-plane roles like Storage Blob Data Contributor grant Entra-authenticated access scoped to exactly the containers needed — no shared secrets involved. Account keys and SAS tokens are shared secrets that violate the 'existing identities' requirement. Anonymous public access exposes data to the internet. Note the RBAC requirement: management-plane roles like Reader do not grant data access; you need the Blob Data roles.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: Your company is replacing on-premises file servers at 20 branch offices. Each office needs a local cache of shared files, but the authoritative copy must live in Azure, and files must be tiered to the cloud when rarely accessed to save local disk. Which solution should you deploy?
options: Premium SSD managed disks attached to a file server VM
Azure File Sync with cloud tiering enabled
Azure Data Box at each office
AzCopy scheduled sync jobs
explain: Azure File Sync with cloud tiering keeps the authoritative copy in Azure Files, caches hot files locally on each Windows Server, and tiers cold file content to the cloud while leaving namespace stubs — exactly the hybrid pattern described. Data Box is one-time offline migration, not ongoing sync. AzCopy copies data but provides no transparent local cache or tiering. A single file-server VM centralizes files but gives no branch-local caching.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: You create a Premium block blobs account for an analytics workload that ingests millions of small telemetry files per hour. A colleague suggests switching to a Standard GPv2 account to save money. What is the key performance reason to keep the Premium block blobs account?
options: Premium block blobs provide consistently low, single-digit millisecond latency for high-transaction workloads
Premium block blobs support NFS 3.0
Premium block blobs include free geo-replication
Premium block blobs support the Archive tier
explain: Premium block blobs (BlockBlobStorage) are built for high transaction rates and large numbers of small objects with consistently low latency — the defining reason to choose them over Standard for telemetry ingestion. They do NOT support the Archive tier (Hot/Cool only). Geo-replication is not free on Premium. NFS 3.0 is a feature of Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2 hierarchical namespace on Standard accounts, not Premium block blobs.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: A storage account firewall is configured to deny all networks except the corporate office public IP range. Developers working from home over VPN report they cannot access blobs, even though the VPN lands them on the corporate network. What is the most likely cause?
options: Blob storage requires a private endpoint for VPN access
The developers must use Storage Explorer instead of AzCopy
The developers need a service SAS instead of account keys
The firewall evaluates the source public IP, and the VPN egress IP is not in the allow list
explain: The storage firewall filters on the source public IP of the connection. VPN clients typically egress to the internet through the VPN concentrator's public IP (or their own ISP if split-tunneled), which differs from the corporate office range in the allow list. SAS tokens authenticate but do not bypass firewall rules. A private endpoint is an alternative design, not the cause. The tool used (Storage Explorer vs AzCopy) is irrelevant to firewall evaluation.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: You need to store VM disk images that will be attached as OS disks to Azure VMs. The images require the highest IOPS per disk and must support 4K native sector sizes for a specific guest OS. Which managed disk and storage combination meets the requirement?
options: Ultra disks with LRS in a supported region
Premium SSD v1 managed disks with ZRS
Standard SSD managed disks with GRS
Standard HDD managed disks with LRS
explain: Ultra disks deliver the highest IOPS/throughput per disk and are the only managed disk type supporting 4K native sector sizes; they are LRS-only in supported regions. Premium SSD v1 tops out lower on IOPS and does not support 4K native. Standard HDD/SSD cannot meet 'highest IOPS' and Ultra disks do not support ZRS or GRS replication — Ultra is LRS only, which is an important exam fact.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: Your Azure Files shares are accessed by Windows clients that are joined to on-premises Active Directory Domain Services. The help desk reports users are prompted for credentials when opening shares, although their AD accounts have NTFS permissions on the files. What should you verify first?
options: That the storage account has an Entra Kerberos identity configured for AD DS authentication
That blob soft delete is enabled on the account
That a private endpoint exists for the storage account
That the share is using the Premium tier
explain: Seamless AD-based authentication to Azure Files requires the storage account to have an identity registered in AD DS (or Entra Kerberos / Entra Domain Services) — without it, Windows clients fall back to storage-account-key authentication and prompt for credentials. NTFS ACLs alone are not enough; the Kerberos identity is the prerequisite. Blob soft delete, share tier, and private endpoints are unrelated to authentication prompts.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: You are designing storage for a new application. The architects require that data at rest be encrypted with keys fully controlled by the company, stored off the storage account, with a different key per storage account for blast-radius isolation. Which design meets all three requirements?
options: Microsoft-managed keys, one key per storage account
Customer-managed keys in a dedicated Key Vault per storage account
Infrastructure encryption with Microsoft-managed keys
A single customer-managed key shared across all storage accounts
explain: Customer-managed keys satisfy 'fully controlled by the company' and 'stored off the storage account' (they live in Key Vault); using a dedicated vault per account gives each account its own key for blast-radius isolation. Microsoft-managed keys fail the control requirement regardless of count. Sharing one CMK across accounts fails the per-account isolation requirement. Infrastructure encryption adds a second Microsoft-managed layer but does not change key ownership.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: A nightly job writes thousands of blobs, then a reporting service reads them once the next morning. The storage account uses the Hot tier, and the finance team complains about transaction costs. The data is never read again after the report runs. Which change reduces cost without breaking the workflow?
options: Switch the account to the Archive tier
Enable blob versioning
Switch to Premium block blobs
Add a lifecycle policy that moves blobs to the Cool tier one day after last modification and deletes them after 30 days
explain: The data is hot for one day then cold forever: a lifecycle rule moving blobs to Cool after one day cuts storage cost, and deleting after 30 days removes the never-read-again waste — all automatic. Archive would break the morning reads (rehydration takes hours). Versioning increases cost by retaining copies. Premium block blobs raise, not lower, transaction and storage costs for this pattern.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: You need to allow an external auditor to download specific blobs over the next 48 hours. Company policy forbids distributing the storage account keys and forbids granting the auditor any Azure RBAC role. Which credential should you issue?
options: A service SAS scoped to the blobs with a 48-hour expiry
An account SAS with full permissions and a 48-hour expiry
A stored access policy with no SAS
The secondary storage account key
explain: A service SAS scoped to just the needed blobs, expiring in 48 hours, grants least-privilege time-boxed access without sharing keys or assigning RBAC roles. An account SAS is broader than necessary (account-level permissions). A stored access policy alone is not a credential — it must back a SAS. Sharing any account key violates the stated policy directly.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: You open Storage Explorer and connect to a storage account using your Microsoft Entra credentials. You can see the list of containers but opening any container returns an authorization error. The portal shows you have the Reader role on the storage account. What is missing?
options: A storage firewall exception for your client IP
An SAS token appended to the connection string
A data-plane RBAC role such as Storage Blob Data Reader
The Contributor role on the resource group
explain: The Reader role is a management-plane role: it lets you list the account and see container names via the control plane, but reading blob data requires a data-plane role such as Storage Blob Data Reader. This is the classic exam distinction between control-plane and data-plane permissions. A firewall issue would block listing too. SAS tokens are an alternative to RBAC, not a fix for missing RBAC. Contributor on the resource group is still management-plane and grants no data access.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: You have a trading application deployed on five Azure VMs. The application is extremely latency-sensitive: requests bounce between the VMs hundreds of times per second, and even sub-millisecond delays hurt fill rates. The VMs must be placed physically close together in the same Azure datacenter. What should you configure?
options: An availability set with three fault domains, to protect against rack-level hardware failures
A virtual machine scale set with overprovisioning enabled, to keep extra capacity warm
A proximity placement group, to co-locate the VMs as close together as possible
An availability zone, to spread the VMs across physically separate datacenters
explain: A proximity placement group pins VMs to a single datacenter and places them physically near each other, minimizing network latency between them — exactly what a chatty, latency-sensitive workload needs. Availability zones and sets do the opposite (spreading VMs for resilience), and scale set overprovisioning only affects provisioning speed, not latency.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: You deploy two identical web server VMs into an availability set. During a scheduled platform maintenance event, Azure reboots some of the underlying hosts. You need to ensure at least one web server keeps running through the maintenance. Which availability set concept provides this guarantee?
options: Fault domains, which group VMs onto separate physical racks to survive hardware failures
Proximity placement groups, which keep VMs in the same datacenter for low latency
Update domains, which group VMs so that only one update domain is rebooted at a time
Availability zones, which place VMs in physically separate datacenters within the region
explain: Update domains are Azure's mechanism for planned maintenance: VMs in the same availability set are divided across update domains, and Azure reboots only one update domain at a time, so the VMs in the others stay up. Fault domains protect against unplanned hardware failures, not scheduled maintenance — a classic exam distinction.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: Your team runs a video-rendering farm as a batch job each night. The job can tolerate interruptions — a render node can be killed and restarted without losing the whole job — and the finance team wants the compute cost as low as possible. Which VM pricing option fits best?
options: Azure Hybrid Benefit, applying existing Windows Server licenses to the VMs
Spot VMs, using spare Azure capacity at a deep discount with eviction possible
Reserved Instances, committing to one year of capacity for up to 72% savings
Dedicated Hosts, reserving whole physical servers for compliance isolation
explain: Spot VMs use spare Azure capacity at steep discounts (up to ~90%), with the trade-off that Azure can evict the VMs when it needs the capacity back. Interruptible batch work like rendering is the textbook Spot workload. Reserved Instances also save money but lock you into a 1- or 3-year term, which is overkill for a nightly batch job.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: Your company runs a production SQL Server VM that has been running continuously for 18 months and will run for at least two more years with a steady, predictable load. Management wants to cut the VM's compute cost without changing the workload. What should you recommend?
options: Enable Azure Hybrid Benefit, which reduces compute cost by up to 72%
Convert the VM to a Spot VM to take advantage of spare capacity pricing
Purchase a 3-year Reserved Instance for the VM's size and region
Move the VM to a B-series burstable size to save on unused CPU credits
explain: A steady, multi-year VM is the ideal Reserved Instance candidate: committing to a 1- or 3-year term for a known size and region yields the deepest compute discount (up to ~72%), and a 3-year term beats a 1-year term. Spot VMs are too risky for production SQL (eviction), and Hybrid Benefit applies existing licenses rather than committing capacity — it stacks with RIs but isn't the primary lever here.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: You have 40 Azure VMs across two resource groups. A new security agent must be installed on all of them by Friday, but the VMs have no public IPs and your team is not allowed to open RDP or SSH access. You need a way to run the installer script on every VM from Azure. Which solution should you use?
options: The Custom Script Extension for Windows and Linux, deployed to each VM to download and run the installer
Azure Bastion, to connect to each VM's private IP and run the installer manually
A Desired State Configuration pull server, which only applies OS configuration baselines
The Run Command feature, which requires opening port 22 or 3389 on each VM's NSG
explain: The Custom Script Extension executes scripts on VMs through the Azure VM agent — no RDP/SSH, no public IP, and fully automatable across many VMs via ARM/Bicep or CLI. Azure Bastion still means 40 manual sessions, Run Command works without open ports (it also uses the VM agent) but is designed for one-off commands, and DSC is for configuration state rather than one-time software installation.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: You are migrating a legacy application from an availability set to a virtual machine scale set. The application requires manual control over VM maintenance events, per-VM availability options, and a mix of fault-domain isolation with a small number of instances. Which scale set orchestration mode meets these requirements?
options: Flexible orchestration mode in a single region without zones, which behaves like a scale set
Flexible orchestration mode, which supports per-VM configuration and availability-set-like maintenance control
Uniform mode with single placement group disabled, which spreads instances across regions
Uniform orchestration mode, which treats all instances as identical and updates them together
explain: Flexible orchestration mode is the recommended replacement for availability sets: each VM gets its own identity, you can spread instances across fault domains or zones, and you retain manual maintenance control per VM. Uniform mode is the classic scale-set model where instances are identical and managed as a group. Microsoft recommends Flexible for most new deployments.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: Your virtual machine scale set runs a stateless web API behind a load balancer. When you roll out a new application version, you need the scale set to upgrade instances in batches, automatically pause the rollout if a batch fails its health probe, and roll back the failed batch. Which upgrade policy should you configure?
options: Manual upgrade policy, so each instance upgrades only when you approve it
Rolling upgrade policy with an application health probe, which upgrades batches and pauses on unhealthy instances
Automatic upgrade policy without a health probe, which upgrades all instances at once
Rolling upgrade policy with overprovisioning disabled, which skips health checks for speed
explain: The Rolling upgrade policy upgrades instances in batches and — when paired with an application health probe (via the Application Health extension) — pauses and rolls back if a batch comes up unhealthy, exactly the safety behavior described. Manual policy requires you to trigger every instance upgrade, and Automatic upgrades all instances simultaneously with no batching control.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: Your virtual machine scale set hosts an e-commerce site. Traffic is steady most of the day, but CPU consistently exceeds 75% for 10+ minutes during the lunch rush, and the site slows down. You need the scale set to add instances automatically during these spikes and remove them afterward, without manual intervention. What should you configure?
options: A metric-based autoscale rule that scales out when average CPU exceeds 75% for 10 minutes and scales in when it drops
The Rolling upgrade policy, which replaces instances with larger VM sizes during high load
A scheduled autoscale profile that adds instances every day at noon
Manual scaling with a runbook that an operator triggers when the site slows down
explain: Autoscale rules based on metrics (like average CPU percentage over a time window) scale the instance count out and back in automatically as demand changes. A fixed schedule can't react to variable spike lengths, upgrade policies handle version rollouts rather than capacity, and manual scaling defeats the 'without manual intervention' requirement.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: You plan to host a production web app on Azure App Service. The release process requires a staging slot so new versions can be warmed up and tested before going live, plus the ability to scale out to multiple instances. The app is currently on the Basic tier. What must you do?
options: Keep Basic and use the Premium-only 'swap with preview' feature instead of slots
Move to the Free tier and use deployment slots, which are included at no cost
Stay on Basic and enable deployment slots, which are available on all tiers
Scale up to the Standard tier or higher, which supports deployment slots and scale-out
explain: Deployment slots require the Standard tier or higher — the Basic (and Free/Shared) tiers do not support slots. This is a distractor check: the correct move is scaling up to Standard, where slots and multi-instance scale-out are both available. Swap with preview is a slot feature, not an alternative to slots, so it cannot help on Basic.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: You swapped your App Service staging slot into production last week and the new version caused intermittent errors that only appeared under real traffic. For the next release, you want to route a small percentage of live production traffic to the staging slot first, verify it, and then complete the swap — with the ability to cancel if problems appear. Which deployment approach should you use?
options: Cloning the production slot to a new app, which creates an independent copy for testing
Swap with preview (multi-phase swap), which lets you validate the staging slot with production settings and a portion of live traffic before completing the swap
A standard slot swap, which exchanges the slots immediately with no validation phase
Zip Deploy directly to the production slot, which overwrites the running app in place
explain: Swap with preview is a two-phase operation: phase one applies production settings to the staging slot so you can validate it under real conditions, and you then choose to complete or cancel the swap — giving you the canary-style safety net described. A standard swap flips everything at once with no preview, Zip Deploy offers no rollback, and cloning creates a separate app rather than a controlled swap.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: Your compliance team requires daily automated backups of an App Service web app, including its files, configuration, and connected Azure SQL database, with the ability to restore to a point in time. What must be in place for App Service Backup to work?
options: An Azure Files premium share mounted to the app and a manual export of the database
A Recovery Services vault in the same region, which stores the backup snapshots
An Azure Storage account in the same subscription to hold the backups, and the app on a Standard tier or higher
A user-assigned managed identity with Owner rights on the subscription
explain: App Service Backup requires the app to be on a Standard tier or higher and an Azure Storage account (in the same subscription) as the backup destination; it can include linked databases in the backup. Recovery Services vaults are for VM and workload backup, not App Service Backup, and while managed identities are common in Azure, the storage account plus supported tier is the actual prerequisite.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: Your App Service web app needs to call an internal API that is only reachable inside your Azure virtual network — the API has no public endpoint. The web app is currently on the Basic tier. What should you configure so the app can reach the internal API?
options: Service endpoints on the API's subnet, which expose the web app to the VNet
Regional VNet integration, which lets the app make outbound calls into the VNet (requires Standard tier or higher)
A private endpoint on the web app, which places the app's inbound traffic inside the VNet
VNet peering between the App Service plan and the virtual network
explain: Regional VNet integration gives the web app outbound access into a VNet, so it can reach the internal API — and it requires Standard tier or higher, so the Basic app must be scaled up. Private endpoints control inbound traffic to the app (the reverse direction), service endpoints are configured on the resource side in the subnet, and App Service plans cannot be VNet-peered directly.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: Your App Service web app intermittently runs out of memory under load, but CPU stays low. During an incident you need more RAM immediately, without adding more instances. Which scaling action should you take?
options: Scale up to a larger pricing tier instance size (e.g., P2v3 to P3v3), which increases CPU and memory per instance
Add a deployment slot, which provides an isolated copy of the app for the extra load
Enable autoscale based on memory percentage, which changes the tier automatically
Scale out to more instances, which adds capacity by duplicating the current instance size
explain: Scaling up changes the VM size of each instance (more CPU/RAM per instance), which directly addresses memory pressure on a single instance. Scaling out adds more instances of the same size — useful for throughput, not per-instance memory. Autoscale adjusts instance count, not tier, and deployment slots are for release management, not capacity.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: Your developers push code to a GitHub repository several times a day, and each push must automatically build, run tests, and deploy to an App Service staging slot. You want a deployment method with first-class CI/CD integration and visible build logs per commit. Which option should you choose?
options: Zip Deploy with a SAS URL, copying a pre-built package to the app on each release
FTP deployment, uploading changed files manually after each commit
Local Git deployment, pushing directly from a developer workstation to the app
GitHub Actions deployment, using a workflow triggered on push to build, test, and deploy
explain: GitHub Actions provides true CI/CD: a workflow triggered by each push can build, test, and deploy to a specific slot, with logs per run. FTP and Zip Deploy are manual or scripted push methods with no build/test pipeline, and Local Git deploys from a workstation rather than from the repository with automated validation.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: You need to run a containerized order-processing API that idles overnight but must handle sudden bursts of messages each morning. The platform should scale the container to zero when idle to avoid charges, scale on queue length, and support multiple revisions for safe rollouts. Which Azure service is the best fit?
options: An App Service web app for containers on the Basic tier, which scales containers to zero
Azure Kubernetes Service, which requires managing node pools for burst capacity
Azure Container Instances, which bills per second and supports scale-to-zero automatically
Azure Container Apps, which provides KEDA-based event-driven scaling to zero and revision management
explain: Azure Container Apps is the serverless container platform with built-in KEDA scalers (including queue-length triggers), scale-to-zero, and managed revisions for traffic splitting between versions. Container Instances is simpler and bills per second but does not natively scale to zero or manage revisions, and AKS adds cluster-management overhead this scenario doesn't need.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: You need to run a single containerized data-validation task that starts in seconds, runs for about five minutes, and must never restart — if it crashes, the failure should be recorded and the container left stopped for investigation. Which Azure Container Instances configuration should you use?
options: Restart policy Never, so a crashed container stays stopped for investigation
Restart policy Always, so the container recovers automatically from any crash
Restart policy OnFailure, so the container retries transient errors
A container group with a sidecar, so a second container monitors the first
explain: The ACI restart policy Never means the container runs once and is never restarted — a crash leaves it stopped so you can inspect the failure, exactly matching the requirement. Always is for long-running services, OnFailure would retry and potentially mask the failure you want to investigate, and a sidecar adds complexity without changing restart semantics.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: You are writing an ARM template that deploys a virtual machine, and it needs an administrator password supplied at deployment time. The password must never appear in deployment logs or in plain text in the template. How should you define this input?
options: As an output value, which is encrypted when returned to the deployer
As a parameter of type secureString, which keeps the value out of logs and deployment history
As a parameter of type string with a defaultValue, which is the simplest way to pass it
As a variable, which is resolved at deployment time and hidden automatically
explain: Parameters typed secureString (or secureObject) are treated as secrets: Azure excludes their values from deployment logs and history. A plain string parameter with a default value would expose the password, variables are for internal computed values (not secret inputs), and outputs are for returning values — they don't protect inputs.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: Your ARM template deploys a storage account, and storage account names must be globally unique. You want the template to generate a unique name deterministically from the resource group so redeployments produce the same name. Which template function should you use?
options: uniqueString(), to generate a deterministic hash from the resource group ID
parameters(), to read a unique name supplied by the operator
resourceGroup(), to return the resource group's location as a suffix
concat(), to join a fixed prefix with the deployment timestamp
explain: uniqueString() creates a deterministic hash from its input — uniqueString(resourceGroup().id) yields the same 13-character value on every deployment to that resource group, making it the standard way to build globally unique names. concat() with a timestamp would change every deployment, parameters() pushes the problem to the operator, and resourceGroup() returns an object whose properties don't provide uniqueness.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: Your team maintains large ARM templates in JSON that have become hard to read and reuse across projects. You want a simpler authoring experience with modules for shared components, while still deploying through the standard ARM deployment pipeline. What should you adopt?
options: Azure Policy, which enforces the template structure at deploy time
Terraform, which replaces the ARM deployment pipeline entirely
The Azure CLI, which removes the need for declarative templates
Bicep, which offers simpler syntax and modules and transpiles to ARM JSON
explain: Bicep is Microsoft's domain-specific language for Azure: cleaner syntax than ARM JSON, native module support for reuse, and it transpiles to standard ARM templates so the existing deployment pipeline is unchanged. Terraform is a different ecosystem, Azure Policy governs compliance rather than authoring, and the CLI is imperative — it doesn't replace declarative templates.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: You need to back up Azure VMs in the East US region using Azure Backup. You create a Recovery Services vault, but the portal will not let you select it as the backup target for those VMs. The vault was created in West Europe. What is the problem?
options: The vault must be in the same region as the VMs it protects
The vault must be in the same resource group as the VMs
The vault must be created after the VMs, or the backup extension fails to install
The vault requires locally redundant storage, which is unavailable in West Europe
explain: A Recovery Services vault used for Azure VM backup must reside in the same region as the VMs it protects — a West Europe vault cannot back up East US VMs. The vault does not need to share the resource group, storage redundancy is a separate vault setting, and creation order relative to the VMs doesn't matter.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: A junior administrator accidentally deleted several Azure VM backups from a Recovery Services vault during cleanup. Your company needs protection against this kind of accidental or malicious deletion of recovery points. Which feature addresses this?
options: Cross-region restore, which copies backups to a secondary region
A resource lock on the vault, which prevents deletion of the vault itself
Soft delete for Azure Backup, which retains deleted backup data for a retention period so it can be recovered
Instant Restore snapshots, which keep VM snapshots in the source storage account
explain: Soft delete for Azure Backup holds deleted backup data for an additional retention period (14 days by default) even after deletion, allowing recovery from accidental or malicious deletes. A resource lock protects the vault resource but not the backup data inside it, Instant Restore is about fast restores from local snapshots, and cross-region restore is about geographic availability — neither guards against deletion.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: Your backup administrator needs to restore a failed Azure VM as fast as possible. The VM is protected by Azure Backup with the default policy, and the most recent recovery point was taken last night. Why might this restore complete in minutes rather than the time a full vault restore would take?
options: Because Instant Restore keeps VM snapshots locally for a few days, and restores can run directly from the snapshot
Because cross-region restore replicates the recovery point to the nearest region
Because soft delete keeps a decrypted copy of the VM in the vault for fast access
Because the Recovery Services vault uses premium storage for all recovery points
explain: Azure VM backup policies keep Instant Restore snapshots in the source storage for a short retention (2 days by default); restoring from a local snapshot avoids transferring data out of the vault, so it completes far faster. Soft delete is a deletion-safety feature, vault storage tier doesn't determine restore speed this way, and cross-region restore is about restoring in a secondary region, not speed.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: You use Azure Site Recovery to replicate VMs to a secondary region. A planned datacenter maintenance window is coming, and you want to fail over with no data loss, then fail back afterward. The primary site is still fully operational. Which statement about this failover is correct?
options: A planned failover shuts down the primary VMs and synchronizes final changes, so no data is lost
A test failover should be used, because it moves production traffic with zero data loss
An unplanned failover is required, because planned failovers always lose the last replication delta
Failback is automatic after a planned failover, with no re-protection needed
explain: A planned failover is designed for exactly this: the source VMs are shut down gracefully and final changes replicate before the secondary VMs start, resulting in zero data loss (lowest RPO). Unplanned failover is for outages where the primary is unreachable and data loss is possible, test failover is isolated and doesn't touch production traffic, and failback always requires re-protecting in the reverse direction.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: A regional outage takes down your primary datacenter, and you trigger an Azure Site Recovery unplanned failover. When choosing a recovery point, you see options labeled 'Latest' and 'Latest processed'. What is the difference between them?
options: Latest includes only application-consistent snapshots, while Latest processed includes crash-consistent ones
Latest minimizes data loss but takes longer to bring up, while Latest processed is faster with potentially more data loss
Latest requires the primary site to be online, while Latest processed works during an outage
Latest is the oldest available recovery point, while Latest processed is the newest one
explain: For unplanned failover, 'Latest' recovery point minimizes data loss (lowest RPO) but takes longer because the VMs must process pending replication data at failover time; 'Latest processed' uses an already-processed point, so failover is faster (lower RTO) at the cost of potentially more data loss. This is the core RPO-vs-RTO trade-off the exam tests for ASR.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: You deploy an ARM template in Incremental mode to a resource group that already contains a storage account and a virtual network created manually last month. The template defines a new virtual machine and an updated configuration for the virtual network. What happens to the manually created storage account?
options: It is moved to a new resource group, because the deployment scope changes
It is deleted only if it has no resource lock, otherwise it is left unchanged
It is left unchanged, because Incremental mode only adds or updates resources defined in the template
It is deleted, because Incremental mode removes resources not defined in the template
explain: Incremental is the default deployment mode: resources in the template are created or updated, and existing resources not in the template — like the manually created storage account — are left untouched. Deleting everything not in the template is what Complete mode does, which is why Complete mode is risky against resource groups containing manually created resources.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: Your company plans a site-to-site VPN between its on-premises network (10.0.0.0/16) and a new Azure VNet. A junior engineer proposes creating the VNet with address space 10.0.0.0/16 to keep addressing simple. You need the VPN tunnel to route correctly once connected. What should you do?
options: Approve the plan; Azure automatically remaps overlapping address spaces when the VPN connects
Create the VNet with 10.0.0.0/16 and enable BGP on the VPN gateway to resolve the overlap
Create the VNet with a non-overlapping address space such as 10.1.0.0/16
Create the VNet with 10.0.0.0/16 and configure NAT on the VPN gateway to translate the overlapping range
explain: A VNet connected to on-premises via VPN or ExpressRoute must not use address space that overlaps the on-premises ranges; Azure cannot distinguish identical routes, so the tunnel will not route correctly. Azure never remaps address space automatically, and BGP does not fix an overlap. Plan non-overlapping space up front, since you can add address space to a VNet later but cannot shrink or change the original range.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: You have three VNets: VNet-A is peered with VNet-B, and VNet-B is peered with VNet-C. There is no peering between VNet-A and VNet-C. A VM in VNet-A needs to communicate with a VM in VNet-C. What is true?
options: Traffic flows automatically through VNet-B because peering is transitive
Enabling 'Allow forwarded traffic' on the VNet-B peerings makes the path transitive
You must create a direct peering between VNet-A and VNet-C, or route the traffic through a hub NVA
Move one of the VMs into VNet-B, because peering only works between directly adjacent VNets
explain: VNet peering is non-transitive: peerings do not chain, so VNet-A cannot reach VNet-C through VNet-B. Connectivity requires a direct VNet-A to VNet-C peering, or a hub-and-spoke design where an NVA or gateway routes between the spokes. 'Allow forwarded traffic' only permits an NVA in a peered VNet to forward packets; it does not create transit routing by itself.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: Your hub VNet has a VPN gateway with 'Allow gateway transit' enabled. A spoke VNet is peered to the hub with 'Use remote gateways' enabled, and spoke VMs reach on-premises successfully. The team now wants to deploy a second VPN gateway inside the spoke VNet for redundancy. What will happen?
options: The deployment succeeds if the new gateway uses a different SKU than the hub gateway
The deployment succeeds but the spoke silently stops using the hub gateway
The deployment succeeds and the spoke gets active-active redundancy
The deployment is blocked: a VNet configured to use remote gateways cannot have its own gateway
explain: A VNet with 'Use remote gateways' enabled cannot deploy its own VPN or ExpressRoute gateway; the setting hands gateway use to the peered hub VNet. Redundancy for the spoke comes from the hub side, for example by deploying the hub gateway in active-active mode. To give the spoke its own gateway, you must first remove the 'Use remote gateways' setting.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: Your company has 150 remote employees on personal laptops with dynamic home IP addresses and no on-premises VPN device. They need secure access to VMs in an Azure VNet. What should you deploy?
options: A point-to-site VPN gateway
An ExpressRoute circuit
A site-to-site VPN gateway
A VNet-to-VNet connection
explain: Point-to-site VPN connects individual client devices directly to the VNet over OpenVPN, IKEv2, or SSTP, and requires no on-premises VPN device or static public IP. Site-to-site needs a compatible on-premises VPN device, VNet-to-VNet connects two Azure VNets, and ExpressRoute is a private dedicated circuit that is far heavier than remote-worker access requires.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: A financial services workload must replicate data to Azure over a connection that never traverses the public internet, per compliance requirements. The link must also support high throughput. Which connectivity option meets the requirement?
options: A site-to-site VPN, because IPsec encryption removes the data from the public internet
A point-to-site VPN with certificate authentication
VNet peering between the on-premises network and Azure
An ExpressRoute circuit
explain: ExpressRoute provides private, dedicated connectivity from on-premises to Azure that does not cross the public internet, which is what the compliance rule demands. VPN connections are encrypted but still traverse the internet. VNet peering only connects Azure VNets to each other, not on-premises networks.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: An NSG on a subnet has two custom rules: 'Allow-Web' (priority 100) allows TCP 443 from 203.0.113.0/24, and 'Deny-BadIP' (priority 200) denies all traffic from 203.0.113.50. Traffic from 203.0.113.50 to port 443 is still being allowed. Why?
options: Deny rules only apply to outbound traffic, not inbound
NSG rules are evaluated from the lowest priority number upward, and 'Allow-Web' (100) matches first
NSG rules take up to 24 hours to take effect
The default 'DenyAllInBound' rule overrides custom rules
explain: NSG rules are processed in priority-number order, lowest first, and the first matching rule wins; lower numbers mean higher precedence.
