'Allow-Web' at priority 100 matches the traffic before 'Deny-BadIP' at 200 is ever evaluated. The fix is to give the deny rule a lower priority number than 100, not a higher one.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: You need an NSG rule that allows Azure platform health probes to reach VMs behind a Standard Load Balancer. The probe source IP addresses change over time and are not published per region as static ranges. What should the rule's source be?
options: The VirtualNetwork service tag
The Internet service tag
The load balancer's frontend public IP address
The AzureLoadBalancer service tag
explain: The AzureLoadBalancer service tag represents the platform health-probe sources and is maintained automatically by Microsoft, so the rule keeps working as probe IPs change. The Internet tag is far too broad, VirtualNetwork covers only VNet address space, and the frontend IP is the destination side of the traffic, not the probe source.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: You create an application security group (ASG) named web-servers in VNet-A and add the NICs of three web VMs in VNet-A. You then try to add the NIC of a web VM in peered VNet-B to the same ASG, but the portal does not list that NIC. Why?
options: All NICs in an ASG must reside in the same VNet; peering does not extend ASG membership
VNet peering must have gateway transit enabled before ASGs span VNets
An ASG supports a maximum of three NICs
ASG members must be in the same subnet, not just the same VNet
explain: Every network interface assigned to an ASG must exist in the same virtual network as the ASG; VNet peering does not change that boundary. To group the VNet-B VM, create a second ASG in VNet-B and reference both ASGs in the NSG rule. There is no three-NIC limit, and gateway transit is unrelated to ASG membership.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: Developers need outbound access to *.windowsupdate.com and *.microsoft.com from a subnet, while all other internet destinations must be blocked. An NSG alone cannot meet this requirement. What should you deploy?
options: A second NSG with a lower-priority allow rule
A NAT gateway with an FQDN allow list
A user-defined route with next hop type Internet
Azure Firewall with application rules allowing those FQDNs
explain: NSGs filter only at layers 3 and 4 (source/destination IP, port, protocol) and cannot match domain names. Azure Firewall application rules provide FQDN-based filtering for HTTP/HTTPS outbound traffic. A NAT gateway supplies a static outbound IP but performs no filtering, and a UDR to Internet does not filter either.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: You create a private endpoint for a storage account in VNet-A and link the privatelink.blob.core.windows.net private DNS zone to VNet-A. VMs in VNet-A resolve the storage account to its private IP correctly. VMs in peered VNet-B still resolve the storage account's public IP address. What is missing?
options: A second private endpoint deployed in VNet-B
Gateway transit enabled on the VNet peering
A private DNS zone link to VNet-B
A service endpoint on the VNet-B subnet
explain: A private DNS zone only answers queries from VNets it is linked to; VNet peering does not inherit DNS zone links. Linking the same private DNS zone to VNet-B lets its VMs resolve the private endpoint IP. Gateway transit, a second endpoint, and service endpoints do not fix name resolution.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: Four VMs sit in the backend pool of a Standard SKU internal load balancer. They communicate with each other, but they cannot reach the internet for OS updates. The subnet NSG allows outbound internet traffic. What is the most likely cause and fix?
options: Internal load balancers block all outbound traffic by design; replace it with a public load balancer
Each VM needs its own Standard public IP for outbound access
Standard Load Balancer provides no default outbound connectivity; attach a NAT gateway to the subnet or add a load balancer outbound rule
The NSG default rules deny outbound internet and must be deleted
explain: Unlike Basic SKU, a Standard Load Balancer gives backend VMs no implicit outbound SNAT, so they cannot reach the internet until you provide explicit outbound connectivity. The supported fixes are a NAT gateway on the subnet or an outbound rule on the load balancer. The NSG default 'AllowInternetOutBound' rule already permits outbound, and a public LB frontend is not required for outbound-only access.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: Your single-region web application needs protection against OWASP Top 10 attacks such as SQL injection and cross-site scripting. It also needs /api/* requests sent to one backend pool and all other requests sent to a different backend pool. Which service and SKU should you deploy?
options: Standard SKU Load Balancer with a WAF add-on
Traffic Manager with geographic routing
Application Gateway with the WAF_v2 SKU and path-based routing rules
Azure Firewall in the hub VNet
explain: Application Gateway is a regional layer-7 load balancer; the WAF_v2 SKU adds managed OWASP protection, and path-based routing rules direct URL paths to different backend pools. Standard Load Balancer operates at layer 4 with no WAF or URL routing, Traffic Manager is DNS-based global routing, and Azure Firewall does not load-balance web traffic.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: You run a web application in East US and West Europe. You need global users routed to the nearest healthy endpoint with near-instant failover, TLS termination at the edge, and URL path-based routing. Which service should you use?
options: VNet peering between the two regions
Standard SKU Load Balancer with a backend pool in each region
Azure Front Door
Traffic Manager with performance routing
explain: Azure Front Door is a global layer-7 reverse proxy with anycast routing: it terminates TLS at the edge, routes to the nearest healthy origin, fails over almost instantly, and supports path-based routing. Traffic Manager is DNS-based, so failover waits on DNS TTL and it never proxies traffic or terminates TLS. A Standard Load Balancer is regional, and VNet peering is not a traffic-routing service.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: A compliance audit requires that traffic from your VNet to Azure Storage never traverse a public IP address, and the storage account must be unreachable from the internet. Which approach meets both requirements?
options: Add an NSG rule denying outbound traffic to the Internet service tag
Create a private endpoint for the storage account via Private Link and set public network access to Deny
Enable a service endpoint for Microsoft.Storage on the subnet
Deploy a VPN gateway in the VNet
explain: A private endpoint maps the storage account to a private IP inside your VNet, so traffic never uses a public address, and setting public network access to Deny closes internet access. A service endpoint keeps the storage public endpoint as the destination, so traffic still targets a public IP. NSGs and VPN gateways do not change how the storage endpoint is addressed.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: Users report intermittent application errors on a VM that you suspect are caused by malformed packets on the wire. You need to capture the actual network traffic on the VM's NIC for two hours and analyze it in Wireshark. What should you use?
options: NSG flow logs with Traffic Analytics
Connection troubleshoot against the application port
IP flow verify, filtered to the VM's NIC
A Network Watcher packet capture saved to a storage account
explain: Network Watcher packet capture records real packets from the NIC into a .cap file you can open in Wireshark. IP flow verify only simulates whether an NSG rule would allow or deny a packet, connection troubleshoot tests TCP reachability hop by hop, and NSG flow logs record flow metadata (5-tuple, bytes, action) without packet payloads.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: You need to chart a VM's 'Percentage CPU' as a daily average over the past 60 days. You never configured diagnostics or a Log Analytics workspace for this VM. Can you get this data?
options: Yes, but only for the last 30 days
No; metrics require a data collection rule before any data is stored
Yes; platform metrics are collected automatically and retained for 93 days, viewable in Metrics explorer
No; without a Log Analytics workspace no historical data exists
explain: Azure platform metrics such as Percentage CPU are collected automatically for every resource at no charge and retained for 93 days, so 60 days of history is available in Metrics explorer with no setup. Log Analytics and data collection rules are needed for logs and guest-OS metrics, not for platform metrics.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: An auditor asks who deleted the 'finance-rg' resource group six months ago. The Azure portal activity log only retains 90 days, but all activity logs have been sent to a Log Analytics workspace with two-year retention. How do you answer the auditor?
options: Open Metrics explorer and chart deletion events over six months
Check Resource Health history for finance-rg
Run a KQL query against the AzureActivity table filtering on the delete operation and the resource group name
Use Network Watcher connection troubleshoot
explain: Administrative operations such as resource group deletion are recorded in the activity log, which lands in the AzureActivity table in Log Analytics. A KQL query filtering OperationNameValue for the delete operation and the resource group name returns the caller identity and timestamp. Metrics track numeric performance, not who-did-what, and Resource Health tracks platform health, not admin actions.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: You need an alert that fires when a scheduled KQL query counting failed sign-ins over the last 15 minutes returns more than 10 results. Which alert type should you create?
options: A metric alert on the sign-in count metric
A Service Health alert
An activity log alert
A log search alert
explain: Log search alerts evaluate a KQL query on a schedule and fire based on the number of results returned, which is exactly this scenario. Metric alerts watch numeric platform or custom metrics against thresholds, activity log alerts fire on control-plane events like resource creation, and Service Health alerts fire on Azure-wide incidents.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: You must notify the security team immediately whenever anyone deletes any VM in the subscription. Which alert type fits, and what does it watch?
options: A metric alert watching VM availability
A Resource Health alert on the VMs
A log search alert querying the Heartbeat table
An activity log alert watching the Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/delete operation
explain: Deleting a VM is a control-plane operation recorded in the activity log, so an activity log alert on the delete operation fires the moment it happens. Metric alerts watch performance numbers, Heartbeat tracks agent connectivity rather than admin actions, and Resource Health reports platform-initiated health events, not user deletions.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: Your on-call rotation changes quarterly, and 40 alert rules currently notify the old team's email addresses. You want future rotations to require updating a single place instead of editing every rule. What should you do?
options: Enable autoscale on the action group
Create an alert processing rule that suppresses the old email addresses
Create one action group containing the on-call contacts and reference it from all 40 alert rules
Export the alert rules to ARM templates and redeploy them each quarter
explain: Action groups decouple notification endpoints from alert rules: many rules can reference one action group, so updating the group's email addresses or SMS numbers updates every rule at once. Alert processing rules suppress or add actions but do not store the contact list itself, and redeploying templates each quarter is unnecessary manual work.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: Your existing alert rules page the network team by email. Management now requires that every Severity 0 alert also trigger a PagerDuty webhook, without editing any of the existing alert rules. What should you configure?
options: An alert suppression rule for all non-Severity 0 alerts
An alert processing rule that adds an action group containing the PagerDuty webhook, filtered to Severity 0
A second action group added manually to each alert rule
A metric alert on the PagerDuty webhook endpoint
explain: Alert processing rules can add action groups to alerts matching a filter (scope, severity, monitor condition) at fire time, without touching the alert rules themselves. Filtering to Severity 0 targets only the critical alerts. Suppression would silence notifications rather than add one, and editing each rule defeats the no-edit requirement.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: Your team suspects an Azure platform problem is affecting VMs in East US, but nobody changed any configuration. Where do you confirm whether Azure is experiencing a region-wide service issue?
options: Log Analytics workspace
Network Watcher
Resource Health for one of the VMs
Service Health
explain: Service Health reports Azure-wide service issues, planned maintenance, and health advisories per region, which is where a platform outage would be published. Resource Health shows the health of your specific resources, not the region. Log Analytics holds your telemetry, and Network Watcher diagnoses network connectivity.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: You receive notice that Azure will perform planned host maintenance affecting one of your VMs next week. Where can you see the maintenance window for that specific VM and whether it will require a reboot?
options: The activity log
Service Health
Resource Health for that VM
Metrics explorer
explain: Resource Health shows per-resource health, including upcoming planned maintenance events with their windows and expected impact for that specific VM. Service Health reports region-wide events without per-VM detail, metrics show performance numbers, and the activity log records past administrative operations.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: You need an interactive report where engineers pick a resource group from a dropdown and see KQL-driven charts of errors and latency, shareable with the whole team. What should you build?
options: A metrics chart saved as a favorite
An Azure Dashboard with pinned metric charts
An Azure Monitor workbook with parameters and KQL queries
A Logic App that emails query results
explain: Workbooks are interactive reports that support parameters (like a resource-group dropdown) and live KQL queries, and they can be shared with the team. Dashboards pin mostly static tiles with limited interactivity, and Logic Apps automate workflows rather than present interactive reports.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: Security policy requires sign-in and audit logs to be retained for two years, but all other logs only 90 days to control cost. Everything flows into a single Log Analytics workspace. How do you meet the requirement most cost-effectively?
options: Send the security tables to a second workspace with two-year retention
Configure table-level retention: 730 days on the security tables, 90 days for the rest
Set the workspace default retention to two years
Export all logs to a storage account and delete them from the workspace
explain: Log Analytics supports per-table retention, so you keep the expensive long retention only on the security tables that need it and the 90-day default everywhere else. Raising the workspace default to two years over-retains every table and raises cost, and exporting to storage loses the queryable log experience the policy implies.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: You enforce a Conditional Access policy that requires phishing-resistant MFA for all users in the tenant. The identity architect insists that the two emergency-access (break-glass) accounts be excluded from this policy, monitored with sign-in alerts, and secured with FIDO2 keys kept in a safe. A junior admin objects that excluding any account weakens security. What is the correct response?
options: The junior admin is right; every account including break-glass must satisfy the MFA policy with no exceptions
The architect is right; emergency-access accounts must be excluded from Conditional Access so a policy misconfiguration cannot lock out all administrators
Delete the break-glass accounts and rely on PIM-eligible Global Administrators instead
Keep the accounts in the policy but exempt them from MFA using the legacy per-user trusted IPs list
explain: Microsoft's documented best practice is to exclude at least one emergency-access account from Conditional Access policies, because a misconfigured policy could otherwise lock every administrator out of the tenant. The accounts are protected instead with long random passwords, FIDO2 keys stored offline, and sign-in monitoring. Requiring them to satisfy the same policy defeats their purpose as a last-resort recovery path. The legacy trusted-IPs list only affects per-user MFA, not Conditional Access.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: You run quarterly Microsoft Entra access reviews on the 'Project Falcon' security group, which contains employees and B2B guest users. Auto-apply results is enabled. A reviewer determines that three guest users no longer need access and denies their continued membership. What happens when the review completes?
options: The guests are converted to member userType so the review can track them
The guests keep access until an administrator manually removes them from the group
The review generates a report, but guest membership can only be removed by deleting the guest accounts
The denied guests are removed from the group automatically
explain: With auto-apply enabled, access reviews enforce reviewer decisions: denied users are removed from the group (or have the role assignment removed) automatically at review end. Guest membership is removed the same way as member membership — there is no requirement to delete the guest account. Options B and C describe manual-only processes that auto-apply specifically eliminates, and userType conversion is unrelated to access reviews.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: Your tenant synchronizes identities with Microsoft Entra Connect. You enable password writeback in the Connect configuration, but SSPR password changes for synchronized users still do not flow back on-premises. The tenant uses the Free edition of Microsoft Entra ID. What is the most likely cause?
options: Password writeback requires Microsoft Entra ID P1 or P2; the Free edition does not support it
Password writeback only works for cloud-only users, not synchronized users
SSPR is not enabled for the synchronized users
The on-premises domain controllers must be upgraded to support writeback
explain: Password writeback is a premium feature requiring Microsoft Entra ID P1 or P2 — it is the exact scenario writeback exists for (synchronized users), so B is backwards. If SSPR itself works in the cloud, SSPR enablement is not the issue; the cloud-to-on-premises leg is what the license gates. Domain controller version is unrelated to the licensing requirement.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: Help desk tickets show that several administrators approve Authenticator push notifications without looking, enabling MFA fatigue attacks. You want every Authenticator approval to require the user to type the number shown on the sign-in screen. Where do you configure this?
options: In the Conditional Access policy, under Session controls
In the legacy per-user MFA service settings, under trusted IPs
In the Authentication methods policy, in the Microsoft Authenticator settings
In Identity Protection, under the MFA registration policy
explain: Number matching is configured in the Authentication methods policy under the Microsoft Authenticator settings, and it applies to push approvals tenant-wide. Conditional Access session controls govern session lifetime and persistence, not authenticator behavior. The legacy per-user MFA settings manage an older method list, and the MFA registration policy only requires users to register — it does not change how approvals are confirmed.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: Your company allows personal laptops to access Microsoft 365, but security requires that any device accessing Exchange Online be marked compliant. Devices are enrolled in Intune with a compliance policy. Which Conditional Access grant control enforces this?
options: Require hybrid Microsoft Entra joined device
Require device to be marked as compliant
Require authentication strength with FIDO2
Require approved client app
explain: The 'Require device to be marked as compliant' grant control blocks access until Intune reports the device compliant — exactly the requirement. Hybrid join alone proves domain join, not compliance state. Authentication strength controls the MFA method, and approved-client-app controls which apps may connect; neither evaluates device compliance.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: Engineers from a partner tenant access your Azure portal resources as B2B guests. They already completed MFA in their home tenant, but your Conditional Access policy prompts them for MFA again, annoying both teams. The partner tenant enforces MFA as strongly as you do. What should you configure?
options: Exclude all guest users from the MFA Conditional Access policy
Assign the guests the Conditional Access Administrator role
Enable password hash sync for the partner tenant
In cross-tenant access settings, configure the inbound trust settings to trust the partner's MFA claims
explain: Cross-tenant access inbound trust settings let you trust MFA, compliant-device, and hybrid-joined claims from the partner tenant, so guests are not re-prompted when their home tenant already satisfied the requirement. Excluding guests from the policy removes the protection instead of recognizing the partner's MFA. The Conditional Access Administrator role delegates policy management, not claim trust, and password hash sync is an internal sync option, not a B2B mechanism.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: Your company operates in three regions. Each region has an IT team that must reset passwords and manage group memberships for users in their region only. They must have no administrative power over users in other regions. What is the least-privilege design?
options: Create an administrative unit per region containing that region's users and groups, and assign the regional admins scoped roles on their administrative unit
Create a separate Microsoft Entra tenant per region
Assign the regional admins the User Administrator role at the tenant level and instruct them to manage only their region
Create one security group per region and assign the admins as group owners
explain: Administrative units scope role assignments to a subset of users, groups, and devices — assigning User Administrator scoped to the region's AU gives exactly regional power and nothing more. Separate tenants fracture identity and collaboration. Tenant-wide User Administrator violates least privilege regardless of instructions. Group ownership manages one group's membership, not password resets or user administration.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: Your company uses pass-through authentication with three authentication agents in the headquarters datacenter. The CIO worries that a total internet outage at headquarters would prevent everyone from signing in to Microsoft 365, even though Microsoft's cloud is healthy. Which authentication method removes this dependency?
options: Federation with Active Directory Federation Services, because it keeps authentication on-premises
Pass-through authentication with additional agents in branch offices
Password hash synchronization, because the password hashes live in Microsoft Entra ID and cloud authentication continues without on-premises connectivity
Smart card authentication with certificate trust
explain: With password hash synchronization, Microsoft Entra ID validates credentials itself using the synced hashes, so sign-in survives a headquarters internet outage. Pass-through authentication always requires live agents reachable from the cloud — more agents do not help if headquarters is offline. Federation keeps the dependency on-premises (worse for this scenario), and smart cards do not change where the credential is validated.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: You need a group to which you will assign the Reader role on a subscription for the finance audit team. The team also wants a shared inbox, a Teams channel, and a SharePoint site for audit workpapers. How should you structure the groups?
options: Create one Microsoft 365 group and assign it the Reader role; it provides the inbox, Teams, and SharePoint plus the role assignment
Create a security group for the Reader role assignment and a separate Microsoft 365 group for the collaboration resources
Create a mail-enabled security group, which provides both the shared inbox and Azure RBAC eligibility
Assign the Reader role to individual users and create a distribution list for the inbox
explain: Security groups are the correct principal for Azure RBAC role assignments, while Microsoft 365 groups exist to back collaboration workloads (Teams, SharePoint, Exchange). Mixing the two overloads one group with unrelated purposes and lifecycle. Mail-enabled security groups add an inbox but not Teams/SharePoint, and per-user assignments plus a distribution list create management overhead the group model exists to avoid.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: A governance rule requires every resource to carry the 'Owner' tag. Hundreds of existing resources lack it, and new deployments sometimes forget it. You want Azure to add the tag automatically with a default value wherever it is missing, without blocking deployments. Which policy effect should the definition use?
options: Deny, which blocks any deployment missing the tag
Audit, which reports missing tags for manual remediation
Disabled, which skips evaluation for tagged resources
Modify, which adds or updates the tag on existing and new resources during evaluation
explain: The Modify effect remediates by adding or updating tags on resources that lack them, covering both existing resources (via a remediation task) and new ones. Deny only blocks non-compliant deployments and never fixes existing resources. Audit only reports. Using Modify with a remediation task is the standard pattern for automatic tag backfill.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: Your enterprise architect designs a management group hierarchy with eight nested levels below the root management group to mirror the org chart. You must tell them the design violates an Azure limit. What is the limit?
options: A hierarchy supports at most six levels of management groups below the root
A hierarchy supports at most three levels of management groups
There is no depth limit; the design is valid
A hierarchy supports at most ten levels, so eight is acceptable
explain: Azure supports up to six levels of management groups in a hierarchy, not counting the root level or the subscription level. An eight-deep design must be flattened. The limit is documented and enforced — deeper nesting is rejected, so 'no limit' and the other numbers are wrong.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: Your company acquires a startup. The startup's Azure subscription must be moved into your Microsoft Entra tenant. The startup's CTO asks whether their existing RBAC role assignments will keep working after the move. What do you tell them?
options: Yes, role assignments transfer with the subscription unchanged
Yes, but only assignments at the subscription scope; resource group assignments are lost
No, changing the subscription's directory permanently deletes all RBAC role assignments, and they must be recreated in the new tenant
No, the subscription cannot change directories at all
explain: When a subscription changes its Microsoft Entra tenant, Azure permanently deletes every RBAC role assignment — the identities they reference live in the old directory. You must re-create assignments for identities in the new tenant after the move. The move itself is supported, so D is wrong, and no scope of assignment survives, so A and B are wrong.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: You apply a ReadOnly resource lock to a production resource group. A Contributor on that resource group tries to deploy a new virtual machine into it, and also tries to read the settings of an existing VM. What happens?
options: Both actions succeed, because ReadOnly only blocks deletions
The deployment fails, but reading the VM settings succeeds
Both actions fail, because the lock suspends the Contributor role entirely
The deployment succeeds after the Contributor confirms an override prompt
explain: A ReadOnly lock blocks all control-plane writes (create, update, delete) while permitting reads — so the deployment is denied and reading settings works. It does not suspend the role or affect data-plane operations, and there is no override prompt; only removing the lock (Owner or User Access Administrator) unblocks writes.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: You configure a PIM role assignment for the Contributor role that requires manager approval on activation. A user who is both eligible for the role and designated as an approver requests activation and then approves their own request in the PIM blade. What happens?
options: The activation succeeds; approvers may approve their own requests
The activation succeeds but is flagged in the audit log for later review
The request is queued until a second approver also approves
PIM blocks self-approval; a different approver must approve the request
explain: PIM does not allow a user to approve their own activation request — this separation-of-duties enforcement is built in. The request stays pending until an eligible approver other than the requestor approves (or it expires). There is no self-approval path and no automatic escalation to a second approver.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: Your platform team defines environments with Azure Blueprints, including policy assignments and role assignments stamped out per environment. Microsoft has deprecated Blueprints. The team needs the same declarative, versioned environment deployment with the ability to block deletion of deployed resources. What should they migrate to?
options: Deployment Stacks, which support declarative deployment with denySettings to block deletes
Template Specs, which provide deny assignments on deployed resources
Azure Policy initiatives, which replace blueprint artifact deployment
Stay on Blueprints; deprecation only affects new blueprint creation
explain: Microsoft deprecated Azure Blueprints and directs customers to Deployment Stacks, which deploy and manage resources as a unit and support denySettings (DenyDelete) to protect deployed resources. Template Specs version templates but do not manage resource lifecycle or create deny assignments. Policy initiatives govern compliance rather than deploying environments. Deprecation means migration is required, not optional.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: The dev/test subscription routinely overspends. You create a budget and want Azure to automatically deallocate all VMs in the subscription when forecasted spending hits 100% of budget — not just send an email. What should you configure?
options: A budget alert with email recipients; the on-call engineer deallocates the VMs manually
An Azure Policy Deny assignment that blocks VM creation at 100% of budget
A budget alert condition on forecasted cost wired to an action group that triggers an Automation runbook to deallocate the VMs
A resource lock applied automatically when the budget threshold is crossed
explain: Budget alerts can invoke action groups, and an action group can trigger an Automation runbook — the supported automation path for cost-triggered remediation like deallocating VMs. Email-only alerts require manual action. Policy Deny cannot evaluate spend, and resource locks are not budget-triggered and would block all management, not just compute cost.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: Your workloads run on varying VM sizes across three regions, and the mix changes every few months. Finance wants a commitment discount on compute but refuses to be locked to specific VM sizes or regions. Which purchasing option fits?
options: Reserved Virtual Machine Instances, scoped to a region and VM size family
Azure savings plan for compute, which applies the discount across VM sizes and regions based on hourly spend commitment
Spot VMs, which offer the deepest discount for flexible workloads
Azure Hybrid Benefit, which discounts compute for any size and region
explain: A savings plan for compute commits to an hourly spend amount and the discount floats across VM families, sizes, and regions — matching variable workloads. Reserved VM Instances lock the discount to a size and region (exchangeable, but not automatic). Spot pricing is deep but evictable, unsuitable as a finance planning commitment. Hybrid Benefit discounts using existing licenses rather than committing spend, and applies per-VM.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: A partner's senior engineer will co-administer your Azure environment for a two-year project. As a guest, they hit directory visibility restrictions and cannot perform some admin tasks your team takes for granted. The partnership is long-term and trusted. What should you do?
options: Give the guest the Global Administrator role; the role overrides guest restrictions
Create a cloud-only member account and share its credentials with the engineer
Move the engineer into your on-premises Active Directory
Invite the partner as a B2B user with userType Member, which removes guest restrictions while keeping their home-tenant identity
explain: B2B users can be invited with userType Member instead of Guest, giving them member-level directory access while they keep their home-tenant credentials — designed for trusted long-term collaborators. A Global Administrator guest still faces guest restrictions in some experiences. Sharing a cloud-only account destroys auditability, and pulling the engineer into on-premises AD is unnecessary when B2B member type exists.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: Developers keep deploying GPU-intensive VM sizes for test workloads, exploding the subscription bill. You want to prevent anyone from deploying VM sizes outside an approved list, while allowing everything else. Which control should you implement?
options: Assign the built-in 'Allowed virtual machine SKUs' Azure Policy definition, listing the approved sizes
Assign the Reader role to developers so they cannot deploy expensive VMs
Apply a CanNotDelete lock to the subscription
Create a budget alert at 50% of the expected spend
explain: The 'Allowed virtual machine SKUs' policy denies VM deployments outside the approved list at deployment time — preventive governance. Reader would stop all deployments, not just expensive ones. A CanNotDelete lock blocks deletions, not creations. A budget alert only notifies after spend occurs; it never prevents the deployment.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: You plan to use dynamic membership groups, Privileged Identity Management for Entra roles, quarterly access reviews, and Identity Protection user risk policies. The tenant currently has Microsoft Entra ID P1. What licensing change is required?
options: No change; P1 covers all four features
Upgrade to P2 is required only for dynamic membership groups
Upgrade to P2; PIM, access reviews, and Identity Protection require P2, while dynamic groups are covered by P1
Downgrade is possible; all four features are in the Free edition
explain: Dynamic groups, Conditional Access, and SSPR are P1 features, but PIM, access reviews, and Identity Protection are P2-only. Since the plan includes the P2 features, the tenant needs P2. Option B reverses the mapping, and the Free edition covers none of these.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: An analytics team created a general-purpose v2 storage account last month and loaded 40 TB of data. They now want to use it as an Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2 account with hierarchical namespace for big-data analytics. What is the correct path?
options: Enable hierarchical namespace on the existing account in the portal; the data is reorganized automatically
Create a new storage account with hierarchical namespace enabled and migrate the data; the namespace setting cannot be changed after account creation
Upgrade the account to Premium block blobs, which enables hierarchical namespace
Enable NFS 3.0 on the existing account, which implicitly activates hierarchical namespace
explain: Hierarchical namespace is a creation-time decision and cannot be enabled on an existing storage account — a new account is required, followed by data migration. Premium block blobs do not support hierarchical namespace at all. NFS 3.0 requires hierarchical namespace rather than enabling it; the dependency runs the other way.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: A Linux analytics cluster needs to mount blob storage over NFS 3.0 for a Hadoop-compatible workload. Which storage configuration supports this?
options: A Premium file shares account with NFS 4.1
A standard GPv2 account with hierarchical namespace disabled
A Premium block blobs account with NFS 3.0 toggled on
A standard GPv2 account with hierarchical namespace and NFS 3.0 protocol support enabled
explain: NFS 3.0 protocol support for blob/object storage requires a GPv2 account with hierarchical namespace enabled (the ADLS Gen2 foundation). Premium file shares support NFS 4.1 for file shares, a different protocol and service. Premium block blobs do not support NFS 3.0, and NFS 3.0 cannot work without hierarchical namespace.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: A business partner must upload weekly reports to your blob storage using SFTP clients they already own. You want to avoid standing up a VM-based SFTP server. What should you do?
options: Enable SFTP support on a GPv2 storage account with hierarchical namespace enabled, and grant the partner container-scoped access
Enable SFTP on any standard GPv2 account; hierarchical namespace is optional
Deploy an Azure VM running an SFTP server with the storage account mounted
Use Azure Data Box to receive the partner's uploads
explain: Azure Blob Storage natively supports SFTP, but it requires hierarchical namespace to be enabled on the account — then local users or Entra identities get container-scoped SFTP access with no VM to manage. SFTP cannot be enabled on non-HNS accounts. A VM-based server reintroduces infrastructure the native feature eliminates, and Data Box is for offline bulk migration, not weekly partner uploads.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: You need to host a single-page application (static HTML, CSS, and JavaScript) with a custom domain, served directly from Azure Storage at the lowest cost. No server-side code is involved. What should you configure?
options: Deploy the files to an Azure Files premium share and expose it with a private endpoint
Upload the files as page blobs in the Hot tier and share the blob URLs
Enable the static website feature on a GPv2 storage account, upload the assets to the $web container, and set the index document
Enable hierarchical namespace and serve the site through SFTP
explain: The static website feature serves content from the special $web container with index and error document support — the purpose-built, cheapest option for static sites. Page blob URLs work but provide no index-document routing or clean hosting semantics. Azure Files is not a web host, and SFTP is a transfer protocol, not an HTTP serving path.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: Two storage accounts in different regions hold the same dataset for a multi-region application. New blobs written to the source account must appear in the destination account automatically within minutes, continuously, without any scheduled job. Which feature should you configure?
options: Geo-redundant storage (GRS) on the source account
Object replication with a replication policy between the source and destination containers
A nightly AzCopy sync scheduled with Task Scheduler
Azure File Sync between the two accounts
explain: Object replication asynchronously copies new and changed block blobs from source to destination containers per a replication policy — continuous and automatic. GRS replicates within one account to its paired region, not to a second account you manage. A scheduled AzCopy is batch-based, not continuous, and File Sync is for Azure Files with Windows servers, not blob-to-blob replication.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: Compliance requires a weekly report listing every blob in 50 containers, including tier, last-modified date, and encryption scope, delivered as a file the auditors can open in Excel. Manually listing containers is impractical. What should you use?
options: Storage Explorer with a container-by-container export
A lifecycle management policy, which generates inventory as a side effect
Diagnostic settings on the storage account
Blob inventory, which generates scheduled CSV or Parquet reports of blob properties
explain: Blob inventory produces scheduled reports (CSV or Parquet) enumerating blobs and their properties — built for exactly this audit scenario. Lifecycle policies move or delete data; they do not report on it. Diagnostic settings capture control-plane and request logs, not a blob catalog. Storage Explorer cannot automate a weekly 50-container report.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: An event-driven pipeline must trigger an Azure Function for every new or changed blob in a container holding millions of objects. Polling container listings is too slow and too expensive in transactions. Which feature gives the pipeline an ordered log of blob changes to consume?
options: The blob change feed, which records create, modify, and delete events per blob in order
Blob versioning, which stores prior copies of each blob
Soft delete for blobs, which retains deleted blobs
The activity log, which records blob-level data operations
explain: The change feed provides a durable, ordered log of blob create/modify/delete events that downstream processors (Functions, Event Grid) consume — far cheaper than listing polling at scale. Versioning keeps prior content, not an event log. Soft delete protects against deletion but emits no consumable stream. The activity log records control-plane operations, not per-blob data changes.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: A financial firm must retain trade records in blob storage for seven years in an unalterable state to satisfy SEC 17a-4. After seven years the records may be deleted. No one — not even administrators — may delete or modify them during the retention period. Which immutability configuration meets the requirement?
options: A legal hold, which the compliance officer can clear at any time
Blob versioning with a 7-year lifecycle rule
A time-based retention policy of seven years on the container, which cannot be shortened once set
Soft delete with a 7-year retention period
explain: A time-based retention policy enforces WORM compliance for a fixed period — it cannot be shortened or removed until it expires, satisfying the regulator. A legal hold is indefinite and clearable at will, so it does not prove a fixed retention. Versioning and soft delete are data-protection features, not immutability; neither blocks an administrator from deleting.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: You want a lifecycle policy that moves blobs to the Cool tier 30 days after they were last read, not 30 days after last modification. In the portal, the 'days after last access' condition is unavailable. What must you enable first?
options: Blob versioning on the storage account
Access time tracking (last access time) on the storage account, which records read operations at a small transaction cost
The Archive tier on the account
Diagnostic settings for read telemetry
explain: Lifecycle rules can only evaluate last-access time if access time tracking is enabled on the account — it is off by default because recording reads costs extra transactions. Versioning tracks writes, not reads. The Archive tier is a destination, not a prerequisite, and diagnostic settings do not feed lifecycle evaluation.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: You are building a two-node Windows Server Failover Cluster in Azure for a clustered SQL Server instance. Both nodes need simultaneous read/write access to the same data disks. Which managed disk configuration supports this?
options: Standard SSD disks with ZRS replication
Premium SSD v2 disks, which support sharing natively on all sizes
Ultra disks with encryption at host
Premium SSD disks with disk sharing enabled (maxShares set to 2 or more)
explain: Shared managed disks — Premium SSD (and Ultra) with maxShares greater than 1 — allow multiple VMs to attach the same disk simultaneously, which failover clustering requires. ZRS replicates within a region but does not share a disk between VMs. Premium SSD v2 does not support shared disks. Encryption at host is unrelated to multi-attach.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: A reporting VM runs on a 512 GiB Premium SSD with a steady 200 IOPS baseline, but month-end jobs spike to 4,000 IOPS for about an hour. Provisioning a disk sized for 4,000 IOPS year-round is wasteful. Which feature handles the spikes cost-effectively?
options: Credit-based bursting on the Premium SSD, which allows temporary bursts above the baseline using accumulated credits
An Ultra disk, which bursts automatically at no extra cost
Zone-redundant storage on the disk, which increases IOPS
A second Standard HDD disk in a storage pool
explain: Premium SSD bursting lets disks accumulate credits during low usage and burst well above baseline for short periods — the economical answer for brief spikes. Ultra disks deliver provisioned (non-bursting) performance you pay for continuously. ZRS changes replication, not IOPS, and adding a Standard HDD does not raise the Premium disk's burst ceiling.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: A security policy requires that VM OS disks be encrypted inside the guest operating system with BitLocker, using keys stored in Azure Key Vault, so the encryption travels with the VHD if it is ever downloaded. Which solution meets the requirement?
options: Server-side encryption with Microsoft-managed keys, which encrypts at the storage layer
Server-side encryption with customer-managed keys, which encrypts at the storage layer
Azure Disk Encryption, which uses BitLocker (Windows) or DM-Crypt (Linux) with keys in Key Vault
Encryption at host, which encrypts data at the VM host level
explain: Azure Disk Encryption encrypts within the guest OS via BitLocker/DM-Crypt and stores the keys (BEK/KEK) in Key Vault — so protection travels with the VHD. Server-side encryption (Microsoft- or customer-managed keys) encrypts at the Azure Storage layer, not inside the guest. Encryption at host encrypts on the physical host, also outside the guest OS.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: You take daily full snapshots of a 4 TiB data disk for backup purposes, and snapshot storage costs are climbing. Only about 50 GiB changes per day. How do you cut snapshot storage cost while keeping daily recovery points?
options: Switch to Standard HDD snapshots, which are free
Use incremental snapshots, where the first snapshot is full and subsequent ones store only the deltas
Delete snapshots older than one day
Move the disk to the Archive tier before snapshotting
explain: Incremental snapshots store only changed blocks after the initial full snapshot, so 50 GiB of daily change costs far less than 4 TiB full copies — while each snapshot remains an independently restorable point-in-time. Deleting old snapshots destroys history rather than optimizing it. There is no Archive tier for managed disks, and snapshot billing is not waived by disk type.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: You need a copy of a managed OS disk from East US available in West Europe to build a golden image there. Managed disks cannot be moved directly between regions. What is the supported sequence?
options: Enable GRS on the disk and read from the secondary endpoint
Attach the disk to a VM in West Europe over VNet peering
Use AzCopy to copy the disk's VHD URI across regions
Create a snapshot of the disk, copy the snapshot to West Europe, and create a new managed disk from the copied snapshot
explain: Snapshots are the cross-region vehicle for managed disks: snapshot the source disk, copy the snapshot to the target region, then create a disk from it. Managed disks have no GRS option and no secondary endpoint. A disk cannot be attached across regions, and managed disks have no directly copyable VHD URI for AzCopy.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: Your Azure Files shares hold department documents that users occasionally delete or overwrite by mistake. You need scheduled backups with file-level restore, managed entirely in Azure with no on-premises infrastructure. What should you use?
options: Azure Backup for Azure Files shares via a Recovery Services vault, with snapshot-based scheduled backups and file-level restore
Azure File Sync with cloud tiering
Blob soft delete on the storage account
Storage account failover to the secondary region
explain: Azure Backup natively protects Azure Files shares with scheduled, snapshot-based backups and item-level restore through a Recovery Services vault. File Sync replicates to Windows servers rather than backing up. Blob soft delete covers blobs, not file shares, and a storage failover is a disaster-recovery operation, not a backup with point-in-time file restore.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: A storage account firewall denies all public network access. Azure Backup fails to back up the file shares, because the backup service cannot reach the storage account. You cannot open the firewall to the internet. What should you enable?
options: A service SAS for the backup service with no IP restriction
A private endpoint in every virtual network in the tenant
The 'Allow trusted Microsoft services to access this storage account' exception on the firewall
Anonymous public read access on the shares
explain: The trusted-Microsoft-services exception lets first-party services such as Azure Backup reach the storage account through the firewall without opening it to the internet. A SAS authenticates but does not bypass firewall rules. Private endpoints in every VNet are overkill and do not help a platform service, and anonymous access defeats the firewall's purpose.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: To save money, an administrator moves 20 TB of blobs to the Archive tier, then deletes half of them 30 days later when a project is cancelled. Finance is surprised by an early-deletion charge. Why?
options: Archive tier deletions always cost the same as the original upload
The Archive tier has a 180-day minimum retention; deleting earlier incurs a prorated early-deletion charge
Deleting from Archive requires rehydration first, which was billed
Early-deletion charges apply only to the Cool tier, so this must be a billing error
explain: Archive carries a 180-day minimum storage duration — deleting before it expires triggers an early-deletion charge for the remaining days. (Cool has a 30-day and Cold a 90-day minimum.) Rehydration is only needed to read data, not to delete it, and the charge here is documented behavior, not a billing error.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: A database backup application writes to an Azure Files premium share and needs a sustained 40,000 IOPS. The current 100 GiB provisioned share tops out far below that. What should you do?
options: Enable SMB multichannel, which multiplies IOPS without resizing
Switch the share to the Hot tier
Add a second share and stripe writes across both
Increase the provisioned size of the premium share, because provisioned IOPS and throughput scale with provisioned capacity
explain: On Premium Azure Files, baseline IOPS and throughput scale with the provisioned share size — the fix for an IOPS ceiling is provisioning more capacity. SMB multichannel improves single-client throughput, not the share's provisioned IOPS limit. There is no Hot tier for premium shares, and striping across shares adds complexity instead of using the designed scaling model.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: A data lake holds finance, HR, and engineering folders. Each department's analysts authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID and must see only their own folder. Coarse container-level access is not sufficient. The storage account has hierarchical namespace enabled. What should you configure?
options: POSIX-style access control lists (ACLs) on the directories, granting each department's Entra group access to its own folder
A separate storage account per department
The Storage Blob Data Reader role on the container for all analysts
Container-level stored access policies per department
explain: Hierarchical namespace enables POSIX-like ACLs on directories and files, providing folder-level least privilege within one account. A container-level RBAC role cannot distinguish folders. Separate accounts work but multiply cost and management. Stored access policies back SAS tokens; they do not evaluate directory-level permissions.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: You perform an unplanned failover of a RA-GRS storage account during a regional outage. After the failover completes and the application is running in the secondary region, what is the replication state of the account?
options: It remains RA-GRS with the regions swapped automatically
It becomes ZRS in the new primary region
It becomes LRS in the new primary region; you must reconfigure geo-replication afterward
Replication pauses until you fail back to the original region
explain: After failover the account is locally redundant (LRS) in the new primary region — geo-replication does not automatically re-establish. You reconfigure GRS/GZRS once the original region recovers (or accept LRS). The account does not become ZRS on its own, and replication to a secondary does not resume until you configure it.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: A legacy workload requires a 4 TiB OS disk on its Azure VM. The VM was created as Generation 1 and the deployment fails when attaching the larger OS disk. What must change?
options: Enable Ultra disks on the Generation 1 VM
Convert the disk to Standard HDD, which supports larger OS disks on Gen1
Attach the 4 TiB disk as a data disk instead of an OS disk
Recreate the VM as Generation 2, which supports OS disks larger than 2 TiB with UEFI boot
explain: Generation 1 VMs are BIOS-based and limited to 2 TiB OS disks; Generation 2 uses UEFI and supports much larger OS disks plus faster boot. Disk type does not change the generation limit. Attaching as a data disk dodges the requirement instead of meeting it — the workload needs a 4 TiB OS disk.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: Your security baseline requires that Azure VMs boot only signed code and that the VM have a virtual TPM for measured boot and disk-encryption key protection. Which VM feature provides both, and what does it require?
options: Trusted launch, providing Secure Boot and vTPM; it requires a Generation 2 VM
Azure Disk Encryption, providing Secure Boot and vTPM on any VM generation
Confidential computing with AMD SEV-SNP, available on Generation 1 VMs
Host-based encryption, which includes vTPM on Generation 1 VMs
explain: Trusted launch bundles Secure Boot and a virtual TPM for measured boot, and it requires Generation 2 VMs (UEFI). Azure Disk Encryption encrypts disks but does not provide Secure Boot or vTPM. Confidential VMs are a separate, more specialized offering. Encryption at host protects data on the physical host and is unrelated to boot integrity.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: You are standardizing monitoring for 200 VMs. A runbook from last year installs the Log Analytics agent (MMA) and connects VMs to the workspace. A colleague says to deploy the Azure Monitor Agent instead. Why is the colleague right?
options: The Log Analytics agent cannot send data to a Log Analytics workspace
The Azure Monitor Agent is free while the Log Analytics agent requires a license
The Log Analytics agent is deprecated; the Azure Monitor Agent with data collection rules is the supported path for new deployments
The Azure Monitor Agent works without any workspace or data collection rule
explain: Microsoft deprecated the Log Analytics agent (MMA/OMS); new monitoring should use the Azure Monitor Agent governed by data collection rules. The old agent does send to workspaces — that is not the issue. AMA still needs a destination and usually a DCR; the difference is supportability and the modern configuration model, not licensing.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: A compliance standard requires the IIS web server role to be installed on all 60 Windows VMs at all times. A one-time script is not enough — drift must be detected and corrected continuously. Which Azure capability should you use?
options: The Custom Script Extension, rerun weekly via a scheduled task
Machine configuration (Azure Policy guest configuration), which audits and remediates desired state continuously
VM Run Command, executed against each VM daily
An Azure Automation update management schedule
explain: Machine configuration (guest configuration via Azure Policy) continuously audits and can auto-remediate desired state such as an installed Windows feature — built for drift control. Custom Script Extension and Run Command are one-time imperative actions with no ongoing enforcement. Update management handles OS patching, not configuration state.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: A VM stops responding to RDP and the VM agent shows as unresponsive, so Run Command and extensions are unavailable. You need an interactive text console to diagnose the boot failure. Boot diagnostics is enabled. What should you use?
options: Azure Bastion, which connects through the VM agent
Packet capture on the VM's NIC
Connection troubleshoot against port 3389
The VM serial console, which provides text-based console access independent of the network and the VM agent
explain: Serial console connects to the VM's serial port through the Azure fabric — no network path and no VM agent required — and works with boot diagnostics enabled (Windows uses the SAC channel). Bastion still needs a responsive guest OS network stack, which a hung VM lacks. Packet capture and connection troubleshoot diagnose network paths, not an unresponsive guest OS.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: A regulator requires that your VMs run on hardware dedicated to your organization — no other tenant's VMs may share the physical servers. Which Azure option satisfies this?
options: Azure Dedicated Host, which reserves entire physical servers for your VMs
An availability zone, which isolates VMs in separate datacenters
A proximity placement group, which pins VMs to one datacenter
A virtual machine scale set with overprovisioning
explain: Dedicated Host allocates whole physical servers to your organization, giving hardware-level isolation for compliance. Availability zones protect against datacenter failure but share hardware across tenants. Proximity placement groups optimize latency, and scale sets manage instance counts — neither addresses hardware tenancy.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: Your VMSS runs a stateless web tier from a marketplace image. You want Azure to automatically apply OS security patches to instances using a rolling upgrade with health checks, without you building custom images. Which feature should you enable?
options: Automatic VM guest patching with a maintenance window
The Rolling upgrade policy for application deployments
Automatic OS image upgrades on the scale set, which rolls out new platform images in batches validated by the application health probe
Spot VMs with eviction policy set to Deallocate
explain: Automatic OS upgrades on VMSS apply the latest platform image across instances in rolling batches, pausing on unhealthy instances via the health probe — no custom image pipeline needed. Guest patching patches the running OS in place rather than upgrading images. The rolling application-upgrade policy deploys your app version, not OS images. Spot eviction policy is about capacity, not patching.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: Your VMSS runs interruptible Spot instances processing queue messages. When Azure evicts an instance, in-flight messages are lost because the VM dies instantly. You need advance warning so the application can finish or requeue work. What should you configure?
options: Overprovisioning on the scale set
Scheduled Events with terminate notification, so the VM receives notice before eviction and can drain gracefully
A proximity placement group for the scale set
The Manual upgrade policy
explain: Scheduled Events deliver a terminate notification to the VM ahead of Spot eviction (and other maintenance), giving the application time to drain or requeue work. Overprovisioning only speeds up scale-out provisioning. Proximity placement affects latency, and the upgrade policy governs version rollouts — neither provides eviction warning.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: Your App Service web app on the Standard tier needs HTTPS on a custom domain. You want a free, auto-renewing certificate with no Key Vault to manage. What should you use?
options: Upload a self-signed PFX certificate
An Application Gateway with a WAF policy
A private endpoint on the web app
An App Service managed certificate bound to the custom domain
explain: App Service managed certificates are free, auto-renewing TLS certificates for custom domains on Standard tier and above — no Key Vault or manual renewal needed. Self-signed certificates trigger browser trust warnings. Application Gateway and private endpoints address traffic routing and network isolation, not certificate issuance.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: Your App Service app on the Basic tier unloads after 20 minutes of inactivity, causing a slow cold start for the first user each morning. The app must stay loaded. What should you enable?
options: Always On, which keeps the worker process loaded during idle periods
A deployment slot, which keeps a warm copy of the app
Autoscale, which adds instances before morning traffic
Application Insights, which pings the app continuously
explain: Always On prevents the idle timeout unload by keeping the app loaded — the direct fix for cold starts. Deployment slots serve release management, not idle behavior. Autoscale adjusts instance count based on metrics, not idle unloading. Application Insights monitors; its availability tests could warm the app incidentally, but that is a hack, not the designed setting.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: Your App Service web app exposes an internal admin portal that must be reachable only from the corporate office public IP range. The main site stays public. What should you configure?
options: A private endpoint on the web app, which makes the whole app private
An NSG on the App Service plan subnet
Access restrictions on the app (or slot), with an allow rule for the office IP range
VNet integration on the app
explain: App Service access restrictions act as an IP allowlist/denylist at the app (or slot) level — you can scope the admin path while the main site stays public. A private endpoint would privatize the entire app. App Service plans do not take NSGs directly, and VNet integration gives the app outbound VNet access rather than filtering inbound callers.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: Every release, you deploy to the staging slot, warm it up, then swap to production manually during a change window. You want the swap to happen automatically once the staging deployment finishes warming up, with no manual step. What should you enable?
options: Swap with preview on every deployment
Auto swap on the staging slot, which swaps it into production automatically after the app initializes
A second production slot that you deploy to directly
Deployment slots on the Basic tier
explain: Auto swap on a slot automatically swaps it into production after deployment and warm-up complete — removing the manual change-window step. Swap with preview adds a manual validation phase, the opposite of automation here. Deploying straight to production loses the warm-up safety, and slots require Standard tier or higher.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: You need to run a containerized ETL task every night at 2 AM. It processes files for about 40 minutes and then must stop completely — it is never a long-running service. Which Azure service fits best?
options: Azure Container Apps (serverless apps), which run continuously
Azure Container Instances with restart policy Always
An App Service web app for containers
Azure Container Apps Jobs, designed for run-to-completion triggered tasks
explain: Container Apps Jobs are built for run-to-completion workloads (scheduled, event-driven, or manual triggers) that start, finish, and stop. Container Apps (the apps resource) targets long-running services. ACI with Always would restart the finished task pointlessly, and App Service for containers hosts web workloads, not batch jobs.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: A container group in Azure Container Instances must resolve and reach an on-premises database over the existing site-to-site VPN. The containers get public IPs by default and cannot reach the private address space. What should you do?
options: Deploy the container group into a delegated subnet of the VNet, giving the containers private VNet addresses that route over the VPN
Assign a public IP to the on-premises database
Enable the Container Instances restart policy OnFailure
Place a Standard Load Balancer in front of the container group
explain: ACI supports VNet integration by deploying the container group into a delegated subnet, placing containers on private VNet IPs that can use the VPN to on-premises. Exposing the database publicly is a security regression. Restart policy and load balancers do not change container network placement.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: Your AKS cluster's system node pool runs on D-series VMs. A new ML workload needs GPU nodes, but you must not disturb the system pool or risk cluster stability. What should you do?
options: Change the system node pool VM size to a GPU SKU
Delete the cluster and recreate it with GPU nodes
Add a user node pool with a GPU VM size and schedule the ML pods there with a node selector or taints
Run the ML workload as a DaemonSet on the system pool
explain: AKS supports multiple node pools: adding a user node pool with GPU SKUs isolates the ML workload while the system pool keeps running cluster services untouched. Resizing the system pool is disruptive and mixes concerns. Recreating the cluster is unnecessary, and DaemonSets on the system pool put user workloads where only system pods belong.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: Pods in your AKS cluster stay in Pending state with 'Insufficient cpu' events during traffic spikes, even though the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler is adding pod replicas. What should you enable?
options: The vertical pod autoscaler, which resizes pod requests
The cluster autoscaler, which adds nodes when pods cannot be scheduled
More aggressive HPA thresholds
A second system node pool
explain: HPA scales pods; when pending pods cannot be scheduled for lack of node capacity, the cluster autoscaler adds nodes. This is the classic two-level scaling distinction the exam tests. VPA resizes existing pod requests, HPA tuning adds more unschedulable pods, and another system pool does not auto-grow with demand.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: Your Azure Function must call an internal API inside a VNet and scale automatically with load. It is currently on the Consumption plan and cannot reach the API. Which hosting plan meets both requirements?
options: Stay on Consumption and add VNet integration
Move to a Dedicated (App Service) plan with Always On but no scaling
Use Container Instances instead of Functions
Move to the Elastic Premium plan, which supports VNet integration and elastic scale
explain: The Consumption plan does not support VNet integration; the Elastic Premium plan adds VNet integration plus elastic scaling (and longer execution times). The Dedicated plan supports VNet but you manage scaling yourself. Switching compute services avoids the question rather than answering it.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: Before deploying an updated Bicep template to the production resource group, you want to see exactly which resources will be created, modified, or deleted — without changing anything. What should you run?
options: A what-if deployment, which previews the changes with no side effects
A Complete mode deployment to a test resource group
The template through the ARM template test toolkit only
A validation deployment, which applies changes in audit mode
explain: What-if analysis previews the create/modify/delete/no-change effects of a deployment without executing it — the pre-deployment safety check. Complete mode to a test group does not show production deltas. The test toolkit lints template syntax rather than predicting changes, and there is no 'audit mode' deployment.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: You want Azure to automatically assess and install OS patches on your VMs on a schedule, rebooting as needed, without you logging in to each machine or managing patch windows per VM. Which patch orchestration should you use?
options: Manual patching through Windows Update on each VM
Custom Script Extension running a patch script monthly
Automatic VM guest patching (patch orchestration set to Azure-orchestrated/AutomaticByPlatform)
VMSS rolling upgrades, which patch standalone VMs
explain: Automatic VM guest patching lets the Azure platform assess and patch VMs on a schedule with safe reboot handling — no per-VM logins. Manual patching and script extensions do not scale and lack platform orchestration. VMSS rolling upgrades apply to scale sets, not standalone VMs.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: You try to resize a running VM from D4s_v5 to E8s_v5 in the portal, but the E-series size is not listed as available. The VM is currently running. What is the most likely reason and fix?
options: The subscription quota is exhausted; request a quota increase
The new size is not available on the current hardware cluster; stop (deallocate) the VM and then resize
E-series sizes require the VM to be Generation 1
Resizing is blocked by the ReadOnly lock on the resource group
explain: A VM can only resize to sizes available on its current hardware cluster while running; moving to a size hosted on a different cluster requires deallocating first so Azure can place it freely. Quota exhaustion produces a different error, E-series runs on Gen2, and a ReadOnly lock would block the resize operation itself rather than hiding the size.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: You need a subnet that provides at least 60 usable IP addresses for VMs. Azure reserves 5 addresses in every subnet. What is the smallest subnet prefix that meets the requirement?
options: A /26 subnet, which provides 59 usable addresses
A /27 subnet, which provides 27 usable addresses
A /25 subnet, which provides 123 usable addresses
A /24 subnet, which provides 251 usable addresses
explain: Azure reserves 5 IPs per subnet (first four and last), so usable = 2^(32-prefix) minus 5: /26 gives 64-5=59 (just short of 60), /25 gives 128-5=123. /25 is therefore the smallest prefix meeting the requirement. The trap is forgetting the 5 reserved addresses and picking /26.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: You are preparing a VNet for a site-to-site VPN gateway. Which subnet configuration is required for the gateway?
options: Any subnet with at least 16 addresses; the gateway finds it automatically
A subnet named 'Gateway' with a /28 prefix
The gateway can share a subnet with VMs as long as no NSG is attached
A subnet named exactly 'GatewaySubnet' with a /27 prefix or larger
explain: The gateway subnet must be named exactly GatewaySubnet and be at least /27 (larger prefixes like /26 are allowed). The name is how Azure identifies it — any other name fails deployment. Gateways cannot share a subnet with VMs, and /28 is below the minimum size.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: Your company uses ExpressRoute with private peering to reach Azure VNets. The CIO wants Microsoft 365 traffic to also travel over ExpressRoute instead of the internet. What should you configure?
options: Microsoft peering on the ExpressRoute circuit, which advertises Microsoft 365 and Dynamics 365 public prefixes
A second ExpressRoute circuit dedicated to Microsoft 365
VNet peering between the VNet and Microsoft 365
A site-to-site VPN with BGP for Microsoft 365 prefixes
explain: Microsoft peering on an ExpressRoute circuit advertises Microsoft public service prefixes (Microsoft 365, Dynamics 365) so that traffic traverses the private circuit. Private peering only reaches your VNets. No second circuit or VNet peering to a SaaS service is needed, and VPN cannot carry Microsoft peering prefixes.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: Your company has two datacenters, each with its own ExpressRoute circuit in a different region. The datacenters need to communicate with each other, and you want that traffic to stay on Microsoft's backbone rather than the internet. What should you enable?
options: VNet peering between the two regions
A site-to-site VPN between the datacenters
ExpressRoute Global Reach, which connects the two ExpressRoute circuits through Microsoft's network
Private peering on both circuits, which automatically bridges them
explain: ExpressRoute Global Reach links two ExpressRoute circuits so on-premises sites communicate over Microsoft's backbone. Private peering connects each site to Azure, not the sites to each other. VNet peering connects Azure VNets, and a VPN would traverse the internet — exactly what the requirement excludes.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: You need a site-to-site VPN that supports BGP and carries traffic to three separate on-premises sites through one Azure VPN gateway. Which gateway type should you deploy?
options: A policy-based VPN gateway, which supports up to 10 tunnels with BGP
A route-based VPN gateway, which supports multiple site-to-site connections and BGP
An ExpressRoute gateway, which natively terminates IPsec tunnels
A point-to-site gateway with RADIUS authentication
explain: Route-based VPN gateways support multiple site-to-site tunnels and BGP; policy-based gateways support a single S2S tunnel, no BGP, and IKEv1 only. ExpressRoute gateways terminate private circuits, not IPsec. Point-to-site serves individual clients, not site connectivity.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: In a hub-and-spoke topology, spoke VNet VMs must send all internet-bound traffic through the Azure Firewall in the hub VNet for inspection. What must you configure?
options: A NAT gateway on each spoke subnet
Gateway transit on the spoke-to-hub peering only
An NSG on the hub firewall subnet allowing outbound internet
A user-defined route for 0.0.0.0/0 with next hop the firewall's private IP on the spoke subnets, and 'Allow forwarded traffic' on the peerings
explain: Forcing spoke internet traffic through the hub NVA requires a default UDR pointing at the firewall's private IP on the spoke subnets, plus 'Allow forwarded traffic' on the VNet peerings so the hub accepts and forwards the packets. A NAT gateway would send traffic directly out, bypassing inspection. Gateway transit shares gateways, not NVA forwarding, and NSGs do not route traffic.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: Security policy requires that all internet-bound traffic from Azure VMs be inspected by the on-premises security stack. The VNet connects to headquarters over ExpressRoute. How do you force VM internet traffic back on-premises?
options: Create a user-defined route for 0.0.0.0/0 with next hop type 'Virtual network gateway' on the VM subnets
Attach an NSG denying outbound internet on the VM subnets
Deploy a NAT gateway and block its public IP on-premises
Enable forced tunneling by setting the VNet's DNS servers to on-premises
explain: Forced tunneling is implemented with a default UDR whose next hop is the virtual network gateway, sending internet-bound traffic down the ExpressRoute/VPN to on-premises inspection. An NSG deny would block traffic rather than redirect it. NAT gateways and DNS settings do not steer routing.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: A VMSS with 200 instances makes thousands of concurrent outbound HTTPS connections for a data pipeline. Connections intermittently fail with SNAT port exhaustion errors. Each instance currently uses the load balancer's default outbound SNAT. What should you deploy?
options: A public IP on every VMSS instance
An internal Standard Load Balancer
A NAT gateway on the subnet, which provides 64,000 SNAT ports per public IP and scales by adding IPs
A larger VM size with more network bandwidth
explain: NAT gateway is the designed fix for SNAT exhaustion: each public IP supplies about 64k SNAT ports and you can attach up to 16 IPs.
