Per-instance public IPs are unmanageable at this scale and less secure. An internal load balancer provides no outbound path, and VM size does not change SNAT port allocation.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: A runbook from 2023 deploys a Basic SKU load balancer for a new zonal web tier. The deployment fails, and the architect says the SKU choice is the problem. What happened, and what should you deploy?
options: Basic SKU now requires an availability set; add the VMs to one
Basic SKU load balancers were retired; deploy a Standard SKU load balancer, which also supports availability zones
Basic SKU is only available in paired regions; deploy in the paired region instead
Basic SKU requires a public IP; the runbook used an internal frontend
explain: Microsoft retired the Basic SKU load balancer (September 30, 2025); new deployments must use Standard, which additionally brings zone redundancy, larger backend pools, and better SLAs. Basic supported internal frontends and had no availability-set requirement — the failure is retirement, not configuration.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: You have a Standard internal load balancer in a hub VNet. Backend servers include VMs in two peered spoke VNets. Which backend pool configuration supports this?
options: NIC-based backend pool, which spans peered VNets automatically
A Basic SKU load balancer, which supports cross-VNet backends
Backend pool by VMSS only
IP address-based backend pool, adding the spoke VMs' private IPs
explain: Standard Load Balancer supports IP-based backend pools, letting you add private IPs from peered VNets (or even on-premises via VPN/ER). NIC-based pools are limited to the load balancer's own VNet. Basic SKU is retired and never supported this topology.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: You deploy an Application Gateway into a subnet that already contains two application VMs, and the deployment fails. What is the rule for Application Gateway subnets?
options: The subnet must be dedicated to Application Gateway instances; no other resources may reside in it
The subnet must be named 'AppGatewaySubnet'
The subnet must have an NSG denying all inbound traffic
The gateway must share the subnet with the backend VMs for low latency
explain: Application Gateway requires a dedicated subnet — only gateway instances may occupy it; VMs or other resources cause deployment failure. There is no required subnet name (unlike GatewaySubnet or AzureBastionSubnet). An NSG is allowed with specific rules, not a deny-all, and sharing the subnet with backends is exactly what the rule forbids.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: You run real-time game servers on custom TCP ports in three regions. You need global users directed to the nearest healthy region with automatic failover. The traffic is not HTTP. Which service should you use?
options: Azure Front Door, which routes custom TCP ports globally
Application Gateway with multi-site listeners
Traffic Manager with performance routing, which works at the DNS level for any protocol
A Standard Load Balancer with backends in all three regions
explain: Traffic Manager is DNS-based and protocol-agnostic, so it directs users to the nearest healthy endpoint for any TCP/UDP workload with failover on endpoint health. Front Door is an HTTP/HTTPS reverse proxy and cannot front raw TCP game traffic. Application Gateway is regional HTTP load balancing, and a Standard Load Balancer is regional, not global.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: Your public website is app.contoso.com resolving to a public IP. Inside your VNet, the same name must resolve to the application's private IP so internal traffic never leaves the VNet. What should you configure?
options: A hosts file entry on every VM
A private DNS zone named contoso.com linked to the VNet, with an A record for app pointing to the private IP
A second public DNS zone for contoso.com
Conditional forwarding on the VNet to the public DNS servers
explain: A private DNS zone with the same name as the public zone (split-brain DNS) lets linked VNets resolve app.contoso.com to the private IP while the internet keeps using the public zone. Hosts files do not scale, a second public zone would conflict publicly, and forwarding to public DNS returns the public IP — the opposite of the goal.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: VMs in your VNet must resolve on-premises hostnames like db.corp.local through the headquarters DNS servers, which are reachable over the VPN. Azure's default DNS cannot resolve corp.local. What should you configure?
options: An NSG rule allowing DNS traffic to headquarters
A private DNS zone for corp.local with manual A records
Azure Bastion in the VNet
Custom DNS servers on the VNet pointing to the headquarters DNS server IPs
explain: Setting custom DNS servers on the VNet makes all VMs use the on-premises DNS servers, which resolve corp.local authoritatively over the VPN. An NSG rule does not change which server answers queries. Manually duplicating records in a private zone creates split-brain drift, and Bastion is remote-access, not name resolution.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: You need ongoing measurement of latency and packet loss between a VM in East US and an on-premises server over the VPN, with alerts if latency exceeds 150 ms. One-off tests are not enough. What should you use?
options: Network Watcher Connection Monitor, which continuously probes and records latency and loss, and can feed alerts
A packet capture on the VM's NIC
IP flow verify run on a schedule
NSG flow logs with Traffic Analytics
explain: Connection Monitor performs continuous synthetic probing between endpoints and records latency/packet loss over time with alerting — built for ongoing SLA monitoring. Packet captures and flow logs are forensic tools, not latency monitors. IP flow verify is a one-time NSG simulation, not a continuous probe.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: After a security incident, you must determine exactly which NSG rule allowed a suspicious inbound connection to a VM last Tuesday, including the rule name and the decision. Which data source provides this?
options: The activity log, which records the connection
A packet capture from last Tuesday
NSG flow logs (version 2) with Traffic Analytics, which record per-flow allow/deny decisions and the rule name
Connection Monitor history
explain: NSG flow logs v2 capture the 5-tuple, the allow/deny decision, and the rule name for each flow — the forensic record needed. The activity log records control-plane operations, not data-plane connections. A packet capture would need to have been running at the time, and Connection Monitor measures synthetic probes, not real traffic decisions.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: A VM cannot reach the internet even though its subnet NSG allows outbound traffic. You suspect a route is overriding the default. Where do you see the actual routes applied to the VM's NIC, including system routes, UDRs, and BGP-propagated routes?
options: In the NSG's effective security rules
In the NIC's effective routes view
In the VNet's address space settings
In the VPN gateway's BGP peer status
explain: Effective routes on the NIC show the merged routing table Azure actually applies: system routes, user-defined routes, and BGP-propagated routes with their sources. Effective security rules show NSG evaluation, not routing. VNet address space and BGP peer status do not reveal the per-NIC route table.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: A developer claims an NSG is blocking their application's traffic to a database VM on port 1433. You want to quickly test whether the NSGs would allow or deny that specific packet, without capturing traffic or changing any rules. What should you use?
options: A packet capture on the database VM's NIC
Connection troubleshoot to port 1433
NSG flow logs filtered to the developer's IP
IP flow verify, which simulates the packet against the effective NSG rules and reports allow or deny
explain: IP flow verify simulates a packet (source, destination, port, protocol) against the effective NSG rules and reports the verdict instantly — no traffic capture or rule changes. Packet capture records real traffic but does not explain the NSG decision. Connection troubleshoot tests reachability hop-by-hop (heavier), and flow logs only show historical flows.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: You are deploying Azure Bastion for RDP/SSH access without public IPs on the VMs. Which subnet is required in the VNet?
options: A subnet named exactly 'AzureBastionSubnet' with a /26 prefix or larger
Any subnet with the name 'Bastion' and a /28 prefix
The existing 'GatewaySubnet', which Bastion can share
No dedicated subnet; Bastion deploys as a VM extension
explain: Bastion requires a dedicated subnet named exactly AzureBastionSubnet, at least /26 (larger prefixes allowed). Like GatewaySubnet, the name is mandatory and sharing with gateways or VMs is not supported. Bastion is a managed platform service, not a VM extension.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: A public IP fronting your customer portal needs always-on traffic monitoring, automatic mitigation of DDoS attacks, and cost protection against scale-out during an attack. Which Azure protection should you enable?
options: An NSG with a deny rule for suspicious source IPs
DDoS IP Protection on the public IP, which provides per-IP monitoring, mitigation SLA, and cost protection
Azure Firewall on the VNet
A WAF policy on the public IP
explain: DDoS IP Protection is the per-public-IP SKU with always-on monitoring, automatic mitigation backed by an SLA, and cost protection for scale induced by attacks. NSGs filter by static rules and cannot mitigate volumetric DDoS. Azure Firewall filters traffic but is not a DDoS mitigation service, and WAF policies protect against application-layer (OWASP) attacks, a different threat class.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: You must collect syslog messages from 80 Linux VMs into a Log Analytics workspace for security analysis. The legacy Log Analytics agent is deprecated. What is the supported configuration?
options: Install the Log Analytics agent and enable syslog in the workspace's legacy settings
Deploy the Azure Monitor Agent to the VMs and create a data collection rule that collects syslog and sends it to the workspace
Enable boot diagnostics on each VM, which forwards syslog automatically
Create a log search alert that queries syslog on each VM directly
explain: The supported path is the Azure Monitor Agent plus a data collection rule (DCR) defining the syslog facilities to collect and the destination workspace. The legacy agent is deprecated for new deployments. Boot diagnostics capture serial console output, not syslog streams, and alert rules query data already ingested — they do not collect it.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: An application team needs to see which processes consume the most CPU on each VM, map application dependencies between VMs, and track performance trends — beyond the basic host metrics in Metrics explorer. What should you enable?
options: A workbook with KQL queries against the AzureActivity table
Service Health alerts for the VMs
Network Watcher packet capture on each VM
VM insights, which collects guest performance data including per-process CPU and dependency mapping
explain: VM insights (via the Azure Monitor Agent and dependency agent data) provides per-process performance, the application dependency map, and trend views. Workbooks visualize data but do not collect guest metrics. Service Health reports platform incidents, and packet capture is network forensics — neither shows process-level CPU.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: You manage 300 VMs across five subscriptions and need a single view of missing updates, plus scheduled patching windows per environment (dev patches Tuesday, production patches Saturday). Which service should you use?
options: Azure Update Manager, which assesses update compliance centrally and applies patches on per-scope schedules
Automatic VM guest patching with identical settings on every VM
Azure Policy DeployIfNotExists to install updates
Manual patching via Run Command on a schedule
explain: Azure Update Manager gives a central compliance dashboard and maintenance configurations with per-scope schedules — exactly the multi-environment patching workflow. Guest patching auto-patches but lacks the central assessment view and differentiated schedules. Policy DeployIfNotExists installs agents/extensions, not OS updates, and Run Command is one-off execution.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: Finance asks you to find wasted compute spend. You suspect several VMs run at under 5% CPU around the clock. Where do you get specific resize or shutdown recommendations backed by Azure's utilization analysis?
options: The activity log, filtered to VM deallocation events
Metrics explorer, which recommends VM sizes automatically
Azure Advisor cost recommendations, which identify underutilized VMs and suggest rightsizing or shutdown
The Azure Status page
explain: Azure Advisor analyzes utilization telemetry and produces concrete cost recommendations (resize underutilized VMs, shut down idle ones). Metrics explorer shows the raw data but makes no recommendations. The activity log records operations, not efficiency analysis, and the status page reports service health.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: You want the infrastructure team notified by SMS whenever Azure schedules planned maintenance affecting the East US region. Which alert type should you create?
options: A Resource Health alert on each VM
A Service Health alert filtered to planned maintenance in East US, wired to an action group with SMS
A metric alert on the VMs' CPU percentage
A log search alert querying the AzureActivity table
explain: Service Health alerts fire on platform events including planned maintenance per region — filtering to East US planned maintenance with an SMS action group matches the requirement. Resource Health is per-resource rather than regional. Metric and log-search alerts watch your telemetry, not Azure's maintenance schedule.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: A VM is unreachable. Nobody on your team changed anything, and Azure's status page shows no regional incident. Where do you check whether the Azure platform itself took the VM down, and what would that look like?
options: Service Health, which shows per-VM platform events
The activity log, which records platform-initiated reboots
Metrics explorer, which annotates platform events on charts
Resource Health for the VM, which would show 'Unavailable' with a platform-initiated cause
explain: Resource Health reports per-resource health including platform-initiated unavailability (host failure, live migration issues) — the right place when no admin action and no regional incident explain the outage. Service Health covers region-wide events, not individual VMs. The activity log records your administrative operations, not platform health, and metrics show performance, not health causes.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: Your Application Gateway WAF is blocking legitimate customer requests, and you need the full request details of blocked transactions to tune exclusions. Where do you enable collection of the WAF logs?
options: In the Application Gateway's diagnostic settings, sending FirewallLogs to a Log Analytics workspace
In the NSG flow logs on the gateway subnet
In the activity log export settings
In the Application Gateway's backend health probe settings
explain: Application Gateway diagnostic settings include the Firewall log category (WAF blocked/allowed request details) routable to Log Analytics. NSG flow logs record layer-3/4 flow metadata, not WAF decisions. The activity log covers control-plane operations, and health probes report backend availability, not request blocking.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: You need a query listing the ten most common error codes in the AppServiceHTTPLogs table over the last 24 hours. Which KQL query does this?
options: AppServiceHTTPLogs | where TimeGenerated > ago(24h) | project ScStatus
AppServiceHTTPLogs | take 10
AppServiceHTTPLogs | where TimeGenerated > ago(24h) | summarize count() by ScStatus | top 10 by count_ desc
AppServiceHTTPLogs | summarize count() | where count_ > 10
explain: The pattern is filter by time, summarize count() by the status column, then top 10 by count_ descending. Option A only projects the column without aggregating, B takes ten arbitrary rows, and D counts all rows into a single number — none ranks error codes by frequency.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: You need a line chart of average request duration in five-minute buckets over the last 6 hours from AppServiceHTTPLogs. Which KQL fragment produces the time series?
options: | summarize avg(TimeTaken) by TimeGenerated | render table
| summarize avg(TimeTaken) by bin(TimeGenerated, 5m) | render timechart
| where TimeTaken > 5m | count
| top 6 by TimeGenerated | project TimeTaken
explain: bin(TimeGenerated, 5m) buckets timestamps into five-minute intervals, summarize computes the average per bucket, and render timechart draws the line chart. Without bin(), each distinct timestamp becomes its own group. C counts slow requests rather than charting averages, and D takes six rows — not a six-hour series.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: Your VMSS shows high average CPU, but you need to know whether a few instances are hot while others are idle. In Metrics explorer, how do you break the Percentage CPU chart down per instance?
options: Change the aggregation from Average to Maximum
Extend the time range to 30 days
Add a second metric for available memory
Apply splitting by the Instance dimension
explain: Splitting (segmenting) a metric by a dimension such as Instance renders one series per VMSS instance, revealing hot versus idle instances. Changing aggregation or time range keeps a single blended line. Adding a memory metric does not decompose CPU per instance — and guest memory is not a platform metric anyway.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: A VM's CPU follows an unpredictable daily pattern, and your static 80% alert threshold pages the team constantly during normal peaks while missing real anomalies at night. Which alert configuration adapts to the learned pattern?
options: A metric alert with dynamic thresholds, which uses machine learning on historical data to set upper and lower bounds
A log search alert with a higher static threshold
An activity log alert on VM start/stop events
A Service Health alert for the region
explain: Dynamic thresholds apply ML to the metric's history and alert on deviations from the learned pattern, cutting noise from normal peaks and catching off-hours anomalies. Raising a static threshold just moves the noise. Activity log and Service Health alerts watch control-plane and platform events, not CPU behavior.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: You need to know within minutes if your public web app stops responding, tested from five geographic locations, with alerts on failure. The app has no agent installed. What should you configure?
options: A log search alert querying the app's logs
Connection Monitor between the regions
An Application Insights standard availability test (URL ping) from multiple locations with an alert rule
A metric alert on the app's CPU percentage
explain: Standard availability tests (URL ping tests) probe the app's endpoint from multiple Azure locations on a schedule and trigger alerts on failure — no agent required. Log queries need ingested data and detect issues indirectly. Connection Monitor tests network paths between your resources, not public endpoint availability. CPU metrics do not prove the app responds to HTTP.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: A request flows through a front-end API, two microservices, and a database. When latency spikes, you need to see the end-to-end trace with each span's duration to find the slow component. Which Application Insights capability provides this?
options: Availability tests, which trace each hop automatically
Distributed tracing (transaction diagnostics), which correlates spans across services using W3C trace context
The activity log, which records the request path
Metrics explorer with splitting by cloud role name
explain: Distributed tracing correlates telemetry across services into one end-to-end transaction view with per-span timings via W3C trace-context propagation. Availability tests only check endpoint up/down. The activity log records Azure control-plane operations, not application requests. Metrics splitting shows aggregates, not individual request traces.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: Your workspace ingests verbose debug logs at high volume. Engineers query them only during rare incident investigations; dashboards and alerts never use them. How do you cut the ingestion cost for these tables?
options: Delete the tables; the data can be regenerated
Set the workspace default retention to 30 days
Export the tables to a storage account and stop ingesting
Switch those tables to the Basic Logs plan, which offers lower-cost ingestion for high-volume, rarely queried data
explain: The Basic Logs table plan reduces ingestion cost for high-volume tables that are queried infrequently, with a subset of KQL capabilities and shorter interactive retention. Deleting data destroys the investigation record. Workspace default retention affects all tables equally, and exporting then stopping ingestion loses the queryable copy entirely.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: A compliance rule requires that all Azure Monitor ingestion and query traffic from your VNets stay on the private network and never traverse the public internet — including agent telemetry uploads. What should you deploy?
options: An Azure Monitor Private Link Scope (AMPLS) connected to a private endpoint, with the DCRs and workspace bound to the scope
A service endpoint for Microsoft.Storage on each subnet
A VPN gateway in each VNet
Private endpoints on every monitored VM
explain: AMPLS with private endpoints keeps monitoring ingestion and query traffic private; binding DCRs and the workspace to the scope enforces it. Service endpoints for Storage do not cover Monitor endpoints. A VPN alone does not change the public endpoints agents target, and VMs do not take private endpoints for this purpose.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: A VM in VNet-A cannot reach a VM in peered VNet-B on port 8080. You want Network Watcher to test the path hop by hop and tell you exactly where the connection fails — source NSG, peering, or destination NSG. What should you run?
options: IP flow verify on the source VM
A packet capture on the destination NIC
Connection troubleshoot from the source VM to the destination on TCP 8080
NSG flow logs on both subnets
explain: Connection troubleshoot tests TCP connectivity hop by hop and reports where it breaks (each NSG evaluation, peering, routing). IP flow verify only simulates one NSG's verdict. Packet capture records traffic but does not diagnose the path, and flow logs show historical flows rather than an active diagnostic.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: You need an alert when any VM's memory usage exceeds 90%. You create a metric alert, but no memory-related metric is available for the VMs. Why, and what must you configure first?
options: Memory metrics are only available on Premium SSD VMs; resize the VMs
Memory is a guest OS metric, not a platform metric; deploy the Azure Monitor Agent with a data collection rule collecting the memory counter
Metric alerts cannot use memory; use a log search alert on the AzureActivity table instead
Memory metrics require the VM to be in an availability zone
explain: Platform metrics cover host-level signals (CPU, disk, network) but not guest-OS memory — collecting it requires the Azure Monitor Agent with a DCR gathering the guest memory performance counter, after which the metric alert can target it. Disk type and zones are unrelated, and the AzureActivity table holds control-plane events, not performance counters.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: Every Severity 0 alert must automatically open a ticket in the company's ServiceNow instance. You do not want to modify the dozens of existing alert rules. How should you implement this?
options: Add a webhook to each alert rule's action group manually
Create a Logic App that polls the activity log every minute
Enable the ITSM connector and add its action to every alert rule
Configure the IT Service Management connector for ServiceNow, then use an alert processing rule filtered to Severity 0 that adds an action group containing the ITSM action
explain: The ITSM action in an action group creates ServiceNow tickets via the IT Service Management connector, and an alert processing rule can attach that action group to all Severity 0 alerts at fire time — no alert-rule edits needed. Manually editing each rule defeats the requirement, and polling the activity log is a fragile workaround for a built-in integration.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: Leadership wants a single dashboard combining Azure Monitor metrics, Prometheus data from AKS, and incident annotations — with Microsoft Entra authentication for viewers. Which service should you deploy?
options: Azure Managed Grafana, which unifies Azure Monitor and Prometheus data sources with Microsoft Entra authentication
An Azure Dashboard pinned with metric charts
A Log Analytics workbook
Azure Data Explorer with a dashboard
explain: Azure Managed Grafana is the multi-source visualization service: native Azure Monitor and Prometheus plugins plus Microsoft Entra ID authentication. Azure Dashboards and workbooks are Azure-data-centric and lack Prometheus federation. Azure Data Explorer dashboards visualize Kusto data, not Prometheus, and add an unnecessary data pipeline.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: Management wants a weekly report of backup job success rates, storage consumption, and missed SLAs across all Recovery Services vaults. The data must be queryable centrally. What should you configure?
options: Export each vault's jobs to CSV manually every week
A log search alert on each vault
Diagnostic settings on the vaults sending backup data to a Log Analytics workspace, then use the Backup Reports workbook
Azure Advisor, which reports backup compliance automatically
explain: Sending vault diagnostic data (AzureBackupReport) to a Log Analytics workspace centralizes job, storage, and policy data, and the Backup Reports workbook visualizes success rates and SLA misses. Manual CSV exports do not scale and are not queryable. Alert rules notify on conditions rather than producing reports, and Advisor does not cover backup reporting.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: Your company partners with Fabrikam for a two-year project. Fabrikam employees need access to a SharePoint site, a Teams team, and an Azure SQL database. Access must be request-based with manager approval, expire automatically at project end, and be reviewable quarterly. What is the best solution?
options: Invite each Fabrikam user as a B2B guest and manually assign licenses and roles, tracking expiry in a spreadsheet
Add all Fabrikam users to one security group with permanent access and no reviews

Configure Fabrikam as a connected organization, bundle the resources into an access package with an approval policy, expiry, and quarterly access reviews, letting users request access through myAccess
Use B2B direct connect so Fabrikam users appear in a shared Teams channel
explain: Entitlement management access packages bundle multiple resources with policy-driven request, approval, lifecycle (expiry), and access reviews — and connected organizations define which external organizations may request them. Manual invites create toil and spreadsheet-tracked expiry is unreliable. A permanent security group has no lifecycle. B2B direct connect only enables Teams shared channels, not SharePoint/SQL governance.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: You configure a Conditional Access policy with the grant control 'Require authentication strength' set to the built-in 'Phishing-resistant MFA' strength. A user who authenticates with SMS one-time codes plus the Authenticator app push notification is blocked. The user insists they completed MFA. Why are they blocked, and what must they use instead?
options: SMS and push are not MFA at all; the user must enroll a password
The user must switch to a phishing-resistant method such as a FIDO2 security key, Windows Hello for Business, or certificate-based authentication
The policy is misconfigured; any MFA method satisfies any authentication strength
The user must be excluded from the policy because their phone cannot do phishing-resistant MFA
explain: The built-in authentication strengths are tiered: SMS, voice, and push notifications satisfy 'Multifactor authentication' but NOT 'Phishing-resistant MFA', which requires FIDO2, Windows Hello for Business, or certificate-based authentication. The user did complete MFA — just not a phishing-resistant form. Excluding the user defeats the policy, and the strength tiers are enforced exactly as configured.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: Legal requires every contractor to accept the company's acceptable-use policy before accessing SharePoint Online, and acceptance must be re-confirmed every 180 days. Emailing PDFs has proven unenforceable. How should you implement this?
options: Create an access review that asks contractors if they read the policy
Use a Conditional Access session control to display the policy at sign-in
Assign contractors the Guest Inviter role so they accept terms during invitation
Create a Terms of Use document and require it in a Conditional Access grant control, with reacceptance set to 180 days
explain: Terms of Use integrated with Conditional Access blocks access until the user accepts the document, and supports periodic reacceptance — enforceable, unlike emailed PDFs. Access reviews verify continued need, not document acceptance. Session controls manage sign-in frequency and persistence, not terms. The Guest Inviter role delegates invitations and has nothing to do with policy acceptance.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: You add custom banned passwords like 'Contoso2026!' to Microsoft Entra password protection. Cloud users are blocked from using them, but on-premises Active Directory users can still set these passwords. The tenant syncs with Microsoft Entra Connect. What must you deploy to enforce the custom banned list on-premises?
options: The password protection DC agent on all domain controllers, plus the proxy service so the agents can download the custom banned list
Smart lockout on the domain controllers, which enforces the banned list automatically
Self-service password reset for the on-premises users
Nothing; the custom banned list syncs to Active Directory through Microsoft Entra Connect automatically
explain: On-premises enforcement requires the password protection DC agent installed on every domain controller; the proxy service is what lets those agents download the custom banned-password list from the cloud (the global banned list works without the proxy). Smart lockout is a separate brute-force defense, SSPR does not push banned lists down, and Connect sync does not carry the custom list to AD.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: You are a Global Administrator in a new tenant, but the Azure portal shows no subscriptions and every resource blade returns an access error. A colleague says Global Administrator should grant full access to everything. What is the correct fix?
options: Wait 24 hours for the role assignment to propagate to Azure RBAC
In Microsoft Entra ID properties, set 'Access management for Azure resources' to Yes, which grants your account User Access Administrator at the tenant root so you can then assign proper RBAC roles
Ask an Owner to assign you Owner on each subscription individually
Convert your account from a guest to a member user
explain: Microsoft Entra directory roles do not grant Azure RBAC permissions by default — the two authorization systems are separate. Elevating 'Access management for Azure resources' grants User Access Administrator at the root management group, after which you assign least-privilege roles and remove the elevation. There is no propagation delay to wait out, and member-vs-guest is unrelated to subscription visibility.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: The help desk needs to invite B2B guests and reset passwords for non-administrative users, but must not manage groups, roles, or conditional access. The built-in User Administrator role is too broad. What is the least-privilege approach?
options: Assign the Authentication Administrator role, which covers guest invitations
Assign the Global Reader role plus the Helpdesk Administrator role
Create a security group and delegate through group ownership
Create a custom Microsoft Entra directory role with only the needed permissions, which requires Microsoft Entra ID P1 or P2
explain: Custom directory roles let you assemble exactly the needed permissions (invite guests, reset passwords for non-admins) and require P1/P2. Authentication Administrator manages authentication methods and registrations, not invitations. Global Reader is read-only. Group ownership manages one group's membership, not password resets or guest invites — and custom directory roles are distinct from Azure RBAC custom roles.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: You assign Microsoft 365 E5 licenses to a dynamic security group via group-based licensing. Most users get licensed, but several show a license error. Investigation shows those users already have Microsoft 365 E3 assigned directly. What is the cause and fix?
options: The users have conflicting service plans between E3 and E5; remove one of the overlapping licenses so the plans no longer conflict
Group-based licensing does not support dynamic groups; convert it to an assigned-membership group
The tenant needs Microsoft Entra ID P2 for group-based licensing
License assignment takes 72 hours to resolve conflicts automatically
explain: Group-based licensing fails when a user holds two SKUs containing the same conflicting service plan (E3 and E5 overlap on services like Exchange); the fix is removing one assignment. Group-based licensing fully supports dynamic groups and requires only P1, not P2. Conflicts never auto-resolve — they persist until the overlap is removed.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: You use Windows Autopilot. You need a dynamic device group that automatically contains all Windows 11 devices so an Autopilot profile and compliance policy target them. Which membership rule should you use?
options: (user.department -eq 'IT'), which captures the device owners
(device.deviceOSType -eq 'Windows') -and (device.deviceOSVersion -startsWith '10.0.22')
(device.managementType -eq 'MDM'), which captures all managed users
(group.objectId -eq 'Autopilot'), which nests the existing group
explain: Dynamic device groups evaluate device.* properties, not user.* — so the rule must test device attributes like deviceOSType and deviceOSVersion (Windows 11 builds start with 10.0.22xxx). User attributes are invalid in device rules. Nesting by objectId is not a supported dynamic-rule pattern, and managementType alone does not filter by OS.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: You install a second Microsoft Entra Connect server for high availability and leave it in the default installed state. Users soon report duplicate objects and sync conflicts. What went wrong, and how should the standby server be configured?
options: Two active export servers are unsupported; the standby must be uninstalled until needed
The standby server should be enabled for staging mode, which imports and synchronizes data but does not export to Microsoft Entra ID or passwords back
The standby server needs its own SQL database to avoid conflicts
Staging mode is only for migration and must be disabled after cutover
explain: Only one Connect server may actively export; a second active server causes duplicate/conflicting exports. Staging mode is the designed standby posture: it performs imports and syncs so it is ready for failover, without exporting anything. A separate SQL database does not fix dual-export conflicts, and staging mode is the high-availability mechanism, not just a migration aid.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: Office users get single sign-on to Microsoft 365 without password prompts, but employees working from home on domain-joined laptops without VPN are prompted for passwords. You use password hash sync with seamless single sign-on. What explains the difference?
options: Seamless SSO requires federation with AD FS, which you have not configured

Seamless SSO authenticates via Kerberos against an on-premises domain controller using the AZUREADSSOACC computer account, so it only works with line-of-sight to a DC; remote users without VPN fall back to password authentication
Password hash sync is broken for remote users
The laptops need to be hybrid-joined before seamless SSO works
explain: Seamless SSO is Kerberos-based: the client must reach a domain controller to get a ticket for the AZUREADSSOACC account. Without VPN there is no line-of-sight to a DC, so SSO silently fails and the user is prompted — password hash sync then validates the password in the cloud. Federation is a different SSO method, hybrid join is not required for seamless SSO, and PHS working proves sync is healthy.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: Finance needs a list of every virtual machine across all 12 subscriptions that is missing the CostCenter tag. Clicking through the portal subscription by subscription is impractical. What is the most efficient approach?
options: Run an Azure Resource Graph query across the subscriptions filtering virtual machines where tags.CostCenter is empty
Assign an Azure Policy and wait for the compliance dashboard
Export Cost Management data, which lists untagged resources
Query the activity log for tag write operations
explain: Azure Resource Graph queries resource properties across subscriptions and tenants in one query — purpose-built for inventory questions like 'which VMs lack this tag.' Policy compliance only reports after a policy is assigned and evaluated. Cost Management reports spend, not tag presence, and the activity log records operations, not current resource state.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: Deploying D-series VMs in West Europe fails with an error that the operation exceeds the approved Standard D-family vCPU quota. Deploying the same VMs in North Europe succeeds. What should you do?
options: Move the subscription to a different Microsoft Entra tenant to reset quotas
Convert the workload to B-series VMs, which share the D-series quota
Request a quota increase for the Standard D family in West Europe; quotas are enforced per VM family, per region, per subscription
Delete unused resource groups in West Europe to free quota
explain: vCPU quotas are scoped per VM family, per region, per subscription — usage in North Europe is irrelevant to West Europe, and deleting resource groups does not change quota. The fix is a quota increase request for that family in that region. Tenant moves and VM-family swaps do not address a regional family quota.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: Your company uses a Microsoft Customer Agreement. A shared networking subscription hosts resources for three departments, each billed to a different invoice section. Finance wants the shared costs split proportionally without creating separate subscriptions. What should you configure?
options: Move each department's resources into its own subscription
A budget per department, which automatically splits the charges
Cost allocation rules, which distribute the shared subscription's costs across the departments' invoice sections or subscriptions
Resource tags, which reassign the charges in the invoice
explain: MCA cost allocation rules redistribute costs of shared subscriptions or resources to other invoice sections or subscriptions — the designed mechanism for chargeback without re-architecting. Budgets only alert on spend, and tags organize and filter costs but do not move charges between invoice sections.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: You bought a 1-year reserved instance for a D-series VM in East US, but the workload permanently moved to West Europe. You want to keep a commitment discount on the relocated workload. What should you do?
options: Move the reservation to West Europe in the portal; reservations are region-portable
Cancel the reservation for a full refund and buy a new one
Buy an Azure savings plan, which cannot be exchanged
Exchange the reservation for a new one of equal or greater value matching the West Europe VM; reservations cannot be moved between regions directly
explain: Reservations are scoped to region and can be exchanged — not moved — for another reservation of equal or greater value, which preserves the commitment. Cancellation refunds are limited and not the designed path. Savings plans apply across regions automatically, so they need no exchange, but that does not help an existing reservation.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: An administrator enables Azure Hybrid Benefit on all Windows Server VMs to cut costs, but the company owns no Software Assurance or qualifying subscriptions. The licensing team flags this. What is the correct action?
options: Remove Hybrid Benefit from the VMs or acquire qualifying Software Assurance; using Windows Server Hybrid Benefit without eligible licenses is non-compliant
Keep Hybrid Benefit; it is available to every Azure customer by default
Convert the VMs to Spot VMs to preserve the discount legally
Hybrid Benefit only applies to Linux, so the setting had no effect anyway
explain: Azure Hybrid Benefit for Windows Server requires active Software Assurance or qualifying subscription licenses — without them, applying the benefit violates licensing terms. The fix is licensing compliance (buy SA) or reverting to pay-as-you-go. Hybrid Benefit is not universal, Spot pricing is unrelated to licensing, and Windows Server Hybrid Benefit is a real, commonly used benefit.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: Under your Microsoft Customer Agreement, a new department needs its own subscription whose charges appear on their invoice section. The department lead asks who can create it. What do you tell them?
options: Any Contributor on the existing subscriptions can create new subscriptions
The EA enrollment account owner must create it; MCA has no equivalent
A user with Owner or Contributor on the billing account, billing profile, or the target invoice section can create the subscription under that invoice section
Only Microsoft support can create MCA subscriptions
explain: MCA billing hierarchy (billing account > billing profile > invoice section) governs subscription creation: principals with Owner/Contributor at the appropriate billing scope can create subscriptions under an invoice section. Subscription-level Contributor grants no billing powers, the EA model does not apply to MCA, and support is not required.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: You assign a built-in guest configuration policy to audit password complexity on Windows VMs. New VMs are evaluated, but existing VMs show as non-compliant with no evaluation data, and no remediation happens. What is missing?
options: Change the policy effect to Deny, which forces evaluation
Exempt the existing VMs and reassign the policy per VM
Guest configuration only supports Linux VMs

The VMs need the Guest Configuration extension (deployed by the policy's DeployIfNotExists), the assignment needs a managed identity with sufficient permissions, and existing resources need a remediation task
explain: Guest configuration evaluation inside the VM requires the Guest Configuration extension; the assignment's managed identity needs permission to deploy it; and like all DeployIfNotExists policies, existing resources need an explicit remediation task. Deny cannot evaluate guest state, guest configuration supports Windows and Linux, and per-VM assignment does not replace the remediation task.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: You are authoring a custom Azure Policy to audit storage accounts that allow non-HTTPS traffic. You need to reference the storage account's HTTPS-only setting in the policy rule. What should you use?
options: The resource's tags, which mirror the HTTPS setting
The policy alias Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/supportsHttpsTrafficOnly in the rule's field
A DeployIfNotExists effect, which reads settings automatically
The resource ID, which encodes the HTTPS configuration
explain: Policy aliases map resource provider properties into policy rules — Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/supportsHttpsTrafficOnly is the alias for the secure-transfer setting. Tags do not mirror the setting, resource IDs encode identity not configuration, and the effect type does not determine which fields a rule can evaluate.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: Security worries that an attacker who steals a user's session cookie could replay it from their own device to access Microsoft 365. The workforce uses compliant, hybrid-joined Windows devices. Which Conditional Access control directly mitigates token replay?
options: The 'Token protection for sign-in sessions' session control, which cryptographically binds tokens to the device so they cannot be replayed elsewhere
Increasing the sign-in frequency to require reauthentication every hour
Requiring password change on next sign-in for all users
Blocking legacy authentication clients
explain: Token protection binds the session tokens to the device identity, so a stolen token is useless on the attacker's device; it requires a compliant or hybrid-joined device. Sign-in frequency shortens session life but does not bind tokens. Password changes and legacy-auth blocks address different attack paths than cookie replay.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: After a credential-stuffing wave, you want cloud accounts to lock after repeated failed sign-ins, with smarter handling for sign-ins from familiar locations. An engineer suggests implementing on-premises AD account lockout policy in the cloud. What should you explain?
options: Cloud lockout must be built with Conditional Access policies; nothing is built in
Microsoft Entra smart lockout is on by default, locks accounts after failed attempts, and distinguishes familiar from unfamiliar locations; it is separate from on-premises AD lockout policy
Smart lockout requires Microsoft Entra ID P2 to function
Smart lockout only applies to B2B guest users
explain: Smart lockout is built into Microsoft Entra ID and enabled by default — no P2 or CA policy required — and it is smarter than a fixed threshold because it weighs location familiarity. It protects cloud authentication only; on-premises AD lockout remains a separate Group Policy concern. It applies to all user types, not just guests.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: A hospital stores patient imaging in blob storage. Requirements: survive a datacenter loss within the primary region, keep the same endpoints, and maintain a secondary-region copy for regional disaster recovery. Cost is secondary. Which redundancy option meets all requirements?
options: ZRS, which protects against zonal failure but keeps no secondary-region copy
GZRS, which combines zone-redundant replication in the primary region with geo-replication to a secondary region
RA-GRS, which adds secondary read access but no zonal protection in the primary region
LRS with AzCopy jobs copying data to a second region
explain: GZRS layers both protections: synchronous zone-redundant replication in the primary region plus asynchronous geo-replication to the paired region. ZRS alone has no secondary region, RA-GRS has no zonal redundancy in the primary, and scripted AzCopy copies are not a managed redundancy option with consistency guarantees.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: You must perform storage account maintenance that requires failing over a GRS account. The primary region is healthy, and zero data loss is mandatory. Which failover type should you choose, and why?
options: Unplanned failover, because it is faster and speed guarantees no data loss
Planned failover is unavailable for GRS accounts; only RA-GRS supports it
Delete the account and recreate it in the secondary region
Planned failover, which requires the primary to be available, ensures all data is replicated before switching, and swaps the primary/secondary roles with no data loss
explain: Planned failover is the graceful path: it only runs when the primary is reachable, drains all pending replication, then swaps roles — zero data loss. Unplanned failover is for true outages and can lose data not yet replicated. Planned failover is supported on GRS/GZRS/RA-GRS accounts alike, and recreating the account is unnecessary and destructive.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: A storage account firewall is set to deny all public networks. VMs in a subnet without public IPs need to read blobs, and traffic must stay on the Azure backbone. No private endpoint exists yet. What is the simplest compliant configuration?
options: Enable a Microsoft.Storage service endpoint on the subnet and add a virtual network rule for that subnet on the storage firewall
Assign public IPs to the VMs and allowlist them on the firewall
Create a SAS token; SAS tokens bypass firewall rules
Enable the firewall's trusted-services exception for all virtual networks
explain: A service endpoint extends the subnet identity to the storage service, and the firewall's virtual network rule then permits that subnet — traffic stays on the Azure backbone with no public IPs. SAS tokens authenticate but never bypass firewall evaluation. The trusted-services exception is for first-party Azure services, not your VMs, and adding public IPs defeats the no-public-IP design.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: You issue a SAS for an external auditor to download blobs. Security requires the SAS to work only from the corporate office public IP range and only over HTTPS, so a leaked URL cannot be abused from elsewhere. Which SAS feature enforces this?
options: A stored access policy, which limits SAS usage to office hours
An account SAS, which implicitly restricts by IP
Signed IP range and signed protocol (HTTPS-only) restrictions on the SAS
The Storage Blob Data Reader role, which replaces the SAS
explain: SAS tokens support signed IP (or IP range) and signed protocol constraints, so the token is rejected from other networks or over plain HTTP. Stored access policies manage expiry/permissions for revocation, not network constraints. Account SAS has no implicit IP restriction, and RBAC is a different credential model that cannot express these URL-level constraints.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: A line-of-business application authenticates to Azure with a managed identity. It needs to generate short-lived, container-scoped credentials for blob uploads, but company policy forbids the application from ever possessing the storage account key. Which SAS type should the application create?
options: An account SAS, which requires the account key to sign
A user delegation SAS, created with Microsoft Entra credentials via OAuth, requiring no account key and valid for up to 7 days
A service SAS with a stored access policy, which requires the account key
A connection string with the account key embedded
explain: User delegation SAS is signed with Entra credentials (the managed identity's OAuth token) instead of the account key, supports container/directory scoping, and is capped at 7 days — matching the no-key policy. Account and service SAS are both key-signed. Embedding the key in a connection string directly violates the policy.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: A lifecycle policy must move blobs under the logs/ virtual directory to the Cool tier after 30 days, while blobs elsewhere in the same container must stay Hot indefinitely. How should you scope the rule?
options: Create a second storage account for the logs
Enable blob index tags on every log blob
Apply the rule to the whole container and exempt the other blobs manually
Use a prefixMatch filter of ['logs/'] in the lifecycle rule so it evaluates only blobs under that prefix
explain: Lifecycle rules accept prefix filters, so one rule can target exactly the logs/ prefix while leaving the rest of the container untouched. A second account is unnecessary architecture, index tags are a different filtering mechanism (useful for tag-based rules), and there is no per-blob exemption workflow for lifecycle evaluation.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: Blobs for 40 projects are spread across a dozen containers with no consistent folder naming. Management wants a lifecycle rule that archives blobs tagged Project=Atlas after 90 days, regardless of container or folder. What enables this?
options: Blob index tags (e.g., Project=Atlas) combined with a lifecycle rule using blobIndexMatch, which filters by tag across containers
Virtual directory naming conventions, which the lifecycle rule can parse
A separate storage account per project
The $web container, which supports tag-based rules
explain: Blob index tags attach queryable key-value metadata to blobs, and lifecycle rules support blobIndexMatch filters — so one rule can act on Project=Atlas blobs anywhere in the account. Lifecycle prefix filters depend on path naming, which the scenario says is inconsistent. Separate accounts or the $web container do not solve cross-container tag filtering.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: Field technicians use Microsoft Entra-joined laptops and work entirely off the corporate network with no VPN and no line-of-sight to a domain controller. They need single sign-on to Azure Files shares using their Entra identities. Which identity source should you configure on the storage account?
options: On-premises AD DS authentication, which requires Kerberos line-of-sight to a domain controller
Storage account key authentication with the key pushed via Intune
Entra Kerberos authentication, which lets Entra-joined clients get Kerberos tickets from Microsoft Entra ID without contacting a domain controller
Anonymous SMB access restricted by firewall
explain: Entra Kerberos issues Kerberos tickets via Microsoft Entra ID itself, so Entra-joined (or hybrid-joined) clients authenticate without DC connectivity — the off-network scenario. AD DS authentication needs DC line-of-sight, account keys are shared secrets with no SSO, and anonymous access provides no identity at all.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: A department needs its Azure Files shares protected with scheduled daily backups, a 30-day retention policy, and file-level restore by the help desk. An engineer proposes scripting share snapshots on a schedule. Why is Azure Backup the better choice?
options: Snapshots cannot be taken on Azure Files shares at all

Azure Backup for Azure Files provides scheduled, policy-driven backups with retention management and item-level restore through a Recovery Services vault, while scripted snapshots leave scheduling, retention, and cataloging to you
Snapshots are stored in the same region and Backup replicates them
Azure Backup is free while snapshots incur charges
explain: Azure Backup turns file-share protection into a managed policy: scheduled backups, retention, and file-level restore with a centralized catalog. Share snapshots are manual point-in-time copies — scriptable, but you own scheduling, retention cleanup, and restore bookkeeping. Snapshots do work on shares, both incur storage charges, and regional replication is a separate design decision.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: A media archive needs a single 80 TiB file share for video masters. The workload is infrequent-access and cost-sensitive, so Premium Files is overkill. What should you configure?
options: Sixteen 5 TiB standard shares striped by the application
A Premium file share, because only Premium supports more than 5 TiB
An Azure Data Box for the archive instead of a share
A standard file share with large file shares enabled, which supports up to 100 TiB per share
explain: Standard file shares with large file shares enabled scale to 100 TiB per share — the cost-effective answer for an 80 TiB infrequent-access archive. Premium is not required for capacity. Striping shares adds application complexity for no reason, and Data Box is a migration transport, not a serving share.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: In an ADLS Gen2 data lake, you set an ACL granting the finance group read access on the /finance directory. New files created in /finance tomorrow are not readable by the finance group, though existing files are. What is missing?
options: Default ACLs on /finance, which propagate to newly created child files and directories; access ACLs apply only to the directory object itself
The Storage Blob Data Reader role on the container
A lifecycle policy that copies permissions to new files
POSIX ACLs are evaluated only at the container level
explain: ADLS Gen2 ACLs come in two flavors: access ACLs govern the object itself, while default ACLs are inherited by newly created children. Setting only the access ACL leaves new files without the grant. RBAC roles are coarser (container-level) and do not replace directory ACLs, and no lifecycle mechanism propagates permissions.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: A vendor must upload files via SFTP into exactly one container. They cannot use Microsoft Entra identities, and you will not share the storage account key. You want key-based SSH authentication scoped to that container. What should you create?
options: A service SAS URL and ask the vendor to use it with their SFTP client
A second storage account with the key shared only with the vendor
An SFTP local user scoped to the container with an SSH public key for authentication
A private endpoint so the vendor can use anonymous SFTP
explain: SFTP local users are identities native to the storage account: you scope each to specific containers with granular permissions and authenticate with SSH keys or passwords — no Entra, no account key. SAS tokens do not authenticate SFTP sessions, a second account still shares a key, and private endpoints do not create identities or permit anonymous access.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: A nightly automation script running on an Azure VM copies blobs between storage accounts with AzCopy. The security team bans storing account keys or SAS tokens in scripts and automation variables. How should the script authenticate?
options: Embed the key in the script but restrict file permissions
Use a SAS token with a 1-year expiry stored in the automation variables
Use Storage Explorer with interactive login on the VM
Run AzCopy with the VM's system-assigned managed identity (azcopy login --identity) and grant it the needed Blob Data roles
explain: A managed identity lets AzCopy authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID and no stored secret; RBAC data roles (e.g., Storage Blob Data Contributor) scope its access. File permissions do not make an embedded key compliant, a year-long SAS is a standing secret, and interactive login cannot run unattended.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: You must migrate 60 TB from an on-premises NAS (SMB shares) to Azure Files with minimal downtime. The migration needs discovery, agent-based transfer, and delta passes so the final cutover window is short. Which service fits?
options: Azure Data Box, which ships a device for offline copy with no delta sync
AzCopy run once from a workstation
Azure Storage Mover, which uses agents on the source network, manages migration projects and jobs, and supports repeated copy passes before cutover
Azure File Sync, which requires Windows Server endpoints and keeps syncing forever
explain: Storage Mover is the online NAS-migration service: deploy agents near the source, define migration projects/jobs, and run multiple copy passes so cutover is fast. Data Box is offline with no incremental sync, a single AzCopy pass means a long cutover, and File Sync is ongoing hybrid sync anchored on Windows Server — not a migration tool.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: You need to ingest 200 TB of historical data into Blob storage. The site has no usable WAN bandwidth, and corporate policy requires using company-owned, BitLocker-encrypted drives rather than a vendor-supplied appliance. Which service should you use?
options: The Azure Import/Export service, which ingests data from customer-supplied BitLocker-encrypted drives shipped to an Azure datacenter
Azure Data Box, which ships a Microsoft-owned device to you
AzCopy over ExpressRoute, which still needs the WAN you lack
Azure Storage Mover, which performs online migration
explain: Import/Export is the customer-drive service: you copy data to your own BitLocker-encrypted disks and ship them; Azure copies the data into Blob storage. Data Box is Microsoft's device (the opposite of the requirement), AzCopy and Storage Mover are online transfers that need the bandwidth you do not have.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: A 128 GiB Premium SSD data disk (P10, 500 IOPS) is throttling a database at peak. You need roughly 2,300 IOPS but do not want to pay for a larger disk's capacity. What should you do?
options: Add a second P10 and stripe them in the guest OS
Convert the disk to Ultra Disk, which requires recreating it
Change the disk's performance tier to a higher tier (e.g., P20-level) without resizing; Premium SSD performance tiers decouple provisioned IOPS from disk size
Enable bursting permanently, which raises the baseline
explain: Premium SSD performance tiers let you raise provisioned IOPS/throughput independently of disk size — you pay the tier price, not for unused gigabytes. Striping adds complexity, Ultra Disk migration is heavier than needed, and bursting only covers temporary spikes above baseline, not a sustained higher baseline.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: A faulty driver update rendered a VM unbootable. You have a snapshot of the OS disk from before the update. You need the VM back on the pre-update OS as fast as possible without rebuilding. What should you do?
options: Restore the entire VM from Azure Backup, which also rolls back the data disks
Deallocate the VM, create a managed disk from the snapshot, and swap the VM's OS disk to the new disk
Attach the snapshot as a data disk and copy the driver files over
Delete the VM and recreate it from the snapshot with a new name
explain: OS disk swap replaces the VM's OS disk with a disk built from the snapshot — the fastest surgical recovery, requiring the VM to be deallocated first. Full backup restore works but also affects data disks and takes longer. Attaching as a data disk does not fix the boot volume, and recreating the VM loses its identity, NIC, and configuration.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: Your team maintains a hardened Windows Server image that must be deployed in five Azure regions, with version history so you can roll back to last month's image. A managed image per region is becoming unmanageable. What should you use?
options: A VHD file copied to a storage account in each region
A snapshot shared across regions
An ARM template that reinstalls the hardening steps each deployment
An Azure Compute Gallery with an image definition and versioned images replicated to all five regions
explain: Azure Compute Gallery provides versioned image definitions with automatic replication to chosen regions — one publishing flow, global availability, and rollback to prior versions. Per-region VHD copies and snapshots have no versioning or lifecycle management, and reinstalling via template on every deploy is slow and drift-prone.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: An administrator tries to detach the OS disk from a running VM to attach it to another VM for offline repair, and the operation fails. The same administrator successfully detaches a data disk from another running VM. What explains the difference?
options: An OS disk cannot be detached while the VM is running; you must deallocate (or delete, keeping the disk) the VM first, while data disks support detach from a running VM
OS disks can only be detached with Azure CLI, not the portal
The VM needs a managed identity to detach its OS disk
Data disks detach only when the VM is deallocated; the second operation should also have failed
explain: Azure blocks detaching the OS disk of a running VM because it is the boot volume; deallocating the VM releases it. Data disks are designed for hot detach/attach. The portal and CLI have the same restriction, managed identity is unrelated, and option D states the rule backwards.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: An analytics workload needs Premium performance for block blobs, and a separate file-share workload needs Premium Files. An architect proposes one Premium storage account for both. Why will this fail?
options: Premium storage accounts do not exist; Premium is only a managed-disk tier

BlockBlobStorage accounts support only block blobs and append blobs, while FileStorage accounts support only file shares — premium account kinds are single-service, so you need one account of each kind
A storage account can hold either blobs or files, never both
Premium performance requires a GPv2 account with hierarchical namespace
explain: Premium account kinds are purpose-built per service: BlockBlobStorage for block/append blobs, FileStorage for file shares, and BlockBlobStorage/PageBlobStorage variants cannot be mixed — you need two accounts. Standard GPv2 accounts can mix blobs and files, but not at Premium performance. Premium storage accounts absolutely exist; the limitation is one premium service per account kind.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: You are sizing VMs for a SQL Server workload that needs a high memory-to-vCPU ratio. The database team proposes D-series VMs because they are labeled 'general purpose.' What should you recommend instead, and why?
options: F-series VMs, which maximize CPU clock speed for compute-bound queries
E-series VMs, which are memory-optimized with a high memory-to-core ratio suited to SQL Server
B-series burstable VMs, which are cheapest for steady database load
M-series VMs, which are required for any SQL Server deployment
explain: E-series VMs are the memory-optimized family — the right fit for SQL Server's memory-hungry buffer pool. D-series is general purpose with a balanced ratio, F-series optimizes CPU over memory, and B-series burstable VMs cannot sustain steady database throughput. M-series offers the largest memory footprints but is overkill unless the workload truly needs it.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: Your SQL Server is licensed per core, and the E16s v3 VM (16 vCPUs) you planned wastes license budget — the workload needs only 4 vCPUs but the full 128 GiB of memory. What should you deploy?
options: A D4s VM, which has 4 vCPUs but far less memory
Two E8s VMs clustered, doubling the license cost
A B-series VM with 4 vCPUs and credit-based bursting
A constrained-vCPU size such as E16-4s v3, which keeps the 128 GiB memory footprint with only 4 active vCPUs
explain: Constrained-vCPU sizes (e.g., E16-4s) reduce the active vCPU count for licensing while preserving the full memory and I/O of the parent size — designed exactly for per-core licensed workloads. Downsizing to a smaller VM sacrifices memory, B-series cannot sustain database load, and clustering multiplies rather than reduces license needs.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: Developers run stateful dev VMs that they deallocate every night to save cost, but they lose all in-memory application state and spend 30 minutes each morning rebuilding it. What feature lets them deallocate while preserving RAM contents?
options: Hibernation, which saves the VM's memory state to the OS disk on deallocate and restores it on start
Snapshots of the OS disk taken nightly
An availability set, which keeps the VM's memory across maintenance
Stopping (not deallocating) the VM, which preserves RAM at full compute cost
explain: Hibernation persists the in-memory state to the OS disk (requiring a Premium SSD OS disk and a supported Generation 2 VM), so a deallocated VM resumes exactly where it left off with no compute charges while stopped. Snapshots capture disk, not RAM. Stopping without deallocating keeps RAM but keeps billing compute. Availability sets are about fault tolerance, not state preservation.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: A trading firm must control exactly when Azure platform maintenance reboots their VMs, restricting it to a Sunday 2–4 AM window. Update domains alone do not give them scheduling control. What should they configure?
options: An availability zone, which eliminates platform maintenance
A proximity placement group, which pins maintenance to one datacenter
A maintenance configuration assigned to the VMs (or their dedicated hosts) defining the allowed maintenance window
Azure Site Recovery, which fails over before maintenance
explain: Maintenance configurations let you define custom windows controlling when platform updates apply to VMs, dedicated hosts, or VMSS. Availability zones do not eliminate maintenance, proximity placement groups control latency not timing, and Site Recovery is disaster recovery — not a maintenance scheduler.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: You need a VMSS web tier that survives the loss of an entire datacenter (availability zone) in the region. A colleague suggests a regional scale set with five fault domains. Why is that insufficient, and what should you deploy?
options: Fault domains span zones automatically; the regional set is fine
A zonal VMSS, which spreads instances across availability zones so the tier survives a zone failure — a regional set stays within one datacenter
An availability set, which is the zone-redundant option
A single VM in each zone managed manually
explain: Zonal VMSS distributes instances across zones, providing zone-level resilience; regional VMSS uses fault domains within a single datacenter and cannot survive a zone outage. Fault domains do not span zones, availability sets are not zone-redundant, and manual per-zone VMs lose the scale set's management benefits.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: Your VMSS runs a stateless API. Occasionally an instance becomes unhealthy and serves errors, but the scale set keeps it until someone manually reimages it. You want Azure to automatically detect and replace unhealthy instances. What should you enable?
options: Autoscale, which replaces unhealthy instances when CPU is high
Manual upgrade policy with faster approval
Overprovisioning, which keeps spare healthy instances
Automatic instance repair with an application health probe, which replaces instances the probe reports as unhealthy
explain: Automatic instance repair monitors the application health probe and replaces unhealthy instances automatically — built for exactly this. Autoscale reacts to metrics, not health. Overprovisioning only affects scale-out provisioning headroom, and upgrade policies govern version rollouts, not health remediation.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: Your VMSS hosts a cache-heavy workload. The oldest instances hold warm caches that take hours to rebuild, while newly added instances are still cold. During scale-in, you must remove the cold newest instances first and never sacrifice the warm ones. Which scale-in policy should you configure?
options: NewestVM, which removes the most recently created instances first, preserving the long-running instances with warm caches
OldestVM, which removes the longest-running instances first
Default, which balances deletions across zones and fault domains rather than strictly by age
Instance protection on every instance, which blocks scale-in entirely
explain: The NewestVM scale-in policy removes the most recently created instances first — exactly the expendable cold-cache instances — preserving the warm long-running ones. OldestVM would destroy the warm caches. Default balances across zones and fault domains rather than by age, and protecting every instance from scale-in defeats autoscaling.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: Your App Service web app must query an on-premises SQL Server. Corporate policy forbids VPN and ExpressRoute for this project, but the on-premises server can make outbound HTTPS connections. The app is on the Standard tier. What should you configure?
options: Regional VNet integration, which requires a VPN or ExpressRoute path to on-premises
A private endpoint on the web app, which only controls inbound traffic
A Hybrid Connection with the Hybrid Connection Manager installed on the on-premises server, relaying TCP traffic without a VPN
An App Service Environment, which mandates ExpressRoute
explain: Hybrid Connections relay TCP traffic through Azure Relay: the on-premises Hybrid Connection Manager makes an outbound connection, so no VPN, ExpressRoute, or inbound firewall rules are needed. VNet integration gives VNet access but cannot reach on-premises without hybrid connectivity. Private endpoints are inbound-only, and an ASE does not remove the need for a network path.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: You have a nightly App Service backup. Before applying a risky configuration change, you want to verify the backup restores correctly — without touching the production app. What should you do?
options: Swap the production slot with staging to test the backup
Restore the backup as a new app (clone), including its settings and database connection strings, and validate there
Delete the production app and restore in place
Download the backup ZIP and inspect it locally
explain: App Service Backup supports restoring as a new app — a clone carrying the files, configuration, and optionally the database — so you can validate recovery with zero production impact. Restoring in place or deleting production is destructive, slot swaps do not test backups, and inspecting a ZIP does not prove the app runs after restore.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: A government contract requires a web application to run on fully isolated, single-tenant infrastructure inside your virtual network, with no shared compute with other customers. Which App Service option meets this requirement?
options: A Premium v3 plan, which is single-tenant by default
A private endpoint on the web app, which isolates the compute layer
An Isolated v2 plan on shared workers with VNet integration
An App Service Environment, which deploys dedicated workers into your VNet as a single-tenant environment
explain: An App Service Environment (ASE) provisions dedicated compute inside your VNet — true single-tenant isolation. Premium plans run on shared workers (private endpoints and VNet integration only isolate networking, not compute). There is no shared-worker 'Isolated' tier; isolation is what the ASE exists to provide.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: Your Durable Functions orchestrator calls DateTime.Now and generates a GUID to name output blobs. In production, orchestrations sometimes produce duplicate blobs or fail on replay. What is the root cause and fix?
options: Orchestrator code replays multiple times and must be deterministic; move DateTime.Now, GUID generation, and other non-deterministic calls into activity functions
The Consumption plan does not support durable orchestrations; move to Premium
Orchestrations cannot write blobs; use a queue trigger instead
Increase the function timeout to allow replays to finish
explain: Durable orchestrator functions replay their code to rebuild state, so any non-deterministic call (DateTime.Now, random numbers, GUIDs, I/O) produces different results on replay — corrupting execution. The pattern is: orchestrator only coordinates, activity functions do the non-deterministic work. Plan and timeout are unrelated to replay semantics.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: A function app exposes an internal admin API that must be reachable only from within the corporate VNet — never from the public internet. Access restrictions with IP rules still leave a public endpoint. What should you configure?
options: VNet integration, which secures inbound traffic to the function app
A service endpoint on the VNet subnet
A private endpoint on the function app, which removes the public endpoint from the equation; note this requires an Elastic Premium or App Service (Dedicated) plan, not Consumption
Azure API Management in front of the function
explain: A private endpoint gives the function app a private IP in the VNet and can disable public network access — true private inbound. VNet integration is for outbound calls from the app. Service endpoints do not privatize the app's endpoint, and API Management adds a gateway but does not remove the function's public surface. The plan requirement (Premium/ASE, not Consumption) is the classic exam trap.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: You deploy a new revision of a Container Apps API and want to canary-test it with 10% of live traffic, keeping 90% on the stable revision, before promoting it fully. How should you implement this?
options: Deploy a second Container App and split traffic with Front Door
Stop the old revision immediately and monitor the new one
Disable ingress until testing completes
Configure traffic splitting on the Container App's ingress to route 90% to the stable revision and 10% to the new revision
explain: Container Apps natively supports multiple active revisions with weighted traffic splitting on its ingress — the built-in canary mechanism.
