A second app with Front Door works but abandons the platform feature, stopping the old revision removes the rollback path, and disabling ingress takes the API offline instead of canarying.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: Your microservices on Container Apps need publish/subscribe messaging and distributed state without each team writing Service Bus and storage SDK code. What should you enable?
options: Azure Service Bus bindings coded into each service
Dapr, whose sidecar building blocks expose pub/sub, state management, and service invocation as local HTTP/gRPC APIs
An AKS cluster, which includes Dapr by default
Event Grid with manual subscription management per service
explain: Dapr (Distributed Application Runtime) runs as a sidecar in Container Apps and provides building blocks — pub/sub, state stores, bindings — so services call a local API instead of infrastructure SDKs. Hand-coding Service Bus clients reintroduces the coupling Dapr removes, AKS does not include Dapr automatically, and Event Grid alone does not provide state management.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: Your AKS cluster runs a supported Kubernetes version, but the team manually upgrades it every few months and once missed a version going out of support. You want Azure to automatically apply patch upgrades. What should you configure?
options: A cluster auto-upgrade channel (e.g., patch), which automatically upgrades the control plane and nodes on the chosen cadence
Node image auto-upgrade only, which upgrades Kubernetes versions
Manual upgrades scheduled in Azure Automation
Recreating the cluster on each new Kubernetes release
explain: Cluster auto-upgrade channels (none, patch, stable, rapid, node-image) automate Kubernetes version upgrades including the control plane. Node-image upgrade only refreshes the OS image, not the Kubernetes version. Manual runbooks and cluster recreation are operational toil the channel eliminates.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: You must back up an AKS cluster's application state — namespace resources plus persistent volume data — on a schedule, with restores managed from the Azure portal. What should you use?
options: VM-level backup of the node pools, which captures etcd and volumes
Manual kubectl exports of YAML stored in Blob storage
Azure Backup for AKS, which installs a backup extension and takes scheduled, vault-managed backups of namespaces and persistent volumes
Azure Site Recovery replication of the nodes
explain: Azure Backup for AKS is the native scheduled backup: the backup extension snapshots persistent volumes and namespace resources into a Recovery Services vault with portal-managed restores. Node VM backups do not capture Kubernetes state coherently, YAML exports miss volume data, and Site Recovery replicates VMs — it is not a Kubernetes-aware backup.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: Compliance requires that the AKS API server have no public endpoint — administrators must reach it only from the corporate VNet. Authorized IP ranges are proposed, but they still leave a public FQDN. What should you deploy?
options: A public cluster with authorized IP ranges, which removes the public endpoint
An Azure Firewall in front of the API server
A private endpoint on each node pool
A private AKS cluster, where the API server gets a private IP and a private DNS zone, with no public FQDN
explain: A private cluster provisions the API server with a private endpoint inside your VNet and no public FQDN — the compliance requirement. Authorized IP ranges filter a still-public endpoint. Firewalls and node private endpoints do not change how the API server is exposed.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: In your AKS cluster, a compromised frontend pod starts scanning backend pods. By default, Kubernetes allows all pod-to-pod traffic. What should you implement to restrict traffic between pods?
options: NSG rules on the node subnets, which filter pod-level traffic precisely
Kubernetes NetworkPolicies enforced by Azure Network Policy Manager or Calico, defining which pods may communicate
A private cluster, which encrypts pod traffic
Taints and tolerations on the node pools
explain: NetworkPolicies are the Kubernetes-native pod-traffic firewall, enforced by a policy engine (Azure NPM or Calico) — default-deny policies stop lateral movement like the scanning described. NSGs operate at node/subnet level and cannot express pod identity. Private clusters change API exposure, not pod traffic, and taints control scheduling, not network flow.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: Every month, the security team publishes a hardened Windows Server image, and VM deployments still use a manually sysprepped VHD from six months ago. You need an automated pipeline that customizes, validates, and distributes the image. What should you adopt?
options: Azure VM Image Builder, which automates customization scripts, validation, and distribution of images to an Azure Compute Gallery
A monthly manual sysprep with stricter checklists
Azure Migrate, which builds images from on-premises servers
Custom Script Extensions run at every VM boot
explain: VM Image Builder is the managed image pipeline: define customization/validation steps once, and it produces versioned images distributed to the Compute Gallery. Manual sysprep does not scale or audit well, Azure Migrate assesses and replicates servers rather than authoring golden images, and per-boot scripts slow every deployment instead of baking the image once.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: A fleet of Windows Server VMs needs security patches applied without reboots, because the application cannot tolerate downtime windows. The VMs run Windows Server 2022 Datacenter: Azure Edition. What should you enable?
options: Automatic VM guest patching, which still reboots the VM
Update Manager maintenance windows, which schedule the required reboots
Hotpatch, which applies security updates in memory without rebooting on supported Azure Edition images
An availability set, which eliminates the need for patching
explain: Hotpatch patches the running OS in memory with no reboot, supported on Windows Server 2022 Datacenter: Azure Edition (and 2025). Guest patching and Update Manager both ultimately reboot. Availability sets keep capacity during reboots but do not remove the reboot requirement itself.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: You run WAF in Prevention mode on Application Gateway. Legitimate requests to /api/search are blocked because a query-string argument contains SQL-like keywords, tripping OWASP rule 942100. You cannot change the application, and every other rule must keep blocking real attacks. What should you configure?
options: A WAF exclusion list targeting that specific query-string argument, so the rule skips it while all other rules keep evaluating normally
Switch the entire WAF policy to Detection mode until the application is rewritten
Disable OWASP rule 942100 globally on the WAF policy
Add an NSG allow rule for the search traffic on the backend subnet
explain: Exclusion lists surgically tune false positives: they omit specific request attributes (headers, cookies, query arguments) from evaluation by specific managed rules, leaving the rest of the protection intact. Switching to Detection mode stops all blocking everywhere, disabling the rule globally weakens every path, and NSGs operate at layers 3/4 — they cannot influence WAF rule matches.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: You are reviewing an old ARM template that creates public IPs with the Basic SKU for a new internet-facing workload. The deployment must be supportable for years. What should you change?
options: Nothing; Basic SKU public IPs are the recommended choice for new workloads
Change the SKU to Standard, because the Basic SKU was retired and Standard is the supported, zone-redundant, secure-by-default option
Remove the public IP and use a private IP with internet routing
Keep Basic but add an availability zone parameter
explain: The Basic SKU for public IPs (and load balancers) was retired — new deployments must use Standard, which is zone-redundant and secure by default (closed to inbound internet unless explicitly allowed). Reusing the retired SKU in a template guarantees deployment failure. Private IPs cannot receive internet traffic directly, and Basic never supported zones.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: Your workloads in three availability zones share one NAT gateway for outbound internet. During a zone outage, outbound connectivity must survive. How should the NAT gateway be configured?
options: Deploy one zonal NAT gateway per zone; a single NAT gateway cannot span zones
Make the NAT gateway zone-redundant (no zone selected) so its data plane spans zones and survives a single zone failure
Attach the NAT gateway to a GatewaySubnet for zone resilience
NAT gateways are regional by default and need no configuration
explain: A NAT gateway with no zone specified is zone-redundant, spreading its data plane across zones to survive a zone failure. A zonal NAT gateway pins to one zone and fails with it. GatewaySubnet is for VPN/ExpressRoute gateways, and NAT gateways are not automatically zone-redundant — the zone selection at creation determines it.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: Your Azure Firewall policy has 40 network rules referencing the same 25 corporate public IP ranges. The company adds a new branch office range, and updating all 40 rules is error-prone. What should you use?
options: A second firewall policy merged with the first
NSG rules instead of firewall rules
Individual FQDNs for each branch
An IP group containing the corporate ranges, referenced by the rules — updating the group updates every rule at once
explain: IP groups are reusable collections of IP addresses/ranges that firewall (and NSG) rules reference; one update propagates everywhere. A second policy adds management overhead, NSGs cannot replace firewall FQDN/TLS functionality and duplicate the same maintenance problem, and FQDNs do not represent raw branch ranges.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: Administrators need RDP access to a VM that has no public IP. The VNet routes all outbound traffic through Azure Firewall. What should you configure on the firewall?
options: A DNAT rule translating the firewall's public IP on port 3389 to the VM's private IP on port 3389
A network rule allowing outbound 3389 from the VM
An application rule allowing the RDP FQDN
A second public IP on the VM itself
explain: DNAT rules translate an inbound destination (firewall public IP + port) to an internal private IP + port — the firewall equivalent of port forwarding. Network rules govern outbound flows, application rules filter HTTP/HTTPS FQDNs (not RDP), and adding a public IP to the VM bypasses the firewall design entirely.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: Your network team configures BGP over a site-to-site IPsec tunnel to Azure. Azure assigns APIPA addresses (169.254.x.x) for the BGP peering by default, but the on-premises router policy requires custom peering addresses from your own APIPA allocation. What should you do?
options: BGP peering addresses are fixed by Azure and cannot be changed
Disable BGP and use static routes instead
Configure custom BGP peering addresses using APIPA addresses (169.254.21.x range) on the Azure VPN connection
Use public IPs for BGP peering instead
explain: Azure VPN gateways support custom APIPA addresses for BGP peering on IPsec connections, letting you align with on-premises addressing policy. The addresses must come from the APIPA range — public IPs are not used for this peering. Disabling BGP loses dynamic routing, and the default addresses are changeable, not fixed.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: Three business units each manage their own Azure Firewall policy, but security mandates a common baseline: deny all high-risk FQDNs everywhere, with each unit adding its own rules on top. How should you structure the policies?
options: Copy the baseline rules into each policy manually and audit quarterly
Create a parent (base) firewall policy with the baseline rules and child policies per business unit that inherit from it
Merge all rules into one policy owned by security
Use NSGs for the baseline and firewall policies for the rest
explain: Firewall policy hierarchy supports parent/child inheritance: the base policy holds the mandated baseline, child policies inherit it and add unit-specific rules — one place to update the baseline. Manual copies drift, a single merged policy removes unit autonomy, and NSGs cannot enforce FQDN-based rules.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: You enable WAF on Application Gateway for a legacy application you fear may break under blocking rules. You want to observe which requests would be blocked for two weeks before enforcing anything. Which mode and configuration should you use?
options: Prevention mode, which logs without blocking
Disabled mode with manual log review
Detection mode only, which never detects anything
Detection mode with a managed rule set (e.g., OWASP 3.2), which logs matched requests without blocking them, then switch to Prevention mode
explain: WAF Detection mode evaluates the managed rule sets (OWASP, Microsoft Bot Manager) and logs matches without blocking — the safe tuning phase. Prevention mode blocks matched requests. There is no log-only prevention variant, and detection without a rule set evaluates nothing.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: Your Application Gateway routes to a backend pool, but the backend application requires an X-Forwarded-Host header and a custom correlation header on every request, which clients do not send. Where should you implement this?
options: A rewrite rule set on the Application Gateway that adds/overwrites request headers before forwarding to the backend
An NSG rule on the backend subnet
A second backend pool with the headers hardcoded
WAF exclusion lists, which inject headers
explain: Application Gateway rewrite rules can add, remove, or overwrite request and response headers (and URL paths/query strings) as traffic passes through — the designed header-manipulation point. NSGs filter packets, not headers. A second pool duplicates infrastructure, and WAF exclusions tune rule matching rather than injecting headers.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: Your Application Gateway (Standard_v2) handles steady traffic but spikes 10x during sales events. You want capacity to scale automatically between 2 and 20 instances. What should you configure?
options: Manual instance count set to 20 at all times
Autoscaling, which is supported on the v2 SKUs with configurable minimum and maximum instance counts
A second Application Gateway for the spikes
Upgrade to the v1 SKU, which autoscales natively
explain: The v2 SKUs (Standard_v2, WAF_v2) support autoscaling with min/max bounds — capacity follows demand. Fixed over-provisioning wastes money, a second gateway adds routing complexity, and the v1 SKU is the one WITHOUT autoscaling (fixed instance counts) — the backwards-causality trap.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: An internal HR application behind Application Gateway must never be reachable from the internet — not even the gateway's frontend. All users are on the corporate VNet. How should you deploy the gateway?
options: A public frontend with an NSG blocking all internet sources
A private-only Application Gateway with a private frontend IP and no public IP address
A WAF_v2 SKU, which is private by default
An internal Standard Load Balancer instead of Application Gateway
explain: Application Gateway supports a private-only deployment: frontend on a private IP with no public IP, so the entire data path stays internal. An NSG in front of a public frontend still leaves a public IP exposed. WAF_v2 is not private by default, and a layer-4 load balancer cannot replace the gateway's layer-7 routing the app relies on.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: Your Front Door routes to two origins. Users intermittently hit a degraded origin that returns HTTP 200 with an error page, so Front Door keeps sending traffic to it. How should you make health probes detect this?
options: Increase the probe interval so the origin recovers between probes
Disable health probes and rely on latency-based routing
Add more origins to dilute the traffic
Configure the health probe with a path that returns non-200 when the application is degraded, since Front Door marks origins unhealthy based on probe responses
explain: Front Door judges origin health by probe responses: a probe path backed by a real application health check returns failure codes when degraded, removing the origin from rotation. A 200-with-error-page fools default probes. Longer intervals delay detection, disabling probes removes health awareness, and more origins do not fix broken health signals.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: Your public web app behind Front Door faces credential-stuffing attacks and bot scraping. You want managed bot protection and rate limiting applied at the edge, before traffic reaches your origins. What should you attach?
options: A WAF policy on Front Door with managed rule sets (including bot protection) and rate-limit rules
An NSG on the origin subnet, which filters edge traffic
Azure Firewall in the origin VNet, which inspects Front Door traffic
A second Front Door instance for the attackers
explain: Front Door WAF policies apply managed rule sets (OWASP, Microsoft Default Rule Set with bot protection) and custom rate-limit rules at the edge POPs — before traffic traverses to origins. NSGs and Azure Firewall sit at the origin and cannot shed edge load, and a second Front Door does not filter anything.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: You need global traffic routing that first sends European users to the EU endpoint group and American users to the US group (geographic), and within each group fails over from primary to secondary (priority). How should you structure Traffic Manager?
options: A single profile with performance routing, which handles both requirements
Two profiles with weighted routing added together
Geographic routing at the subnet level only
Nested Traffic Manager profiles: a top-level geographic profile whose endpoints are child profiles using priority routing
explain: Nested profiles combine routing methods: the parent geographic profile steers by user location, and each child priority profile handles failover within its region. A single profile uses one routing method only — performance routing optimizes latency, not geography-then-priority. Weighted routing splits by ratio, and subnet-level routing is a different feature.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: Your company offers a SaaS API hosted in your VNet. Enterprise customers want to consume it over private IP addresses from their own VNets, without VPNs and without your API ever getting a public endpoint. What should you deploy on your side?
options: A private endpoint in each customer's VNet, created by you
A Private Link service backed by your Standard Load Balancer, which customers consume via their own private endpoints after your approval
VNet peering to every customer VNet
A VPN gateway per customer
explain: Private Link service is the provider-side construct: you expose your service (fronted by a Standard LB) and customers create private endpoints in their VNets, subject to your approval workflow. You cannot create endpoints in their VNets. Peering to every customer does not scale and merges address spaces; per-customer VPNs are operational heavy.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: On-premises servers use the corporate DNS forwarders and need to resolve names in Azure private DNS zones (e.g., privatelink.blob.core.windows.net). The ExpressRoute circuit is up. What should you deploy in Azure?
options: A public DNS zone with the private records
Conditional forwarders on the Azure VMs
A DNS private resolver inbound endpoint in the VNet, with on-premises DNS forwarding private-zone queries to it
An Azure Firewall DNS proxy with custom rules
explain: The private DNS resolver's inbound endpoint receives DNS queries from on-premises (via ExpressRoute/VPN) and resolves private DNS zones — the hybrid name-resolution path. Public zones would expose private names, conditional forwarders on VMs do not help on-premises servers, and the firewall DNS proxy serves VNet-internal forwarding, not inbound hybrid queries.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: You currently use NSG flow logs on 50 subnets for traffic analysis. Microsoft guidance says to modernize, and you want flow data at the VNet level with a simpler enablement model. What should you migrate to?
options: VNet flow logs, the successor to NSG flow logs, enabled at VNet, subnet, or NIC scope and feeding Traffic Analytics
Packet capture on every NIC, which replaces flow logs
Connection Monitor, which records the same flow tuples
Diagnostic settings on the virtual network, which capture flow logs natively
explain: VNet flow logs supersede NSG flow logs with broader scope options (VNet/subnet/NIC) and the same Traffic Analytics integration — the documented migration path. Packet capture records payloads rather than flow summaries, Connection Monitor tests connectivity rather than logging flows, and generic diagnostic settings do not emit flow logs.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: An ExpressRoute-connected analytics workload pushes massive east-west traffic between on-premises and Azure VMs. The ExpressRoute gateway is becoming a throughput bottleneck. What feature lets traffic bypass the gateway directly to the VNet?
options: ExpressRoute Global Reach, which connects two circuits together
FastPath, which sends traffic directly to VMs in the VNet, bypassing the gateway data path — requiring a high-performance gateway SKU
Microsoft peering, which is for SaaS traffic only
A second ExpressRoute circuit for load balancing
explain: FastPath improves the data path by bypassing the ExpressRoute gateway for VNet-destined traffic, raising throughput — it requires a high-performance gateway SKU (UltraPerformance/ErGw3AZ) and must be enabled on the peering. Global Reach links circuits, Microsoft peering targets Microsoft SaaS, and a second circuit adds cost without removing the gateway bottleneck.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: Your active-standby VPN gateway takes several minutes to fail over during Azure maintenance, dropping connections. You need both tunnel endpoints active so failover is near-instant. What should you deploy?
options: A policy-based VPN gateway, which is active-active by default
An active-active VPN gateway with two public IPs and two instances, using BGP for fast route convergence
Two separate site-to-site connections on the same gateway
ExpressRoute, which is the only active-active option
explain: Active-active gateways run two instances with two public IPs; both tunnels carry traffic and BGP converges routes quickly on failure — the near-instant failover design. Policy-based gateways are active-standby only. Two connections on one active-standby gateway still fail over slowly, and ExpressRoute is a different (private-circuit) technology, not a VPN mode.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: You are designing a Virtual WAN hub that must inspect all spoke-to-spoke and spoke-to-internet traffic with Azure Firewall, managed centrally. What should you deploy?
options: A standard Virtual WAN hub with user-defined routes on each spoke
A Network Virtual Appliance in each spoke VNet
A secured virtual hub, which integrates Azure Firewall (or a supported NVA) into the hub with routing intent to inspect inter-spoke and internet traffic
An ExpressRoute gateway in every spoke
explain: A secured virtual hub embeds Azure Firewall directly in the Virtual WAN hub, and routing intent steers spoke and branch traffic through it — centralized inspection without per-spoke appliances. Standard hubs route without inspection, per-spoke NVAs multiply cost and management, and spoke gateways address connectivity, not inspection.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: You deploy Azure Monitor Agent with data collection rules across VNets that use Azure Monitor Private Link Scopes. Log ingestion fails, though the agents show healthy. The DCRs reference the workspace directly. What is missing?
options: The agents need public IPs to reach the workspace
Data collection endpoints (DCEs) associated with the DCRs, which provide the private ingestion endpoints the agents use instead of public ones
A second Log Analytics workspace in each VNet
Diagnostic settings on each VM
explain: Data collection endpoints give DCRs private ingestion endpoints; without a DCE, agents under AMPLS cannot reach the ingestion path even though the agent is healthy. Public IPs would defeat the private-link design, extra workspaces do not fix ingestion routing, and diagnostic settings collect platform logs rather than agent data.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: Security wants Windows Security event logs in the workspace but only logon/logoff events (4624/4625), not the full noisy event stream, to control ingestion cost. The VMs use Azure Monitor Agent. Where should you implement this filtering?
options: On each VM with a local event subscription
In the Log Analytics workspace retention settings
With a log search alert that deletes unwanted rows
A transformation in the data collection rule using KQL to filter events before ingestion
explain: DCR transformations apply KQL at ingestion time — filtering rows or dropping columns before data is stored — which cuts ingestion cost at the source. Workspace retention shortens storage life but you still pay ingestion. Alerts do not delete data, and per-VM subscriptions are unmanageable at scale.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: An application writes JSON logs to a custom file path on each VM. You need these logs queryable in Log Analytics alongside platform data, collected via Azure Monitor Agent. What should you create?
options: A custom log collection via a data collection rule targeting the file path; the data lands in a custom table with the _CL suffix
A storage account file share mounted to each VM
An Application Insights availability test against the log file
A workbook that reads the file over SMB
explain: AMA custom logs use a DCR to collect text/JSON files into a custom Log Analytics table, which always carries the _CL suffix. Storage shares store files but do not make them queryable, availability tests check endpoints rather than collecting logs, and workbooks query ingested data — they cannot reach VM-local files.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: Your AKS clusters expose Prometheus metrics endpoints. You want a managed Prometheus-compatible store with PromQL, integrated with Azure Monitor alerts and Grafana, without running your own Prometheus servers. What should you deploy?
options: A self-hosted Prometheus StatefulSet in each cluster
Container insights only, which stores PromQL natively
Azure Monitor managed service for Prometheus, which ingests remote-write metrics and integrates with alert rules and Azure Managed Grafana
Log Analytics custom logs for the metric exposition format
explain: The managed service for Prometheus is the Azure-native PromQL store: clusters remote-write to it, and it plugs into Azure Monitor alerting and Managed Grafana. Self-hosting reintroduces operational burden, Container insights is a logs/metrics solution without PromQL, and stuffing exposition-format metrics into custom log tables loses the Prometheus query model.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: After onboarding AKS to monitoring, developers ask where to find their pods' stdout and stderr logs and container CPU/memory time series. Which solution provides both?
options: VM insights on the node pools, which shows only host metrics
Container insights, which collects container logs (stdout/stderr) and metrics into Log Analytics
Service Map, which shows logs per pod
Azure Advisor, which recommends log queries
explain: Container insights is the AKS monitoring solution: it collects container stdout/stderr logs and performance metrics into the Log Analytics workspace. VM insights covers node hosts, not container logs. Service Map visualizes dependencies rather than storing logs, and Advisor gives recommendations, not telemetry.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: An application broke right after a deployment, and nobody admits to changing anything. You need a timeline of what changed on the resource group — property edits, SKU changes, deployments — over the last 14 days. What should you use?
options: Metrics explorer, which charts configuration changes
The activity log alone, which only shows the last 90 days of control-plane operations without property diffs
Resource Health history
Change Analysis, which tracks resource property changes and presents a timeline of what changed and when
explain: Change Analysis records resource property changes and renders a before/after timeline — built for 'what changed' investigations. Metrics track numbers, not configuration. The activity log shows operations but not property-level diffs over time in a timeline view, and Resource Health tracks platform health, not configuration edits.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: During an outage, you need to see which VMs, processes, and external services a failing application depends on, to find the broken dependency. The VMs run Azure Monitor Agent. What should you open?
options: Service Map (VM insights dependency visualization), which maps VM-to-VM, process, and external connections
A Log Analytics workbook with a static architecture diagram
Network Watcher topology, which shows VNet layout only
The activity log, which lists dependency failures
explain: Service Map discovers and visualizes live dependencies — processes, ports, and connections between VMs and external services — from agent data. Static diagrams go stale, Network Watcher topology shows network layout rather than application dependencies, and the activity log records management operations, not runtime connections.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: Your Application Insights app has no custom alerts, yet you receive a notification that failure rates tripled in the last hour. No one configured a rule for this. What generated it?
options: Azure Advisor, which sends failure notifications
A metric alert created automatically for every app
Smart Detection, which uses machine learning to detect anomalies like failure spikes and notifies automatically
Service Health, which monitors your application code
explain: Smart Detection is Application Insights' built-in anomaly detection: it learns normal patterns and auto-notifies on deviations such as failure or performance anomalies — no rule configuration needed. Advisor gives best-practice recommendations, metric alerts require explicit creation, and Service Health reports Azure platform incidents, not your code's behavior.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: An API endpoint is intermittently slow, and you need code-level timing — which method and line consume the time — captured automatically when latency spikes, in production, without attaching a debugger. What should you enable?
options: Snapshot Debugger, which captures variable state on exceptions
Application Insights Profiler, which captures code-level execution traces triggered by load or on demand
Log streaming, which shows console output
A load test in Azure Load Testing
explain: Profiler records method-level timing traces in production, triggered automatically (e.g., by load) or on demand — pinpointing hot code paths. Snapshot Debugger captures state at exception moments, not performance traces. Log streaming shows console output, and load tests generate traffic rather than diagnosing code.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: A production exception occurs once a day with no reproducible pattern. You need the full call stack plus local variable values at the moment of the exception, without stopping the application or deploying a debug build. What should you use?
options: Profiler, which captures timing but not variable state
Remote debugging attached to the production instance
Crash dumps collected manually after each occurrence
Application Insights Snapshot Debugger, which captures snapshots with local variables on exceptions with minimal overhead
explain: Snapshot Debugger collects a snapshot — call stack plus local variable values — when a configured exception fires in production, without stopping the app. Profiler captures performance traces, not exception state. Remote debugging production risks the service, and manual dumps are reactive toil rather than automatic capture.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: Every Severity 1 alert must trigger a POST to the company's incident-management webhook, which requires Azure AD authentication — not an anonymous URL. Which action group action meets this securely?
options: A secure webhook action using Azure AD authentication, triggered via an alert processing rule filtered to Severity 1
An email action to the webhook URL
An SMS action containing the webhook payload
A Logic App action without authentication
explain: Action groups support webhook actions, and secure webhooks authenticate with Azure AD — the correct credentialed integration. An alert processing rule scoped to Severity 1 adds it without editing rules. Email and SMS cannot POST payloads, and unauthenticated Logic App triggers violate the auth requirement.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: Patching windows every Sunday 2–4 AM generate hundreds of expected alerts that page the on-call team. You want those alerts suppressed during the window without disabling the alert rules. What should you configure?
options: Delete the alert rules every Saturday and recreate them Monday
Disable the action groups permanently
An alert processing rule with a suppression action on a recurring Sunday 2–4 AM schedule
A second set of alert rules with higher thresholds
explain: Alert processing rules support suppression on a schedule — alerts still fire and are recorded, but notifications are silenced during the maintenance window. Deleting/recreating rules loses history and risks gaps, disabling action groups affects all hours, and duplicate rules with higher thresholds create management sprawl.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: Compliance requires every security-related log retained for 7 years in cheap immutable storage, while engineers keep querying the last 90 days in Log Analytics. What should you configure?
options: Extend the workspace retention to 7 years for all tables
Data export (continuous export) of the workspace tables to a storage account, keeping interactive retention at 90 days
A weekly manual export to CSV
Archive the workspace itself after 90 days
explain: Data export continuously streams ingested data to a storage account (and/or event hub) for long-term cheap retention, while the workspace keeps a short interactive retention for queries. Seven-year workspace retention is prohibitively expensive, manual exports are unreliable, and archiving the workspace would end queryability.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: Your workspace ingests 500 GB/day of predictable security logs, and pay-as-you-go ingestion is the largest line item. Commitment tiers were considered but do not fit the procurement model. What alternative reduces ingestion cost for steady high volume?
options: Delete half the data sources
Switch to the Basic Logs plan for all tables
Reduce retention to 30 days, which lowers ingestion cost
A capacity reservation on a dedicated cluster, which commits to daily ingestion volume at a lower effective rate than pay-as-you-go
explain: Capacity reservations (on a dedicated Log Analytics cluster) commit to a daily ingestion volume for a discounted rate versus pay-as-you-go — designed for steady high-volume workloads. Retention affects storage cost, not ingestion. Basic Logs suits rarely-queried tables, not the primary security tables engineers query, and deleting sources destroys visibility.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: A privacy request requires deleting one customer's personal data from a Log Analytics table. Retention policies only age out whole tables, and the data is 60 days old. What is the supported way to remove specific data?
options: Purge the specific data from the table using the purge API, understanding it is irreversible and subject to throttling and audit
Delete the workspace and recreate it
Wait for retention to expire the data
Run a KQL delete query against the table
explain: The purge API is the supported mechanism for targeted data removal (e.g., GDPR erasure) — it is asynchronous, irreversible, throttled, and audit-logged. KQL has no delete capability, waiting for retention does not satisfy an erasure request timeline, and deleting the workspace destroys all tenants' data.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: You manage 300 on-premises servers onboarded to Azure Arc. You need a central view of which servers are missing security patches and the ability to schedule patching across them like Azure VMs. What should you use?
options: Microsoft Defender for Cloud only, which assesses but does not patch
WSUS on each server with manual reporting
Azure Update Manager, which assesses and patches Azure Arc-enabled servers on schedules like native VMs
Azure Automation runbooks written per server
explain: Azure Update Manager natively manages Arc-enabled servers: periodic patch assessment plus scheduled patch installation, mirroring the Azure VM experience. Defender assesses posture but does not orchestrate patching, WSUS is per-server toil without central scheduling, and hand-written runbooks reinvent the managed service.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: An auditor asks for a list of every change made to production resources in the last 30 days — who changed what and when — queryable across subscriptions. The activity log retention in the portal is only 90 days but querying it at scale is painful. What is the most efficient query path?
options: Export activity logs to CSV per subscription
Query the resourcechanges table in Azure Resource Graph, which records resource property changes across subscriptions
Check each resource's activity log blade individually
Use Change Analysis screenshots
explain: The Resource Graph resourcechanges table exposes resource change history queryable with KQL across subscriptions — the at-scale answer. Per-subscription CSV exports and per-resource blades do not scale, and Change Analysis is an interactive troubleshooting view rather than a queryable audit source.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: You want a standard set of Azure Monitor alert rules (e.g., VM CPU, disk space, backup failures) deployed automatically to every new subscription, following Microsoft's recommended baselines. What should you use?
options: Manually create the alerts in each subscription
An ARM template run by hand per subscription
Azure Policy AuditIfNotExists, which only reports missing alerts
Azure Monitor Baseline Alerts (AMBA), which provides policy initiatives and templates deploying recommended alert rules consistently
explain: AMBA (Azure Monitor Baseline Alerts) packages Microsoft's recommended alert baselines as deployable policy initiatives and templates — consistent alerts on every subscription automatically. Manual creation and hand-run templates do not scale or stay consistent, and audit-only policies never deploy the alerts.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: You migrated IIS log collection from the retired Log Analytics agent to Azure Monitor Agent. The IIS logs stopped arriving, though the agent is healthy and the DCR exists. What is the most likely missing piece?
options: The DCR's data source must explicitly include the IIS log files/directories; AMA collects only what the DCR's data sources define, unlike the legacy agent's workspace-level configuration
IIS logs require a private endpoint on the VM
The workspace must be upgraded to the premium tier
IIS logging is unsupported with AMA
explain: AMA is DCR-driven: nothing is collected unless a data source in the DCR defines it — including the IIS log path. The legacy MMA used workspace-level collection configuration, so migrations commonly miss redefining sources. IIS is fully supported with AMA, no private endpoint or premium tier is required for basic collection.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: Five teams each wrote their own KQL to compute 'failed sign-ins per user per hour,' and the logic has drifted between teams. You want one canonical, reusable definition in the workspace that everyone queries by name. What should you create?
options: A saved workbook per team with the query pasted in
An alert rule per team duplicating the logic
A KQL function (stored query) in the workspace defining the logic once, which teams call by name with parameters
A data export of the raw sign-in logs
explain: Stored KQL functions define reusable query logic once — teams call the function by name (optionally with parameters), eliminating drift. Duplicated workbooks and alert rules preserve the divergence, and exporting raw data does not standardize the computation.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: You assign the Virtual Machine Contributor role to a security group. You make a contractor eligible for membership in that group through PIM for Groups, with activation requiring MFA and approval. The contractor activates their group membership. What access does the contractor now have, and for how long?
options: Permanent membership in the group with no time limit
Virtual Machine Contributor assigned directly to the contractor, independent of the group
Membership in the group only for the configured activation duration, inheriting the group's Virtual Machine Contributor role while active
Read access on the group object only; role assignments on groups never flow to members
explain: PIM for Groups governs group membership itself: an eligible user activates and becomes a member only for the configured duration. While active, they inherit any Azure RBAC roles assigned to the group — no direct role assignment is created. Permanent membership would defeat the just-in-time model, and role assignments on groups do flow to members; that is the entire point of assigning roles to groups.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: You configure PIM role settings for the Contributor role. The security team requires that no eligible assignment be standing: every eligible assignment must carry a defined end date. Which role setting enforces this?
options: Allow permanent eligible assignment
Expire eligible assignment after a specified period, with permanent eligible assignments disallowed
Maximum activation duration
Require approval to activate
explain: PIM role settings offer two eligible-assignment duration options: allow permanent eligible assignments, or expire eligible assignments after a specified period. Selecting the expiry option with permanent assignments disallowed forces every eligible assignment to have an end date. Maximum activation duration limits how long each activation session lasts rather than the assignment itself, and approval governs the activation step rather than assignment lifetime.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: You must apply a Conditional Access policy only to corporate-owned Windows devices, excluding personally owned devices even when they are Microsoft Entra joined. The device extension attribute extensionAttribute1 is set to CorpManaged on corporate devices. How should you scope the policy?
options: In the policy conditions, configure Filters for devices with an include rule matching extensionAttribute1 equals CorpManaged
Create a dynamic device group; Conditional Access cannot evaluate device attributes directly
Use the Device platforms condition and select Windows
Require hybrid Microsoft Entra join; only corporate devices are hybrid joined
explain: Filters for devices let a Conditional Access policy target devices by properties such as extension attributes, so the include filter on extensionAttribute1 scopes the policy precisely to corporate devices. The platform condition cannot distinguish ownership, and hybrid join describes a trust type rather than ownership. Dynamic groups can approximate this, but filters are the direct, purpose-built mechanism.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: Two tenants collaborate daily in shared Teams channels. Users complain about switching tenants and re-authenticating. You want members of the partner tenant to access the shared channel with their home credentials, without a guest object in your tenant and without tenant switching. What should you configure?
options: Invite each user as a B2B guest and add them to the team
Create cloud-only member accounts for each partner user
Set up cross-tenant synchronization to provision the partner users into your tenant
Configure B2B direct connect with mutual trust in cross-tenant access settings
explain: B2B direct connect enables shared channels where external users authenticate with their home tenant credentials — no guest object is created in your tenant and no tenant switching is required. Standard B2B collaboration creates guest objects and requires switching. Cross-tenant synchronization provisions B2B collaboration users (still guest-type objects), and duplicate member accounts destroy single-identity auditability.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: Password hash sync stops working after a firewall change and users cannot sign in. You want proactive email alerts if sync errors occur again in the future. What should you use?
options: An Azure Policy audit assignment on the Connect server
Microsoft Entra Connect Health with alert notifications configured for synchronization errors
A Log Analytics workspace with manual event-log collection from the server
Service Health alerts for Microsoft Entra ID
explain: Connect Health monitors the synchronization components and raises alerts on sync errors — the purpose-built monitoring for this scenario. Service Health reports Azure service incidents, not the health of your own sync infrastructure. Manual event-log collection rebuilds what Connect Health already provides, and Azure Policy governs resource compliance rather than monitoring sync operations.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: You run pass-through authentication with a single authentication agent on one server. The security team requires sign-in to survive the loss of any single server. What is the minimum change that meets the requirement?
options: Install additional pass-through authentication agents on separate servers; authentication requests are automatically distributed across the available agents
Enable password hash sync as a backup; pass-through authentication supports only one agent
Deploy a second agent on the same server for redundancy
Switch to federation; pass-through authentication cannot be made highly available
explain: Pass-through authentication supports multiple agents, and the service automatically distributes authentication requests across the healthy ones — so agents on separate servers survive any single server loss. The one-agent limit is a misconception. A second agent on the same server does not survive that server failing, and federation is a different authentication method rather than a high-availability fix for pass-through.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: New hires must register passwordless authentication (FIDO2 keys) on day one, but they have no existing MFA method to satisfy the MFA registration policy. The help desk needs a short-lived credential to bootstrap them. What should the help desk issue?
options: A permanent exclusion from the MFA registration policy
The user's password read over the phone
A Temporary Access Pass with a short lifetime and single use
A PIM activation of the Global Administrator role
explain: A Temporary Access Pass is designed exactly for bootstrapping strong authentication: it is time-limited, can be restricted to one-time use, and satisfies sign-in requirements so the new hire can register FIDO2. Permanent policy exclusions and phone-shared passwords undermine the security baseline, and Global Administrator is wildly excessive for onboarding.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: Your tenant still manages MFA through the legacy per-user MFA controls and password reset through the legacy SSPR policy. Microsoft recommends converging on a single management point for all authentication methods and registration. What should you migrate to?
options: Keep both legacy policies; they are functionally equivalent to the converged model
Conditional Access session controls
Per-user MFA states with number matching enabled
The Authentication methods policy, using its migration control to move settings from the legacy MFA and SSPR policies
explain: The Authentication methods policy is the converged place to manage all authentication methods, and its migration control moves configuration from the legacy multifactor authentication and self-service password reset policies. Keeping the legacy policies preserves the fragmented management Microsoft is retiring. Session controls govern session lifetime, and per-user MFA states are the legacy model being replaced — not the destination.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: You draft a Conditional Access policy that blocks access from non-compliant devices. Before enforcing it, you want to see which real sign-ins it would affect without blocking anyone. What should you do?
options: Enable the policy in enforce mode and monitor help desk tickets
Set the policy to Report-only and review the sign-in logs and Conditional Access insights
Apply the policy to a single user and extrapolate the impact
Use the What If tool; there is no report-only evaluation mode
explain: Report-only mode evaluates the policy against live sign-in traffic and records what would have happened, without enforcing any grant or block — the safe way to measure blast radius. Enforcing first and watching tickets risks a real outage. A single-user test does not represent tenant traffic, and the What If tool simulates one hypothetical sign-in rather than observing real traffic patterns.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: HR requires that when an employee termination date arrives, their account is disabled, their sessions are revoked, and their licenses are removed automatically. Which feature implements this offboarding flow?
options: A Microsoft Entra ID Governance lifecycle workflow: a leaver workflow triggered on the employee leave date
A Conditional Access policy that blocks the user
An access review in which the reviewer denies the user
A PIM eligible assignment that expires
explain: Lifecycle workflows automate joiner, mover, and leaver processes on schedule-based triggers such as the employee leave date, executing tasks like disabling accounts, revoking sessions, and removing licenses. A Conditional Access block stops access but leaves the account enabled and licensed. Access reviews remove group or role membership, not the account itself, and PIM governs role assignments rather than account lifecycle.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: Only 40 percent of users have registered for MFA. You want to nudge the rest with sign-in prompts over 14 days that they can snooze, without blocking anyone who has not registered yet. What should you use?
options: A Conditional Access policy requiring MFA registration, in enforce mode
Per-user MFA set to Enforced for all users
An MFA registration campaign in the Authentication methods policy targeting the unregistered users
A Terms of Use policy requiring MFA setup
explain: A registration campaign nudges targeted users at sign-in with a snoozable prompt over a configurable number of days — encouragement without enforcement. The Conditional Access MFA registration control blocks unregistered users until they register, which is enforcement rather than a nudge. Per-user Enforced forces registration at next sign-in immediately, and Terms of Use presents consent text rather than driving MFA setup.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: A user reports being blocked from SharePoint Online. You need to determine which Conditional Access policies applied to that specific sign-in attempt. What is the fastest investigation path?
options: Reproduce the sign-in yourself from the user's device
Disable policies one by one until access works
Ask the user to try a different browser
Use the Conditional Access What If tool with the user, application, and sign-in conditions to see which policies would apply
explain: The What If tool simulates policy evaluation for a given user, application, and context, showing exactly which policies apply and with what result — the fastest diagnostic. Disabling policies one by one is disruptive and slow, reproducing the sign-in requires the user's device and context, and switching browsers does not diagnose policy evaluation.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: Security policy states that only administrators may invite guest users, but currently any employee can invite guests from Teams. Where do you restrict this?
options: In External Identities external collaboration settings, set the guest invite setting to administrators only
In Conditional Access, create a policy blocking guest invitations
Remove the Teams license from all employees
In PIM, require approval for guest role activation
explain: External collaboration settings control who can invite guests — anyone in the organization, member users, or only users with specific admin roles. Conditional Access governs access to resources, not the invitation action itself. Removing Teams licenses breaks collaboration entirely, and PIM governs role activation rather than guest invitations.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: You assign a regulatory compliance initiative at the management group scope. Two subscriptions need a stricter allowed-locations list than the initiative default, but you do not want to duplicate the initiative. What should you do?
options: Create a second initiative with hardcoded locations
Use initiative parameters at assignment time to override the allowed locations for those assignments
Edit the built-in initiative definition to change the default
Apply a resource lock tagged with the locations
explain: Initiatives expose parameters, and each assignment can supply different parameter values — so the same initiative enforces stricter locations in those two subscriptions without duplication. Built-in initiative definitions cannot be edited. A second initiative duplicates maintenance overhead, and resource locks prevent deletion rather than governing deployment locations.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: Each quarter you must certify that only the right people hold the Global Administrator role. Reviewers should confirm or remove each assignment, and denied assignments must be removed automatically. What should you configure?
options: A Conditional Access policy targeting the admin portals
PIM activation alerts for the role
A Microsoft Entra access review scoped to the Global Administrator role with auto-apply results enabled
An Azure Policy assignment that audits role members
explain: Access reviews can target Microsoft Entra directory roles: reviewers certify each assignment, and with auto-apply enabled, denied assignments are removed automatically at review end. Conditional Access controls access sessions rather than reviewing assignments. PIM alerts notify on activation but do not certify membership, and Azure Policy audits resource compliance rather than adjudicating role membership.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: For the finance application, users must reauthenticate every 8 hours even when their session is otherwise valid. All other applications keep the default session lifetime. How should you scope this requirement?
options: Set the tenant-wide session timeout to 8 hours
Configure the persistent browser session control to Never
Use the legacy per-user MFA trusted IPs list
Create a Conditional Access policy targeting the finance application with a Sign-in frequency session control of 8 hours
explain: The Sign-in frequency session control forces reauthentication on the configured interval, and scoping the policy to the finance application leaves every other app on the default lifetime. A tenant-wide timeout would punish all applications. The persistent browser session control governs the 'stay signed in' experience rather than reauthentication frequency, and the trusted-IPs list is a legacy per-user MFA setting unrelated to session lifetime.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: Users complain they must complete two separate setup flows: one for multifactor authentication and one for password reset. You want a single registration experience that sets up both. What should you enable?
options: Combined security information registration for SSPR and MFA
Two Conditional Access policies, one per registration flow
Per-user MFA in the Enabled state
Self-service password reset without any registration
explain: Combined security information registration merges the MFA and SSPR setup into one flow, so users register their authentication methods once for both purposes. Additional Conditional Access policies do not change the registration user experience. Per-user MFA states control enforcement rather than the registration flow, and SSPR fundamentally requires registered authentication methods to verify identity.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: Tier-1 support must reset passwords and manage licenses for standard users, but must never reset an administrator's password or manage administrative roles. Which role provides this least-privilege access?
options: Global Administrator
Authentication Administrator
User Administrator at tenant scope
Helpdesk Administrator (Password Administrator)
explain: Helpdesk Administrator (also called Password Administrator) resets passwords and manages licenses for non-administrative users only — exactly the scoped requirement. Authentication Administrator is broader: it can require users to re-register MFA and reset passwords for some administrators. User Administrator manages all users including administrators, and Global Administrator is full tenant control.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: Access to the finance system requires the requester's manager to approve first, then the finance data owner to approve, and the granted access must expire after 90 days. Where do you configure this?
options: A security group with two designated owners
PIM with two approvers configured on the role
An entitlement management access package with a multi-stage approval request policy and an access expiration setting
Two Conditional Access policies evaluated in sequence
explain: Access packages support multi-stage approval workflows (sequential approvers) together with time-limited access that expires automatically. A security group with two owners provides no approval workflow or expiration. PIM multi-approver settings apply to role activation rather than resource access requests, and Conditional Access policies evaluate sign-in conditions rather than approving access requests.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: A deployment to a new subscription fails with: the subscription is not registered to use namespace Microsoft.Cdn. The template is valid and RBAC permissions are sufficient. What is the fix?
options: Assign the Contributor role at a higher scope
Move the subscription to a different tenant
Redeploy using incremental mode
Register the Microsoft.Cdn resource provider on the subscription
explain: Each subscription must register the resource providers for the resource types it deploys — an unregistered namespace blocks deployment regardless of RBAC or template validity. Higher-scope RBAC does not substitute for provider registration, the tenant is irrelevant to the error, and deployment mode does not affect provider registration state.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: Compliance requires that all storage traffic use HTTPS and that plain HTTP requests be rejected. Where do you enforce this account-wide?
options: Enable Secure transfer required on the storage account
Create a service SAS that specifies the HTTPS-only protocol
Disable the Allow Blob public access setting
Add a storage firewall rule denying port 80
explain: Secure transfer required rejects HTTP requests at the account level for all services. A SAS protocol restriction applies only to that SAS token, not the account. The public-access setting controls anonymous reads rather than the transport protocol, and the storage firewall filters source networks rather than enforcing HTTPS.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: Auditors require that no container or blob can ever be made anonymously readable, even if an owner misconfigures a container ACL. What is the strongest enforcement?
options: Set every container ACL to private manually
Set Allow Blob public access to Disabled at the storage account level
Remove the Storage Blob Data Contributor role from all users
Enable soft delete on the storage account
explain: Disabling Allow Blob public access at the account level overrides any container or blob ACL, making anonymous access impossible even after a misconfiguration. Manual private ACLs can be changed back at any time. Removing RBAC roles would break legitimate authenticated access, and soft delete provides recovery rather than prevention.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: A script corrupted thousands of blobs 6 hours ago; the corrupted versions are now the current versions. You need the account's block blob data restored to its state from 8 hours ago. What should you use?
options: Undelete each blob individually
Read the data back from the secondary region endpoint
Point-in-time restore for block blobs, rolling the data back to 8 hours ago
Fail over the storage account to the secondary region
explain: Point-in-time restore rolls block blob data back to an earlier point, which addresses corrupted overwrites — the exact scenario soft delete alone cannot fix, since undelete only restores deleted blobs rather than prior versions of overwritten ones. The secondary endpoint holds a replica of the same corrupted state, and failover changes which region is primary rather than rewinding data.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: You need continuous, Azure-managed backup of block blobs with point-in-time recovery, without managing backup policies per container. Which approach fits?
options: Copy blobs to a second account with a scheduled AzCopy job
Rely on RA-GRS replication
Take manual snapshots before each write
Enable operational backup for blobs, which provides managed continuous protection with point-in-time restore
explain: Operational backup for blobs is the Azure-managed continuous data protection for block blobs, giving point-in-time restore without per-container policy management. Scheduled AzCopy copies are do-it-yourself backup with gaps. RA-GRS is replication, not backup — it replicates corruption and deletions too. Manual snapshots before every write do not scale and are not managed recovery.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: A user deletes an entire Azure file share. You need to recover the share within the retention window. Which feature enables this?
options: Soft delete for Azure file shares
Blob versioning
Manually created file share snapshots
Storage account failover
explain: Soft delete for Azure file shares retains deleted shares for the configured retention period so they can be recovered. Blob versioning applies to blobs, not file shares. Snapshots protect files within an existing share but do not recover a deleted share itself. Failover changes the primary region rather than restoring deleted data.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: You provision a Premium file share with 8,000 IOPS. Actual usage averages 500 IOPS, but the bill reflects the full provisioned performance. Why?
options: Billing is miscalculating; open a support ticket
Premium file shares use a provisioned billing model: you pay for the provisioned IOPS and throughput whether or not you use them
You must enable bursting to switch to usage-based billing
The share is deployed in the wrong region
explain: Premium file shares bill on provisioned capacity — the IOPS and throughput you configure — not on consumed performance, so over-provisioning wastes money regardless of actual usage. The fix is to lower the provisioned size to match the workload. Bursting allows temporary performance above baseline rather than changing the billing model, and region does not determine the billing model.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: Linux clients mount an Azure Files NFS 4.1 share. Security requires encryption in transit for the NFS traffic. What should you configure?
options: Enable Secure transfer required only
Switch the clients to SMB instead of NFS
Configure Kerberos authentication with encryption (krb5p) for the NFS 4.1 share
Add a service endpoint to the client subnet
explain: NFS 4.1 on Azure Files supports Kerberos security flavors, and krb5p provides authentication plus encryption of data in transit. Secure transfer required governs REST and SMB traffic rather than NFS encryption. Switching protocols avoids rather than solves the requirement, and a service endpoint changes network routing without encrypting the NFS payload.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: Your security policy requires storage account keys to be rotated every 30 days, but application teams keep missing the rotation window while keys sit hardcoded in configuration files. You want Azure to rotate the keys automatically while applications always retrieve the current key from a central secret store. What should you configure?
options: Calendar reminders emailed to the application teams
A service SAS with a 30-day expiry redistributed every month
Disable key-based access immediately and require every application to be rewritten for managed identity
A Key Vault managed storage account, where Key Vault stores the keys as secrets and regenerates them automatically on the configured schedule
explain: A Key Vault managed storage account puts the key lifecycle under Key Vault control: it stores both account keys as secrets and regenerates them on the schedule you configure, so applications reading the secret from Key Vault always receive the current key. Email reminders do not enforce rotation, and redistributing a monthly SAS is the same manual toil in another form. Disabling key access may be the long-term goal, but it forces an immediate application rewrite rather than solving the rotation problem.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: Microservices need a durable buffer for work items up to 64 KB, with at-least-once delivery and poison-message handling at minimal cost. Ordering guarantees and transactions are not required. Which messaging option fits best?
options: Azure Storage Queues
Azure Service Bus Premium
Event Hubs with consumer groups
Storage blob leases
explain: Storage Queues provide simple, cheap, durable queuing with at-least-once delivery and poison-queue handling — matching every stated requirement. Service Bus Premium adds ordering, sessions, and transactions at a much higher price, which the scenario explicitly does not need. Event Hubs is an event-streaming service rather than a work queue, and blob leases implement distributed locking rather than messaging.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: You need a schemaless key-attribute store for billions of rows at TB scale with partition-key queries, at the lowest possible cost. You do not need global distribution, secondary indexes, or a sub-10ms SLA. Which should you choose?
options: Azure Cosmos DB with the Table API
Azure Table storage
Azure SQL Database
Blob storage with index tags
explain: Azure Table storage is the low-cost massive key-attribute store, billed far below Cosmos DB for this pattern. Cosmos DB with the Table API adds global distribution, SLAs, and secondary indexing at a premium the scenario does not need. SQL Database is relational rather than key-attribute, and blob index tags support blob discovery rather than serving as a queryable table store.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: You built and generalized (sysprep) a reference Windows VM. You need to deploy 50 identical VMs from it repeatedly over the next year, with versioning and cross-region availability. What should you create from the reference VM?
options: A managed disk snapshot
An Azure Backup recovery point
A VM image, stored in Azure Compute Gallery for versioning and replication
A blob copy of the VHD
explain: A generalized VM image is the artifact designed for repeated deployment of identical VMs, and the Compute Gallery adds versioning plus replication to other regions. Snapshots capture a point-in-time disk state for restore rather than templated deployment. Backup recovery points serve restore scenarios, and a raw VHD blob copy is the legacy unmanaged-disk pattern without gallery features.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: You must deploy a monitoring agent and a configuration package to hundreds of existing and new VMs across regions, versioned, without maintaining custom scripts per VM. What should you use?
options: Custom Script Extension with a hardcoded installer URL per region
Copy the installer to each VM with AzCopy
A file share mounted at boot on every VM
VM applications in Azure Compute Gallery, referenced by version in the VM and VMSS models
explain: VM applications package, version, and replicate line-of-business applications in the Compute Gallery so VMs and scale sets install a specific version declaratively. Per-region script URLs and manual AzCopy distribution have no versioning or lifecycle management. A boot-mounted file share distributes files but does not install or version applications.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: The security baseline requires TLS 1.2 as the minimum for all storage data-plane connections. Where do you enforce this?
options: Set Minimum TLS version to 1.2 on the storage account
Enable infrastructure encryption on the account
Require private endpoints for all access
Enable blob versioning
explain: The Minimum TLS version setting on the storage account enforces the TLS floor for data-plane connections. Infrastructure encryption adds a second Microsoft-managed encryption layer at rest rather than controlling transport security. Private endpoints control network routing rather than the TLS version, and blob versioning is a data-protection feature unrelated to transport encryption.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: Your old runbooks read classic Storage Analytics logs ($logs) for request diagnostics, but new requests no longer appear there. What is the current approach?
options: Re-enable Storage Analytics in the portal; it remains fully supported
Classic Storage Analytics logging is retired; use diagnostic settings to send StorageBlobLogs and StorageFileLogs to a Log Analytics workspace or storage account
Enable the blob change feed instead
Use Azure Advisor for request diagnostics
explain: Classic Storage Analytics metrics and logging were retired; diagnostic settings are the replacement for request-level diagnostics on storage services. Re-enabling is not possible. The change feed records data-plane blob changes rather than request diagnostics, and Advisor produces recommendations rather than request logs.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: You need to copy 2 TB of blobs between two storage accounts in different tenants. You hold a SAS for the destination only. Which statement about AzCopy is true?
options: AzCopy cannot copy data across tenants
You must download the data and re-upload it through your workstation
AzCopy performs a server-side asynchronous copy between accounts; authenticate to the source with its own SAS or Entra identity and to the destination with the SAS you hold
Cross-account copies require Azure Data Box
explain: AzCopy copy operations between storage accounts run server-side and asynchronously — data does not flow through your workstation — and each side authenticates independently, so cross-tenant copies work when you hold valid credentials for both sides. A download-then-upload pattern wastes bandwidth and time. Data Box is for offline bulk migration, not account-to-account copies.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: With blob versioning enabled, legal requires that one specific version of a contract blob be protected from deletion or overwrite while other versions remain mutable. What should you apply?
options: A container-level time-based retention policy
Account-level soft delete
An Azure Policy definition denying deletes
A version-level immutability policy (legal hold) on that blob version
explain: Version-level immutability with a legal hold protects a specific blob version as WORM while leaving other versions mutable. A container-level retention policy applies to every blob in scope rather than one version. Soft delete enables recovery rather than preventing deletion, and an Azure Policy deny is governance rather than legal-hold immutability.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: You must rehydrate 500 GB of archived blobs for analysis while keeping the archive copies intact as a fallback. What is the safest method?
options: Copy the blobs to new blobs in the Hot tier, leaving the archive-tier sources untouched
Change the tier of the archive blobs to Hot in place
Move the blobs to the Cool tier first, then to Hot
Enable versioning and then change the tier in place
explain: Rehydrating via copy to new Hot-tier blobs preserves the original archive copies as a fallback; in-place tier changes convert the archive copy, removing the fallback once rehydration completes. Staging through Cool adds unnecessary steps, and versioning does not preserve the archive-tier copy during an in-place tier change.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: Your static website hosted on the $web container needs a custom domain with HTTPS. Storage static websites cannot terminate TLS for a custom domain directly. What is the recommended approach?
options: Upload the TLS certificate into the $web container
Front the storage static website with Azure CDN or Front Door, and configure the custom domain with managed HTTPS there
Enable SFTP on the account to provide TLS
Switch to a Premium block blobs account
explain: A CDN or Front Door endpoint in front of the $web origin provides the custom domain with managed TLS termination — the documented pattern. A certificate placed in $web is served as content rather than used for TLS. SFTP secures file transfers rather than HTTPS hosting, and Premium block blobs do not add custom-domain TLS termination.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: On-premises Windows clients access Azure Files over SMB, and the network team requires encryption in transit. What is true of Azure Files SMB encryption?
options: SMB encryption requires a separate per-client license
Azure Files only supports unencrypted SMB 2.1
SMB 3.x with AES encryption is negotiated when clients connect with SMB 3.0 or later; require SMB 3.x-capable clients
Encryption in transit requires a private endpoint
explain: Azure Files supports SMB 3.x encryption in transit: clients negotiating SMB 3.0 or later get AES-encrypted traffic, so the control is ensuring clients use SMB 3.x. There is no per-client encryption license. Private endpoints change network routing rather than enabling encryption, and unencrypted-only SMB 2.1 is not the Azure Files behavior.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: You over-provisioned a 4 TB Premium SSD data disk, but only 500 GB is used. You want to shrink it to 1 TB to cut cost. What is true?
options: Shrink the disk in the portal; billing adjusts immediately
Use AzCopy to shrink the disk in place
Detaching and reattaching the disk shrinks it automatically
Managed disks cannot be shrunk; create a new smaller disk and migrate the data
explain: Azure managed disks support increasing size only — shrinking is not supported. The supported path is creating a new smaller disk and copying the data over. The portal offers no shrink operation, AzCopy copies blobs rather than resizing disks, and detach/reattach cycles never change provisioned size.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: A stateless batch-processing scale set reimages nodes frequently. You want the fastest possible reimage with no managed-disk cost for the OS disks. Which OS disk option fits, and what is its key limitation?
options: Ephemeral OS disks, stored on the VM's local temp storage; the OS disk is recreated from the image on reprovisioning and cannot be resized
Premium SSD v2 OS disks with bursting enabled
Standard HDD OS disks with read-only host caching
Ultra disks as OS disks in every region
explain: Ephemeral OS disks live on the VM's local temporary storage, so reimaging is fast and there is no separate managed-disk charge — ideal for stateless workloads. The tradeoff is that the OS disk is not persisted independently: it is recreated from the image, and operations like resizing are unsupported. Premium SSD v2 and Ultra disks are regular managed disks with their own costs and constraints.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: A network-intensive VM needs the lowest latency and highest packets-per-second, bypassing the virtual switch in the host. What should you enable on the NIC?
options: IP forwarding
Accelerated networking (SR-IOV)
A public IP address on the NIC
A proximity placement group on the NIC
explain: Accelerated networking uses SR-IOV to give the VM direct access to the physical NIC, bypassing the host virtual switch for lower latency, reduced jitter, and higher throughput.
