q: Most clients of your blob storage are on the public internet outside Azure. You want blob egress to leave the Microsoft network as close to each client as possible to reduce latency. Which routing preference should you select?
options: Microsoft network routing, which keeps traffic on the backbone the longest
A private endpoint for each client region
Internet routing, which egresses traffic near the client for lower latency
ExpressRoute Microsoft peering for all clients
explain: Internet routing exits the Microsoft network close to the client, minimizing latency for internet-distributed users. Microsoft network routing does the opposite: it carries traffic on the backbone as far as possible, which suits clients inside Azure. Per-region private endpoints are impractical for public clients. ExpressRoute requires dedicated circuits per client network.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: You need an object replication policy between a storage account in your tenant and one in a partner’s tenant. Both accounts were created this year, and the portal blocks the cross-tenant policy. What must you set?
options: Enable hierarchical namespace on both accounts
Configure a private endpoint spanning the two tenants
Set the blob access tier to Hot on both accounts
Set AllowCrossTenantReplication to true on both storage accounts
explain: New storage accounts disallow cross-tenant object replication by default; setting AllowCrossTenantReplication to true on both the source and destination permits the policy. Hierarchical namespace is unrelated to replication tenancy. Private endpoints do not bridge tenants for replication policy. Access tier does not gate cross-tenant policies.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: A VDI project wants to keep using unmanaged disks (page blobs) for its golden images but requires zone-redundant storage for them. The design specifies a Premium storage account with ZRS. What is wrong with this design?
options: Premium page blob accounts support only LRS, so zone-redundant unmanaged disks are not possible
Unmanaged disks cannot use premium storage at all
ZRS requires the Archive tier on premium accounts
Page blobs must be converted to block blobs before ZRS can be enabled
explain: Premium page blob accounts — the home of unmanaged disks — support only LRS, so zone redundancy is unattainable for unmanaged disks; the fix is managed disks, which do offer zone-redundant options. Unmanaged disks live on premium page blob accounts, so B is false. The Archive tier is unavailable on premium accounts. No blob-type conversion creates zone redundancy.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: A storage account uses GRS. Compliance now requires zone redundancy in the primary region instead of geo-redundancy, so you want ZRS. The portal does not offer a direct GRS-to-ZRS conversion. What is the supported path?
options: Fail over the account, which converts GRS to ZRS automatically
Convert in two steps: GRS to GZRS (or LRS), then to ZRS
Enable ZRS on the secondary region, which mirrors it back to the primary
Delete and recreate the account as ZRS, because redundancy can never be changed
explain: A direct GRS-to-ZRS conversion is not supported; the documented path goes through an intermediate SKU such as GZRS or LRS first. Failover changes the primary region, not the redundancy type. There is no secondary-side ZRS toggle. Redundancy can be changed on existing accounts within the supported transition paths.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: A data-science team moves 5 TB of training snapshots to the Cold tier for the quarter. After 40 days, new regulations require the data moved back to Hot immediately. Finance flags an extra charge beyond the rehydration fee. Why?
options: The Cold tier requires 180 days minimum; the remaining 140 days were billed
Deleting blobs from the Cold tier is not permitted
The Cold tier has a 90-day minimum retention; moving blobs to another tier after 40 days incurs a prorated early-deletion charge for the remaining 50 days
Cold tier blobs can only be deleted through lifecycle management policies
explain: The Cold tier carries a 90-day minimum retention commitment; early deletion, overwrite, or tier change triggers a prorated charge for the remaining days. The 180-day minimum belongs to the Archive tier. Deletion from Cold is fully permitted. Lifecycle policies are one way to manage data, not the only way to delete it.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: A rendering farm reads large files from a Premium Azure Files share over SMB, but single-client throughput plateaus well below the share’s limit. The clients support SMB 3.1.1. What should you enable on the storage account to raise per-client throughput?
options: NFSv4.1 protocol on the share
The Archive tier for the share
A service endpoint for the client subnet
SMB Multichannel, which uses multiple network connections per SMB session
explain: SMB Multichannel aggregates multiple TCP connections per session, lifting single-client throughput toward the share’s limit. Switching to NFS changes the protocol rather than fixing SMB throughput. The Archive tier applies to blobs and would make data offline. A service endpoint changes network routing, not per-client throughput.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: You replicate VMs from East US to West US with Azure Site Recovery. The source VMs sit in VNet-Prod-East. During a failover, the VMs must land in VNet-Prod-West with the correct subnets so application tiers can communicate. What should you configure in the recovery setup?
options: Network mapping between the source and target virtual networks
VNet peering between East US and West US
A site-to-site VPN between the two regions
An Azure Firewall in each region with identical rules
explain: Network mapping tells Site Recovery which target network and subnets each replicated VM joins at failover, preserving the tier topology. VNet peering connects networks but does not place failed-over VMs into them. A VPN is unnecessary between Azure regions for this. Firewalls filter traffic; they do not assign VMs to networks.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: A branch office has a single Windows file server with 2 TB of shared folders. There are no Azure VMs at the branch. You need offsite backup of the file shares three times a day with file-level restore. What should you deploy?
options: Azure File Sync with cloud tiering
The Microsoft Azure Recovery Services (MARS) agent on the file server, backing up to a Recovery Services vault
An Azure Backup Server (MABS) installation at headquarters
Scheduled AzCopy copies of the shares to blob storage
explain: The MARS agent backs up files, folders, and system state directly from an on-premises server to a Recovery Services vault, up to three times daily, with item-level restore — exactly this scenario. File Sync replicates files rather than versioning backups. MABS is the heavier backup-server product for larger estates. AzCopy copies data with no backup catalog or point-in-time restore.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: Your App Service uses deployment slots. The staging slot connects to a test database through a connection string, while production uses the production database. After each swap, the staging slot keeps pointing at the production database. What should you configure?
options: Enable auto swap on the production slot
Clone the production settings into staging before every swap
Mark the connection string as a deployment slot setting so it stays with its slot during swaps
Store the connection string in Azure Key Vault instead of app settings
explain: Marking an app setting or connection string as a slot setting pins it to that slot, so it does not travel during a swap — the standard fix for per-environment values. Auto swap changes when swaps happen, not what moves. Manually cloning settings before every swap is toil that will be forgotten. Key Vault changes where the secret lives, not swap behavior.

q: Users report intermittent 500 errors from your App Service app. Investigation shows one of the three instances serves errors while the others are healthy, yet traffic keeps reaching the faulty instance. Which feature automatically stops routing to the bad instance?
options: Always On for the web app
Application Insights availability tests
Autoscale rules based on the HTTP error count
The App Service health check with a path that returns 200 when the instance is healthy
explain: The App Service health check pings a configured path on every instance and pulls unhealthy ones out of the load balancer rotation until they recover. Always On only keeps the app loaded; it does not detect unhealthy instances. Availability tests probe from outside and cannot remove an instance. Autoscale adds or removes capacity but does not quarantine a sick instance.

q: A line-of-business web app on App Service must authenticate users with Microsoft Entra ID, but the development team cannot modify the application code. What should you enable?
options: App Service Authentication (Easy Auth) with Microsoft Entra ID as the identity provider
A Conditional Access policy requiring hybrid-joined devices
Client certificate authentication on the app’s TLS binding
IP access restrictions limited to the corporate range
explain: App Service Authentication adds sign-in with providers like Microsoft Entra ID at the platform layer, requiring zero code changes. Conditional Access refines access decisions but does not add authentication to the app itself. Client certificates are a different credential type. IP restrictions control network reachability, not user authentication.

q: The platform team standardized on App Service for hosting, including its custom domains and deployment slots. A new Python API is delivered only as a Docker image in ACR. How can it run on the existing App Service plan?

Web App for Containers, deploying the custom container image from the registry
Azure Container Instances fronted by the App Service
An Azure Functions Premium plan
explain: Web App for Containers runs a custom Docker image on App Service, keeping the plan, domain, and slots. A code deployment expects source code, not a container image. Container Instances is a separate service that cannot sit behind App Service this way. Functions is a different compute model for event-driven code.

q: A VM exhibits strange behavior that the platform team attributes to the underlying host. Restarting the VM from the portal does not help because it stays on the same host. What should you do to move the VM to healthy hardware?
options: Stop and start the VM from inside the guest operating system
Resize the VM to a larger size
Redeploy the VM, which moves it to a new host within the region
Enable accelerated networking on the VM’s network interface
explain: Redeploying moves the VM to a new physical host in the region, which is the remediation for suspected host problems. A portal restart keeps the VM on the same host. An OS-level stop/start likewise stays put. Resizing may or may not change hosts and is not the designed remediation. Accelerated networking affects NIC performance, not host health.

q: A developer is writing an Azure Function that runs when a message arrives on a Service Bus queue and writes the result to Blob storage. They ask which parts are triggers and which are bindings. What is the correct explanation?
options: Both the queue and the blob are triggers because both start the function
The queue is a binding and the blob is the trigger
Triggers and bindings are interchangeable names for the same concept
The Service Bus queue is the trigger that invokes the function; the blob storage connection is an output binding for declarative data access
explain: A function has exactly one trigger — the event that invokes it, here the queue message — while bindings declaratively connect inputs and outputs such as blob storage without boilerplate code. Two triggers cannot exist on one function. Swapping the roles inverts the model. Triggers and bindings are distinct concepts with distinct purposes.

q: An HTTP-triggered function on the Consumption plan processes large uploads and sometimes runs for 8 minutes, but executions are terminated at 5 minutes. The code cannot be split into smaller functions. What is the maximum execution time you can configure, and where?
options: Up to 10 minutes, via the functionTimeout setting in host.json
Unlimited, by setting functionTimeout to -1 on the Consumption plan
60 minutes, which is the Consumption plan default
The timeout cannot be changed; the function must be rewritten
explain: On the Consumption plan the default timeout is 5 minutes and functionTimeout in host.json can raise it to a maximum of 10 minutes. An unbounded timeout (-1) is not honored on Consumption. The default is 5 minutes, not 60. No rewrite is needed when 8 minutes fits within the configurable 10-minute ceiling.

q: A serverless team loves the Consumption plan’s scale-to-zero billing but needs staging slots to validate function code before it serves production traffic. What is the path to deployment slots?
options: Nothing; Consumption plan function apps support deployment slots natively
Move the function app to a Premium plan (or App Service plan / App Service Environment), because slots are not available on Consumption
Enable Always On, which unlocks slots on the Consumption plan
Convert the function’s triggers into bindings to enable slots
explain: Deployment slots for function apps require the Premium plan, an App Service plan, or an App Service Environment — Consumption does not offer them. Always On is a separate keep-warm setting and does not create slots. Triggers versus bindings is a code model choice unrelated to deployment infrastructure.

q: Your container registry currently uses the admin user credentials in Kubernetes deployment pipelines. Security requires removing shared credentials and using Azure RBAC identities instead. What should you do?
options: Rotate the admin user password on a monthly schedule
Enable the admin user on a second registry for redundancy
Disable the admin user and grant the AcrPull role to the workload’s managed identities
Move the container images to a public registry
explain: Disabling the admin user removes the shared credential, and the AcrPull RBAC role gives each workload identity least-privilege pull access. Rotating the password keeps the shared-credential anti-pattern. A second registry duplicates the problem. A public registry abandons access control entirely.

q: CI builds push hundreds of images weekly, and untagged manifests pile up in ACR, driving storage costs higher every month. Which registry feature automatically cleans up untagged manifests past a configured age?
options: A lifecycle management policy on the underlying storage account
Geo-replication of the registry to a cheaper region
Content trust signing on the repositories
A retention policy for untagged manifests on the registry
explain: ACR retention policies automatically purge untagged manifests older than the configured days, which is the built-in cleanup for CI churn. Storage lifecycle policies do not manage registry manifests. Geo-replication copies data rather than deleting it. Content trust signs images; it does not clean up untagged ones.

q: You are designing AKS networking. Pods need direct VNet IP addresses so on-premises firewalls can filter pod traffic by IP, but the VNet address space is limited. Which consideration matters most when choosing the network plugin?
options: Azure CNI assigns VNet IPs to every pod, so you must plan address space for the maximum pod count; kubenet uses overlay IPs and conserves VNet space but hides pod IPs behind node IPs
Kubenet assigns VNet IPs to pods while Azure CNI hides them behind NAT
Both plugins consume identical amounts of VNet address space
Azure CNI is only available for Windows node pools
explain: With Azure CNI each pod consumes a VNet IP, so address planning must cover peak pod counts — the price of per-pod IP visibility. Kubenet conserves VNet space with an overlay network, but pod traffic appears sourced from node IPs. Option B inverts the two plugins. Their address consumption differs fundamentally. Azure CNI works for Linux and Windows pools.

q: The security team forbids storing service principal secrets anywhere in the AKS cluster, but workloads still need Key Vault secrets at runtime. Which approach gives pods Azure identity without persisted credentials?
options: Mount the service principal certificate as a Kubernetes secret
Azure AD Workload Identity with federated credentials, so pods receive Microsoft Entra tokens without any stored secrets
A private endpoint from each pod to the Key Vault
Share the cluster admin kubeconfig with the pods
explain: Workload Identity uses federated credentials so each pod gets short-lived Entra tokens with no secrets stored anywhere in the cluster. Mounting a certificate as a Kubernetes secret keeps the secret anti-pattern. A private endpoint controls network path, not authentication. The admin kubeconfig grants cluster control, not Key Vault access, and sharing it is a security failure.

q: You need to run a web container and a logging sidecar container that must start and stop together, communicate over localhost, and share a volume. You want no orchestrator to manage. Which Azure Container Instances construct fits?
options: Two separate container groups in the same virtual network
An init container followed by the web container
A single container group containing both containers, which share lifecycle, localhost networking, and volumes
Two revisions of one container app
explain: Containers in one container group share a lifecycle, localhost network, and volumes — the sidecar pattern without an orchestrator. Separate groups do not share localhost or lifecycle. An init container runs to completion before app containers start rather than alongside them. Revisions belong to Container Apps, a different service.

q: In Azure Container Instances, a sidecar must finish downloading configuration from Key Vault before the main container starts serving traffic. Which container type enforces this startup ordering?
options: Set both containers to restart Always so they eventually synchronize
Run the download inside the main container’s startup script instead
Deploy the download as a separate container group and poll for completion
Define the download as an init container, which runs to completion before application containers start
explain: Init containers are the designed mechanism for ordered setup: they run to completion before any application container starts. Restart policies govern post-termination behavior, not startup order. Polling a separate container group is fragile and unordered. Stuffing setup into the application startup script conflates concerns and delays readiness signaling.

q: Site Recovery replicates a SQL Server VM. The DBA rejects crash-consistent recovery points for restores, insisting the recovery capture quiesced application state including in-memory data. Which recovery point type meets this, and what produces it?
options: Application-consistent recovery points, produced with VSS writers on Windows to quiesce the application
Crash-consistent recovery points, which automatically flush application memory
Network-consistent recovery points captured by the virtual network gateway
Incremental snapshots, which are always application-consistent
explain: Application-consistent recovery points use VSS writers to quiesce the application so in-memory state is flushed to disk before the snapshot. Crash-consistent points capture only disk state, like pulling the power cord. There is no network-consistent recovery point type. Incremental snapshots are crash-consistent by default.

q: Before a planned datacenter migration, you want to validate that failed-over VMs boot and the application works, without disrupting production or ongoing replication. What should you run?
options: A planned failover during business hours
A test failover into an isolated test network, which leaves production and replication untouched
An unplanned failover followed by an immediate failback
A backup restore of the VMs into the secondary region
explain: A test failover boots replicas in an isolated network purely for validation, with zero impact on production or the replication relationship. A planned failover is a real cutover with downtime. An unplanned failover treats the primary as lost. A backup restore is a different recovery mechanism, not a failover drill.

q: A regional outage takes down East US, where your Recovery Services vault lives. Leadership asks whether VM backups can be restored in the paired region right now. The vault uses default settings. What do you tell them?
options: Yes — backup data is automatically available in the paired region
Yes, after opening the vault firewall to the secondary region
No — cross-region restore is opt-in and was never enabled, so restores are only possible from the primary region
Yes, by converting the vault to a Backup vault during the outage
explain: Cross-region restore is an opt-in vault setting that replicates backup data to the secondary region; without it, restores are only possible from the primary region. There is no automatic secondary-region availability. The vault firewall governs network access, not restore geography. Recovery Services vaults already protect VM backups — no conversion exists or is needed.

q: The CIO will not approve any one- or three-year cloud commitments this fiscal year, but the go-live weekend needs guaranteed M-series capacity in West Europe. Which approach secures the capacity with no term commitment?
options: A Reserved Instance for the M-series VMs
A Spot VM deployment with eviction protection
An availability set with managed disks
An on-demand Capacity Reservation for the VM size in the region, billed at pay-as-you-go rates with no term commitment
explain: On-demand Capacity Reservation guarantees the VMs will be available in the region and size you need, billed at standard pay-as-you-go rates with no term commitment — the exact fit for a go-live weekend. Reserved Instances require a one- or three-year term for their discount. Spot VMs are interruptible and offer no guarantee. Availability sets provide fault isolation, not capacity guarantees.

q: A hub VNet needs a VPN gateway. The engineer creates a subnet called VpnGatewaySubnet and the gateway deployment fails validation. Which subnet naming rule applies to VPN gateways?
options: The gateway subnet must be named exactly GatewaySubnet
VPN gateways require a /24 subnet at minimum
The subnet must be delegated to Microsoft.Network/virtualNetworkGateways
VPN gateways can only be deployed into subnets with an NSG attached
explain: Azure requires the gateway subnet to carry the exact name GatewaySubnet; any other name causes the deployment to fail. The recommended size is /27 or larger, not /24 minimum. Gateway subnets are not delegated to a service. An NSG is not required on the gateway subnet.

q: A site-to-site VPN between Azure and the on-premises firewall shows the connection as Not Connected, and IKE negotiation never completes. Address spaces are correct on both sides. What is the most likely cause?
options: The Azure VNet address space overlaps the on-premises range
The pre-shared key does not match on both sides of the connection
BGP is not enabled on the Azure gateway
The GatewaySubnet is missing a user-defined route
explain: IKE negotiation fails when the pre-shared (shared) key differs between the Azure connection and the on-premises device — the classic cause of a tunnel that never establishes. Overlapping address spaces cause routing problems after establishment, not IKE failure. BGP is optional for route-based VPNs. The gateway subnet must not carry user-defined routes in a standard deployment.

q: An architect designs ExpressRoute Global Reach linking US and German sites, which sit in different geopolitical regions. The design review flags the Standard SKU circuits as a blocker. What is the SKU prerequisite?
options: Enable FastPath on both circuits
Add Microsoft peering to both circuits
Upgrade both circuits to the Premium SKU, which is required for Global Reach across geopolitical regions
Deploy a VPN gateway in each region as a backup path
explain: Global Reach between different geopolitical regions requires the Premium SKU on the circuits; Standard cannot do it. FastPath bypasses the gateway for throughput and latency but does not enable Global Reach. Microsoft peering carries Microsoft 365 and public-service traffic, not site-to-site Global Reach. A VPN backup does not satisfy the Global Reach requirement.

q: A Standard Load Balancer fronts web VMs. When a VM’s application hangs, the load balancer keeps sending traffic to it for several minutes before marking it unhealthy. You want unhealthy VMs detected within about 30 seconds. What should you tune?
options: The NSG rule priorities on the backend subnet
The load balancing distribution mode (hash-based)
The idle timeout on the load balancing rule
The health probe interval and unhealthy threshold so failures are detected faster
explain: Detection speed is governed by the health probe: a shorter interval combined with a lower unhealthy threshold marks a dead backend faster. NSG priorities do not affect probe timing. The distribution mode chooses how connections spread, not how failures are detected. Idle timeout controls how long idle connections persist, not health detection.

q: An application behind a Standard Load Balancer stores session state in each VM’s memory with no shared cache. Users are randomly logged out as requests land on different VMs. What should you configure on the load balancer?
options: Session persistence (source IP affinity) so each client sticks to one backend VM
An inbound NAT rule for each backend VM
A higher idle timeout on the load balancing rule
An additional frontend IP configuration
explain: Session persistence pins a client to the same backend VM, which is the fix for in-memory session state without a shared cache. Inbound NAT rules expose individual VMs for management, they do not steer application traffic. Idle timeout keeps connections open longer but does not pin clients. Another frontend IP adds entry points without affinity.

q: The support team needs SSH access to any of 12 Linux VMs sitting in a Standard Load Balancer backend pool. The VMs have no public IPs, and the load balancer has a single public frontend. How do you expose per-VM SSH?
options: Add a load balancing rule for port 22 targeting the backend pool
Create inbound NAT rules mapping a unique frontend port to port 22 on each VM
Assign the load balancer’s public IP directly to each VM’s network interface
Open port 22 on the backend subnet NSG and nothing else
explain: Inbound NAT rules map a distinct frontend port to port 22 on a specific VM, giving per-VM SSH through one public IP. A load balancing rule would spray SSH sessions across the pool instead of reaching a chosen VM. A public IP cannot be attached to multiple NICs. An NSG rule alone provides no path through the load balancer.

q: A partner’s firewall only allows traffic from an approved list of source IPs. Your VMs sit behind a Standard Load Balancer, and you want their outbound traffic to present allow-listed addresses without adding a NAT gateway. What gives you explicit control of outbound source IPs?
options: A second backend pool dedicated to outbound traffic
An inbound NAT rule for port 443
An outbound rule defining SNAT with specific public IP addresses
A health probe on port 443
explain: Outbound rules let you define exactly which public IPs are used for outbound SNAT, giving the predictable source addresses the partner needs. Backend pools serve inbound load balancing, not outbound identity. Inbound NAT rules handle inbound management access. Health probes monitor backend health; they do not shape outbound traffic.

q: Outbound connections from a NAT gateway-backed workload keep failing under load with SNAT exhaustion. The gateway uses a single public IP. Which scaling option increases the available SNAT ports?
options: A second NAT gateway on the same subnet
An application security group
A user-defined route for 0.0.0.0/0
A public IP prefix (up to /28), giving the NAT gateway up to 16 addresses and far more SNAT ports
explain: Attaching a public IP prefix (up to /28, 16 addresses) multiplies the SNAT port inventory, which is the designed scaling path for SNAT exhaustion. Only one NAT gateway can serve a subnet. An application security group organizes NICs; it adds no ports. A default route changes path selection, not port capacity.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: A developer is convinced that a NIC-level NSG without custom rules blocks traffic that the subnet NSG allows. The subnet NSG permits inbound 443 from the internet. How do the two NSGs interact?
options: Traffic is allowed: subnet and NIC NSGs are both evaluated, and traffic flows when either allows it and neither denies it
Traffic is blocked: the NIC NSG must explicitly allow whatever the subnet NSG allows
The subnet NSG is ignored whenever a NIC NSG exists
Only the NIC NSG applies to inbound traffic
explain: All NSGs in the path are evaluated together: traffic is permitted if any NSG allows it and no NSG denies it, so the subnet allow rule carries the traffic. There is no requirement to duplicate allows on the NIC. Neither NSG is ignored when both exist. Inbound evaluation considers both, not just the NIC.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: An Application Gateway (Standard_v2) deployed in a single availability zone went down with a zonal outage, taking the application offline. How should you redeploy the gateway for zone resilience?
options: Deploy a second gateway in another region and front both with Traffic Manager
Deploy the v2 gateway as zone-redundant across multiple availability zones
Enable autoscaling, which automatically spreads instances across zones
Move the gateway to the Basic SKU
explain: Application Gateway v2 supports zone-redundant deployment, spreading instances across zones so one zone’s failure does not take the gateway down. A second region addresses regional disaster, not zonal resilience. Autoscaling adjusts instance count, not zone placement. The retired Basic SKU has no zone redundancy.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: Marketing launches two brands, each needing its own hostname and backend pool, but infrastructure will only approve a single Application Gateway. How can one gateway serve both hostnames with separate backends?
options: Two separate Application Gateways
Path-based routing with a single listener
Multi-site hosting with host-based listeners for each domain
Two frontend IPs with identical listeners
explain: Multi-site hosting creates listeners keyed on hostnames, routing each domain to its own backend pool from a single gateway. Two gateways are unnecessary cost and complexity. Path-based routing splits on URL paths, not hostnames. Identical listeners on two frontends cannot distinguish the domains.

q: Your Application Gateway terminates TLS for the application. Users who type http:// are served the site insecurely instead of being redirected to https://. What should you add?
options: An NSG rule blocking port 80
A second backend pool dedicated to HTTP traffic
A WAF exclusion for port 80
An HTTP listener with a redirect configuration pointing to the HTTPS listener
explain: A redirect configuration on the HTTP listener sends clients to the HTTPS listener, which is the standard HTTP-to-HTTPS upgrade on Application Gateway. Blocking port 80 breaks those users instead of redirecting them. A second backend pool does not redirect anything. WAF exclusions tune rule matches, not redirects.

q: Your Front Door (Standard SKU) routes to an App Service origin. Security now requires a managed WAF with bot protection at the edge and a private connection from Front Door to the origin. What must you change?
options: Upgrade to Azure Front Door Premium, which adds the managed WAF and Private Link to origin; Standard does not offer them
Enable the WAF on the Standard SKU, where it is included but disabled by default
Place an Application Gateway WAF in front of Front Door
Configure a private endpoint on the Standard SKU origin group
explain: The managed WAF (including bot protection) and Private Link connectivity to origins are Premium-tier capabilities; Standard has neither. There is no dormant WAF to enable on Standard. Putting a gateway in front of Front Door inverts the traffic flow. Private endpoints to origins require the Premium tier.

q: A legacy service must move regions with minimal risk. The plan is to run old and new endpoints in parallel, starting with a small traffic share on the new endpoint and growing it over days. Which Traffic Manager routing method implements the split?
options: Priority routing with West Europe as priority 2
Weighted routing with weights such as 90 and 10
Geographic routing based on user location
Performance routing to the closest endpoint
explain: Weighted routing distributes traffic proportionally to the assigned weights, which is the mechanism for gradual migration. Priority routing is active-passive failover, not proportional. Geographic routing steers by user location. Performance routing steers by latency, not by your chosen ratio.

q: Private endpoints are deployed for several PaaS services, and the team is hand-creating A records in each privatelink DNS zone — a process that already caused an outage from a typo. What automates DNS record creation when a private endpoint is deployed?
options: A public DNS A record pointing at the private IP
Conditional forwarders on the VNet’s custom DNS servers
A private DNS zone group on the private endpoint, which auto-registers the required DNS records
A service endpoint for Microsoft.Storage on the subnet
explain: A private DNS zone group linked to the private endpoint automatically creates the A records mapping the private FQDN to the endpoint IP. A public DNS record for a private IP will not resolve correctly inside the VNet. Conditional forwarders are a manual alternative, but the zone group is the designed automation. A service endpoint does not create DNS records.

q: An Azure Firewall network rule must allow Windows Update traffic from a subnet. Microsoft publishes the update endpoints as a group that changes over time. What should you reference in the rule instead of maintaining IP lists?
options: A static list of Microsoft IP ranges stored in an IP group
An application rule with a wildcard FQDN
A service tag for Windows Update
The WindowsUpdate FQDN tag in the network rule
explain: FQDN tags such as WindowsUpdate are maintained by Microsoft for use in Azure Firewall network rules, tracking the changing endpoint set automatically. A static IP list goes stale. Application rules use explicit FQDNs rather than tags. Service tags are an NSG construct, not a Firewall network-rule one.

q: Your Azure Firewall currently logs traffic to known malicious IP addresses but still allows it through. You want the firewall to deny traffic to those destinations. Which threat intelligence mode should you select?
options: Alert and deny, which blocks traffic to the threat-intelligence matched destinations
Alert only, which silently blocks the traffic
Off, which logs the traffic for later review
Detection mode on the firewall policy
explain: Alert and deny both logs and blocks traffic to malicious IPs and domains flagged by threat intelligence. Alert only logs without blocking — the current behavior described. Off disables the feed entirely. Detection versus prevention modes are Application Gateway WAF concepts, not Firewall threat intelligence modes.

q: Two VNets were peered an hour ago, but VMs on each side still cannot reach the other. The portal shows the peering in the Initiated state. What step was missed?
options: A user-defined route between the two VNets
The matching peering from the second VNet back to the first; the status becomes Connected only when both sides are created
A VPN gateway in each VNet
An NSG rule explicitly allowing peering traffic
explain: VNet peering requires a peering resource on both sides; a single-sided peering stays Initiated and passes no traffic until the remote side is created and the status becomes Connected. No user-defined routes are needed for basic peering. Gateways are only required for gateway transit scenarios. Default NSG rules already allow intra-VNet traffic.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: A network virtual appliance (NVA) in the hub VNet must exchange routes dynamically with the Azure VPN gateway using BGP, instead of relying on static user-defined routes. What should you deploy?
options: A second VPN gateway dedicated to the NVA
ExpressRoute Global Reach between the hub and the branches
Azure Route Server, which peers via BGP with both the NVA and the Azure gateways
A load balancer with HA ports in front of the NVA
explain: Azure Route Server speaks BGP to the NVA and to Azure’s gateways, injecting dynamic routes both ways and replacing static UDR maintenance. A second gateway adds no BGP peering to the NVA. Global Reach links ExpressRoute sites, it does not peer with NVAs. An HA-ports load balancer fronts the NVA for traffic, not for route exchange.

q: Spoke traffic routed to a hub NVA firewall never emerges on the other side — the NVA silently drops it. Routes and NSGs check out. Which NIC setting must be enabled for the appliance to forward transit traffic?
options: Accelerated networking
A public IP address on the NIC
An application security group
IP forwarding on the NIC
explain: A NIC drops packets not addressed to itself unless IP forwarding is enabled, which is mandatory for any NVA that routes or inspects transit traffic. Accelerated networking improves throughput but does not permit forwarding. A public IP is unrelated to transit forwarding. An application security group only organizes NICs for NSG rules.

q: Your team debates whether to alert on a numeric threshold (CPU above 90%) or to run scheduled queries over detailed event records for the same condition. Which guidance distinguishes Azure Monitor metrics from logs?
options: Use metrics for near-real-time numeric threshold alerting and lightweight dashboards; use logs for rich, queryable diagnostics and root-cause analysis
Metrics and logs are interchangeable, so always use logs because they retain data longer
Metrics require a Log Analytics workspace, while logs do not
Logs cannot trigger alerts, so use metrics for all alerting
explain: Metrics are lightweight numeric time series suited to fast threshold alerts and dashboards; logs carry rich structured records suited to deep KQL investigation. They are not interchangeable — each fits different questions. Metrics do not require a workspace; logs do. Log search alerts are a core alert type, so logs absolutely can trigger alerts.

q: You enable diagnostic settings on a Key Vault. You want audit-style control-plane events without the full verbose data-plane log volume. Which log category selection achieves this?
options: Select allLogs, which includes only audit events
Select the Audit category group instead of allLogs, to collect control-plane audit events without full data-plane verbosity
Diagnostic settings cannot separate audit events from data-plane logs
Send the subscription activity log instead of using diagnostic settings
explain: Diagnostic settings offer category groups such as Audit and allLogs; the Audit group collects control-plane audit events without the verbose data-plane streams. allLogs selects everything, the opposite of the goal. Separation is exactly what category groups provide. The activity log covers subscription control-plane events, not the vault’s resource diagnostics.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: A Microsoft announcement retires the VM series your production cluster uses. You need automatic notification of future retirement and deprecation announcements for your subscriptions. Which Service Health alert type covers these?
options: A Resource Health alert for unavailable VMs
A metric alert on VM CPU utilization
A Service Health alert for the Health advisories incident type
An activity log alert for VM delete operations
explain: Service Health advisories carry deprecation and retirement notices, and Service Health alerts can notify on that incident type. Resource Health reports per-VM platform health, not service retirements. A CPU metric alert measures performance. An activity log alert fires on control-plane operations your team performs, not on Microsoft announcements.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: Leadership wants a single shared portal page combining live metric charts, log query results, and resource inventory that the whole operations team can view. What should you build?
options: A KQL function saved in the workspace
An Azure Policy initiative assignment
An Azure Automation runbook
An Azure dashboard with pinned metric charts, log query tiles, and resource tiles, shared with the team
explain: Azure dashboards pin heterogeneous tiles — metric charts, log query results, resource lenses — onto one shareable page. A KQL function is reusable query logic, not a visual page. A Policy initiative governs configuration. A runbook automates tasks; it does not present a dashboard.

q: Two Log Analytics tables share a device ID column. You need one result set combining sign-in failures with device details for the same devices. Which KQL operator merges tables on a shared key?
options: join on the common device ID field, which merges rows from both tables on the key
union, which is the only operator that combines tables
summarize, which merges tables automatically
render, which joins tables for visualization
explain: The join operator merges rows from two tables on a shared key, which is the correlation mechanism here. union stacks result sets vertically rather than correlating them. summarize aggregates rows within tables. render only visualizes results already produced.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: An application writes unstructured text log lines like ‘2026-10-18 ERROR PaymentService timeout after 30s’. You need to extract the severity, component, and message into columns. Which KQL operator should you use?
options: extend with split() only, because parse cannot handle free text
The parse operator with a pattern matching the log format
The join operator against a lookup table
The serialize operator
explain: The parse operator extracts structured fields from free text using a pattern, which is its designed purpose. split() can work for trivial delimiters but parse handles the mixed format cleanly. join correlates tables rather than parsing text. serialize only marks a result set as ordered.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: During a production deployment, you want to watch request rate, failures, and server performance in near real time with about one-second latency to validate the rollout. Which Application Insights feature provides this?
options: The five-minute aggregated metrics explorer
A scheduled log search alert
Live Metrics, which streams telemetry with near-real-time latency during the deployment
The daily continuous export of telemetry
explain: Live Metrics streams key performance indicators with roughly one-second latency, built for watching deployments as they happen. Metrics explorer aggregates over minutes. Log search alerts notify on conditions rather than streaming live data. Continuous export delivers telemetry in bulk for offline analysis.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: A runbook still configures Application Insights SDKs with an instrumentation key. Microsoft ended support for instrumentation key ingestion on March 31, 2025. What should you migrate to?
options: A newly generated instrumentation key, which renews support
The Log Analytics workspace ID as the ingestion identifier
Anonymous ingestion with no identifier
The Application Insights connection string, which identifies the resource and its ingestion endpoint
explain: Connection strings are the supported ingestion configuration: they identify the Application Insights resource and its regional endpoint. Generating a new instrumentation key does not restore support. The workspace ID alone is not an ingestion configuration. Anonymous ingestion is not a supported pattern.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: You are creating a new Application Insights resource. The portal no longer offers a ‘classic’ option and requires a Log Analytics workspace. Why?
options: Classic Application Insights was retired; new resources must be workspace-based, storing telemetry in Log Analytics
Classic mode is still available, but only through the command line
Workspace-based mode is optional and only used with Microsoft Sentinel
Classic resources were simply renamed, not retired
explain: Support for classic Application Insights ended and all new resources are workspace-based, with telemetry stored in the linked Log Analytics workspace for unified querying. There is no CLI back door for classic creation. Workspace-based mode is the standard, not a Sentinel-only option. Classic was retired, not renamed.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: Traffic from a VM to on-premises never arrives. Routing is suspected, and you need to confirm which next hop the platform selects for the destination. Which Network Watcher diagnostic answers this?
options: IP flow verify
Next hop, which evaluates the effective routes and reports where the packet would be sent
Packet capture
Connection troubleshoot
explain: Next hop evaluates the VM’s effective routes for a given destination and reports the hop type and address, directly answering the routing suspicion. IP flow verify tests whether NSGs allow or deny a packet. Packet capture records traffic rather than predicting routing. Connection troubleshoot tests end-to-end connectivity rather than the route decision.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: A site-to-site VPN tunnel is down. You want Network Watcher to check gateway health, IKE statistics, and connection status in one guided troubleshooting run. What should you use?
options: VPN gateway packet capture
The effective routes view on the gateway subnet
Network Watcher VPN troubleshoot, which diagnoses gateway and connection health
A log search alert on the gateway metrics
explain: Network Watcher’s VPN troubleshoot runs guided diagnostics over the gateway and its connections, surfacing health and IKE state. Packet capture records packets rather than diagnosing the tunnel. Effective routes show routing, not tunnel health. A log alert notifies on conditions instead of running diagnostics.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: Several VMs stopped sending custom logs to the workspace. You want to check whether the monitoring agents on those VMs are still communicating with Azure Monitor. Which table should you query?
options: AzureActivity
SigninLogs
Usage
The Heartbeat table, which records agent connectivity per computer
explain: The Heartbeat table logs a record per agent per interval, so missing heartbeats pinpoint agents that stopped communicating. AzureActivity holds subscription control-plane events. SigninLogs hold identity sign-ins. Usage tracks ingestion volume for billing, not agent health.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: A VMSS needs 10 instances on weekdays and 3 instances on weekends, plus metric-based scaling during weekday peaks. How should you configure autoscale?
options: A default profile plus a recurring schedule profile for weekends with different instance limits, combined with metric-based rules
Two separate scale sets, one for weekdays and one for weekends
Manual scaling every Friday and Monday
A single metric rule, because schedule profiles cannot combine with metric rules
explain: Autoscale supports multiple profiles: a default profile with metric rules for weekday peaks and a recurring weekend schedule profile with its own capacity limits. Two scale sets duplicate infrastructure and cost. Manual scaling is toil that will be missed. Schedule profiles and metric rules combine freely.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: You want an alert when a VM’s health changes from Available to Unavailable, but not when it was already Unavailable. Which alert conditions should you use?
options: An activity log alert on VM power operations
A Resource Health alert with conditions on both current resource status and previous resource status
A metric alert on the VM availability percentage
A Service Health alert for the region
explain: Resource Health alerts expose current and previous resource status as conditions, so you can fire only on the Available-to-Unavailable transition. An activity log alert sees operations you perform, not platform health transitions. A metric availability percentage is a different signal. Service Health alerts cover regional incidents, not per-VM transitions.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: A log search alert evaluates every 15 minutes over the last 60 minutes of data. An engineer asks whether an incident from 45 minutes ago will be caught. Which statement is true?
options: It will be missed, because the alert only examines the last 15 minutes
The evaluation frequency must equal the time window for the alert to work
It will be included, because the time window (the lookback) is 60 minutes even though evaluations run every 15 minutes
Log alerts cannot look back further than their evaluation frequency
explain: Frequency is how often the query runs; the time window is how far back each run looks — a 60-minute window catches the 45-minute-old incident on every 15-minute evaluation. The window is independent of the frequency. There is no requirement that the two values match, and windows routinely exceed frequencies.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: A microservices application has 12 services calling each other. During incidents you need a visual topology showing the components, their dependencies, and which links have failing calls. Which Application Insights view provides this?
options: The Service Map from VM insights
A Log Analytics workbook table
The Azure Resource Graph explorer
The Application Map, which renders application components and their dependency health
explain: The Application Map draws the application’s component topology from distributed telemetry, highlighting failing dependencies. Service Map shows VM and process-level dependencies, a different layer. A workbook table lists data without the topology view. Resource Graph explores Azure resource inventory, not application call graphs.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: Compliance requires Log Analytics data encrypted with a customer-managed key from your Key Vault. The workspace ingests 20 GB per day on pay-as-you-go pricing. What must you deploy first?
options: A Log Analytics dedicated cluster on a 100 GB/day commitment tier, because customer-managed keys are configured at the cluster level
A second workspace in the same region
A private endpoint on the Key Vault only
An Azure Policy denying Microsoft-managed keys
explain: Customer-managed keys for Azure Monitor are configured on a Log Analytics dedicated cluster, which requires a 100 GB/day commitment tier — so the workspace must be linked to such a cluster first. A second workspace changes nothing about key configuration. A private endpoint secures vault network access but does not enable CMK. No policy can conjure the cluster prerequisite.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: Security logs must be retained for two years for compliance but are queried rarely. Interactive retention for two years is too expensive. Which table plan fits?
options: The Analytics plan with 730-day interactive retention
The Auxiliary plan, which offers cheap long-term retention with limited query capabilities, typically via search jobs
The Basic plan with the daily cap disabled
Exporting to blob storage and deleting the data from the workspace
explain: The Auxiliary plan is priced for long-term, rarely queried retention and is queried through search jobs rather than interactive KQL. Two years of Analytics-plan interactive retention is the expensive option being avoided. The Basic plan offers cheap short retention (days), not years. Exporting and deleting sacrifices in-platform queryability.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: You need to run an analytical query over 18 months of Auxiliary-plan logs — far too much data for an interactive query timeout. How should you execute it?
options: Increase the workspace daily cap
Run the query in the portal with a longer timeout setting
Use a search job, which runs the query asynchronously with results delivered to a storage account
Export the tables to CSV files first
explain: Search jobs execute long-running queries asynchronously over large data volumes and deliver results to storage, which is the designed path for Auxiliary-plan analytics. The daily cap governs ingestion, not query timeouts. Portal query timeouts cannot be extended arbitrarily. Manual CSV export is toil that search jobs replace.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: Archived security logs from last year must be queried interactively for an audit. The data sits in the workspace’s long-term archive. What must you do before running KQL against it?
options: Query it directly; archived data is queryable just like hot data
Move the workspace to a dedicated cluster
Enable the Basic Logs plan on the table
Restore (rehydrate) the archived data into the hot cache for the needed time range, then query it
explain: Archived data is not directly queryable; you must restore (rehydrate) the relevant time range into the interactive tier before KQL can touch it. Direct queries against the archive return nothing. A dedicated cluster does not change archive queryability. The Basic plan is a separate cheap-retention tier, not an archive restore mechanism.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: Identity Protection flags a user sign-in as medium sign-in risk because it originated from an unfamiliar location. Your sign-in risk policy targets medium and high risk sign-ins. Which grant control is appropriate, and how does this differ from a user risk policy?
options: Require Terms of Use acceptance; user risk policies use the same grant control
Require multifactor authentication for the risky sign-in; a user risk policy instead requires a secure password change to remediate leaked credentials
Block access permanently; sign-in risk can never be remediated
Require a compliant device; user risk policies cannot set grant controls
explain: A sign-in risk policy evaluates each sign-in attempt, so requiring MFA re-verifies the user in the moment. A user risk policy deals with compromised credentials (for example, leaked in a breach), which MFA cannot fix — it requires the user to change their password, remediating the risk. A permanent block is excessive for medium risk, and Terms of Use does not verify identity.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: Attackers are tricking users into entering device codes on phishing pages, then hijacking the authenticated sessions. You must block the device code flow tenant-wide while keeping normal browser and mobile app sign-ins working. Where do you configure this?
options: In Conditional Access, under Conditions > Authentication flows, targeting the device code flow
In the Authentication methods policy, by disabling device code as an MFA method
In Identity Protection, by raising the sign-in risk threshold to High
In the legacy per-user MFA settings, by blocking remembered devices
explain: The Authentication flows condition lets a policy block the device code flow specifically while other flows keep working. Device code flow is an OAuth flow, not an MFA method, so the authentication methods policy cannot block it. Risk thresholds react to risky sign-ins rather than disabling a flow type, and per-user MFA settings are legacy and unrelated to OAuth flows.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: Staff use shared kiosk PCs in branch lobbies to open a web portal federated with Microsoft Entra ID. Users close the browser without signing out, and the next person inherits the previous user session. Which Conditional Access session control fixes this?
options: Sign-in frequency of 8 hours
Require hybrid Microsoft Entra joined device
Require approved client app
Persistent browser session set to Never persist
explain: The persistent browser session control governs whether a session survives the browser being closed; Never persist forces reauthentication on the next launch. Sign-in frequency controls session lifetime, not browser-close behavior. Device join and approved-client-app are grant controls that do not address shared-device session persistence.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: An administrator deletes the production key vault by mistake. Soft delete is enabled with the default retention. On day 10, another administrator tries to permanently purge the vault to clean up. What controls this, and how do you recover?
options: Nothing; any privileged administrator can purge a soft-deleted vault at any time
Soft delete alone blocks purges for the full 90 days
Purge protection, if enabled beforehand, blocks the purge; you then recover the vault any time within the 90-day retention window
Deleted vaults can only be rebuilt manually; recovery is impossible
explain: Purge protection is the opt-in setting that prevents permanent deletion during the 90-day soft-delete retention; without it, a sufficiently privileged user can purge the vault. Recovery uses the recover-deleted-vault operation, not a manual rebuild. Soft delete alone still permits purging, so the protection must be enabled before the incident.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: You restrict a key vault with the firewall set to deny all public networks, reachable only through a private endpoint. Azure Backup then fails to protect VM disk-encryption keys stored in the vault. What is the least-privilege fix?
options: Enable the Allow trusted Microsoft services to bypass this firewall setting on the vault
Disable the vault firewall entirely
Assign the Azure Backup service principal the Owner role on the vault
Move the keys into a storage account
explain: The trusted-services bypass lets first-party Azure services reach the vault while the firewall still blocks everything else. Disabling the firewall removes network protection entirely. Owner is a management-plane role and grants no data-plane access. Keys cannot be stored in a storage account.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: You move a virtual machine from RG-Old to RG-New in the same subscription. Validation fails. RG-Old carries a ReadOnly resource lock; the VM itself has no lock. What is the cause and the fix?
options: ReadOnly locks never affect moves; the VM must be deallocated first
The ReadOnly lock on the source resource group blocks moving resources in or out; remove the lock, perform the move, then reapply it
You need a CanNotDelete lock on RG-New before moving
Move the lock object itself to RG-New and retry
explain: A ReadOnly lock on a resource group prevents moving resources in or out of it (a ReadOnly lock on the resource itself would not block its own move). Remove the group-level lock, perform the move, and reapply it. Deallocation is not required for moves, and lock objects cannot be moved between groups.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: A Visual Studio subscription hosts dev/test VMs. Mid-month the VMs stop and the portal shows the subscription disabled for reaching its spending limit. No quota request was ever made. What happened, and how do you restore service?
options: The subscription was canceled; you must create a new one
The vCPU quota was exceeded; request a quota increase
The spending limit on the dev/test offer was reached, disabling services for the rest of the billing period; remove the spending limit to re-enable them
The budget action group stopped the VMs; raise the budget
explain: Dev/test offer types such as Visual Studio subscriptions carry a spending limit that disables services when reached; removing the limit restores them. Quota exhaustion blocks new deployments but does not stop running VMs. Budgets only notify or trigger action groups — they never disable a subscription.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: Compliance requires quarterly certification where each employee manager confirms their direct reports still need their group memberships. You run one access review covering the Sales and Engineering groups. How do you route each decision to the right manager?
options: Create a separate access review for every employee
Assign the Global Administrator as the sole reviewer for all memberships
Enable auto-apply results and skip reviewer configuration
Set the reviewers to Managers of users so each member manager attests their continued need
explain: The Managers of users reviewer option routes each user access decision to their own manager, so one review covers both groups. A single administrator cannot meaningfully attest for everyone, per-employee reviews are unmanageable, and auto-apply enforces decisions without making them.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: An administrator updates a user department on-premises at 9:05 AM. At 9:10 AM Microsoft Entra ID still shows the old value, breaking a dynamic group rule. The administrator runs Start-ADSyncSyncCycle -PolicyType Delta and the value updates minutes later. What does this demonstrate?
options: Directory synchronization runs on a 30-minute schedule by default; the command forced an early delta cycle
Dynamic groups only re-evaluate once per hour
Attribute changes replicate instantly; the command was unnecessary
Delta syncs cannot carry attribute changes; a full sync is required
explain: Microsoft Entra Connect synchronizes every 30 minutes by default, so directory changes can lag; a manual delta sync forces an immediate cycle. Dynamic groups re-evaluate when the directory changes. A full synchronization is only needed after filtering or schema changes, not for routine attribute edits.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: A subsidiary on Microsoft Entra Cloud Sync wants to (1) synchronize computer objects for Hybrid Join and (2) write cloud-created groups back to on-premises Active Directory. Which statement is true?
options: Both scenarios are supported in Cloud Sync
Computer objects synchronize, but group writeback does not
Neither is supported: Cloud Sync does not synchronize device objects and does not support group writeback — use Connect Sync for these
Group writeback works, but computer objects do not synchronize
explain: Documented Cloud Sync limitations include no device-object synchronization (required for Hybrid Join) and no group writeback, alongside no password or device writeback and object-count limits. Microsoft Entra Connect Sync supports both scenarios, so it remains the right choice here.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: You need a dynamic user group containing all Sales department members except B2B guests. Which membership rule is correct?
options: (user.department -eq 'Sales') — guests are excluded automatically
(user.department -eq 'Sales') and (user.userType -ne 'Guest')
(user.userType -eq 'Member') — department cannot be combined with userType
Dynamic rules cannot reference userType
explain: userType is a valid dynamic-rule property; combining a department equality check with userType not-equal-to Guest expresses exactly the requirement. Guests are not excluded automatically, and rule clauses combine freely with -and.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: Security requires every Contributor role activation to record a support ticket number and to last no more than 4 hours. Where do you enforce both requirements?
options: In the Conditional Access policy protecting the Azure portal
On the role assignment expiration date
In the quarterly access review configuration
In the PIM role settings for Contributor: require ticket information on activation and set the maximum activation duration
explain: PIM role settings govern activation-time requirements (MFA, justification, ticket information, approval) and cap how long each activation lasts. Conditional Access does not control PIM activation fields. The assignment expiration controls how long eligibility lasts, not each activation. Access reviews attest to continued need; they do not constrain activations.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: You build an access package that should grant a SharePoint site and an Azure subscription, but neither resource appears as selectable in the package designer. What must you do first?
options: Add the resources to the entitlement management catalog that will host the access package
Assign the resources directly to the users instead
Create the access package in the partner tenant
Enable B2B direct connect for the resources
explain: Catalogs are the inventory of resources in entitlement management; an access package can only include resources already added to its catalog. Direct assignment bypasses the package model entirely. The package lives in your own tenant, and B2B direct connect is a Teams collaboration feature unrelated to resource selection.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: You create an access package for partner users with a policy allowing Contoso users to request access. Contoso users cannot find or request the package. What is missing?
options: The package must use auto-assignment instead of a request policy
External users are not supported in access packages
Contoso must be onboarded as a connected organization before its users can request access
The partner users need the Global Administrator role in your tenant
explain: Request policies for users outside your directory require their home organization to exist as a connected organization first. Auto-assignment is a different policy type, not a fix for discoverability. External users are a primary access-package scenario, and requestors need no administrative role.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: A GitHub Actions workflow deploys to Azure with a client secret that expires every 6 months; the last expiry broke deployments until someone noticed. What is the durable fix?
options: Store the secret in the repository so the team can see it
Extend the secret lifetime to 24 months
Switch the workflow to a user-assigned managed identity
Configure a federated credential on the app registration trusting the GitHub organization and repository; the workflow exchanges a GitHub OIDC token for an Azure token with no stored secret
explain: Workload identity federation removes secrets entirely — GitHub mints a short-lived OIDC token that Azure trusts via the federated credential. A longer-lived secret only delays the next outage. Managed identities exist on Azure resources, not on GitHub-hosted runners, so they cannot authenticate the workflow.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: You exempt a legacy storage account from a Deny policy blocking public network access. Auditors ask whether the exemption accepts the risk or records compensating controls. Which category distinction answers them, and what helps users who hit the Deny?
options: Exemptions have no categories; create a second policy instead
Use category Waiver when the risk is accepted or Mitigated when compensating controls exist; add a non-compliance message to the policy guiding users to the approved pattern
All exemptions are Waivers; non-compliance messages are not supported
Delete the policy assignment at that scope instead of exempting
explain: Policy exemption categories distinguish Waiver (risk accepted) from Mitigated (controls in place), which is exactly the distinction auditors need. A non-compliance message surfaces guidance when Deny blocks a deployment. Deleting the assignment would remove protection from the whole scope rather than scoping the exception.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: You remove the Production management group. It held three subscriptions and carried several policy assignments. What happens to the subscriptions and those assignments?
options: The subscriptions move under the parent management group; assignments made at the deleted scope are removed
The subscriptions are deleted together with the group
The subscriptions keep the policies as orphaned assignments forever
Deletion is blocked until the subscriptions are moved out first
explain: Deleting a management group reparents its subscriptions to the immediate parent group; policy and RBAC assignments scoped to the deleted group are removed, while assignments inherited from higher scopes remain. Subscriptions themselves are never deleted by this operation, and child subscriptions do not block the delete.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: Finance bought a one-year VM reservation but the project was canceled in month 3, leaving most of the commitment unused. They request a full cancellation and refund. What do you tell them?
options: Full cancellation with a complete refund is always available
Unused reservation hours are refunded automatically at month end
Cancellations are capped at $50,000 in a 12-month rolling window, and you pay for unused reservation capacity regardless — cancel up to the cap and exchange or consume the remainder
Reservations can never be canceled
explain: Microsoft caps reservation cancellations at $50,000 per rolling 12 months and bills unused capacity — a reservation is a use-it-or-lose-it commitment. Exchange to a different region, size, or family is the other lever for repurposing commitment. Neither automatic refunds nor unlimited cancellation exist.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: A budget has a 100%-of-forecast alert wired to an action group that deallocates VMs. Spend crosses 100% at 2 PM, but the runbook fires at 11 PM. The engineer insists the alert is broken. What is the correct explanation?
options: Budget alerts are real-time; the action group must be misconfigured
Forecast alerts only trigger on actual cost, never on forecasted cost
Budgets evaluate every 5 minutes like metric alerts
Budget alerts evaluate against usage data that refreshes periodically — often with hours of delay — so they are not real-time triggers; design automation with that latency in mind
explain: Budget evaluation depends on the cost and usage pipeline, which can lag by up to about a day; late firing is normal, not a malfunction. Forecast alerts are a supported condition distinct from actual-cost alerts. Metric-alert evaluation frequencies do not apply to budgets.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: A Conditional Access policy targets All users and All workload identities with a grant requiring compliant devices. After enabling it, users are fine but an Azure Function managed identity can no longer read Key Vault secrets. What is the cause and the fix?
options: Key Vault requires the policy to target users only
The policy evaluates the function workload identity too, and a service principal cannot satisfy a device-compliance grant — exclude that managed identity from the policy
Managed identities can never be excluded from Conditional Access
Assign the function a device compliance certificate
explain: Workload identities are first-class Conditional Access targets; a device-based grant control is unsatisfiable by a service principal. A targeted exclusion for the workload identity restores the function while keeping user coverage intact. Service principals can be excluded, and device certificates do not apply to them.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: You move 10 TB of logs to the Cool tier on October 1 to cut costs. On October 10 the project is canceled and you delete all the blobs. The bill still shows a full month of Cool storage charges for that data. Why?
options: The Cool tier requires a 90-day minimum retention
Deleted blobs are held in soft delete for 30 days by default
Blobs deleted from the Cool tier before 30 days incur an early-deletion charge for the remaining days
Lifecycle policies are the only way to delete Cool tier blobs
explain: The Cool tier carries a 30-day minimum retention: deleting earlier triggers an early-deletion charge for the days remaining in the 30-day window. The 90-day minimum belongs to the Cold tier, not Cool. Soft delete is a separate opt-in feature, and blobs can be deleted directly at any time.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: An analytics team wants premium block-blob performance for millions of small telemetry files AND hierarchical namespace features (atomic directory renames, POSIX ACLs) in a single storage account. What do you tell them?
options: Create a premium block blobs account and enable hierarchical namespace on it
Store the telemetry in premium page blobs
Use Azure Data Lake Storage Gen1
Use a standard general-purpose v2 account with hierarchical namespace enabled — premium block blob accounts do not support hierarchical namespace
explain: Premium block blob (BlockBlobStorage) accounts do not support hierarchical namespace, so the two features are mutually exclusive in one account. A standard GPv2 account with HNS enabled delivers directory semantics and POSIX ACLs at standard performance. Premium page blobs back disks rather than telemetry lakes, and ADLS Gen1 is retired.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: An analyst holds Storage Blob Data Contributor at the container scope of an ADLS Gen2 account, but has no POSIX ACL entries on /finance. They can still read files under /finance. Why does the missing ACL not block them?
options: ACLs are only evaluated for service principals, not users
Azure RBAC is evaluated first; when a data-plane role assignment authorizes the operation, the POSIX ACLs are not evaluated — an ACL cannot take away what the role grants
Storage Blob Data Contributor automatically writes matching ACL entries
The analyst must also appear in a deny ACL for the access to work
explain: Authorization checks Azure RBAC role assignments before POSIX ACLs: if a data-plane role such as Storage Blob Data Contributor grants the operation, access is allowed and ACLs are never consulted. ACLs apply to users and service principals alike, roles do not create ACL entries, and no deny entry is needed.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: A data pipeline renames a directory containing 50,000 files in ADLS Gen2 from /staging to /production. The operation finishes in seconds with no data copied. A colleague worries the rename duplicated all the data. What do you explain?
options: Directory renames in a hierarchical namespace are atomic metadata operations; no data is copied and no duplication occurs
The rename copied every file and then deleted the originals, but the copy was instant
Renames are only atomic for empty directories
You must use AzCopy copy plus delete for renames of this size
explain: In a hierarchical namespace, renaming a directory is a single atomic metadata operation regardless of how many files it contains — a key advantage over flat blob storage, where a rename is a copy plus delete per blob. No data movement or duplication happens, and AzCopy is unnecessary.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: You must copy 5 TB of blobs from a Hot storage account to another account and land them directly in the Cool tier to save cost. A two-step copy-then-change-tier job doubles the work. How do you do it in one step?
options: Copy the blobs, then run a lifecycle policy to change the tier
Only the Archive tier can be set during a copy
Destination tiers cannot be set during a copy operation
Use AzCopy copy with the --block-blob-tier Cool flag to set the destination tier during the transfer
explain: AzCopy copy accepts --block-blob-tier to set Hot, Cool, Cold, or Archive on the destination blobs as they land, eliminating the second pass. A lifecycle policy would work but adds delay and a second operation. Tier selection at copy time is fully supported.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: You back service SAS tokens with stored access policies so each of 8 partner integrations can be revoked independently on one container. The portal rejects creating the 6th policy. What is the limit, and what is the workaround?
options: There is no limit; the portal has a bug
The limit is 10 policies per storage account
A container supports at most 5 stored access policies; split integrations across containers, or use user delegation SAS where Entra-based access fits
Stored access policies cannot back service SAS tokens
explain: A container can have at most five stored access policies, so eight independent revocation groups need more containers or a different credential type. User delegation SAS tokens are Entra-backed and revocable by revoking delegation keys. Stored access policies are designed specifically to back service SAS tokens.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: A production VM data disk is Standard HDD and throttles the workload. You need Premium SSD. The VM is running. What is required to change the disk type?
options: Stop (deallocate) the VM, change the managed disk SKU, then start the VM
Disk SKU can be changed on a running VM with no impact
Only OS disks require deallocation for SKU changes
SKU changes are impossible; you must create a new disk and copy the data
explain: Changing a managed disk storage type requires the VM to be stopped and deallocated first — this applies to both OS and data disks. There is no live SKU conversion, and no data copy is needed since the conversion happens in place on the same disk.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: An application on an Azure VM writes its working files to the D: drive. After a host maintenance event moves the VM, all working files are gone while the OS and data disks are intact. What happened?
options: The data disks were encrypted during maintenance
The D: drive is the temporary disk backed by local host storage; its contents do not survive host moves, redeploys, or resizes
The VM was deleted and recreated
Azure Backup restored an older snapshot
explain: The temporary disk lives on the physical host local SSD, so its contents are lost whenever the VM moves hosts — maintenance, redeploy, resize, or stop/deallocate. Durable data belongs on OS or data disks. The VM was not deleted and no backup restore occurred.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage
