q: The team debates which offline device to order for a 20 TB NAS-to-Blob migration with no usable WAN: the 100 TB Data Box or Data Box Disk. Which is right-sized, and why?
options: Azure Data Box (100 TB) — the only offline migration option
Azure Data Box Disk — it supports up to 100 TB
AzCopy over a temporary mobile hotspot
Azure Data Box Disk (up to eight 8 TB disks, roughly 40 TB total) fits 20 TB; the full Data Box at 100 TB is oversized for this job
explain: Data Box Disk handles up to about 40 TB across eight 8 TB disks — the right size for 20 TB — while Data Box targets up to 100 TB. Both are offline options, so Data Box is not the only one. AzCopy requires usable WAN bandwidth, which the site lacks.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: An on-premises application connects over ExpressRoute private peering and must read blobs. The storage account exposes a VNet service endpoint that Azure VMs use successfully, but the on-premises app cannot reach storage. Why?
options: Service endpoints extend to on-premises networks over ExpressRoute
ExpressRoute private peering blocks storage traffic
Service endpoints only work for subnets inside Azure VNets; on-premises traffic over ExpressRoute needs a private endpoint, or the public endpoint with firewall rules
The application needs a site-to-site VPN instead
explain: Service endpoints are scoped to Azure VNet subnets and do not extend to on-premises networks, even over ExpressRoute. On-premises clients must use a private endpoint or the storage public endpoint secured with firewall rules. Private peering carries the traffic fine; a VPN would not change the endpoint limitation.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: You configure customer-managed keys for a storage account. The key vault firewall denies public access, and key wrap/unwrap operations start failing. The storage account uses its system-assigned managed identity. What is the fix that keeps the firewall?
options: Enable the Allow trusted Microsoft services to bypass this firewall setting on the vault, or give the vault a private endpoint reachable by the storage service
Disable the key vault firewall
Switch back to Microsoft-managed keys
Assign the storage managed identity the Owner role on the vault
explain: The trusted-services bypass lets first-party Azure services (including Storage) reach the vault while the firewall still blocks everything else; a private endpoint is the stricter alternative. Disabling the firewall or abandoning CMK weakens the design. Owner is a management-plane role and grants no key permissions.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: An operator deletes a container holding 2,000 blobs. The storage account has container soft delete enabled with 14-day retention. What can you recover?
options: Only the empty container; the blobs are permanently lost
The container together with all the blobs it held, restored as a unit within the retention window
The blobs only if blob soft delete was also enabled
Nothing; container deletion is always permanent
explain: Container soft delete restores the deleted container along with its contents as a unit during the retention window. Blob-level soft delete is a separate feature and is not a prerequisite. Without container soft delete, the deletion would indeed be permanent.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: A worker dequeues a queue message that needs 5 minutes of processing, but the message becomes visible again after 30 seconds and gets processed twice. What should the worker do?
options: Decrease the queue dequeue-count threshold
Authenticate with a service SAS instead
Delete the message before processing starts
Periodically update the message to extend its visibility timeout while processing continues
explain: The visibility timeout hides a dequeued message; long-running work must extend it with update-message calls or the message reappears and duplicates processing. Deleting first loses the message if processing fails. Dequeue count drives poison-message handling, not visibility. The credential type is irrelevant.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: A nightly AzCopy sync mirrors on-premises files to Blob storage. Files deleted at the source remain in the destination container forever, confusing the reporting job. What flag fixes this?
options: Sync deletes destination extras by default; the job must be misconfigured
Set --overwrite=false
Set --delete-destination to mirror semantics so files missing at the source are removed from the destination
Replace the job with Azure Data Box
explain: By default AzCopy sync is additive and leaves destination-only files alone; --delete-destination enables true mirroring so deletions propagate. --overwrite controls whether existing files are recopied, not deletions. Data Box is a one-time offline migration, not a nightly sync tool.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: You must copy the logs/2026/ virtual directory — including all of its subdirectories — from one container to another with AzCopy. The command copies only the top-level files. Which flag is missing?
options: --overwrite=true
--recursive to traverse subdirectories
--block-blob-tier Hot
--include-pattern to match everything
explain: AzCopy copies only the top level by default; --recursive traverses the full directory tree. --overwrite controls whether existing destination files are recopied. --block-blob-tier sets the destination tier. --include-pattern filters by name but does not enable recursion.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: You issued a user delegation SAS to a contractor. The contract ends early and you must invalidate the SAS immediately. It is not backed by a stored access policy. What do you do?
options: Revoke the user delegation keys on the storage account, which invalidates every outstanding user delegation SAS
Delete the contractor Entra account
Rotate the storage account access keys
User delegation SAS tokens cannot be revoked
explain: Revoking the user delegation keys invalidates all user delegation SAS tokens at once — blunt, but the supported emergency revocation. Deleting the Entra account does not invalidate already-issued tokens. Rotating account keys has no effect on user delegation SAS, which is keyed off the delegation keys instead.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: You create a private endpoint for a storage account selecting the blob subresource. VMs reach blobs privately, but Azure Files SMB traffic still goes over the public endpoint. Why?
options: Private endpoints automatically cover every subresource
SMB cannot use private endpoints
Each storage subresource (blob, file, dfs, queue, table) needs its own private endpoint and private DNS zone
The private DNS zone for blob is misconfigured
explain: Private endpoints are per subresource: the blob endpoint covers only blob traffic, so file shares need their own endpoint with the privatelink.file.core.windows.net zone. SMB works fine over a private endpoint once the file endpoint exists. The blob DNS zone is unrelated to the file traffic path.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: You enable Azure Disk Encryption on a VM in West Europe using a key vault in North Europe. The extension fails, although the vault has the enabled-for-disk-encryption access policy. What is wrong?
options: The disk-encryption access policy is unnecessary and causes the failure
Azure Disk Encryption requires Premium SSD disks
Encryption works with a vault in any region; just retry the extension
The key vault must be in the same region as the VM; use a vault in West Europe
explain: Azure Disk Encryption requires the key vault to be in the same region as the VM — the enabled-for-disk-encryption access policy is necessary but not sufficient. The disk type is irrelevant to this failure, and retrying will not fix a region mismatch.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: You try to create a VM with a Premium SSD v2 OS disk and the deployment fails validation. A colleague suggests using the v2 disk anyway for better performance. What is true?
options: Premium SSD v2 cannot be used as an OS disk or with Azure Compute Gallery; use Premium SSD v1 or another supported type for the OS disk
Premium SSD v2 works as an OS disk in every region
The failure is caused by the VM size, not the disk type
Premium SSD v2 OS disks require Ultra disk caching
explain: Premium SSD v2 has documented limitations: it cannot back an OS disk and cannot be used with Azure Compute Gallery images. Use Premium SSD v1 (or Standard SSD) for OS disks and reserve v2 for data disks. The VM size is unrelated to this validation failure.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: For a quarterly regulator requirement, 30 TB of blob data must leave Azure on physical media — the site cannot download it over the WAN. Which Data Box order type does this?
options: Download it with AzCopy over the internet
Place an Azure Data Box export order: Microsoft copies the blobs onto the device and ships it to you
Data Box only supports imports into Azure
Enable read-access geo-redundancy and read from the secondary
explain: Data Box supports export orders that copy data out of Azure onto the device for shipment — the designed path for offline egress. Data Box is not import-only. AzCopy needs the WAN capacity the site lacks, and geo-redundant reads still require network transfer.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: Your VMSS uses a rolling upgrade policy. During OS image upgrades, serving capacity temporarily drops because instances are taken offline to upgrade. You want upgrades to keep full capacity throughout. What should you configure?
options: Enable maxSurge on the rolling upgrade policy so replacement instances are created before old ones are removed
Switch the upgrade policy to manual
Increase the number of fault domains
Enable overprovisioning on the scale set
explain: maxSurge provisions extra (surge) instances during a rolling upgrade, so capacity never dips while instances are replaced. A manual policy still takes instances offline without adding capacity. Fault domains protect against hardware failure, not upgrade capacity. Overprovisioning affects scale-out provisioning speed, not upgrades.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: Two running VMs must join a new proximity placement group for lower latency, but the platform rejects adding them. How do you get them into the PPG?
options: Proximity placement groups only support virtual machine scale sets
Restart the VMs so the platform re-evaluates placement
Delete and recreate the VMs inside the PPG; an existing VM cannot be added to a PPG after creation
Move the PPG into the VMs resource group
explain: PPG membership is fixed at VM creation time — there is no supported operation to add an existing VM to a group, so you must recreate the VMs inside it. Restarting does not change physical placement. PPGs support both single VMs and scale sets, and the group location is unrelated.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: You must deploy 12 identical VMs (VM-01 through VM-12) from one ARM template without duplicating the resource block 12 times. Which construct does this?
options: A separate nested template for each VM
The reference() function on a loop variable
A deployment script that calls the REST API 12 times
A copy loop on the VM resource using copyIndex() to generate the unique names
explain: A copy loop iterates the resource deployment and copyIndex() produces the per-instance names — the standard way to stamp out N identical resources. Nested templates add indirection without solving repetition. reference() reads runtime state of existing resources, and a deployment script is imperative toil the declarative loop replaces.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: Compliance requires a VM to move from Availability Zone 1 to Availability Zone 2. There is no change-zone action in the portal. How do you relocate it?
options: Change the zone on the VM configuration blade
There is no in-place zone change; recreate the VM in the target zone, for example from a snapshot of its disks
Open a support ticket to change the zone
Deallocate the VM and the zone updates automatically
explain: The availability zone is fixed at VM creation and cannot be changed in place — the supported path is to recreate the VM in the target zone from its disks or snapshots. There is no portal toggle and no support-driven zone move. Deallocation preserves the original zone.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: Developers leave 40 dev/test VMs running overnight, wasting budget. You want each VM to shut down automatically at 7 PM daily without building a central runbook. What should you enable?
options: Auto-shutdown on each VM with a 7 PM schedule
An autoscale rule on the VMs
An Azure Policy that denies compute after hours
Convert the VMs to Spot instances
explain: The built-in auto-shutdown feature schedules a daily shutdown per VM with optional notifications — no automation account needed. Autoscale applies to scale sets, not single VMs. Policy can deny deployments but cannot schedule shutdowns, and Spot eviction is unpredictable, not scheduled.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: A stateful application on Azure VMs must drain connections gracefully before Azure host maintenance reboots the host. How can the application learn that a maintenance event is coming?
options: Poll the Azure status page for maintenance announcements
Enable boot diagnostics on the VM
Read the VM activity log
Query the Instance Metadata Service scheduled events endpoint (169.254.169.254), which signals upcoming freeze, reboot, and redeploy events
explain: IMDS scheduled events give the guest advance notice of platform maintenance so applications can drain gracefully. The status page reports regional incidents, not per-host maintenance. Boot diagnostics capture console output, and the activity log records control-plane operations after the fact.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: One VMSS instance runs a singleton coordination service that must never be removed by scale-in, while the other instances are disposable. How do you shield that specific instance?
options: Raise the scale-in CPU threshold
Enable instance protection on instance 3 against scale-in (and optionally scale-set actions)
Set the upgrade policy to manual
Move instance 3 to a different scale set
explain: Per-instance protection shields specific instances from scale-in and scale-set operations — the precise tool for preserving warm state. Threshold changes affect all instances equally and do not target one. The upgrade policy governs updates, not scale-in, and instances cannot be moved between scale sets.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: A Custom Script Extension downloads an installer using a SAS token. The token currently sits in plain text in the template parameters file. How should you pass the secret to the extension?
options: Leave it in settings; the extension encrypts settings automatically
Embed the SAS token in the script file stored in blob storage
Pass the secret through the extension protectedSettings, which are encrypted in transit and at rest
Make the container public so no SAS token is needed
explain: Extension protectedSettings are encrypted — the designed channel for secrets. Plain settings are visible in deployment history. Embedding the token in the script merely moves the exposure. A public container removes authentication entirely.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: Ten apps share one Premium App Service plan. One app needs 10 instances at peak; the others are fine with 2. Scaling the whole plan to 10 wastes capacity. What should you configure?
options: Per-app scaling, so the busy app scales to 10 instances independently within the shared plan
A second Premium plan hosting all ten apps
Autoscale rules on the plan only
Deployment slots for the busy app
explain: Per-app scaling lets an individual app scale independently while sharing the plan, so only the busy app consumes the extra instances. Plan-level autoscale scales every app together. A second plan for all apps doubles cost, and slots are for staging, not scaling.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: A web app must survive an availability-zone outage in the region. It currently runs on a Standard App Service plan. What is required?
options: Enable zone redundancy in place on the Standard plan
Deploy a second Standard plan in another zone and load-balance between them
Zone redundancy requires an Isolated (ASE) plan
Redeploy onto a new Premium v2/v3+ plan with zone redundancy enabled and enough instances; it cannot be switched on for the existing Standard plan
explain: Zone redundancy requires Premium v2 through v4 plans, is set at plan creation, and needs a minimum instance count — Standard plans do not support it and existing plans cannot be converted in place. Two Standard plans do not make one app zone-redundant, and an Isolated plan is a heavier solution than required.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: The security team centrally manages TLS certificates in Key Vault with auto-renewal. Your App Service must use one of those certificates without manual PFX uploads. What should you configure?
options: Upload the PFX to the app and set a calendar reminder to renew it
A Key Vault certificate reference in the app TLS/SSL settings, with the app managed identity granted certificate Get permission on the vault
Store the certificate in a storage account container
Use the free App Service managed certificate and point it at the vault
explain: A Key Vault reference lets App Service pull the certificate through the app managed identity, so renewals in the vault flow to the app automatically. Manual PFX upload requires manual renewal. Certificates cannot be served from storage accounts, and the free managed certificate does not integrate with Key Vault.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: An App Service web app needs a background task that continuously processes queue messages, deployed and scaled together with the app, without provisioning Functions or Container Apps. What should you use?
options: A continuous WebJob packaged and deployed with the web app
A deployment slot running the task
Always On by itself
A second App Service plan for the task
explain: WebJobs run background work inside the App Service context — continuous or triggered — and scale with the app. Deployment slots are for staging code versions. Always On only keeps the app loaded; it does not execute jobs. A second plan is unnecessary cost and complexity.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: A container in Azure Container Instances is repeatedly terminated with an out-of-memory error under load. The image itself is healthy. What should you adjust?
options: Set the container group restart policy to Never
Add a second container to the group
Raise the memory request/limit for the container in the container group definition
Move the workload to a smaller VM size
explain: ACI containers receive the CPU and memory in their resource requests; repeated OOMKills mean the memory limit is too low. Restart Never suits run-to-completion jobs, not memory pressure. More containers do not raise per-container memory, and serverless ACI has no VM sizes.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: You design a Durable Functions workflow: an orchestrator fans out 20 parallel checks and aggregates the results, while a separate long-lived entity tracks approval state across days. Which function types do you implement?
options: Three orchestrator functions chained together
HTTP-triggered functions only
A single activity function that does everything
An orchestrator function for workflow control, activity functions for the parallel checks, and an entity function for the approval state
explain: Durable Functions separates concerns: orchestrators define deterministic workflow control, activities perform the units of work, and entities hold long-lived state. Chaining orchestrators for parallel work breaks the model, and stuffing everything into one activity loses fan-out, replay, and state benefits.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: A function app needs a database connection string from Key Vault, rotated monthly by the security team, without redeploying the app or writing Key Vault SDK code. What should you configure?
options: Hardcode the secret in app settings and redeploy monthly
Embed the secret in the function code
A Key Vault reference (@Microsoft.KeyVault(SecretUri=...)) in app settings, with the app system-assigned managed identity granted Secrets User on the vault
A storage SAS token in app settings
explain: Key Vault references resolve at runtime through the managed identity, so monthly rotations are transparent — no redeploy, no SDK code. Hardcoding plus monthly redeploys is pure toil, embedding secrets in code is a security failure, and a SAS token is a storage credential, not a Key Vault mechanism.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: Your Container Apps microservices need private-only networking: no public ingress, plus outbound access to a database in the corporate VNet. Which environment configuration delivers this?
options: A Container Apps environment with external ingress
A Container Apps environment with a custom VNet and internal ingress
Public ingress locked down with IP restrictions
Azure Container Instances with a public IP
explain: A custom VNet with internal ingress keeps all traffic private — no public endpoint exists to attack — while VNet integration reaches the database. External ingress is public by definition. IP restrictions still expose a public endpoint, and ACI with a public IP misses the requirement entirely.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: A container in Azure Container Instances needs a database password at runtime. Passing it as a plain environment variable exposes it in the container group definition. What should you use?
options: Bake the password into the container image
Pass the password as a command-line argument
Store the password in a mounted config file share
A secure environment variable so the value is hidden from the API and portal (ideally sourced from Key Vault at deployment time)
explain: Secure environment variables keep values out of the plain-text container group definition returned by the API and portal. Baking secrets into images is worse — anyone with the image has the secret. Command-line arguments are equally visible, and ACI has no native config-map concept.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: A container group runs a file-processing job that must survive container restarts and share files between two containers in the group. ACI local storage is ephemeral. What should you mount?
options: An Azure Files share as a volume, accessible to both containers in the group
A managed disk attached to the container group
Blob storage mounted over NFS
The underlying host node disk
explain: Azure Files SMB volumes persist independently of container restarts and can be shared between containers in a group. ACI does not support managed disk attachment, and there is no host disk available in the serverless container model.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: Security requires container image pulls to stay on the private network. Your AKS cluster is in a VNet with no internet egress, and image pulls from your Azure Container Registry fail. What should you configure?
options: Enable the ACR admin user
A private endpoint for the registry in the VNet with private DNS, so pulls stay on the Microsoft backbone
Make the registry publicly accessible
Pull the images from Docker Hub instead
explain: A private endpoint with the privatelink.azurecr.io zone keeps registry traffic on the private backbone — the network fix the scenario needs. The admin user controls authentication, not network reachability. Making the registry public violates the requirement, and Docker Hub does not host your private images.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: Your app image is built FROM a Microsoft .NET base image. When Microsoft patches the base image for a CVE, your app image stays vulnerable until someone manually rebuilds it. How do you automate the rebuild?
options: A scheduled task that rebuilds the image every night
Wait for Dependabot alerts and rebuild manually
An ACR Task with a base image trigger that rebuilds your image automatically whenever the base image updates
Rebuild manually after each Patch Tuesday
explain: A base image trigger watches the upstream image and rebuilds your image on every base update — closing the CVE window automatically. Nightly rebuilds waste build minutes when nothing changed, and manual rebuilds depend on someone noticing. Dependabot alerts do not rebuild container images.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: Remote developers need point-to-site VPN access. You want them to authenticate with their Microsoft Entra credentials and MFA instead of distributing client certificates to every laptop. Which P2S configuration supports this?
options: IKEv2 with machine certificates only
SSTP with RADIUS authentication only
A policy-based (static routing) VPN gateway
OpenVPN protocol with Microsoft Entra authentication on a route-based gateway
explain: OpenVPN with Microsoft Entra authentication lets P2S clients sign in with user credentials and MFA — no client certificates to distribute. IKEv2 P2S relies on certificates. Policy-based gateways do not support point-to-site at all.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: You must connect two VNets in different Azure regions with encrypted traffic over the Microsoft backbone. Policy forbids VNet peering for these VNets. What should you deploy?
options: A site-to-site VPN from each VNet to on-premises
VNet-to-VNet VPN connections using a VPN gateway in each VNet
ExpressRoute with private peering
Public IPs on the VMs with IPsec between them
explain: VNet-to-VNet connections use a VPN gateway in each VNet to build an encrypted tunnel over the backbone without peering. Site-to-site is for on-premises connectivity. ExpressRoute is heavier than needed for VNet-to-VNet, and manual VM-level IPsec is unsupported toil.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: You resize a VPN gateway from VpnGw1 to VpnGw3 for higher throughput. During the operation, both site-to-site tunnels drop for an extended period. Was this expected?
options: Yes — resizing a gateway SKU tears down and recreates the gateway, dropping all connections; plan a maintenance window
No — gateway SKU changes are hitless
Only point-to-site connections drop; site-to-site stays up
Tunnels drop only when BGP is enabled
explain: A gateway resize redeploys the gateway instances, so every S2S and P2S connection drops during the operation — it must be scheduled. There is no hitless SKU change, and BGP has nothing to do with the outage.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: You enable ExpressRoute Microsoft peering, but you only want Microsoft 365 prefixes advertised to your network — not Dynamics 365 or Azure public IPs. How do you limit the advertised prefixes?
options: A user-defined route on the gateway subnet
An NSG on the peering
A route filter selecting the Microsoft 365 BGP community values, applied to the Microsoft peering
Disable private peering
explain: Route filters choose which BGP community prefixes (Microsoft 365, Dynamics 365, etc.) are advertised over Microsoft peering. UDRs control traffic forwarding, not BGP advertisements. NSGs filter packets, not routes, and private peering is a separate peering for RFC1918 traffic.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: A workload needs more than 10 Gbps of private connectivity to Azure with MACsec encryption on the physical links. Standard ExpressRoute circuits cannot meet either requirement. What should you order?
options: Two standard circuits with load balancing
ExpressRoute Direct with 100 Gbps ports and MACsec support
A VpnGw5 gateway pair
Azure Front Door
explain: ExpressRoute Direct provides 10/100 Gbps router ports with MACsec on the physical links — the only option meeting both requirements. Bonding standard circuits does not add MACsec or 100 Gbps ports. VPN gateways top out far below this throughput, and Front Door is a public ingress service.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: VMs in a VNet must resolve each other by hostname without anyone managing A records manually. You link a private DNS zone to the VNet. What must the link enable for automatic record lifecycle?
options: Manual A records for every VM
A public DNS zone linked to the VNet
Conditional forwarding to on-premises DNS
Auto-registration on the virtual network link, so VM DNS records are created and cleaned up automatically
explain: Auto-registration on the VNet link manages A records with the VM lifecycle — created on deployment, removed on deletion. Manual records are toil and go stale. Public zones do not resolve private IPs, and conditional forwarding is for hybrid name resolution, not VM records.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: Your public DNS zone contoso.com is hosted at your registrar. You want Azure DNS to authoritatively serve the branch.contoso.com subdomain. What must you configure?
options: An Azure private DNS zone for the subdomain
A CNAME record pointing at the subdomain
An Azure DNS zone for branch.contoso.com plus NS records delegating it in the parent contoso.com zone
An A record for every host in the subdomain
explain: Standard DNS delegation: create the child zone in Azure DNS and add NS records for it in the parent zone so resolvers are referred to Azure. A private zone is not publicly resolvable. A CNAME cannot delegate a zone, and per-host A records in the parent defeat the purpose of delegation.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: You run an active-passive pair of regional web endpoints. All traffic must go to the primary; the secondary serves only if the primary fails health checks. Which Traffic Manager routing method does this?
options: Priority (failover) routing
Weighted routing
Geographic routing
Multivalue routing
explain: Priority routing sends all traffic to the highest-priority healthy endpoint and fails over in order — the active-passive pattern. Weighted splits traffic by ratio. Geographic routes users by location. Multivalue returns multiple healthy endpoints at once.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: Your Front Door-fronted site serves large product images that rarely change. Every request currently reaches the origin, adding latency and egress cost. What should you enable?
options: WAF rate limiting
Caching on the Front Door route so edge points of presence serve the images
A Private Link connection to the origin
Session affinity on the origin group
explain: Edge caching lets Front Door POPs serve static content directly, cutting origin load, latency, and egress. WAF rate limiting protects against abuse but does not cache. Private Link secures origin connectivity, and session affinity is for stateful apps — neither reduces origin hits.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: You add shop.contoso.com as a custom domain on Front Door. Browsers warn about the certificate. What must you configure for trusted HTTPS?
options: Upload the certificate to each origin server
Serve the site on the default azurefd.net hostname instead
Front Door cannot serve HTTPS on custom domains
Enable the Front Door-managed certificate (or bring your own) for the custom domain so Front Door terminates TLS with a trusted certificate
explain: Front Door can provision and auto-renew a managed certificate for your custom domain (validated via DNS), or you can bring your own from Key Vault. Origin certificates do not cover the edge hostname clients connect to. HTTPS on custom domains is fully supported.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: A compliance scan flags your Application Gateway for accepting TLS 1.0 connections. Where do you enforce a minimum TLS version and cipher suites?
options: On the backend VMs behind the gateway
In the WAF exclusion list
In the gateway SSL policy (predefined or custom), applied where the gateway terminates TLS
In the health probe settings
explain: The SSL policy controls the frontend TLS handshake — minimum version and cipher suites — at the termination point. Backend VM TLS is a separate end-to-end concern. WAF exclusions tune rule false positives, not TLS, and health probes do not negotiate client TLS.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: During VMSS scale-in behind Application Gateway, in-flight requests to removed instances fail. You want the gateway to stop sending new requests to a deregistering backend while letting existing connections finish. What should you enable?
options: Connection draining on the backend HTTP settings
Cookie-based affinity
WAF prevention mode
A longer health probe interval
explain: Connection draining gracefully retires backends: no new connections are sent, but in-flight ones complete. Cookie affinity provides client stickiness, not graceful removal. WAF mode governs blocking behavior, and probe intervals only affect failure detection speed.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: European users must reach the EU web endpoint and American users the US endpoint for data-residency reasons, while failover within each region is handled separately. Which Traffic Manager routing method enforces this?
options: Weighted routing
Priority routing
Performance routing
Geographic routing, mapping each user location to its endpoint
explain: Geographic routing maps the end-user location to a designated endpoint — the data-residency pattern. Weighted splits traffic by ratio, priority is active-passive failover, and performance routes by measured latency regardless of borders.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: You deploy SQL Server Always On availability groups behind a Standard Load Balancer. The listener requires Direct Server Return behavior for the SQL traffic. Which load balancing rule setting enables this?
options: HA ports rule
Floating IP (Direct Server Return)
An inbound NAT rule
Source IP session persistence
explain: Floating IP enables Direct Server Return: the backend sees the original destination IP, which SQL Always On listeners require. HA ports is the all-protocols/all-ports rule type for NVA scenarios. Inbound NAT rules are for administrative access to individual VMs, and session persistence only affects distribution.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: One Standard Load Balancer must expose two public IPs: one for the web tier and one for the API tier, each with its own load balancing rules. Is this supported?
options: Yes — a load balancer supports multiple frontend IP configurations, each with its own rules and backend pools
No — a load balancer supports only one public IP
Only on the Basic SKU
Only by deploying two load balancers
explain: Standard Load Balancer supports multiple frontend IPs, each with independent rules, probes, and backend pools — a standard multi-tenant front-end design. The single-IP limit does not exist, and Basic SKU is retired for new deployments anyway.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: You attach a NAT gateway to a subnet but associate a Basic SKU public IP with it. The deployment fails. What is required?
options: Basic SKU works with NAT gateway in the same region
NAT gateway requires dynamic public IPs
NAT gateway requires Standard SKU public IPs or a Standard public IP prefix
Associate a private IP with the NAT gateway instead
explain: NAT gateway only supports Standard SKU public IPs and prefixes — Basic SKU is incompatible and retired for new deployments. Dynamic versus static allocation is not the issue, and NAT gateway fundamentally needs public IPs for outbound internet translation.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: A workload holds long-lived outbound TCP connections through a NAT gateway. Connections are silently dropped after 4 minutes of idleness. What should you adjust?
options: The NSG rule timeout
The NAT gateway TCP idle timeout, configurable up to 120 minutes
The VM TCP keepalive settings only
Switch outbound traffic to a Basic load balancer
explain: The NAT gateway idle timeout defaults to 4 minutes and is configurable up to 120 minutes — the direct fix for dropped idle connections. NSGs have no idle timers. TCP keepalives mitigate but do not change the gateway setting, and Basic load balancer outbound is unrelated.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: You try to delete the default AllowVnetInBound NSG rule to implement a default-deny posture, and the portal refuses. What is the correct approach?
options: Default rules can be deleted with PowerShell
Delete the NSG and recreate it without defaults
Default-deny is impossible in Azure networking
Default rules cannot be deleted or modified; create a custom Deny rule with a lower priority number (for example 100) that is evaluated before them
explain: NSG default rules are immutable — lower priority numbers are evaluated first, so a custom Deny at priority 100 overrides the Allow defaults at 65000+. PowerShell cannot delete them either, and recreating the NSG brings the same defaults back.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: An NSG must allow inbound HTTPS from Azure DevOps hosted agents and Azure Storage, whose published IP ranges change weekly. Maintaining manual IP lists keeps breaking. What should you use in the rule source?
options: Application security groups
A dedicated public IP per service
Service tags such as AzureDevOps and Storage, which track the Microsoft-published ranges automatically
Allow 0.0.0.0/0 on port 443
explain: Service tags represent Microsoft-published IP ranges that update automatically — the designed replacement for hand-maintained lists. Application security groups group VM NICs, not service ranges. Opening 443 to the internet abandons least privilege.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: You need your Azure Firewall to detect known malicious traffic patterns using intrusion signatures, starting in monitor-only mode to assess impact before blocking. Which feature and mode do you use?
options: IDPS in Alert mode first, then move to Alert and deny
Threat intelligence in Off mode
WAF on the firewall policy
Network rules with FQDN filtering
explain: Azure Firewall Premium IDPS offers Alert (monitor-only) and Alert and deny modes — start in Alert to measure impact, then enforce. Threat intel is IP and domain reputation, a related but separate control. WAF lives on Application Gateway and Front Door, not the firewall.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: Your KQL query returns request durations in milliseconds. The report needs a column showing seconds. Which operator adds the computed column?
options: take
extend DurationSec = DurationMs / 1000.0
summarize
join
explain: extend adds a calculated column to each row — the operator for derived values. summarize aggregates rows into groups. take limits the row count. join merges two tables on keys.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: You need sign-in failures from the last 7 days only. Which KQL filter expresses this correctly?
options: where TimeGenerated < ago(7d)
where TimeGenerated == last(7d)
take 7d
where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
explain: ago(7d) evaluates to the timestamp seven days ago, so greater-than selects everything more recent. Less-than would select data older than seven days. take limits row count rather than filtering by time, and last(7d) is not valid KQL.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: Management asks: how many distinct users had failed sign-ins today? Which aggregation answers this?
options: summarize dcount(UserPrincipalName)
summarize count()
summarize sum(Failures)
take 1
explain: dcount returns the distinct count of a column — exactly distinct users. count() counts rows, inflated by users with multiple failures. sum() needs a numeric column and does not deduplicate. take only limits rows.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: Failed logons are recorded in both the SigninLogs table and a custom SecurityEvents_CL table. You need one result set searching both tables. Which operator combines them?
options: join
parse
union SigninLogs, SecurityEvents_CL
extend
explain: union stacks tables vertically into one result set for cross-table searching. join merges rows on matching keys. parse extracts structured fields from text. extend adds computed columns.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: A KQL query aggregates VMSS average CPU into one row per evaluation. You need an alert when that value exceeds 85%. Which log alert logic fits — and when is number of results the right choice instead?
options: Number of results; metric measurement is never used with log alerts
Metric measurement is only available for platform metric alerts
Number of results with the threshold set to 85
Metric measurement on the aggregated value; number of results fits fire-when-any-rows-match scenarios such as error events
explain: Metric measurement evaluates an aggregated numeric value against a threshold — right for average CPU > 85. Number of results fires based on row presence, which fits error-event detection. Setting a row-count threshold of 85 would alert on 85 rows, not 85% CPU, and metric measurement is a first-class log alert type.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: A new engineer needs a visual map of how the hub and spoke VNets, VPN gateways, and peerings connect. Which Network Watcher feature renders this?
options: The Topology view, which diagrams VNets, subnets, gateways, and peerings
IP flow verify
Next hop
Connection Monitor
explain: The Topology view draws the network layout including peerings and gateways. IP flow verify tests whether NSGs would allow a packet. Next hop shows the effective route for a destination. Connection Monitor measures latency and loss over time.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: Your incident webhook parses alert JSON, but the payload shape differs between metric alerts and log alerts, breaking the parser. How do you standardize it?
options: Write and maintain a parser per alert type
Enable the common alert schema on the action group so every alert type uses one payload shape
Switch all actions to email
Disable log alerts so only metric alerts fire
explain: The common alert schema normalizes the webhook payload across alert types, so one parser handles everything. Per-type parsers are maintenance toil. Email does not fix webhook parsing, and disabling log alerts removes needed coverage.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: You enable diagnostic settings on a storage account but only see account-level metrics; no blob read logs appear even though the app reads blobs heavily. What is missing?
options: Storage accounts cannot log blob read operations
You must enable metrics only; logs are unavailable
Data-plane diagnostic settings are configured per service — enable them on the blob service (and queue, table, or file as needed), not just the account
Blob logging requires premium performance storage
explain: Blob, queue, table, and file services each have their own diagnostic settings under the storage account; account-level settings alone do not capture data-plane logs. Blob read logging is fully supported on standard storage once the blob-service diagnostics are enabled.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: Your runbook sets retention days to 365 on diagnostic settings that send logs to a storage account. New deployments ignore the setting. What changed?
options: Retention now requires premium storage accounts
The retention setting moved to the Log Analytics workspace
365 days exceeds the maximum allowed retention
Microsoft deprecated retention-by-days on diagnostic settings; manage retention with lifecycle management policies on the storage account instead
explain: Retention policies on diagnostic-settings storage destinations were retired; lifecycle management rules on the storage account are the replacement for aging data out. The storage tier is irrelevant, the workspace has its own separate retention, and no 365-day maximum is the issue.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: An order-processing VMSS drains a Service Bus queue. CPU stays low even when the queue backs up with 50,000 messages, so CPU-based autoscale never fires. How should autoscale react to the backlog?
options: Scale the VMSS on the Service Bus queue message-count metric, so instance count follows the real backlog
Raise the CPU scale-out threshold to 95%
Enable predictive autoscale for the queue pattern
Scale on the VMSS data-disk queue depth metric
explain: Autoscale supports custom metrics such as Service Bus queue message counts — the true backlog signal when work is queue-bound and CPU is flat. Raising the CPU threshold makes firing even less likely. Predictive autoscale forecasts from history but does not observe the queue. Data-disk queue depth measures storage contention, not message backlog.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: An administrator deletes a Log Analytics workspace by mistake. It held 60 days of security logs needed for an audit next week. What is the recovery path?
options: Deleted workspaces can never be recovered
Re-create the workspace; the data re-ingests automatically
Recover the soft-deleted workspace within 14 days; data is retained through the soft-delete window
Restore the workspace from Azure Backup
explain: Workspace deletion is soft: you can recover the workspace with its data within 14 days. Re-creating starts with an empty workspace — historical data does not re-ingest. Azure Backup does not protect Log Analytics workspaces.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: One VM must send performance counters to the operations workspace and security events to a separate security workspace. The VM runs Azure Monitor Agent. How do you configure this?
options: Install a second monitoring agent on the VM
Associate two data collection rules — one per workspace — with the VM; Azure Monitor Agent supports multiple DCR associations
An agent can only target a single workspace
Reinstall the legacy Log Analytics agent
explain: Azure Monitor Agent multi-homes through multiple data collection rule associations, each routing to its own workspace. A second agent is unnecessary, the single-workspace limit applied to the legacy agent model, and the Log Analytics agent is deprecated.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: A VMSS web tier gets a sharp traffic ramp every weekday at 8 AM. Reactive metric autoscale always lags about 10 minutes, causing slow responses. What should you enable?
options: A higher static CPU threshold
Manual scaling every morning at 7:55 AM
Schedule-based profiles only
Predictive autoscale, which uses machine learning on historical patterns to scale out ahead of the forecasted load
explain: Predictive autoscale learns the daily pattern and provisions capacity before the ramp, eliminating the reactive lag. Higher thresholds still react late. Manual and schedule-only approaches are rigid and miss variations in the pattern.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: An autoscale rule scales out at 75% CPU and in at 40%. The instance count oscillates every few minutes during a gradual ramp, churning VMs. What should you tune?
options: Increase the cooldown periods so scaling actions settle before the next evaluation
Lower both thresholds
Disable scale-in entirely
Add more autoscale profiles
explain: Cooldown periods let a scaling action take effect before the opposing rule is evaluated — the direct fix for flapping. Lowering thresholds makes oscillation worse. Disabling scale-in wastes money, and more profiles do not dampen the cycle.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: You need failed sign-ins where the client app was any of three legacy protocols: IMAP, POP3, or SMTP. The ClientAppId column holds the protocol name. Which filter is the cleanest?
options: where ClientAppId == 'IMAP' or ClientAppId == 'POP3' or ClientAppId == 'SMTP'
where ClientAppId in ('IMAP', 'POP3', 'SMTP')
take 3
where ClientAppId has 'mail'
explain: The in operator tests set membership cleanly in one predicate. Chained or-equalities work but are verbose and error-prone. take limits rows rather than filtering. has does substring matching, which is imprecise for exact protocol names.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: Database VMs must receive only Security and Critical updates; driver and feature updates are banned by policy. How do you scope the Update Manager schedule?
options: Update Manager installs every classification; filtering is impossible
Manage patching with WSUS instead
Exclude unwanted updates by KB number only
In the maintenance configuration, include only the Security and Critical update classifications
explain: Maintenance configurations filter by update classification, so the schedule installs only Security and Critical updates. Per-KB exclusion is toil that never ends. WSUS is an on-premises tool, and classification filtering is a built-in capability.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: Azure Advisor shows cost and reliability recommendations, but the Security category is empty even though you suspect misconfigurations. What is the most likely reason?
options: Advisor has no security recommendation category
Security recommendations appear only for classic resources
Advisor security recommendations come from Microsoft Defender for Cloud; enable a Defender plan to populate them
You need the Global Administrator role to see them
explain: Advisor surfaces Defender for Cloud findings as its security recommendations — without a Defender plan enabled, the category stays empty. The category exists for all resource types, and the Reader role is sufficient to view Advisor.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: You must onboard 200 existing VMs to VM insights (performance plus the dependency Map view) without touching each machine. What is the most efficient approach?
options: Assign the built-in Azure Policy initiative for VM insights, which deploys Azure Monitor Agent, the data collection rule, and the associations at scale
RDP into each VM and install the agent manually
Enable VM insights in the portal one VM at a time
Reinstall the legacy Log Analytics agent on all VMs
explain: The built-in initiatives use Policy remediation to deploy AMA, the DCR, and associations across the fleet — the at-scale path. Manual installation does not scale to 200 VMs. The legacy Log Analytics agent is deprecated and cannot provide the current VM insights experience.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: Finance wants automatic notification of unusual daily spend spikes without anyone maintaining budget thresholds per team. Which feature detects anomalies against historical patterns?
options: Budgets with forecast alerts
Cost Management anomaly alerts, which apply machine learning to historical spend and flag unusual deviations
Advisor cost recommendations
Manual cost exports reviewed weekly
explain: Anomaly alerts learn normal spend patterns and flag deviations with no thresholds to maintain — the hands-off option finance asked for. Budgets require explicit thresholds per scope. Advisor recommends rightsizing, not spend anomalies, and manual exports are the toil being replaced.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: The finance data warehouse needs Azure cost data delivered daily as CSV files. The team currently downloads them manually from the portal. What should you configure?
options: A Power BI manual refresh schedule
Activity log exports to storage
Cost Management scheduled exports to a storage account with daily CSV delivery
A budget with an action group
explain: Scheduled exports automate daily (or monthly) cost data delivery to blob storage in CSV format for downstream ingestion. The activity log carries control-plane events, not cost data. Budgets alert on spend but do not export datasets, and manual refreshes keep the toil.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: Your company rolls out a line-of-business mobile app for field technicians. The app does not support Intune enrollment, and technicians will not enroll their personal phones in MDM. You must still ensure corporate data inside the app is protected by policy when accessed from those phones. Which Conditional Access grant control should you require?
options: Require approved client app
Require app protection policy
Require compliant device
Require Hybrid Microsoft Entra joined device
explain: The Require app protection policy grant control enforces an Intune app protection (MAM) policy on the client app, which protects corporate data without device enrollment. Require approved client app only checks that the app is on the approved list and does not enforce the protection policy. Compliant device and Hybrid Microsoft Entra joined device both require device management or domain join, which the unenrolled personal phones cannot satisfy.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: You send a B2B invitation to contractor@fabrikam.com. The contractor opens the invitation email but tries to redeem it by signing in with a different address, contractor.personal@outlook.com. What happens?
options: Redemption succeeds and the guest account is created under the personal address
Redemption fails; the guest must redeem using the invited email address, or you must send a new invitation to the correct address
Redemption succeeds after a 24-hour verification delay
The invitation is automatically reissued to the personal address
explain: B2B redemption is tied to the invited email address; signing in with a different address fails because the redemption cannot match the invitation. The fix is to redeem with the invited address or send a fresh invitation to the right address. There is no automatic reissue or verification delay, and the guest account is never silently created under a different address.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: You run Microsoft Entra Connect with an on-premises Exchange hybrid deployment. A new Microsoft 365 group is created in the cloud, and the on-premises file server team wants to use that group for an on-premises shared folder ACL. Which feature makes the cloud group visible on-premises, and as what object type does it appear?
options: Password writeback; the group appears as a security group
Device writeback; the group appears as a mail-enabled security group
Directory extension attribute sync; the group appears as an organizational unit
Group writeback; the group appears as a distribution group in on-premises Active Directory
explain: Group writeback is the optional Microsoft Entra Connect feature that writes Microsoft 365 groups back to on-premises Active Directory, where they appear as distribution groups (it requires on-premises Exchange). Password writeback syncs passwords, device writeback syncs device objects for Conditional Access, and directory extension sync replicates custom attributes - none of them create group objects on-premises.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: Your help desk is overwhelmed by password resets. You pilot passwordless sign-in where users approve a sign-in on their phone with no password typed. Which Microsoft Entra authentication method enables this flow?
options: Authenticator app phone sign-in: the user registers the Authenticator app and enables phone sign-in, then approves sign-ins from the phone
SMS sign-in: the user receives a code by text message
Temporary Access Pass: the user enters a time-limited passcode
FIDO2 security key: the user inserts a hardware key
explain: Phone sign-in through the Microsoft Authenticator app is the passwordless method where the user approves the sign-in on their phone instead of typing a password. SMS sign-in still involves entering a code, a Temporary Access Pass is a bootstrap credential used to register passwordless methods rather than the ongoing sign-in method, and FIDO2 uses a physical security key rather than the phone approval flow described.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: You enable seamless single sign-on for a tenant synchronized with Microsoft Entra Connect. Users on domain-joined machines get SSO to cloud apps. Six months later SSO stops working for everyone at the same time, and you discover the Kerberos decryption key is stale. Which object holds that key, and what is the fix?
options: The Microsoft Entra Connect sync service account; reset its password
The user password hashes in Microsoft Entra ID; force a full password hash sync
The AZUREADSSOACC computer account in each on-premises forest; roll its Kerberos decryption key (Microsoft Entra Connect normally rolls it automatically every 30 days)
The federation trust certificate; renew the token-signing certificate
explain: Seamless SSO creates the AZUREADSSOACC computer account in on-premises Active Directory, and Microsoft Entra Connect rolls its Kerberos decryption key every 30 days; if rollover breaks, SSO fails tenant-wide until the key is rolled again. The sync service account password and password hashes are unrelated to Kerberos SSO, and there is no federation certificate involved because seamless SSO is not federation.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: You configure a PIM-eligible role assignment that requires approval. A user activates the role and waits for a decision. As the designated approver, where do you review and act on the pending request, and what happens if you take no action?
options: In PIM under Approve requests; approvers get email notifications and the request expires if not acted on within the configured approval timeout
In the Microsoft Entra audit logs; the request is auto-approved after 24 hours
In the Access reviews blade; the request converts to a permanent active assignment
In the Conditional Access blade; the request waits until the next directory sync cycle
explain: Pending PIM activation requests are reviewed in the PIM Approve requests view, approvers receive email notifications, and requests expire after the approval timeout rather than being auto-approved. Audit logs are read-only history and cannot approve anything, access reviews recertify existing access on a schedule, and Conditional Access has no role in PIM approvals.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: Your company ends a managed-services contract. The provider had access to your subscriptions through Azure Lighthouse. You must revoke their delegated access immediately. What should you do?
options: Delete the provider administrators user accounts in your tenant
Ask the provider to delete their own Microsoft Entra tenant
Disable all affected subscriptions until the contract dispute is resolved
In your tenant, remove the Lighthouse delegation (Azure Lighthouse, Delegations, Remove delegation), which revokes their cross-tenant access
explain: Lighthouse delegations are removed from the customer tenant, and removing the delegation immediately revokes the service provider cross-tenant access. The provider users live in the provider tenant, so deleting local accounts does nothing; asking them to delete their tenant is not your call; and disabling subscriptions disrupts your own workloads unnecessarily.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: Two project teams share one storage account. Team Alpha users have Storage Blob Data Reader at the account scope but must only read blobs tagged Project=Alpha; Team Beta users must only read blobs tagged Project=Beta. Managing per-container role assignments for hundreds of containers is impractical. What should you do?
options: Assign Storage Blob Data Reader separately on every container for each team
Issue shared access signatures scoped to each blob
Add an ABAC condition to each team role assignment comparing the user custom security attribute with the blob index tag; both the role action and the condition must evaluate true for access
Enable the storage firewall and filter by team office IP ranges
explain: Attribute-based access control adds a condition to the role assignment, so one assignment per team enforces tag-scoped access - the role data action and the condition must both hold. Per-container assignments do not scale, SAS tokens are shared secrets that bypass identity, and the storage firewall filters networks rather than users.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: Your tagging strategy assigns 60 tags per resource (cost center, owner, environment, project, plus dozens of compliance tags). Deployments start failing at the tagging step. What is the cause?
options: Tags are limited to 10 per resource group
Azure allows a maximum of 50 tags per resource; you must consolidate to 50 or fewer
Tag names are limited to 32 characters
Tags cannot be applied by ARM templates
explain: Azure enforces a limit of 50 tags per resource (and per resource group and subscription), so the 60-tag design fails at deployment. The limit is not 10, tag names allow far more than 32 characters, and ARM templates apply tags normally - the count is the problem.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: You configure SSPR for the tenant with Number of methods required to reset set to 1. A Global Administrator forgets their password and uses the reset portal. How many authentication methods will they be required to provide?
options: Two: administrator accounts always fall under the fixed two-gate password reset policy, which cannot be changed, regardless of the tenant user policy
One, matching the tenant policy
Zero; administrators must contact support instead of using SSPR
Three, because Global Administrator is the highest-privilege role
explain: Microsoft enforces a fixed two-gate reset policy for accounts holding administrator roles, and this policy cannot be changed - it overrides the tenant setting of one method. Administrators are always enabled for SSPR, they are not routed to support, and there is no three-method requirement.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: Your workforce operates only in the United States and Germany. You want to block authentication attempts from every other country. Which Conditional Access configuration achieves this?
options: An access review of all users outside the US and Germany
A sign-in frequency policy of one hour
A legacy per-user MFA trusted IP list
A named location covering all countries except the US and Germany, with a policy that blocks access from that named location
explain: Named locations support countries and regions, so a policy targeting all users with a Block grant for the all-other-countries named location enforces geo-blocking. Access reviews recertify access but do not block sign-ins, sign-in frequency controls session lifetime rather than location, and the legacy trusted-IPs list only affects per-user MFA, not Conditional Access.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: Your company signs an Enterprise Agreement. Finance wants separate invoices per business unit and a single place to manage the overall monetary commitment. Which EA hierarchy provides this?
options: Management groups hold the commitment; subscriptions invoice separately by default
Resource groups map to departments; each department gets its own enrollment
Departments group accounts, accounts own subscriptions, and the enrollment holds the monetary commitment
Billing profiles replace departments for invoice separation
explain: The EA hierarchy is enrollment (monetary commitment) to departments (cost and invoice separation) to accounts to subscriptions. Management groups are a governance hierarchy, not a billing one; resource groups do not map to EA departments; and billing profiles are the MCA construct, not EA.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: After moving from an Enterprise Agreement to a Microsoft Customer Agreement, finance asks where to view and pay the invoice now. What should you tell them?
options: Invoices are issued per billing profile under the MCA billing account; finance views and pays them in the billing profiles view
Invoices appear inside Cost Management under each subscription
The EA portal continues to issue the invoices
Invoices are sent by email only; there is no portal view
explain: Under MCA, the billing account contains billing profiles and each billing profile generates its own invoice, which is where finance works. Cost Management shows usage and cost analysis, not invoices; the EA portal does not serve MCA billing; and invoices are viewable in the portal, not email-only.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: You add contoso.com as a custom domain in Microsoft Entra ID. The portal shows the domain as Unverified. What must you do to verify it?
options: Assign a Global Administrator as the domain owner
Create the TXT (or MX) verification DNS record at your DNS provider using the value shown in the portal
Wait 72 hours for automatic verification
Purchase the domain through Microsoft 365
explain: Domain ownership is proven by adding the portal-provided TXT or MX record at the domain DNS hoster. Assigning roles or waiting does not verify ownership, and the domain can be hosted anywhere - it does not need to be purchased through Microsoft.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: A GitHub Actions workflow must deploy to Azure with no long-lived secret stored in the repository. The team creates a user-assigned managed identity for the workflow. How does the workflow authenticate as that identity without a client secret?
options: By enabling a system-assigned managed identity on the GitHub repository
By using the managed identity principal ID as a password
By opening the Key Vault firewall to GitHub-hosted runner IP ranges
By adding a federated credential on the managed identity that trusts the GitHub OIDC issuer, so GitHub short-lived tokens are exchanged for Microsoft Entra tokens
explain: Federated credentials on a user-assigned managed identity establish trust with an external OIDC issuer (issuer, subject, audience api://AzureADTokenExchange), enabling secretless authentication. System-assigned identities cannot attach to GitHub, the principal ID is an identifier rather than a secret, and firewall rules do not authenticate anyone.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: HR wants new hires to automatically receive a Microsoft Entra account, license assignment, and group memberships on their start date, driven by the HR system feed. Which feature should you configure?
options: A Conditional Access policy scoped to new users
An access review for the new-hires group
A joiner lifecycle workflow triggered by the HR-driven provisioning feed
A dynamic group with a start-date membership rule
explain: Lifecycle workflows automate joiner, mover, and leaver tasks - creating accounts, assigning licenses, and adding group memberships - from HR data. Conditional Access controls sign-in conditions rather than provisioning, access reviews recertify existing access, and dynamic groups manage membership only without creating accounts or assigning licenses.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: Security wants a report listing every virtual machine that is missing the Azure Monitor Agent, without blocking any deployments. Which policy effect should the definition use?
options: Deny
AuditIfNotExists
DeployIfNotExists
Disabled
explain: AuditIfNotExists flags resources where a related resource or configuration is missing, producing the compliance report without blocking or changing anything. Deny would block deployments, DeployIfNotExists would install the agent (remediation rather than reporting), and Disabled evaluates nothing.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: To control cost and sprawl, architects want only virtual machines, storage accounts, and virtual networks creatable in the dev subscription; every other resource type must be blocked at creation time. Which built-in policy definition achieves this?
options: Allowed resource types
Allowed locations
Allowed virtual machine SKUs
Require a tag on resources
explain: The Allowed resource types definition denies any resource type not on the permitted list. Allowed locations restricts regions rather than types, Allowed virtual machine SKUs restricts VM sizes only, and tag policies enforce tagging rather than blocking resource types.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: Legal requires that employees may only invite B2B guests from fabrikam.com and contoso.com; invitations to any other domain must be blocked tenant-wide. Where do you configure this?
options: A Conditional Access policy that blocks those domains
An access package policy per allowed domain
The tenant verified domains list
External collaboration settings: collaboration restrictions with an allowlist containing the two domains
explain: Collaboration restrictions in the External Identities external collaboration settings provide tenant-wide allow and deny lists for B2B invitation domains. Conditional Access cannot block invitation targets by domain, access packages govern access to resources rather than who can be invited, and verified domains are for domains you own rather than guest domains.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: You move a subscription from ManagementGroup-A to ManagementGroup-B. ManagementGroup-A had three policy assignments; ManagementGroup-B has one. What happens to policy enforcement on the subscription?
options: ManagementGroup-A policies remain permanently attached to the subscription
All policy assignments are deleted and must be recreated
The subscription stops inheriting ManagementGroup-A policies and starts inheriting ManagementGroup-B policies
The move is blocked until you remove the policy assignments
explain: Policy and RBAC assignments are inherited from the current management group parent, so moving the subscription changes which assignments apply - nothing is copied, duplicated, or deleted by the move itself. Assignments are never permanently attached by a move, and the move is not blocked by existing assignments.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: You must copy only *.log files from a directory tree containing thousands of mixed file types into a blob container, preserving the folder structure. Which AzCopy syntax filters the transfer to the log files?
options: azcopy copy with --recursive only, which copies every file
azcopy sync with --delete-destination to mirror deletions
azcopy copy with --include-pattern='*.log' (optionally combined with --recursive)
azcopy list with --include-pattern, which transfers the matching files
explain: The --include-pattern (and --exclude-pattern) flags filter AzCopy transfers by file name pattern, so only *.log files are copied. --recursive alone copies everything, --delete-destination mirrors deletions to the destination which is dangerous rather than filtering, and azcopy list only lists without transferring.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: You are designing an Azure Table Storage schema for 50 million IoT telemetry entities, queried mostly by device ID over time ranges. Which partition-key strategy gives the best performance and allows atomic batch writes per device?
options: A single constant partition key for all entities so queries scan one partition
The event timestamp as the partition key
A random GUID per entity as the partition key
The device ID as the partition key with the timestamp in the row key, keeping each device entities together for partition-scoped queries and entity group transactions
explain: Using the device ID as the partition key colocates each device data for efficient partition-scoped queries and enables entity group (batch) transactions, which are limited to a single partition. A single constant partition key creates a throttled hot partition, timestamps scatter one device data across partitions, and random GUIDs prevent both efficient range queries and batching.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: After an unplanned failover of a GRS storage account, an application with a hardcoded 24-hour DNS cache cannot reach the storage endpoint for about an hour. What best explains this?
options: DNS changes from the failover can take up to about an hour to propagate; applications should honor short TTLs and retry rather than hardcoding long DNS caches
Failover deletes the secondary endpoint permanently
GRS failover requires manual storage key rotation before endpoints work
The account converts to LRS and the secondary endpoint never returns
explain: After failover the DNS records change and propagation can take up to about an hour, so long client-side DNS caches delay cutover - the documented guidance is short TTLs and retry logic. The old secondary becomes the new primary rather than being deleted, no key rotation is required for failover, and while the account becomes LRS after failover the endpoint itself keeps working.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: A legacy application stores unmanaged disk VHDs as page blobs and needs premium performance for them. Which storage account kind should you create?
options: BlockBlobStorage
PageBlobStorage (premium page blobs)
FileStorage
Standard general-purpose v2 with the Hot tier
explain: Premium page blobs (PageBlobStorage) is the premium account kind designed for page blobs such as unmanaged disk VHDs. BlockBlobStorage holds block and append blobs only, FileStorage holds file shares only, and general-purpose v2 page blobs run at standard performance tiers.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: You start a server-side copy of a 2 TB blob between storage accounts. The copy request is accepted. Before pointing the production workload at the destination blob, what must you confirm and why?
options: That the source blob was deleted to free space
That the storage account keys were rotated after the copy
That the destination blob tier was changed to Hot
That the copy completed (copy status shows success), because server-side copy runs asynchronously and the destination is not usable until it finishes
explain: Server-side copy is asynchronous: you must poll the copy status until it reports success before using the destination. Deleting the source early is the classic trap because the copy reads from the source, and key rotation or tier changes are unrelated to copy completion.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: After migrating off SFTP-based uploads, security asks you to remove the SFTP endpoint from the storage account while keeping blob and Data Lake access working. The account has hierarchical namespace enabled. What should you do?
options: Delete the storage account and recreate it without SFTP
Disable hierarchical namespace on the account
Turn off the SFTP setting on the storage account; blob, Data Lake, and other endpoints are unaffected
Rotate the storage account keys to invalidate SFTP credentials
explain: SFTP is a toggle on hierarchical-namespace-enabled accounts, so disabling it removes only the SFTP endpoint while everything else keeps working. Hierarchical namespace cannot be disabled after creation, key rotation does not remove a protocol endpoint, and recreating the account is destructive overkill.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: An Azure VM uses an unmanaged OS disk stored as a page blob. An administrator tries to delete the VHD blob directly and gets an error that the blob is leased. What is the correct action?
options: Break the lease (or delete the VM and disk properly first): the infinite lease protects the VHD while the VM exists, and deleting it out from under the VM corrupts the deployment
Wait 60 seconds for the lease to expire on its own
Rotate the storage account keys to release the lease
Move the blob to the Archive tier to release the lease
explain: VM disks hold an infinite lease precisely to prevent accidental deletion; you must break the lease or delete the VM through the compute resource provider first. Infinite leases never expire on their own, and neither key rotation nor tier changes affect leases.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: You deploy a VM in availability zone 2 and try to attach an Ultra disk that was created in zone 1. The attachment fails. What is the cause?
options: Ultra disks require zone-redundant configuration across all zones
Ultra disks are zonal: the disk and the VM must be in the same availability zone
Ultra disks cannot be attached to zonal VMs at all
The VM needs accelerated networking enabled first
explain: Ultra disks are zonal resources, so the disk must be created in the same zone as the VM. They are LRS-only rather than zone-redundant, they attach fine to zonal VMs when co-located, and accelerated networking is unrelated to disk attachment.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: You need the highest IOPS for a database data volume and select Ultra disks. Your template also tries to use an Ultra disk as the OS disk and fails validation. Why?
options: Ultra disks exceed the maximum OS disk size
Ultra disks require Premium SSD v2 as the OS disk type
The region does not support Ultra disks
Ultra disks are supported only as data disks, not as OS disks
explain: Ultra disks can only be data disks; the OS disk must be Premium SSD (v1 or v2), Standard SSD, or Standard HDD. Size limits, region support, and the OS disk type choice are not the issue - the disk role is.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: A single VM with no availability set runs a critical database. You need its OS and data disks to survive a datacenter (zone) failure within the region. Which managed disk redundancy option provides this?
options: Standard HDD with LRS
Premium SSD with LRS
Premium SSD with ZRS
Ultra disk with GRS
explain: Premium SSD supports ZRS, which synchronously replicates the disk across availability zones - the only managed-disk zone redundancy option. Standard disks and Ultra disks are LRS-only, and Ultra disks have no GRS option.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: You take a snapshot of a production data disk for a test environment. You try to attach the snapshot directly to a test VM and the portal rejects it. What is the required step?
