options: Create a managed disk from the snapshot, then attach the new disk to the VM
Copy the snapshot to the Archive tier first
Convert the snapshot back into a page blob
Enable soft delete on the snapshot
explain: Snapshots are point-in-time copies, not attachable disks: you create a managed disk from the snapshot and attach that disk. Archive tiering, blob conversion, and soft delete are unrelated to making a snapshot usable by a VM.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: An application puts 2 MB JSON payloads onto an Azure Storage queue and receives errors. What is the issue, and what is the recommended pattern?
options: Queues require a premium storage account; upgrade the account kind
A queue message is limited to 64 KB; store the payload in a blob and put a pointer message on the queue
Storage queues do not support JSON payloads; switch to XML
The message visibility timeout is too short for large payloads
explain: Queue messages are limited to 64 KB, so the standard claim-check pattern stores the payload in blob storage and queues a small pointer message. Queues work on standard accounts, JSON is fully supported, and visibility timeout controls reprocessing timing rather than message size.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: A lifecycle rule deletes base blobs 90 days after modification. Months later, storage costs barely drop. Investigation shows most blobs have snapshots and the blobs are still present. What is wrong?
options: Lifecycle management cannot delete blobs at all
The rule must move blobs to the Archive tier before deleting
Snapshots are deleted automatically after 90 days regardless
The delete action only applies to the blob subtypes selected in the rule: blobs with snapshots or previous versions are never deleted until the rule also targets snapshots and versions
explain: Lifecycle management will not delete a base blob until its snapshots and previous versions are deleted, so the rule must include those blob subtypes in the delete action. Lifecycle deletes blobs normally, archive-first is not required, and snapshots are never auto-deleted by the base-blob rule.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: Ransomware protection requires blob backups stored offsite in a separate vault with one-year retention, restorable to an alternate location. The current operational backup keeps data inside the source account. What should you configure?
options: Blob versioning only
A second storage account with an object replication policy
Azure Backup vaulted backup for blobs using a Backup vault, with a backup policy defining the schedule and retention
Soft delete with 365-day retention
explain: Vaulted backup for blobs copies data offsite into the Backup vault on a defined schedule with policy-driven retention and supports restore to an alternate location. Operational backup stays in the source account, versioning and soft delete are in-account protections rather than offsite copies, and object replication is replication rather than backup.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: A queue-triggered function fails on a malformed message; the message keeps reappearing and failing, clogging the queue. Which pattern handles this?
options: Move the message to a poison queue after it exceeds the maximum dequeue count, so it can be inspected without blocking the queue
Increase the visibility timeout indefinitely
Delete and recreate the storage account
Disable the function permanently
explain: After exceeding the maximum dequeue count, the message is moved to the poison queue (<queuename>-poison) for inspection while healthy messages keep processing. Raising the visibility timeout only delays redelivery, and deleting the account or disabling the function is destructive rather than diagnostic.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: All applications access storage through Microsoft Entra RBAC roles, but a compliance audit finds one legacy app still authenticating with a storage account key. You want the storage account itself to reject any key-based or SAS authentication. Which setting enforces this?
options: Enable the storage firewall with default deny
Set Allow storage account key access to Disabled (allowSharedKeyAccess=false)
Enable SFTP on the account
Set the minimum TLS version to 1.2
explain: Disallowing shared key access blocks all key-based and SAS authentication, leaving Microsoft Entra ID (RBAC) as the only authentication path. The firewall filters networks rather than authentication methods, SFTP adds a protocol, and minimum TLS controls transport security rather than credential types.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: A nightly AzCopy sync copies on-premises files to a blob container. Analysts sometimes edit blobs directly in the portal during the day, and the nightly sync must never overwrite a destination blob that is newer than the source file. Which flag should you add?
options: --delete-destination=true
--recursive
--overwrite=true
--overwrite=ifSourceNewer
explain: The --overwrite flag controls AzCopy behavior on existing blobs: true overwrites unconditionally, false skips existing files, and ifSourceNewer overwrites only when the source is newer, which is exactly the requirement. --delete-destination deletes destination files missing from the source (destructive mirroring, not protection), and --recursive only controls subdirectory traversal.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: You need revocable delegated access to blobs and want a stored access policy so you can revoke without rotating keys. A colleague suggests attaching the stored access policy to an account SAS. Why will this not work?
options: Stored access policies can only be used with account SAS, not service SAS
Account SAS tokens cannot have expiry times
Stored access policies can only back a service SAS (container or blob scoped), not an account SAS or user delegation SAS
Stored access policies require a premium storage account
explain: Stored access policies group permissions for service SAS on blob, file, queue, and table resources; account SAS and user delegation SAS do not support them. Account SAS can only be revoked by rotating keys, and user delegation SAS by revoking the delegation key - the policy mechanism is exclusive to service SAS.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: You design a telemetry pipeline on a premium block blobs account and require geo-redundant replication to a secondary region. The portal only offers LRS and ZRS. Why?
options: Premium block blobs accounts support only LRS and ZRS; GRS and GZRS are not available for this account kind
Geo-redundancy requires hierarchical namespace to be enabled first
The region does not support any redundancy options
You must enable SFTP before geo-redundancy appears
explain: Per Microsoft Learn, premium block blobs (BlockBlobStorage) support only LRS and ZRS - geo-redundant options require a standard general-purpose v2 account. Hierarchical namespace and SFTP are unrelated to redundancy choices, and the portal correctly reflects the account kind limits.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: Security forbids exporting a managed disk over the public internet. You need a copy of a VHD for forensic analysis from an on-premises workstation connected via ExpressRoute. How do you export the disk privately?
options: Generate a SAS URL with GrantAccess and download it over the internet
Create a disk access resource with a private endpoint, enable private access on the disk, and export through the private link
Copy the disk to a Cool-tier blob first
Take a snapshot and download it from the Azure portal
explain: A disk access resource with a private endpoint enables private export of managed disks over the private link, keeping traffic off the public internet. SAS-based GrantAccess exports traverse the public endpoint, tier changes do not affect the network path, and portal snapshot downloads also use public SAS URLs.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: After a partially failed ARM template deployment, a VM configuration has drifted from its model (an extension is missing) but the VM is running fine. You want Azure to reconcile the VM with its model without moving it to another host or rebooting. Which action should you take?
options: Redeploy the VM to a new host
Reapply the VM configuration, which re-applies the model (extensions and settings) in place
Restart the VM
Delete and recreate the VM from the template
explain: The Reapply action reconciles the VM with its ARM model - reinstalling extensions and settings - without moving hosts or rebooting. Redeploy moves the VM to a new node with downtime, a restart does not fix model drift, and recreating the VM is destructive.

q: After a slot swap, users hit a cold application for 30 seconds while caches build. You want the staging slot warmed with synthetic requests to specific pages before the swap completes. What should you configure?
options: Custom warm-up using applicationInitialization in web.config, so the platform issues the specified warm-up requests during the swap
Always On
Auto-swap
Health check
explain: The applicationInitialization section defines custom warm-up requests that App Service executes against the staging slot before the swap completes. Always On keeps the app loaded but does not warm specific pages pre-swap, auto-swap only triggers the swap automatically, and health check monitors instances without warming them.

q: You configure scheduled backups for a Standard-tier web app to a storage account whose firewall denies all public access. The backups fail. What is the cause and the fix?
options: Backups require the Premium tier; scale the app up
The storage account must be in a different subscription than the app
Enable Allow trusted Microsoft services on the storage account
App Service backup does not support firewall-enabled or private-endpoint storage accounts; use a storage account without firewall or private endpoint restrictions
explain: Microsoft documents that firewall-enabled and private-endpoint storage accounts are not supported as App Service backup destinations - the trusted-services bypass does not cover App Service backup. Standard tier supports backup, the storage account must be in the same subscription rather than a different one, and tier or subscription changes do not address the firewall limitation.

q: A Premium-plan function app has 2 always-ready instances. During a flash sale it needs up to 40 instances for ten minutes, then scales back. You want to allow the burst while capping cost exposure. Which setting controls the maximum scale-out?
options: The Consumption plan execution timeout
functionAppScaleLimit set to 2
The Premium plan maximum burst setting (optionally tightened per app with functionAppScaleLimit)
The number of pre-warmed instances
explain: The Premium plan maximum burst setting caps how far the app scales beyond its always-ready instances, and functionAppScaleLimit can impose a lower per-app cap. Pre-warmed instances set the minimum rather than the maximum, the timeout limits execution duration, and setting functionAppScaleLimit to 2 would prevent the burst entirely.

q: A container app needs a database connection string. You must not store the secret in the Container Apps configuration or in the container image. What is the recommended approach?
options: Bake the secret into the container image
Reference the secret from Azure Key Vault using the container app managed identity (Key Vault secret reference)
Pass the secret as a plain environment variable
Store the secret in a ConfigMap
explain: Container Apps supports referencing Key Vault secrets via the app managed identity, so the secret value never lives in the app configuration or image. Baking secrets into images, passing them as plain environment variables, or using ConfigMaps all expose the secret in recoverable form.

q: Your private AKS cluster must use the central networking team private DNS zone (privatelink.eastus.azmk8s.io) instead of the system-created zone, so DNS records land in the hub subscription. What is required?
options: Create the cluster with --private-dns-zone pointing to the existing zone resource ID, using a user-assigned managed identity with Private DNS Zone Contributor and Network Contributor roles
Enable the API server public FQDN
Peer the cluster VNet to the public internet
Use kubenet networking instead of Azure CNI
explain: A custom private DNS zone requires passing its resource ID at cluster creation plus a user-assigned managed identity holding Private DNS Zone Contributor and Network Contributor roles so AKS can manage records. A public FQDN defeats the private design, internet peering is unrelated to DNS, and the network plugin does not control the private DNS zone.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: Pods fail with ImagePullBackOff pulling from your Azure Container Registry. The cluster uses managed identity and the registry admin user is disabled. What is the fix?
options: Enable the ACR admin user and embed its password in the pod spec
Make the registry publicly accessible
Restart all cluster nodes
Grant the cluster kubelet identity AcrPull on the registry (az aks update --attach-acr)
explain: The attach-acr operation assigns the AcrPull role to the kubelet managed identity, which is the managed-identity way to authorize image pulls. Enabling the admin user introduces a shared credential that policy disabled, public access does not fix authentication, and restarting nodes grants no RBAC permissions.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: You want boot diagnostics screenshots for troubleshooting VM boot issues but have no storage account and do not want to manage one. What should you configure?
options: Disable boot diagnostics
Create a premium storage account in another region
Enable boot diagnostics with the managed storage account option (platform-managed)
Install the Azure Monitor Agent on the VM
explain: Boot diagnostics supports a platform-managed storage option, so screenshots and serial logs are captured without a customer storage account. Disabling diagnostics loses the data, a separate account adds management overhead, and the Azure Monitor Agent collects guest OS logs rather than boot screenshots.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: A container in Azure Container Instances occasionally deadlocks while its main process keeps running, so ACI never restarts it. How do you make ACI detect and restart the unhealthy container?
options: Set the container group restart policy to Always
Configure a liveness probe (HTTP, TCP, or exec) so ACI restarts the container when the probe fails
Increase the container memory limit
Deploy a second container group as a standby
explain: Liveness probes detect application-level hangs and trigger a container restart on probe failure. The restart policy governs behavior after termination rather than health detection, more memory does not fix a deadlock, and a standby group adds cost without detecting the unhealthy container.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: An autoscale rule tries to grow a Uniform-mode scale set to 150 instances, but it stalls at 100. The template never set singlePlacementGroup. What is the cause and the fix?
options: Autoscale maximum defaults to 100; raise the autoscale maximum
The subscription core quota is 100
The load balancer supports only 100 backend instances
singlePlacementGroup defaults to true, capping the set at 100 VMs; set it to false for up to 1,000 instances across multiple placement groups
explain: A Uniform scale set defaults to a single placement group with a maximum of 100 VMs; setting singlePlacementGroup to false allows up to 1,000 instances across multiple placement groups. The autoscale maximum and subscription quota are separate limits that were not hit here, and Standard load balancers support far more than 100 backends.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: You enable scheduled backup for a web app with a linked Azure SQL database. After a restore drill, the files are back but the database is empty. The backup was configured for files only. What should you have included?
options: Nothing; the backup automatically includes all linked databases
A separate Recovery Services vault for the database
The linked database in the backup configuration: App Service backup can include connected Azure SQL, MySQL, and PostgreSQL databases alongside files and settings
A manual BACPAC export before each backup
explain: App Service backup supports including linked Azure SQL Database, MySQL, and PostgreSQL databases, but they must be selected in the backup configuration - a files-only backup skips them. The backup never includes databases automatically, a Recovery Services vault is not used for App Service backup, and manual exports defeat the purpose of scheduled backups.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: A development AKS cluster sits idle every night and weekend. You want to stop compute charges during idle hours without deleting the cluster. What should you do?
options: Use az aks stop and az aks start to deallocate the cluster when idle and bring it back when needed
Delete the node pools every night and recreate them each morning
Scale the system node pool to zero nodes
Pause the subscription
explain: AKS stop deallocates all cluster nodes (stopping compute charges) while preserving the cluster configuration, and start brings it back. Deleting node pools destroys configuration, system node pools cannot scale to zero, and subscriptions cannot be paused.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: You decommission a VM but legal requires its backups retained for three years. In the Recovery Services vault you stop protection for the VM. Which option preserves the existing recovery points?
options: Stop backup and delete backup data
Stop backup and retain backup data
Delete the vault
Disable soft delete on the vault
explain: Stopping protection with retain data keeps the existing recovery points according to their retention settings. Deleting backup data purges them, deleting the vault destroys everything including other workloads, and soft delete is a safety net against accidental deletion rather than a retention mechanism.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: Finance needs daily backups kept 30 days, weekly backups kept 12 weeks, and monthly backups kept 7 years for a file server. Which backup policy structure supports this?
options: Three separate Recovery Services vaults
Operational backup only
A snapshot-only policy
A backup policy with tiered retention: daily, weekly, monthly, and yearly (GFS) retention points
explain: Azure Backup policies support Grandfather-Father-Son style retention with daily, weekly, monthly, and yearly retention points in a single policy. Multiple vaults are unnecessary overhead, operational backup applies to blobs rather than file servers, and snapshots alone do not provide multi-year retention.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: One container app needs GPUs and dedicated compute with no noisy neighbors, while another app in the same environment is fine on serverless pay-per-use. How do you satisfy both in a single Container Apps environment?
options: Deploy two separate Container Apps environments
Run both apps on the Consumption profile
Add a Dedicated (or GPU) workload profile to the environment and assign the demanding app to it, leaving the other app on Consumption
Move the GPU app to Azure Container Instances
explain: Workload profiles let one environment mix the Consumption profile (serverless, scale to zero) with Dedicated profiles including GPU SKUs, assigning each app to the right profile. Separate environments add management overhead, Consumption cannot provide GPUs or dedicated compute, and moving to ACI abandons the shared environment.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: A web app uses regional VNet integration. Traffic to Azure SQL via private endpoint works, but internet-bound traffic from the app still egresses through the App Service public infrastructure instead of the VNet firewall. What setting forces all outbound traffic through the VNet?
options: Enable Route All on the VNet integration (WEBSITE_VNET_ROUTE_ALL=1)
Add a private endpoint for the web app
Enable access restrictions on the app
Scale the app to the Premium tier
explain: By default only RFC1918 traffic uses VNet integration; Route All sends all outbound traffic through the VNet so it hits the firewall. A private endpoint controls inbound private connectivity, access restrictions filter inbound callers, and scaling does not change outbound routing.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: You run Spot VMs for a batch workload. When Azure needs the capacity back, you want the VMs deallocated rather than deleted so OS disks and state persist for later resume. Which eviction policy should you choose?
options: Delete
Deallocate (Stop/Deallocate)
Redeploy
Evict to another region
explain: The Deallocate eviction policy stops the VM while keeping its disks and state for later resume. Delete removes the VM, redeploy is not an eviction policy, and there is no cross-region eviction option.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: You want full control over when each scale set instance receives a new image - no automatic rolling upgrades. Which VMSS upgrade policy should you set?
options: Automatic
Rolling
Automatic OS image upgrade
Manual: you trigger upgrades explicitly per instance or for the whole set
explain: The Manual upgrade policy means instances only update when you initiate the upgrade, giving full control over timing. Automatic and Rolling policies upgrade on their own schedule, and automatic OS image upgrades apply platform images without your trigger.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: A web API must only accept requests from clients presenting a specific client certificate (mutual TLS). Where do you enforce this in App Service?
options: In the storage account firewall
In a WAF policy on Application Gateway only
By enabling incoming client certificates and setting the client certificate mode to Required on the app
By enabling HTTPS Only on the app
explain: App Service supports incoming client certificates with modes including Required, which enforces mutual TLS at the front end. HTTPS Only encrypts traffic without authenticating clients, a WAF policy is a different tier solution, and the storage firewall is unrelated to the web app.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: You have an HTTP-triggered function. External partners need a key that works only for this one function, while your CI pipeline needs a key that works for all functions in the app. Which key types should you issue?
options: A function key for the partners and a host key for the CI pipeline (reserving the master key for administration)
The master key for everyone
The storage account key for both
A SAS token for the function URL
explain: Function keys scope to a single function, host keys scope to all functions in the app, and the master key is reserved for administrative access. Sharing the master key violates least privilege, and storage keys or SAS tokens do not authorize function invocations.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: A VPN gateway must support both site-to-site IPsec from headquarters and point-to-site connections from remote workers. The gateway was created as policy-based. What must change?
options: Recreate the gateway as route-based: point-to-site requires a route-based (dynamic routing) VPN gateway and cannot coexist with policy-based
Add a second public IP to the existing gateway
Enable BGP on the policy-based gateway
Nothing; policy-based gateways support point-to-site
explain: Point-to-site requires a route-based VPN gateway; policy-based gateways support site-to-site only. The gateway type cannot be changed in place, so you recreate it. A second public IP enables active-active rather than P2S, and BGP alone does not make a policy-based gateway support P2S.

q: You must ensure traffic from a subnet to a compromised external IP range is dropped silently inside Azure, without sending it to any appliance. Which user-defined route next-hop type should you use?
options: Virtual appliance
Internet
None: the None next hop drops (blackholes) the traffic
Virtual network gateway
explain: A next hop of None discards matching packets, which is the blackhole pattern. Virtual appliance forwards to an NVA, Internet sends the traffic out to the public internet, and virtual network gateway routes toward on-premises or ExpressRoute - none of which drop the traffic.

q: A subnet route table has a 0.0.0.0/0 route to the firewall (forced tunneling), but ExpressRoute BGP is injecting a competing default route that wins. How do you make your user-defined route take effect?
options: Delete the ExpressRoute circuit
Disable BGP route propagation on the route table so only your user-defined routes apply
Add a more specific route on the firewall
Enable IP forwarding on the subnet VMs
explain: Route tables have a disable BGP route propagation setting; with it on, BGP-learned routes are ignored and your UDRs govern routing. Deleting the circuit is overkill, a more specific route does not suppress propagation, and IP forwarding applies to NVA appliances rather than route selection.

q: You need to load-balance traffic across public frontends in East US and West Europe, with automatic failover if an entire region fails. Which load balancer tier supports this?
options: Regional Standard load balancer
Basic load balancer
Gateway load balancer
Cross-region (Global tier) load balancer with the regional load balancers as its backends
explain: The cross-region Global tier sits above regional load balancers to distribute traffic across regions with failover. Regional and Basic load balancers are single-region, and the Gateway load balancer chains network virtual appliances rather than balancing across regions.

q: You must insert a third-party firewall appliance transparently into the traffic path for multiple application subnets, without re-architecting routes per subnet. Which service chains the NVA into the data path?
options: Azure Firewall
Application Gateway
Gateway Load Balancer, which chains NVAs transparently and is referenced from the subnets
Traffic Manager
explain: Gateway Load Balancer is purpose-built for transparent NVA chaining in the data path. Azure Firewall is Microsoft managed firewall rather than a chaining mechanism for third-party appliances, Application Gateway is an HTTP load balancer, and Traffic Manager is DNS-based global routing.

q: The central security team deploys a Virtual Network Manager security admin rule denying RDP from the internet across all VNets. An app team has an NSG rule allowing RDP from the internet on their subnet and is surprised RDP is blocked. Why?
options: Security admin rules are evaluated before NSG rules, and a Deny terminates evaluation: the central deny cannot be overridden by the NSG allow
NSG rules always override Virtual Network Manager rules
The NSG allow rule needs a lower priority number to win
Virtual Network Manager rules only apply to outbound traffic
explain: Security admin rules always evaluate before NSG rules, and Deny (like Always Allow) terminates evaluation, so the central deny stands regardless of the NSG. NSG priority numbers only order rules within the NSG, and security admin rules apply to both inbound and outbound traffic.

q: You need to inspect encrypted HTTPS traffic leaving the VNet for data exfiltration, decrypting and re-encrypting it with your enterprise CA. Which Azure Firewall SKU and feature provides this?
options: Standard SKU with application rules
Premium SKU with TLS inspection
Basic SKU with network rules
Any SKU with threat intelligence in Alert mode
explain: TLS inspection is a Premium SKU-only feature that decrypts outbound TLS for inspection. Standard application rules filter by FQDN without decrypting payloads, and threat intelligence modes detect known-malicious destinations rather than inspecting encrypted content.

q: A developer needs occasional Bastion access to a single test VM and wants the cheapest option with no dedicated subnet or public IP to manage. Which should you choose?
options: Bastion Standard with 50 scale units
Bastion Basic in AzureBastionSubnet
A jumpbox VM with a public IP
Bastion Developer SKU: shared infrastructure with no VNet or subnet required, the lowest-cost option for dev and test
explain: The Developer SKU runs on shared infrastructure with no dedicated subnet or public IP, making it the cheapest fit for occasional dev/test access. Basic and Standard require AzureBastionSubnet plus a public IP, and a jumpbox VM adds patching and management overhead.
