q: You configure point-to-site with client address pool 10.0.0.0/24, but the VNet itself uses 10.0.0.0/16. Clients connect but cannot reach any VM. What is the misconfiguration?
options: The tunnel type is wrong
The root certificate was never uploaded
The point-to-site address pool overlaps the VNet address space: the pool must not overlap the VNet or on-premises ranges
The gateway SKU is too small for the client count
explain: The P2S client address pool must not overlap the virtual network address space (or on-premises ranges); overlapping ranges break routing to VMs. Tunnel type and certificates affect whether clients connect at all rather than routing, and SKU affects throughput rather than reachability.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: Your VNet is in Subscription A. The ExpressRoute circuit lives in Subscription B in the same tenant. You create the circuit connection from your VNet side. What does the circuit owner need to provide?
options: An authorization key generated on the circuit, which you enter when creating the connection
The circuit public IP address
Nothing: same-tenant circuits connect automatically
A VPN pre-shared key
explain: Cross-subscription ExpressRoute connections require the circuit owner to generate an authorization key that the VNet owner redeems. Same-tenant does not auto-authorize, circuits have no public IP to share, and pre-shared keys belong to VPN connections rather than ExpressRoute.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: An NSG on a VM subnet denies all outbound traffic, and DNS resolution for Azure resources breaks. You add an allow rule for outbound DNS. Which destination must remain reachable for Azure-provided DNS?
options: 168.63.129.16: the Azure platform DNS virtual IP
The VNet gateway private IP
explain: 168.63.129.16 is the Azure platform IP that provides DNS (plus health probes and DHCP); blocking it breaks name resolution for Azure resources. Public resolvers like 8.8.8.8 or 1.1.1.1 are not the platform DNS path, and the gateway IP does not serve DNS.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: You deploy a new VM with no public IP, no NAT gateway, and no load balancer outbound rules. It cannot reach the internet, though an identical VM deployed last year can. What changed?
options: The NSG default rules were changed
The region lost internet connectivity
New VMs always require a public IP for any outbound access
Default (implicit) outbound access is retired for new VMs: explicit outbound connectivity (NAT gateway, load balancer outbound rules, or a public IP) is now required
explain: Microsoft retired default outbound access for new VMs (September 30, 2025): new VMs need an explicit outbound method, while existing VMs kept working. NSG defaults did not change, the region is fine, and a public IP is only one of the explicit options rather than a universal requirement.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: You run an app in East US (primary) and West US (standby). Traffic must go to East US unless it is unhealthy, then fail over to West US. How do you configure this in Front Door?
options: Two separate Front Door profiles, one per region
A Traffic Manager profile with weighted routing
One origin group containing both origins, with priority set so East US is primary and West US is failover, and health probes driving the switch
An NSG rule prioritizing East US
explain: Front Door origin groups support priority-based failover: the primary origin serves traffic while health probes monitor it, and traffic shifts to the lower-priority origin on failure. Two profiles cannot fail over between each other, Traffic Manager is a separate DNS-based service, and NSGs filter traffic rather than routing it.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: After a regional failover, some clients keep hitting the failed region for several minutes while others fail over immediately. The Traffic Manager profile uses priority routing. What best explains the delay for those clients?
options: DNS TTL and client-side DNS caching: clients cache the resolved endpoint for the TTL duration, so failover time depends on TTL expiry
Traffic Manager only health-checks endpoints once per hour
Priority routing does not support failover
The failed endpoints must be manually re-enabled before traffic moves
explain: Traffic Manager is DNS-based, so clients and resolvers cache the endpoint for the TTL; failover is only as fast as cache expiry. Health probes run frequently, priority routing does support failover, and endpoints fail back automatically once healthy.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: Developers want to SSH from their local terminals through Bastion instead of the browser, and transfer files. The current Bastion host is Basic SKU. What must change?
options: Nothing: Basic SKU supports native client connections
Upgrade to Standard SKU (or higher) and enable native client support: native client connections require Standard or higher
Deploy a VPN gateway alongside Bastion
Open port 22 to the internet on each VM
explain: Native client connections (local SSH/RDP clients, plus file transfer) require the Standard SKU or higher; Basic is browser-only. A VPN is an alternative access path rather than the fix, and opening SSH publicly defeats the purpose of Bastion.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: An Application Gateway marks healthy backends as unhealthy because the default probe hits the app root path, which returns a 302 redirect. The app exposes /healthz returning 200. What should you configure?
options: A WAF exclusion for the redirect
A rewrite rule to change the probe path
A larger backend pool
A custom health probe targeting /healthz with the expected 200 status (and host header if the app requires it)
explain: Custom health probes let you set the path, interval, expected status code, and host header so the gateway judges health correctly. WAF exclusions address false-positive blocks rather than probing, rewrite rules modify client requests, and pool size does not fix probe configuration.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: You want all DNS queries from VNet workloads to flow through Azure Firewall for logging and filtering, without configuring each VM DNS settings individually. Which feature should you enable?
options: A user-defined route for 0.0.0.0/0 to the firewall
An Azure Private DNS resolver
DNS proxy on Azure Firewall: the firewall listens on port 53 and proxies and filters DNS queries
A dedicated DNS forwarder VM
explain: The firewall DNS proxy feature makes Azure Firewall intercept and proxy DNS on port 53, enabling logging and FQDN filtering in network rules. A UDR routes traffic but does not proxy DNS, the Private DNS resolver is a separate service, and a forwarder VM adds management overhead.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: Remote workers use a mix of Windows, macOS, and Linux laptops. You configure point-to-site with the SSTP tunnel type only. macOS and Linux users cannot connect. What is the issue?
options: SSTP is supported only on Windows clients: enable OpenVPN and/or IKEv2 for macOS and Linux
Point-to-site does not support macOS or Linux at all
The client address pool is exhausted
Microsoft Entra authentication requires SSTP
explain: SSTP is Windows-only; OpenVPN (SSL) and IKEv2 support macOS and Linux clients. Point-to-site fully supports those platforms via the other protocols, pool exhaustion would affect all clients, and Entra authentication works with OpenVPN rather than requiring SSTP.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: At the edge, you need to add a custom response header and redirect HTTP to HTTPS before traffic reaches the origins. Which Front Door feature should you use?
options: A network security group
A Front Door rules set (rules engine) attached to the route: header manipulation and URL redirects at the edge
A storage lifecycle management policy
A Private Link service
explain: The Front Door rules engine modifies requests and responses and performs redirects at the edge before traffic hits origins. NSGs filter network traffic, lifecycle policies manage blob data, and Private Link provides private connectivity - none of them rewrite HTTP at the edge.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: You create a Traffic Manager profile for app failover. What DNS record should you create so clients resolve your custom domain through Traffic Manager?
options: An A record pointing to the VM public IP
An MX record pointing to the profile
A TXT record with the profile name
A CNAME record pointing your domain to the profile <profilename>.trafficmanager.net DNS name
explain: Traffic Manager works by CNAME: your domain CNAMES to the profile DNS name, and Traffic Manager resolves it to the healthy endpoint. An A record bypasses Traffic Manager entirely, and MX or TXT records do not route application traffic.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: You need to find failed sign-ins where the client app name includes Exchange anywhere in the string, case-insensitively. Which KQL operator should you use?
options: == 'Exchange'
has 'Exchange'
contains 'Exchange'
startswith 'Exchange'
explain: contains performs a case-insensitive substring match, which finds Exchange anywhere in the value. has matches whole terms (token-based) rather than substrings, == requires an exact match, and startswith only matches at the beginning of the string.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: When a critical alert fires, you must notify all subscription Owners, but team membership changes frequently and you do not want to maintain an email list. Which action group notification should you use?
options: A webhook pointing at a static distribution list
Email the Azure Resource Manager role (Owners): the action resolves the current role members dynamically
An SMS to a single phone number
A push notification to one user
explain: The Email Azure Resource Manager Role action notifies whoever currently holds the selected RBAC role, so no list maintenance is needed as the team changes. Webhooks, SMS, and push target fixed endpoints that you must maintain yourself.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: After each deployment, you want a marker on the Application Insights charts showing when the new version went live, so performance regressions can be correlated with releases. What should you create?
options: A workbook per release
A daily analytics data export
A custom log table for release events
Release annotations (deployment markers) on the Application Insights resource
explain: Release annotations place deployment markers directly on Application Insights metric charts, making it easy to correlate regressions with releases. Workbooks visualize data without marking releases, exports move data elsewhere, and a custom table does not overlay markers on the charts.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: You build an Azure dashboard and share it with the support team. They can open it but see no-access errors on some tiles. What controls their access to the underlying data?
options: Azure RBAC on the underlying resources: sharing grants access to the dashboard, but each tile still enforces RBAC on its data source
The dashboard built-in password
The number of tiles pinned
The subscription spending limit
explain: A shared dashboard requires RBAC on the dashboard resource itself plus read access to every underlying data source; tiles fail where the viewer lacks data permissions. There is no dashboard password, and tile count or spending limits do not cause per-tile access errors.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: You need one alert rule that notifies the ops team of any service issue or planned maintenance affecting Virtual Machines or Storage in East US or West US. How should you scope the Service Health alert?
options: Create four separate alert rules, one per service per region
Use Resource Health alerts instead
Create a single Service Health alert selecting multiple services and multiple regions
Use an activity log alert on the subscription
explain: A single Service Health alert rule can cover multiple services and multiple regions, which is the intended design for broad operational coverage. Separate rules add toil without benefit, Resource Health tracks per-resource availability rather than service events, and activity log alerts do not fire on service health events.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: You stream resource logs to a Log Analytics workspace. One team wants per-resource-type dedicated tables for granular retention; another wants the legacy combined table. Which diagnostic setting controls this?
options: The workspace daily cap
The destination table mode: Azure diagnostics (single combined table) versus resource-specific (dedicated tables per resource type)
The alert rule severity
The action group common alert schema
explain: Diagnostic settings offer Azure diagnostics mode (one combined table) and resource-specific mode (dedicated tables such as StorageBlobLogs). The daily cap limits ingestion volume, severity classifies alerts, and the alert schema shapes notifications - none of them change the table layout.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: A query returns 40 columns but the report needs only TimeGenerated, Computer, and EventID. Which operator trims the result to those columns?
options: extend
summarize
take
project: selects exactly the specified columns
explain: project selects the named columns (with project-away and project-rename variants for refinement). extend adds computed columns rather than removing them, summarize aggregates rows, and take limits the row count rather than the columns.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: You collect custom logs with the Azure Monitor Agent. The same data must land in a Log Analytics workspace for querying and in Event Hubs for the SIEM. Where do you configure the two destinations?
options: In the data collection rule (DCR): a single DCR supports multiple destinations, including Log Analytics workspaces, Event Hubs, and Storage
In the VM network security group
In the alert rule
In the storage account firewall
explain: Data collection rules define both data sources and destinations, and one rule can fan out to a workspace, Event Hubs, and Storage simultaneously. NSGs and firewalls control network traffic rather than telemetry routing, and alert rules consume data rather than routing it.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: In Resource Health, a VM shows a status of Degraded. What does this state mean?
options: The VM has been deleted
The VM is running normally with no detected issues
The VM is running but Azure has detected a performance-impacting issue: between Available and Unavailable
The VM was deallocated by the user
explain: Resource Health uses four states: Available (healthy), Degraded (running with detected issues), Unavailable (down due to a platform event), and Unknown (no data). Degraded does not mean deleted or user-deallocated - it signals a detected problem worth investigating.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: When an alert fires you need to run an Azure Automation runbook, call an internal HTTPS endpoint, and trigger an Azure Function for enrichment. Which action group capabilities cover all three?
options: Email notifications only
An Automation runbook action, a webhook action, and an Azure Function action: action groups natively support runbooks, webhooks, functions, logic apps, and ITSM connectors
SMS notifications only
A single Azure mobile app push notification
explain: Action groups provide native action types for Automation runbooks, generic webhooks, Azure Functions, Logic Apps, and ITSM tools, covering all three integrations. Email, SMS, and push are notification channels for people rather than system integrations.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: You alert on storage queue length to drive autoscale decisions. Queue length is a point-in-time gauge, and you want the alert to evaluate the latest value rather than the sum over the window. Which aggregation should the metric alert use?
options: Total
Count
Sum of averages
Maximum (or Average): for gauge metrics like queue length, evaluate the latest or peak value rather than summing samples
explain: Queue message count is a gauge, so summing samples across the evaluation window is meaningless - Average, Maximum, or Minimum reflects the actual queue depth. Total and Count suit cumulative or event-count metrics rather than point-in-time gauges.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: You want a weekly compliance report of missing patches every Monday, but actual patching must only happen during the Saturday maintenance window. How do you configure this in Azure Update Manager?
options: Create a periodic assessment schedule for Mondays and a separate patch deployment schedule for Saturdays
Enable automatic VM guest patching only
Run a one-time update deployment each Saturday
Use Azure Policy to install the patches
explain: Update Manager separates assessment schedules (scan and report compliance) from deployment schedules (install patches), so each runs on its own cadence. Automatic guest patching installs without a controlled window, one-time deployments do not repeat, and Azure Policy assesses compliance but does not install patches.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: Azure Advisor flags several single-instance VMs and recommends moving them to availability zones. Which Advisor category does this fall under, and why zones?
options: Cost: zones are cheaper than availability sets
Security: zones encrypt data at rest
High availability: zone-redundant deployment survives a datacenter failure, unlike a single zone or a single VM
Operational excellence: zones improve resource tagging
explain: Advisor high-availability recommendations push architectures that survive zone failure, and availability zones provide that datacenter-level isolation. Zones are not a cost, encryption, or tagging feature.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: Without changing application code, you want to see SQL query durations and HTTP call latencies for your app in Application Insights. Which capability provides this?
options: Custom events that you instrument manually in code
Automatic dependency tracking: the SDK auto-collects SQL, HTTP, and Azure SDK calls with their durations
Availability tests
The Azure Monitor Agent on the VM
explain: The Application Insights SDK automatically collects dependency telemetry - SQL queries, HTTP calls, Azure Storage and Service Bus operations - with durations and no code changes. Custom events require instrumentation, availability tests probe endpoints synthetically, and the Azure Monitor Agent collects VM guest logs rather than app dependencies.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: Your Log Analytics bill spiked. You need to identify which tables ingested the most billable data in the last seven days. Which query approach works?
options: Query the AzureActivity table
Check the storage account metrics
Estimate from the table names
Query the Usage table filtering where _IsBillable is true, summarizing Quantity by DataType
explain: The Usage table records ingestion per table with the _IsBillable flag, so filtering on it and summarizing by DataType ranks billable ingestion. AzureActivity tracks control-plane operations rather than ingestion, storage metrics do not cover workspace ingestion, and guessing from names is not data.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: Your incident process must distinguish a regional outage, a planned maintenance window, a new feature announcement, and a security advisory. Which Service Health event types map to these?
options: Service issues, planned maintenance, health advisories, and security advisories: the four Service Health event types
All four are activity log events
All four are Resource Health events
Service issues only; the rest arrive by email
explain: Service Health tracks exactly four event types: service issues (outages), planned maintenance, health advisories (feature changes), and security advisories. The activity log covers control-plane operations, Resource Health covers per-resource availability, and all four types are available in the portal and via alerts rather than email only.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: You configure alert routing: Sev 0 and Sev 1 page the on-call engineer, Sev 2 and 3 create tickets, Sev 4 only logs. A colleague asks what the severity scale means. How do you explain it?
options: Severity runs 1 to 5, with 5 most critical
Severity is informational only and does not affect routing
Alert severities run Sev 0 (critical) to Sev 4 (verbose); a lower number means higher urgency
Severity maps to the resource pricing tier
explain: Azure Monitor alert severities run from Sev 0 (critical) through Sev 4 (verbose), with lower numbers indicating higher urgency - which is why paging uses Sev 0 and 1. There is no Sev 5, severity actively drives routing, and it is unrelated to pricing tiers.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: From a VM Monitoring blade you run a log query and it automatically scopes to that VM data. You then open Logs from the workspace and the same query returns data for all VMs. What explains the difference?
options: The VM blade query is broken
Resource-context (resource-centric) queries scope to the selected resource; workspace-context queries span the whole workspace
The workspace daily cap filtered the first query
RBAC blocks the workspace-scoped query
explain: Opening Logs from a resource runs the query in resource context (scoped to that resource), while opening Logs from the workspace runs it in workspace context across all data. The same KQL behaves differently because the initial scope differs - the query is not broken, and caps or RBAC are not the cause.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: A query over 30 days of SecurityEvent data times out. It filters on EventID first and applies the TimeGenerated filter last. What is the most effective optimization?
options: Add more columns with project
Increase the workspace daily cap
Union additional tables into the query
Filter on TimeGenerated first: time filtering prunes partitions before expensive predicates run, which is the primary KQL performance rule
explain: TimeGenerated filtering first lets the engine skip irrelevant data partitions before evaluating other predicates; applying it last forces a full scan. project does not reduce scanned data, the daily cap limits ingestion rather than query speed, and union widens the scan further.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: Compliance asks for an audit trail of who ran which KQL queries against the Log Analytics workspace last month. Which table provides this?
options: LAQueryLogs: the workspace query-audit table recording query text, user, and execution details
AzureActivity
Heartbeat
The storage account $logs container
explain: LAQueryLogs captures an audit record of queries executed against the workspace, including who ran them. AzureActivity logs control-plane operations rather than queries, Heartbeat tracks agent availability, and $logs covers storage analytics rather than the workspace.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: Your company launches a partner portal — a SaaS app registered in your Microsoft Entra tenant. You want partner employees to register themselves using their Google accounts or an email one-time passcode, with zero IT involvement per user. What should you configure?
options: Have an administrator send individual B2B invitations from the Entra admin center for every partner
Create a self-service sign-up user flow for the application, adding Google as an identity provider and enabling email one-time passcode
Publish the app through an entitlement management access package so partners can request access
Turn on Security Defaults, which automatically enables self-service sign-up for external users
explain: Self-service sign-up user flows in Microsoft Entra External ID let external users register themselves for an application using federated identity providers like Google or an email one-time passcode — exactly the zero-touch requirement. Per-user B2B invitations work but defeat the self-service goal. Access packages govern access for users who are already provisioned or invited; they are not a self-registration page. Security Defaults enforces MFA and blocks legacy auth tenant-wide and has nothing to do with external self-registration.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: A Conditional Access policy must require phishing-resistant MFA for administrators. One admin argues that Microsoft Authenticator phone sign-in already counts as phishing-resistant, so no hardware keys are needed. Is the admin correct?
options: No; the phishing-resistant strength covers FIDO2 security keys/passkeys, Windows Hello for Business, and certificate-based authentication — Authenticator phone sign-in is passwordless but not phishing-resistant
Yes; any use of the Microsoft Authenticator app satisfies the phishing-resistant authentication strength
Yes, but only when number matching is enabled for Authenticator push notifications
No; phone sign-in is not MFA at all, so it cannot satisfy any MFA requirement
explain: Microsoft classifies FIDO2/passkeys, Windows Hello for Business, and certificate-based authentication as phishing-resistant; Authenticator phone sign-in is passwordless but NOT phishing-resistant, so the admin is wrong. Number matching hardens push approvals against MFA fatigue but does not change the method's phishing-resistance classification. Option D overcorrects: phone sign-in is a valid second factor that satisfies a plain 'require MFA' grant — it just does not satisfy the phishing-resistant strength.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: In cross-tenant access settings you leave the default inbound trust with MFA claims untrusted, then add an organizational entry for partner tenant Contoso and enable trust for multifactor authentication claims from Contoso. A Contoso guest who completed MFA in their home tenant signs in to your tenant. Which setting applies?
options: The default settings apply, because defaults always win over organizational entries
The guest is prompted for MFA again, because trust settings only apply to B2B direct connect
The organizational settings for Contoso take precedence, so the guest is not re-prompted for MFA
Both settings merge, so the guest must complete MFA in both tenants
explain: Organizational (per-tenant) entries take precedence over the default settings, so Contoso's trust entry governs and the home-tenant MFA claim is honored without a second prompt. Defaults apply only to external organizations with no specific entry — they never override one. Trust settings apply to B2B collaboration guests, not only direct connect, and there is no merge behavior that would double-prompt the user.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: You transfer billing ownership of a production subscription to another Microsoft Customer Agreement billing account in the same tenant, WITHOUT selecting 'Move subscription tenant'. What is the effect on the running resources and RBAC assignments?
options: Resources are redeployed under the new billing account and all RBAC assignments are recreated automatically
All RBAC role assignments are permanently deleted, exactly as in a tenant move
The subscription is disabled until the new billing admin accepts the transfer request
Resources keep running untouched and existing RBAC assignments are maintained; only which billing account pays changes
explain: Transferring billing ownership without moving the tenant only changes who pays — resources keep running and RBAC assignments are preserved. The recipient accepts the request and selects a payment method, but the subscription is not disabled in the interim. RBAC is wiped only when you also move the subscription to a different Microsoft Entra tenant. Nothing is redeployed: billing ownership is a billing-scope change, not a resource move.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: You need to deploy an ARM template that assigns an Azure Policy initiative at the management group scope. When you run New-AzManagementGroupDeployment, the command fails asking for a location, even though management groups are not regional. Why is the location required?
options: Deployment metadata is stored in a region, so every management-group-scope deployment must specify a location
The location determines which region the policy initiative is enforced in
Management groups are regional resources, so the location picks the right one
The location is only required for Bicep files; ARM JSON templates do not need it
explain: The deployment object itself — its metadata and state — is stored by Azure Resource Manager in a region, so a location is mandatory even at management group scope; it has no effect on where the policy applies. Enforcement scope comes from the deployment target (the management group), not the location. Management groups are global rather than regional, and the location requirement applies equally to ARM JSON and Bicep.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: A contractor needs the Contributor role on one resource group for exactly the six weeks of a migration project. You want them to activate the role themselves when needed, with no standing access afterward. What should you configure in PIM?
options: An active (permanent) assignment for six weeks, then manually remove it
An eligible assignment with a defined start and end date covering the six weeks
An eligible assignment with no end date; PIM automatically expires eligibility after 30 days
A time-bound active assignment that the contractor activates through My Roles
explain: Eligible assignments can carry explicit start and end dates, giving just-in-time activation during the project window with automatic expiry afterward — no standing privilege and no manual cleanup. An active assignment grants standing access for the whole period, the opposite of just-in-time. PIM does not auto-expire open-ended eligible assignments, and active assignments never require activation, so D contradicts itself.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: You create a custom Azure RBAC role that must let application support read secrets from a specific Key Vault but grant no management-plane rights on the vault itself. Which permission block should the role definition use?
options: Actions containing Microsoft.KeyVault/vaults/secrets/read
Actions containing Microsoft.KeyVault/vaults/* with a NotActions entry for management operations
DataActions containing Microsoft.KeyVault/vaults/secrets/getSecret/action
DataActions containing Microsoft.KeyVault/vaults/write
explain: Key Vault secret values are data-plane operations governed by DataActions such as getSecret/action, while vault configuration is the management plane under Actions. An Actions entry with a secrets/read-style string targets the wrong plane and grants no data access. A wildcard Actions grant with NotActions carve-outs still only covers the management plane and would hand over vault management rights — the opposite of least privilege.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: Your on-premises Active Directory has 50 OUs, but only the 'Corp-Users' and 'Corp-Groups' OUs should synchronize to Microsoft Entra ID. Service accounts in the other OUs must never become cloud objects. Where do you configure this?
options: In the Entra admin center under a Hybrid management sync-exclusions blade
By moving the unwanted OUs into a separate Active Directory forest
By assigning Deny permissions on the Microsoft Entra Connect service account for those OUs
In Microsoft Entra Connect sync configuration, using OU-based filtering
explain: OU-based filtering is the built-in Microsoft Entra Connect sync option that limits synchronization to selected OUs — exactly the requirement. There is no sync-exclusions blade in the admin center; filtering is configured in the Connect wizard and synchronization rules. A separate forest is unnecessary upheaval, and AD permission hacks on the service account are unsupported and would break sync health rather than filter cleanly.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: You assign a DeployIfNotExists policy that deploys diagnostic settings to every VM. Compliance shows non-compliant VMs but nothing is remediated, and the assignment has no managed identity configured. What is missing?
options: The policy assignment needs a managed identity with rights to perform the deployment, plus a remediation task for the existing VMs
DeployIfNotExists policies remediate automatically; the non-compliant state means the policy definition is invalid
The assignment needs the Owner role on the subscription before any evaluation occurs
A CanNotDelete lock must be removed from the VMs before remediation can run
explain: DeployIfNotExists (and Modify) effects execute their deployments under the assignment's managed identity, so without one the deployment step has no credentials and existing non-compliant resources are never fixed — you must also create a remediation task for resources that already exist. Evaluation itself needs no identity. Owner on the scope is not required (the identity only needs rights for the specific deployment), and locks are irrelevant when the root cause is the missing identity.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: An administrator deletes a cloud-only user account by mistake. Thirty minutes later the help desk asks whether the account, its group memberships, and licenses can be recovered without recreating everything. What do you tell them?
options: Deleted users are gone immediately; recreate the account and reassign everything
Restore the user from Deleted users within 30 days; group memberships and attributes are recovered
Only the UPN is recoverable; group memberships must be rebuilt manually
Restoration is only possible if the user held a P1 license before deletion
explain: Soft-deleted users sit in Deleted users for 30 days and can be restored with their group memberships and attributes intact. There is no instant permanent deletion on this path and no license prerequisite for restore. Licenses are freed at deletion and may need reassigning, but the identity and its memberships come back — option C understates what a restore recovers.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: Your company builds a SaaS application that customers in other Microsoft Entra tenants will consent to and sign in to. How should you configure 'Supported account types' on the app registration?
options: Accounts in this organizational directory only (single tenant)
Accounts in any organizational directory and personal Microsoft accounts, to maximize reach
Accounts in any organizational directory (multitenant)
Personal Microsoft accounts only, since customers are external
explain: Multitenant ('accounts in any organizational directory') lets other tenants consent to and use the app — the SaaS requirement. Single-tenant restricts the app to your own directory, blocking external customers entirely. Adding personal Microsoft accounts pulls in consumer identities a B2B SaaS app does not need, and personal-accounts-only would exclude the organizational customers altogether.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: You configure SAML SSO for a third-party HR application as an enterprise app. HR requires that only members of the 'HR-Staff' group can sign in, but today anyone in the tenant who finds the URL can get in. What should you change?
options: Create a Conditional Access policy that blocks all users except HR-Staff
Convert the enterprise application into an app registration
Enable Privileged Identity Management for the enterprise application
Set Assignment required to Yes on the enterprise application and assign the HR-Staff group
explain: The 'Assignment required?' (user assignment required) setting makes the application enforce user/group assignment at SSO time — unassigned users are denied. A Conditional Access block policy could work but is the heavy indirect route when the app has the native control. An enterprise app already has an app registration behind it, so 'converting' is meaningless, and PIM governs role activation, not application SSO access.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: Your tenant has Microsoft Entra ID P1. You need a Conditional Access grant control that requires FIDO2 security keys for admins but a different method mix for everyone else, as a named reusable strength per audience. Can you build this with custom authentication strengths?
options: Yes; custom authentication strengths (up to 15 per tenant) are available with P1
No; custom authentication strengths require Microsoft Entra ID P2
No; authentication strengths only support the three built-in options and cannot be customized
Yes, but Conditional Access itself requires P2 so you must upgrade first
explain: Custom authentication strengths are a P1 capability — you can define up to 15, combining methods like FIDO2 and Authenticator to match each audience. P2 adds risk-based policies, Identity Protection, and PIM, not the strengths feature. The three built-in strengths exist alongside custom ones, and Conditional Access as a whole is P1, so D misstates the licensing.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: You plan to manage membership of the 'SQL-Admins' security group through PIM for Groups. The group has 40 eligible members, but only 10 users currently hold Microsoft Entra ID P2 licenses. What is the licensing requirement?
options: Only the users who will actually activate membership need P2; the rest can remain unlicensed
Every user eligible for membership in the PIM-managed group needs a P2 (or Entra ID Governance) license
No licenses are needed because group membership is not a directory role
One P2 license assigned to the group object covers all members
explain: Microsoft requires P2 (or Entra ID Governance) for every user eligible for membership or ownership in a PIM-for-Groups managed group — not just those who activate. Licenses are per-user and can never be assigned to cover a group object. PIM for Groups is a P2 feature regardless of whether directory roles are involved, so C is wrong.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: Users complain the Microsoft Entra sign-in page looks generic, which makes phishing emails harder to spot. You want the tenant logo, a background image, and custom sign-in page text. Where do you configure this, and what license is needed?
options: Conditional Access > Custom controls; requires P2
Intune > Company Portal branding; requires Intune licenses
Microsoft Entra ID > Company branding; requires P1
Authentication methods > FIDO2 policy; requires P1
explain: Company branding in Microsoft Entra ID customizes the sign-in experience (banner logo, background image, sign-in page text) and is a P1 feature. Conditional Access custom controls integrate external authentication providers, not page visuals. Intune Company Portal branding affects the Intune app, not the browser sign-in page, and the FIDO2 policy governs passkey registration, not visuals.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: Your tenant uses Active Directory Federation Services (federated sign-in) with Microsoft Entra Connect, and password hash sync is deliberately disabled for compliance. The help desk asks whether federated users can still use SSPR with password writeback. What is the correct answer?
options: No; password writeback for federated users requires password hash sync to be enabled
No; SSPR is only supported for cloud-only and password-hash-synced users
Yes, but only if you switch the tenant to pass-through authentication first
Yes; password writeback supports federated, pass-through, and password-hash-synced users — PHS is not a prerequisite
explain: Password writeback works for all three hybrid sign-in methods — federated (AD FS), pass-through authentication, and password hash sync — because the writeback channel is independent of how sign-in validates credentials. PHS is not required, and PTA is not a prerequisite either; federated users are explicitly supported, so neither a method switch nor enabling hash sync is needed.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: You discover that a tenant-wide User Administrator accidentally reset the password of a break-glass emergency account. You want a boundary so that only explicitly designated admins can modify the emergency accounts — even tenant-wide role holders. What should you use?
options: A restricted management administrative unit containing the emergency accounts
A standard administrative unit containing the emergency accounts
A Conditional Access policy scoped to the emergency accounts
A CanNotDelete resource lock on the user objects
explain: A restricted management administrative unit blocks modifications — password resets, property changes, deletes — from any administrator not assigned at that AU's scope, including tenant-wide User Administrators. A standard AU only scopes the admins you assign; it does not block tenant-wide admins from acting on its members. Conditional Access governs sign-in, not directory modifications, and resource locks apply to Azure resources, not directory user objects.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: Finance wants a separate budget for each of the company's 12 project resource groups, with alerts per project. A colleague claims budgets can only be created at the subscription scope. Is that correct?
options: Yes; Azure budgets exist only at the subscription scope
No; budgets can be scoped to a management group, subscription, or resource group
No; budgets can be scoped to individual resources but not resource groups
Yes, but you can simulate per-RG budgets with one subscription budget and 12 alert rules
explain: Budgets support management group, subscription, and resource group scopes, so one budget per project resource group is the direct design. There is no per-resource budget scope, and a single subscription budget cannot partition spend tracking per resource group for alerting — scope is what partitions the tracking.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: You apply a CanNotDelete lock at the resource group level on 'rg-prod'. A Contributor then tries to delete a single virtual machine inside rg-prod. What happens?
options: The delete succeeds; locks apply only to the object they are placed on
The delete succeeds because the Contributor role overrides locks
The delete is blocked; locks set on a parent scope are inherited by child resources
The delete is queued until an Owner approves it in the activity log
explain: Locks are inherited — a lock on a resource group protects every resource inside it, so the VM delete is denied. The lock does not care which role attempts the delete; even an Owner cannot delete a locked resource without first removing the lock. Option A confuses locks with something scope-local, and there is no approval-queue mechanism for lock conflicts.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: Your SSPR policy still allows security questions as a verification method, and 300 users registered answers years ago. What should you plan for?
options: Nothing; security questions remain a fully supported long-term SSPR method
Disable security questions today and users who registered them will keep working indefinitely
Security questions are being promoted to a phishing-resistant method, so expand their use
Migrate users to Authenticator app or phone methods; Microsoft is retiring security questions for SSPR in March 2027
explain: Microsoft announced retirement of security questions for SSPR in March 2027 due to guessability and social-engineering risk — users relying on them will be unable to reset passwords after that date. They are the opposite of phishing-resistant, and administrator accounts already cannot use them. The correct move is proactive migration to supported methods in the Authentication methods policy, not waiting for the enforcement date.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: You manage a legacy general-purpose v1 storage account that you want to use with lifecycle management and the Cool access tier. What is the supported upgrade path to general-purpose v2?
options: Perform the in-place upgrade to GPv2 from the storage account configuration; no data migration is needed
Create a new GPv2 account and use AzCopy to migrate; v1 accounts cannot be upgraded
Upgrade to Premium block blobs first, then convert to GPv2
Enable hierarchical namespace on the v1 account, which automatically upgrades it to v2
explain: Azure supports an in-place upgrade of GPv1 (Storage kind) to GPv2 (StorageV2) with no downtime or data movement — it unlocks access tiers, lifecycle management, and other v2 features. Creating a new account and migrating is unnecessary work. Premium block blobs is a different account kind, not a stepping stone, and hierarchical namespace cannot be enabled on an existing account at all.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: You prepare an Azure Import/Export job to ship 40 TB on customer-owned drives. Compliance requires the drives to be encrypted and the job metadata tracked with journal files. What must you do before shipping?
options: Encrypt the drives with Azure Disk Encryption and upload a CSV manifest to the storage account
Encrypt the drives with BitLocker and use the WAImportExport tool to prepare the drives and generate journal files
Ship the drives unencrypted; Azure encrypts them automatically on receipt
Format the drives as ReFS and email the drive serial numbers to the Azure data center
explain: Import/Export requires drives encrypted with BitLocker, and the WAImportExport tool prepares the drives, copies the data, and produces the journal files the datacenter uses to drive the import. Azure Disk Encryption is a VM-disk feature, not the drive-prep mechanism for Import/Export. Drives are never accepted unencrypted, and there is no email-based manifest process — the journal files are the tracking mechanism.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: An application writes work items to an Azure Storage queue and a worker processes them within minutes. The team assumes failed messages stay in the queue forever for later inspection. What is the actual default behavior?
options: Messages persist indefinitely until explicitly deleted
Messages expire after 24 hours by default
Messages expire after 7 days by default unless a different TTL is set
Messages are moved to a poison queue after 7 days automatically
explain: Queue messages have a default time-to-live of 7 days, after which they are deleted — you must set an explicit TTL (or -1 for never expire) to change that. There is no infinite retention by default. Poison queues are a pattern you build yourself using dequeue-count thresholds; the platform never moves messages there automatically.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: You enable static website hosting on a storage account for a marketing site. Visitors to the site root should see the homepage, and broken links should show a branded error page instead of raw XML. What must you configure?
options: Upload the pages to the $root container and set the container ACL to Blob
Enable the static website feature only; the portal auto-generates both pages
Set a default document in the CDN endpoint configuration
Specify an index document name (for example index.html) and an error document path (for example 404.html) in the static website settings
explain: Static website hosting serves the configured index document for directory roots and the configured error document (e.g., 404.html) for missing blobs — both are explicit settings alongside the $web container. The portal does not generate these pages, CDN default-document settings do not apply to the storage static-website endpoint itself, and content must live in the $web container, not $root.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: You need to get 20 TB of VHD files into Azure as managed disks using an Azure Data Box. In what form should the VHDs be uploaded to the Data Box?
options: As page blobs, from which you then create managed disks
As block blobs, which Data Box converts to managed disks automatically
As files in Azure Files, then converted with AzCopy
As table entities describing the disk layout
explain: Data Box import for managed disks works by uploading the VHDs as page blobs; you then create managed disks from those page blobs. Block blobs cannot back managed disks and Data Box performs no automatic conversion. Azure Files and table storage are unrelated to the managed-disk import path.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: A Linux team mounts a premium NFS 4.1 Azure file share. Security requires that the root user on client VMs cannot act as root against the share — root requests must be mapped to an anonymous identity — while regular users keep their own UIDs. Which root squash setting should you apply?
options: NoRootSquash, which leaves the client root user mapped to root on the share
AllSquash, which maps every UID and GID to the anonymous user
DisableSquash, which turns off all identity mapping for the share
RootSquash, which maps only UID/GID 0 to the anonymous UID/GID
explain: RootSquash maps requests from UID/GID 0 (root) to the anonymous user (65534) while leaving all other UIDs untouched — exactly the requirement. NoRootSquash (the default) leaves root as root, which is what security wants to avoid. AllSquash would also neutralize root, but it anonymizes every user, breaking the requirement that regular users keep their identities. DisableSquash is not a real setting.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: A storage account firewall denies all public traffic. An Azure Synapse workspace (a specific resource instance) must read data from the account, but it has no stable public IP and is not in your VNet, so VNet and IP rules cannot cover it. How do you grant it access?
options: Add a resource instance rule allowing that specific Synapse workspace through the storage firewall
Enable the trusted-services bypass, which covers any Azure resource instance
Assign the Synapse workspace the Storage Blob Data Reader role; RBAC bypasses the firewall
Create a private endpoint on the Synapse workspace side
explain: Resource instance rules allow specific Azure resource instances that cannot be isolated through VNet or IP rules — the documented purpose of this rule type. The trusted-services bypass covers a fixed list of first-party Azure services, not arbitrary customer resource instances like a Synapse workspace. RBAC authorizes data access but never bypasses network rules, and private endpoints are created on the storage account side (per sub-resource), not on the client service.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: You still run two legacy unmanaged OS disks (page blobs in a storage account). Before a risky maintenance window you want a point-in-time copy of each disk. What is the correct approach?
options: Use Azure Backup, which only supports managed disks, so first convert the disks
Take a blob snapshot of each page blob; unmanaged disks support page-blob snapshots
Copy the page blobs to block blobs and snapshot those instead
Export the disks with a SAS URL and re-upload them after maintenance
explain: Unmanaged disks are page blobs, and page blobs support blob snapshots — the legacy, supported way to capture a point-in-time copy. Converting to managed disks is a bigger migration than a pre-maintenance safety copy needs. Block blobs cannot back a disk and copying there first adds pointless steps, and exporting/re-uploading is not a snapshot at all.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: An integration needs read access to blobs in two different containers in the same storage account for 24 hours. A developer proposes creating one service SAS. What should you tell them?
options: One service SAS covers the whole storage account, so the plan works
Create two service SAS tokens, one per container — or use an account SAS instead
Use an account SAS, which can delegate access across containers and even services in the account
Service SAS is the only SAS type that supports read access to blobs
explain: An account SAS can delegate access to resources across the storage services (blob, file, queue, table) and multiple containers, so one token covers both containers. A service SAS is scoped to a single container, blob, share, or queue — it cannot span two containers, which is the flaw in the developer's plan. Option B is a workable fallback, but the question asks for the single-token answer; D is simply false since account SAS supports read too.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: A developer accidentally commits an ad-hoc service SAS (signed with the storage account key, no stored access policy) to a public GitHub repository. The token is valid for 30 more days. What must you do to invalidate it?
options: Delete the commit from the repository history
Shorten the token's remaining lifetime in the portal
Create a stored access policy with the same name to override the token
Rotate the storage account keys the SAS was signed with
explain: An ad-hoc SAS is validated purely against the account-key signature and its embedded expiry — there is no server-side token record to delete, so rotating the signing key is the only invalidation path (accepting that it also invalidates other tokens and connection strings using that key). Deleting the commit does not un-expose the token, issued tokens cannot be edited, and a stored access policy only governs tokens created with reference to it — it cannot retroactively capture an ad-hoc token. This is why production SAS should use stored access policies or user delegation SAS.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: You configure blob object replication between two storage accounts, but no block blobs replicate. Both accounts are GPv2 in supported regions. What is the most likely missing prerequisite?
options: Blob versioning must be enabled on both the source and destination accounts
The destination account must use the Premium performance tier
Object replication requires the source account to be ZRS
Both accounts must be in the same region
explain: Object replication requires blob versioning enabled on both source and destination accounts — replication copies are tracked as versions, so without it nothing replicates. The destination tier and source redundancy are irrelevant to the feature, and cross-region replication is the normal design (same-region is allowed but not required). Note the destination account is also fixed once the replication policy is created.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: Compliance requires that blobs in the 'hr-docs' container use a different customer-managed key than the rest of the storage account. What is the cleanest way to implement this?
options: Create a separate storage account for hr-docs with its own key
Set a default encryption scope on the hr-docs container pointing at the second key
Enable infrastructure encryption on the storage account
Rotate the account-level customer-managed key weekly
explain: Encryption scopes let you set a default scope per container (backed by a different key in Key Vault), so hr-docs gets its own key without a second account. A separate account works but is heavyweight when scopes exist. Infrastructure encryption adds a second platform-managed layer account-wide rather than per-container key separation, and rotating the account key changes the key for everything, not just hr-docs.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: You create an Azure Policy that requires a lifecycle management policy on every storage account, and it flags your premium block blobs account as non-compliant. The team asks you to add a lifecycle rule to that account. What do you tell them?
options: Add the lifecycle rule; premium block blobs support lifecycle management like GPv2
Convert the account to GPv2 first, then add the lifecycle rule
Lifecycle management is not supported on premium block blob accounts; use a GPv2 account for tiering rules or manage the data manually
Enable hierarchical namespace on the account, which unlocks lifecycle management
explain: Lifecycle management is not supported for premium block blob storage accounts — the policy expectation itself is wrong for this account kind. Premium block blobs cannot be converted to GPv2 in place, and hierarchical namespace is not supported on premium block blob accounts at all. The correct responses are to exempt the account or move tiering workloads to a GPv2 account.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: You configure Azure Disk Backup for a production VM's data disks. During setup you must designate a resource group for snapshots. What is stored in that resource group?
options: The Recovery Services vault metadata and backup policies
Full independent copies of the VM configuration
The disk encryption keys for the backed-up disks
Incremental snapshots of the disks, managed by the Backup service
explain: Azure Disk Backup stores its incremental snapshots in the designated snapshot resource group; the Backup service manages their lifecycle there. Vault metadata and backup policies live in the Backup vault itself, not the snapshot resource group. The snapshots hold disk data — not VM configuration copies — and encryption keys stay in Key Vault, never in a snapshot resource group.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: A lifecycle management rule must move only blobs tagged Project=Falcon to the Cool tier, leaving untagged blobs in Hot. The blobs share one container with no usable naming prefix. How do you scope the rule?
options: Apply blob index tags to the blobs and use a blobIndexMatch filter in the lifecycle rule
Use a prefixMatch filter on the container name
Filter the rule by blob metadata key Project
Create one lifecycle rule per blob
explain: Lifecycle rules support blobIndexMatch filters that match blob index tags, so tagging Project=Falcon and filtering on the tag scopes the rule precisely. prefixMatch filters on blob name prefixes, which do not exist here. Blob metadata is not a lifecycle filter dimension — only prefixes and index tags are. Per-blob rules do not exist; rules operate at the account level with filters.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: A partner asks for SFTP access to an Azure Files share on your storage account. The account already has hierarchical namespace and SFTP enabled. What do you tell them?
options: Enable the SFTP protocol toggle on the file share itself
SFTP is supported only against blob containers, not Azure Files shares — use SMB or NFS 4.1 for the share
SFTP works on file shares, but only with Active Directory authentication
Upgrade the account to premium file shares to unlock SFTP
explain: Azure SFTP support targets Blob Storage (block blob containers) — it does not work against Azure Files shares, regardless of toggles or tier. There is no per-share SFTP switch, and no authentication or tier change enables it. File shares are accessed over SMB or NFS 4.1; SFTP clients should be pointed at blob containers instead.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: A data engineer with the Contributor role on a storage account tries to set POSIX ACLs on an ADLS Gen2 directory and gets Access Denied. Contributor was expected to be 'full access'. What is missing?
options: The Contributor role must be assigned at the container scope instead of the account scope
The engineer needs the Reader role in addition to Contributor
The engineer needs the Storage Blob Data Owner role, which grants data-plane ACL management
POSIX ACLs can only be managed with the storage account keys
explain: Managing ACLs is a data-plane operation, and Contributor (like Owner) covers only the management plane — so even an account-scope Contributor gets Access Denied on ACL operations. Storage Blob Data Owner grants the data-plane rights to set ACLs. Moving the Contributor assignment to container scope does not change the plane, Reader adds nothing, and account keys are not required when RBAC data roles exist.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: You try to delete a container that holds VHD page blobs with infinite leases. The delete fails. What must you do first?
options: Delete the storage account and recreate it without the container
Wait for the leases to expire; infinite leases eventually lapse
Remove any stored access policies defined on the container
Break the active leases on the blobs, then delete the container
explain: A container holding leased blobs cannot be deleted until the leases are broken (or released). Infinite leases never expire on their own, so waiting is futile — this is also why VHDs use infinite leases. Stored access policies govern SAS revocation, not leases, and deleting the whole storage account is absurd overkill for a container delete.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: Your team receives an Azure Data Box for a 60 TB migration. Which methods can they use to copy data onto the device?
options: Copy data over SMB, NFS, or REST to the Data Box shares
The Data Box automatically pulls data from your storage accounts once connected
Only the Azure Data Box Gateway virtual appliance can load data onto it
Only AzCopy over a private endpoint is supported
explain: Data Box exposes its shares over SMB and NFS (plus a REST interface), and you copy data to it with normal file-copy tools, Robocopy, or AzCopy. The device never pulls data itself. Data Box Gateway is a separate virtual-appliance product, not the load mechanism, and AzCopy is one option among several — not the only one.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: Ransomware encrypted the current version of a critical blob, but blob versioning captured clean prior versions. What is the fastest self-service restore?
options: Open a support ticket to restore the blob from the version
Promote the clean version to become the current base blob
Enable soft delete and wait for the retention period to lapse
Copy the version to a new storage account and swap the connection strings
explain: Promoting a version (copying the version over the base blob) instantly restores the clean content as current — a self-service operation with no ticket needed. Soft delete protects against deletion, not overwrites, and waiting accomplishes nothing. Copying to another account adds pointless steps when the version already sits alongside the blob.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: A serverless function app must reach a private SQL database over the VNet and avoid cold starts on its HTTP endpoints, while still scaling to zero when idle. It runs on Linux. Which hosting plan fits?
options: Consumption plan
Premium plan
Flex Consumption plan
Dedicated (App Service) plan
explain: Flex Consumption adds VNet integration and optional always-ready instances to serverless scale-to-zero billing on Linux — exactly the ask. The classic Consumption plan has no VNet support. Premium supports VNet and pre-warmed instances but keeps at least one instance always allocated (no scale to zero, higher cost floor). Dedicated is not serverless at all.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: Your AKS workloads have spiky GPU and memory needs, and maintaining right-sized node pools has become guesswork. You want the platform to provision the optimal VM SKU automatically for pending pods and consolidate aggressively. You currently use the cluster autoscaler. What should you do?
options: Keep the cluster autoscaler and add a node pool per SKU
Enable node auto-provisioning alongside the cluster autoscaler for best results
Switch the workloads to virtual nodes with ACI
Enable node auto-provisioning (NAP) and disable the cluster autoscaler
explain: NAP (built on Karpenter) provisions right-sized VMs on the fly for pending pods and consolidates aggressively, but it cannot run alongside the cluster autoscaler — one system must own node scaling, so you disable the autoscaler when enabling NAP. Adding more pools is the manual guesswork you want to escape, and virtual nodes (ACI) are a burst mechanism, not SKU optimization.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: You plan an AKS cluster that will run 5,000 pods, but the VNet has only a /24 left for the cluster subnet. Which network plugin approach makes this feasible?
options: Azure CNI Overlay, where pods get IPs from a separate overlay CIDR and only nodes consume VNet IPs
Azure CNI with a pod subnet carved from the same /24
kubenet with a user-defined route table
Azure CNI Node Subnet sharing node and pod IPs from the /24
explain: With Azure CNI Overlay, pods are assigned IPs from a private overlay CIDR logically separate from the VNet, so the /24 only needs to cover nodes — 5,000 pods fit. Both flat CNI modes assign pod IPs from VNet address space, which a /24 cannot hold for thousands of pods. The trade-off to know: pod IPs are SNAT'd behind node IPs and are not directly reachable from outside the cluster.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: You must back up 20 on-premises Hyper-V VMs and their SQL Server workloads to a Recovery Services vault. Which solution fits?
options: Install the MARS agent on each VM
Deploy Azure Backup Server (MABS) on-premises
Enable Azure Site Recovery replication for the VMs
Install the Azure Monitor agent on each VM
explain: Azure Backup Server (MABS) is the on-premises backup server that protects multiple machines and workloads (VMs, SQL) to a Recovery Services vault. The MARS agent backs up a single server's files and folders directly — it is not designed for multi-VM workload protection. Site Recovery is disaster-recovery replication, not backup, and the Azure Monitor agent collects telemetry, not backups.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: After failing over on-premises VMs to Azure with Site Recovery, the primary site is restored. What is the correct failback sequence?
options: Run a planned failover immediately; reprotection happens automatically
Delete the Azure VMs, then re-enable replication from on-premises
Reprotect the Azure VMs so they replicate back on-premises, run a planned failover, commit it, then re-protect the on-premises machines
Run a test failover to the on-premises site and commit it as the failback
explain: Failback follows four stages: reprotect the Azure VMs (replicate back to on-premises), planned failover from Azure to on-premises, commit, then re-protect the on-premises machines to restore forward protection. Planned failover is not available until reprotection produces recovery points. Deleting the Azure VMs destroys the replicated state you need, and a test failover creates an isolated copy — it is a drill, not a failback.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: Your team runs a function app on the Flex Consumption plan and wants blue-green deployments using deployment slots with auto-swap. What should you tell them?
options: Configure deployment slots on the Flex Consumption app; slots are supported on every Functions plan
Move the app to the classic Consumption plan, which supports deployment slots with auto-swap
Flex Consumption supports slots, but auto-swap requires upgrading within the plan
Deployment slots are not supported on Flex Consumption (or Consumption); use the Premium or Dedicated plan for slot-based blue-green deployments
explain: Deployment slots exist only on the Premium and Dedicated (App Service) plans — neither Flex Consumption nor classic Consumption supports slots, so there is nothing to enable or upgrade within Flex. Moving to classic Consumption does not help since it also lacks slots. The correct path for slot-based blue-green deployments with auto-swap is the Premium or Dedicated plan.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: To save cost, an operator shuts down a VM from inside the guest OS. The VM shows 'Stopped' in the portal but compute charges continue. Why?
options: An OS-level shutdown leaves the VM in the Stopped state with compute still allocated; you must stop/deallocate it from Azure to release the allocation
Billing stops only after the VM is deleted
The VM must be stopped from the serial console for billing to stop
Compute charges always continue for 24 hours after any shutdown
explain: Shutting down from inside the guest OS stops the OS but Azure keeps the compute allocation (and bills for it) — the portal shows Stopped, not Stopped (deallocated). Stopping from the portal, CLI, or PowerShell deallocates the VM and releases the compute allocation, ending compute charges (storage charges continue). There is no 24-hour billing tail and no need to delete the VM.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: You need a Compute Gallery image that will deploy 50 identical web servers. How should you prepare the source VM?
options: Capture it as specialized so each VM keeps the source computer name
Generalize the VM (Sysprep on Windows, deprovision on Linux) before capturing
Take a snapshot of the OS disk and share the snapshot directly
Enable hibernation on the source VM before capture
explain: Gallery images meant for many VMs must be generalized — Sysprep (Windows) or agent deprovision (Linux) strips machine-specific identity so each deployment gets a unique identity. A specialized image preserves the source identity and suits only single-VM copies. Snapshots are not deployable gallery images, and hibernation is unrelated to imaging.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: You need to attach an Ultra Disk to an existing production VM, but Ultra Disk compatibility cannot be enabled on it. What is the cause?
options: Ultra Disks require the VM to be stopped (deallocated) first
Ultra Disks can only be used as OS disks
Ultra Disk compatibility must be enabled when the VM is created; it cannot be enabled afterward
Ultra Disks require a Premium SSD v2 data disk to already be attached
explain: The 'Enable Ultra disk compatibility' setting is a creation-time property of the VM — it cannot be toggled on an existing VM, so you must recreate the VM with the setting enabled and then attach the Ultra Disk. Stopping/deallocating does not unlock it. Ultra Disks are data-disk-only (never OS disks), and there is no Premium SSD v2 prerequisite.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: A regulated workload requires hardware-based trusted execution environment (TEE) isolation with AMD SEV-SNP, without rewriting the application. Which VM option provides this?
options: Trusted launch VMs with Secure Boot and vTPM
Dedicated Hosts for hardware isolation
Confidential containers on ACI
Azure confidential VMs (DCasv5/ECasv5 series)
explain: Azure confidential VMs (DCasv5/ECasv5) use AMD SEV-SNP to provide a hardware-based TEE that encrypts VM memory, with lift-and-shift compatibility. Trusted launch adds Secure Boot and vTPM but not SEV-SNP memory encryption. Dedicated Hosts give single-tenant hardware isolation, not a TEE, and confidential containers require containerizing the application.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: Your CI pipeline needs the public nginx:latest image from Docker Hub available in your Azure Container Registry for AKS deployments, without installing Docker on the build agent. What is the best approach?
options: Run az acr import with --source docker.io/library/nginx:latest to pull the image server-side into ACR
Push the image with docker push directly to Docker Hub from the pipeline
Enable ACR admin credentials and configure the AKS nodes to pull from Docker Hub
Use az acr build to rebuild nginx from source on every pipeline run
explain: az acr import copies the image registry-to-registry entirely server-side — no Docker daemon or local pull/push is needed, and it avoids Docker Hub rate limits at deploy time. Pushing to Docker Hub does not place the image in ACR. Having nodes pull from Docker Hub directly reintroduces rate limits and external dependency, and rebuilding nginx from source on every run is wasteful when the upstream image can simply be imported.

q: Your team runs microservices on Azure Container Apps and wants new event-driven functions to live in the same environment with KEDA autoscaling, Dapr, and VNet connectivity — without managing Kubernetes. How should you host the functions?
options: Deploy them to a Consumption plan function app in the same resource group
Host the function apps on Azure Container Apps (Microsoft.App resource provider, kind=functionapp)
Run the functions on AKS with the virtual-kubelet ACI connector
Deploy the functions to an App Service Environment
explain: Azure Functions on Azure Container Apps runs function apps natively in the Container Apps environment (kind=functionapp), inheriting KEDA event-driven scaling, Dapr, VNet connectivity, and revision management alongside your microservices. A Consumption plan is a separate hosting model without the shared environment. AKS with virtual nodes is heavier than required, and an ASE is a dedicated App Service footprint — not the shared serverless container environment asked for.

q: An App Service web app throws intermittent errors that never appear in the portal's log stream because the instances recycle. You need application logs retained for 30 days for post-incident analysis. What should you configure?
options: Enable Application Insights Profiler on the app
Increase the App Service plan to Premium so logs are retained automatically
Enable application logging to Blob storage in the App Service diagnostics settings
Open the Kudu console and copy the log files manually each day
explain: App Service diagnostics can write application logs to Blob storage, where they persist independently of instance recycles for as long as your retention policy keeps them. The log stream and filesystem logs are ephemeral on recycled instances. Profiler captures performance traces, not application log retention; scaling the plan does not retain logs; and manual Kudu copies are not a sustainable retention strategy.

q: You bind three custom hostnames to one App Service app, each needing its own TLS certificate. A junior admin suggests buying three public IP addresses for IP-based SSL. What is the correct guidance?
options: IP-based SSL is required; SNI is not supported on App Service
Assign one certificate to all three hostnames with a wildcard only
Upload the certificates to Key Vault and reference them from the app settings
Use SNI SSL bindings — one IP address serves all hostnames with their own certificates
explain: SNI SSL lets multiple hostnames with different certificates share a single IP address — the TLS handshake's server-name indication selects the right certificate. IP-based SSL dedicates an IP per certificate and is only needed for legacy clients without SNI support. A single wildcard only works if the hostnames share a domain pattern, and Key Vault references supply certificates but do not change the binding model.

q: Your container app serves traffic on its default FQDN. Marketing wants it on shop.contoso.com with HTTPS. The app has external ingress enabled. What should you do?
options: Add a custom domain to the container app and bind a managed certificate for shop.contoso.com
Create a CNAME record only; Container Apps issues certificates automatically for any CNAME
Deploy an Application Gateway in front of the container app for TLS termination
Custom domains require switching the app to internal ingress first
explain: Container Apps supports adding custom domains to an app with external ingress, including a managed certificate for TLS — then you point the DNS record at the app FQDN. A CNAME alone provides no certificate. An Application Gateway in front is unnecessary when the platform handles domains and certificates natively, and internal ingress would remove external access rather than enable a public domain.

q: Your AKS API server has a public endpoint, and security wants only the corporate office public IP range to reach it — without making the cluster private. What should you configure?
options: Deploy Azure Firewall in front of the API server
Configure API server authorized IP ranges with the office CIDR
Enable the cluster's private DNS zone
Assign an NSG to the AKS node subnet blocking all inbound traffic
explain: API server authorized IP ranges restrict which public IPs can reach a public API server endpoint — the exact control for this requirement without going private. A private cluster is the alternative the scenario explicitly rules out. Azure Firewall cannot front the managed API server, and an NSG on the node subnet governs node traffic, not the control-plane endpoint.

q: You set up Azure Site Recovery to replicate on-premises VMware VMs to Azure, but replication never starts. The configuration server is healthy. What component is most likely missing on the source VMs?
options: The Azure Monitor agent
The Microsoft Entra Connect sync agent
The Site Recovery mobility service agent
The Azure Backup MARS agent
explain: The mobility service agent must be installed on each source machine to capture and replicate disk writes to Azure — without it, replication never starts even with a healthy configuration server. The Azure Monitor agent collects telemetry, Entra Connect syncs identities, and the MARS agent performs backups; none of them drive Site Recovery replication.

q: Your team publishes golden images in an Azure Compute Gallery. Another subscription in the same tenant needs to deploy VMs from those images, but must not be able to modify or delete the gallery. How do you share it?
options: Export the image versions as VHDs and copy them to the other subscription's storage
The gallery is automatically visible to every subscription in the tenant
Enable cross-subscription replication targets in the gallery
Grant the other subscription's users the Reader role on the gallery with Azure RBAC
explain: Sharing a gallery is done with Azure RBAC — Reader on the gallery (or image definition/version) lets the other subscription deploy VMs without modify/delete rights. Galleries are not tenant-visible by default. Exporting VHDs is manual toil that bypasses versioning, and replication targets control where image versions are replicated geographically, not who can access them.
