q: Your function app uses AzureWebJobsStorage with a connection string, and security wants stored secrets eliminated. The app has a system-assigned managed identity. What should you do?
options: Enable identity-based connections for AzureWebJobsStorage and grant the identity the Storage data roles it needs
Move the connection string into Key Vault references; the app still authenticates with the key
Enable the function app's admin key rotation schedule
Switch the storage account to premium to unlock identity authentication
explain: Functions supports identity-based connections for AzureWebJobsStorage — the managed identity authenticates to Storage, eliminating the stored key, once granted the needed data roles (Blob/Queue/Table data roles). Key Vault references still use the account key at runtime, just stored elsewhere. Admin keys authorize the Functions host API, not storage, and the storage tier has nothing to do with identity authentication.

q: Your AKS node pool reimages slowly during upgrades, and you want faster node provisioning with lower managed-disk cost. The nodes are stateless. Which OS disk option helps?
options: Premium SSD v2 OS disks
Ephemeral OS disks, stored on the VM cache/temp disk
Ultra Disks as OS disks
Shared managed disks for the node pool
explain: Ephemeral OS disks place the OS on the VM's local cache/temp storage, so reimages are fast and no managed-disk cost accrues — ideal for stateless node pools like AKS. Premium SSD v2 cannot be used as an OS disk. Ultra Disks are data-disk-only, and shared disks are for clustered data workloads, not node OS disks.

q: A branch office connects to Azure with a site-to-site VPN, but the on-premises VPN device sits behind a NAT router and IKE negotiation fails. What should you verify?
options: That the Azure VPN gateway uses a Basic SKU, which supports NAT devices
That the connection uses policy-based routing
That NAT traversal (NAT-T) is in play — Azure VPN gateways encapsulate traffic in UDP 4500 when a NAT device is detected
That the branch uses a public IP from the Azure address space
explain: When a VPN device sits behind NAT, NAT traversal encapsulates ESP in UDP port 4500 so the NAT device can translate it — Azure VPN gateways support NAT-T. The Basic SKU is legacy and not the fix, policy-based versus route-based is unrelated to NAT, and the branch must use its own public IP, never Azure address space.

q: Your ExpressRoute circuit runs at 1 Gbps but utilization has dropped permanently, and finance wants it reduced to 500 Mbps. What is the supported path?
options: Select 500 Mbps on the circuit Configuration page; the downgrade applies without downtime
Open a support ticket to throttle the port to 500 Mbps
Enable the Premium add-on, which allows bandwidth reduction
Deprovision the circuit and provision a new one at 500 Mbps; bandwidth cannot be reduced in place
explain: ExpressRoute bandwidth can be increased in place (given port capacity) but never decreased — reducing bandwidth requires deprovisioning the circuit and reprovisioning a new one. The portal offers no downgrade option, support cannot throttle a provisioned port, and the Premium add-on changes features, not this constraint.

q: You create an Azure private DNS zone for corp.internal and link a VNet. A junior admin asks where to create the NS records to delegate the zone, as they would in public DNS. What do you tell them?
options: Private DNS zones get an SOA record automatically; NS delegation is not used — resolution comes from the VNet links
Create NS records pointing at Azure's 168.63.129.16 resolver
Delegate the zone from the public parent zone with NS records
NS records are required but Azure hides them from the portal
explain: Azure private DNS zones are authoritative via their VNet links and carry an automatic SOA record — there is no NS delegation model like public DNS, because resolution is scoped to linked VNets rather than the public hierarchy. 168.63.129.16 is the platform resolver clients use, not an NS target, and no public parent delegation applies to a private zone.

q: An NSG must allow inbound HTTPS from 40 branch-office public IPs across 5 port ranges to a web tier. A colleague creates 45 separate rules. What is the better approach?
options: NSGs only support one address and one port range per rule, so 45 rules are required
Use one augmented security rule with multiple source addresses and multiple port ranges
Use an application security group per branch office instead
Move the web tier to a new VNet; NSGs cannot filter by source IP
explain: Augmented NSG rules accept multiple source/destination addresses and multiple ports/port ranges in a single rule — one rule replaces the 45. Application security groups group VM NICs, not external public IPs, and NSGs absolutely filter by source IP; a new VNet solves nothing.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: You need OWASP Top-10 managed protections plus bot mitigation on your Front Door-fronted web app. Your Front Door profile is currently Standard tier. What must you change?
options: Nothing; Standard includes the managed rule sets
Switch the WAF policy to Detection mode on Standard
Upgrade to Front Door Premium and attach the Microsoft Default Rule Set and Bot Manager rule set
Move the WAF to an Application Gateway WAF_v2 instead
explain: Managed rule sets (Default Rule Set 2.1, Bot Manager) are a Front Door Premium-only feature — Standard supports only custom rules, so you must upgrade and attach the managed sets. Detection versus Prevention is a policy mode, not a tier unlock, and moving to Application Gateway changes the architecture instead of using the Front Door WAF you already have.

q: An external contractor without Azure credentials needs RDP access to a single VM for a week. Your Bastion host is Basic SKU. What is the cleanest solution?
options: Give the contractor a guest account and portal access to the VM blade
Email the contractor the VM's public IP and open RDP to the internet
Shareable links work on Basic SKU; just create one for the VM
Upgrade Bastion to Standard and create a shareable link for the VM
explain: Bastion shareable links let users without Azure portal access connect to a specific VM through Bastion — but the feature requires Standard (or Premium) SKU. Basic does not support it. A guest account plus portal access is heavier and broader than needed, and exposing RDP to the internet defeats the purpose of Bastion.

q: Your Azure Firewall must allow outbound HTTPS to any host under *.contoso.com for a SaaS integration, but the exact hostnames change frequently. Which rule type supports this?
options: An application rule with the FQDN target *.contoso.com
A network rule with destination *.contoso.com
A DNAT rule translating *.contoso.com
An IDPS signature for the contoso.com domain
explain: Firewall application rules support FQDNs including wildcards like *.contoso.com — designed for exactly this dynamic-SaaS case. Network rules work on IPs/ports and do not accept FQDNs or wildcards. DNAT rules handle inbound translation, not outbound FQDN filtering, and IDPS signatures detect threats rather than allowlisting destinations.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: You associate a route table with Subnet-A, then try to associate a second route table with the same subnet for a migration. The portal rejects it. Why?
options: Route tables can only be associated at the VNet level, not the subnet level
A subnet can be associated with only one route table at a time
The subnet needs a NAT gateway before a second route table can attach
Route tables must be in the same resource group as the VNet to associate
explain: A subnet can have exactly one route table association — one table can be linked to many subnets, but not the reverse. For migration, you edit the existing table or swap the association. Route tables associate at subnet level (not VNet), NAT gateways are unrelated, and cross-resource-group association is allowed within the subscription.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: You use Traffic Manager with Priority routing: primary in East US, secondary in West US. East US recovers after an outage. What happens to new DNS resolutions?
options: Traffic stays on West US until you manually fail back the endpoints
Traffic splits 50/50 between the endpoints until the TTL expires on all clients
Traffic automatically fails back to the East US primary once its probes succeed
The West US endpoint must be disabled before traffic returns to East US
explain: Priority routing always prefers the highest-priority healthy endpoint — when the primary's probes succeed again, Traffic Manager automatically fails traffic back; no manual step is needed. There is no 50/50 split (that is Weighted routing), and disabling the secondary is unnecessary and would remove your failover target.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: Your VPN gateway runs Generation 1 VpnGw1 and you need Generation 2 throughput. You try to resize the SKU in the portal but Gen2 SKUs are not offered. What is the required path?
options: Resize to VpnGw1AZ first, which converts the gateway to Gen2 automatically
Open a support ticket to convert the generation in place
Wait for the automatic platform upgrade of all Gen1 gateways
Delete the Gen1 gateway and recreate it as Gen2; generation changes require redeployment with downtime
explain: Resizing works within a generation, but Gen1 to Gen2 requires deleting and recreating the gateway — new public IP, reconfigured connections, and downtime. There is no in-place generation conversion and no support-ticket shortcut. (Gateways already on Standard public IPs are being moved to Gen2 by the platform over time, but an on-demand Gen1-to-Gen2 change remains delete-and-recreate.)
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: You must peer VNet-A in your tenant with VNet-B in a partner's Microsoft Entra tenant. Address spaces do not overlap. What is required to establish the peering?
options: Network Contributor permissions in both subscriptions — for example, a user from each tenant added as a guest in the opposite tenant with Network Contributor on the VNet
Both VNets must be moved into the same subscription first
A VPN gateway in each VNet; peering does not work across tenants
Global Administrator in both tenants
explain: Cross-tenant peering is supported; the requirement is Network Contributor in both subscriptions, commonly done by adding each tenant's user as a guest in the opposite tenant with Network Contributor on the respective VNet. No subscription move is needed, no gateways are required (that is VNet-to-VNet VPN, a different connectivity type), and Global Admin is far beyond the network-scoped permission required.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: Your VPN gateway must survive a zonal datacenter failure. Which SKU choice provides zone redundancy?
options: Any Generation 1 SKU, which is zone-redundant by default
A zone-redundant SKU such as VpnGw1AZ
The Basic SKU with two public IPs
An active-active Gen1 gateway, which is inherently zone-redundant
explain: Zone-redundant VPN gateways use the AZ SKUs (VpnGw1AZ through VpnGw5AZ). Generation 1 non-AZ SKUs are not zone-redundant, Basic is a legacy SKU without the feature, and active-active provides instance redundancy within whatever zones the SKU deploys to — it does not by itself make a Gen1 gateway zone-redundant.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: Attackers are credential-stuffing your login page at 2,000 requests/minute from rotating IPs. You want Front Door WAF to block client IPs exceeding 100 requests/minute to /login. Where do you configure this?
options: In the Front Door origin group health probe settings
With a managed Default Rule Set exclusion for /login
With a custom WAF rate-limit rule (RateLimitRule) matching /login, threshold per client IP per minute
With a Traffic Manager weighted profile in front of Front Door
explain: A custom WAF rate-limit rule (rule type RateLimitRule) enforces a per-client-IP request threshold over 1 or 5 minutes, optionally scoped by match conditions like the /login URI — exactly the ask. Health probes check origin health, managed rule sets detect exploit signatures rather than rate-limit, and Traffic Manager does DNS routing, not request throttling.

q: You manage 200 VNets with Azure Virtual Network Manager and need to apply security admin rules to all production VNets, with membership updating automatically as new production VNets are created. What should you use?
options: A static network group with manually added VNets
An Azure Policy initiative assigned separately to each VNet
One NSG per VNet with identical rules
A dynamic network group using Azure Policy-based conditions such as tags
explain: VNM network groups support dynamic membership driven by Azure Policy conditions (such as tags), so new production VNets join automatically and security admin rules apply to the whole set. Static groups require manual upkeep, and per-VNet initiatives or NSGs multiply management overhead — the dynamic group is the designed solution.

q: Your zone contoso.com is hosted in Azure DNS. You need the zone apex (contoso.com itself) to resolve to your Traffic Manager profile. A CNAME at the apex is not allowed by DNS standards. Which record type should you use?
options: An alias record set pointing at the Traffic Manager profile
An A record with the Traffic Manager's current IP address
An NS record delegating the apex to Traffic Manager
A TXT record referencing the Traffic Manager profile
explain: Azure DNS alias records let the zone apex point directly at Azure resources like Traffic Manager or Front Door — the supported answer to the apex-CNAME problem, and the alias follows the target if its addresses change. A static A record breaks when the profile's IPs change, NS records delegate subzones rather than aliasing, and TXT records are not resolvable as addresses.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: Each customer gets a subdomain like customer42.apps.contoso.com in your private DNS zone, and new customers are onboarded daily. Creating a record set per customer is becoming toil. What is the cleaner approach?
options: Delegate a child zone per customer with NS records
Create a wildcard record set such as *.apps.contoso.com resolving to the app frontend
Enable auto-registration on the VNet link for the customer names
Use a single A record and rely on the HTTP Host header
explain: A wildcard record set (*.apps.contoso.com) resolves every current and future customer subdomain with one record — the designed answer for dynamic subdomains. Per-customer child-zone delegation multiplies zone management. Auto-registration only covers VM hostnames in linked VNets, not arbitrary customer names, and a single A record cannot distinguish subdomains at DNS resolution time.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: A line-of-business app talks to Azure SQL over the public endpoint using the SQL port, and security wants to allowlist the FQDN rather than IPs in Azure Firewall. Which rule configuration works?
options: A network rule allowing TCP 1433 to the SQL FQDN
A DNAT rule forwarding the SQL FQDN
An application rule allowing the MSSQL protocol to the SQL FQDN
An IDPS allowlist entry for the SQL domain
explain: Firewall application rules support HTTP, HTTPS, and MSSQL protocols with FQDN targets — an MSSQL application rule allowlists the SQL FQDN without tracking IPs. Network rules match IPs/ports and cannot take FQDNs. DNAT rules handle inbound port translation, not outbound FQDN allowlisting, and IDPS is a threat-detection engine, not an allowlist mechanism.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: Your Traffic Manager profile fronts two web apps whose health endpoint is /healthz on port 8080 over HTTPS. The default HTTP port-80 probe of / marks both endpoints Degraded. What should you configure?
options: A longer DNS TTL so clients keep using the last-known healthy endpoint
Switch the routing method from Performance to Priority
Add a nested Traffic Manager profile for each endpoint
Configure a custom probe with HTTPS protocol, port 8080, and path /healthz
explain: Traffic Manager lets you customize the endpoint monitor: protocol (HTTP/HTTPS), port, and path — so an HTTPS probe of /healthz on port 8080 matches what the apps actually serve. The default probe (HTTP, port 80, path /) is what wrongly marks them Degraded. TTL only affects DNS caching, routing method does not change probe behavior, and nested profiles add hierarchy without fixing the probe mismatch.

q: Your Front Door frontend is shop.contoso.com, but the origin web app expects the Host header internal-api.contoso.com and returns 404 otherwise. Where do you fix the Host header sent to the origin?
options: Set the Origin host header to internal-api.contoso.com on the Front Door origin
Add a URL rewrite rule on the Front Door route
Add internal-api.contoso.com as a second custom domain on the frontend
Create a WAF exclusion for the Host header
explain: The Origin host header setting controls the Host header Front Door sends to the origin with each request — setting it to internal-api.contoso.com fixes the 404. A rewrite rule changes the URL path, not the Host header. Adding a frontend custom domain changes what clients request, not what the origin receives, and WAF exclusions tune rule evaluation, not headers.

q: You design an active-active site-to-site VPN gateway for higher availability. How many public IP addresses does the active-active gateway require?
options: None; active-active gateways use private IPs only
Two — one public IP per gateway instance
Three — two for the instances plus one for the BGP peer
One shared public IP that floats between the instances
explain: An active-active VPN gateway runs two instances, each requiring its own public IP — the on-premises device establishes tunnels to both. A single floating IP defeats the purpose of two independent instances. BGP peering uses the instance IPs (or APIPA addresses), not a third public IP, and gateway instances always need public IPs for the tunnels.

q: You need a pie chart of VM counts by operating system type from the last 30 days of AzureActivity data. Which KQL completes the query? AzureActivity | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | summarize count() by OSType ...
options: | render table
| order by count_ desc
| render piechart
| take 10
explain: The render operator with piechart visualizes the summarized results as a pie chart — the requested output. render table just lists rows, take 10 truncates the data, and order by sorts without visualizing. Note the time filter comes first for performance, then summarize, then render.

q: You need the list of distinct operation names that appear in AzureActivity this week — one row per operation, no duplicates. Which KQL operator should you use?
options: summarize count() by OperationName
project OperationName
top 10 by TimeGenerated
distinct OperationName
explain: distinct returns one row per unique value of the column — exactly the deduplicated list asked for. summarize count() by OperationName also deduplicates but adds a count column (useful when you want frequencies, not a plain list). project keeps duplicates, and top just limits rows.

q: From SigninLogs you need two numbers in one row: total sign-ins and how many of them failed (ResultType != 0). Which aggregation expression gives the failed count?
options: failed = countif(ResultType != 0)
failed = dcount(ResultType)
failed = sum(ResultType)
failed = count() where ResultType != 0
explain: countif counts only rows satisfying the predicate, so summarize total = count(), failed = countif(ResultType != 0) yields both numbers in one row. dcount counts distinct values (wrong metric), sum adds the numeric codes (meaningless), and 'count() where' is not valid KQL syntax — the filter belongs inside countif.

q: Your KQL query uses ago(7d) in four different where clauses, and you want a single named value you can change in one place. What should you declare at the top of the query?
options: A datatable with one row
A let statement, for example: let cutoff = ago(7d);
A print statement assigning the value
A stored function in the workspace
explain: The let statement binds a name to an expression (scalar, table, or function) for reuse throughout the query — change it once, everywhere updates. A datatable defines tabular constants, not scalar reuse. print outputs values rather than declaring variables, and a stored function is workspace-level overhead for a single-query constant.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: A high-volume table was switched to the Basic Logs plan to cut ingestion cost. The team asks how long they can query it interactively, and whether they can alert on it. What is the correct answer?
options: 8 days interactive; alerts are supported
90 days interactive; alerts are supported
30 days interactive (fixed); log alerts are NOT supported on Basic plan tables
12 months interactive; only metric alerts are blocked
explain: Basic Logs tables have a fixed 30-day interactive retention period (the older 8-day figure is outdated) and do not support log alerts or full Analytics-plan query features — longer retention comes from archive settings plus search jobs. Alerting on the table requires the Analytics plan. The 8-day number appears in older documentation and should not be used.

q: A production SQL Server VM must install patches during the maintenance window but must NEVER reboot automatically — the DBA team reboots manually afterward. Which reboot setting should the Update Manager schedule use?
options: Always
IfRequired
RebootOnly
Never
explain: The Never reboot setting installs updates without rebooting, leaving the manual reboot to the DBAs. Always reboots unconditionally and IfRequired reboots when an update demands it — both violate the requirement. RebootOnly is a legacy Automation Update Management enum value, not an Update Manager schedule setting (which uses Always, IfRequired, or Never).

q: The on-call engineer wants critical alerts delivered as push notifications to the Azure mobile app on their phone. Which action group action type should you add?
options: Azure mobile app push notification
Email to an ARM role
SMS to the engineer's number
Voice call to the engineer's number
explain: The Azure mobile app notification action type pushes alerts to the Azure mobile app — the requested channel. Email-to-ARM-role notifies role members by email, not push. SMS and voice are valid action types but deliver to the phone's messaging/dialer, not as Azure mobile app push notifications.

q: You create an availability test from 5 locations. You want an alert only when the site is genuinely down — not when a single location has a network blip. How should the alert rule be configured?
options: Alert when any single location fails once
Alert when the average failed locations is greater than or equal to 3 over 5 minutes
Alert only after all 16 possible locations fail
Disable the alert and watch the Availability dashboard manually
explain: The availability alert condition is based on failed-location count over a window (default: 3 failed locations over 5 minutes) — requiring multiple locations filters out single-location blips while catching real outages. Alerting on any single failure pages for transient network issues. Tests support up to 16 locations, but the alert does not require all of them to fail, and manual dashboard-watching is not alerting.

q: You want Azure VM platform metrics (CPU, disk, network) queryable with KQL alongside your log data, so one workbook can correlate metrics and events. Where do you send the metrics?
options: Nowhere; platform metrics cannot leave the Metrics data store
To an Event Hubs namespace only
To a Log Analytics workspace via the resource's diagnostic settings
To a storage account as JSON blobs
explain: Diagnostic settings can route platform metrics to a Log Analytics workspace, making them queryable in KQL next to logs for unified workbooks. Metrics do live in the Metrics store by default, but they are not trapped there. Event Hubs and storage are valid diagnostic destinations, but neither makes metrics KQL-queryable — only the Log Analytics destination does.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: You onboard a production AKS cluster to Container insights and want baseline alerting aligned with Microsoft's recommended signals. Which set of conditions should you implement?
options: Only Azure Activity Log alerts for cluster create/update operations
Only Prometheus recording rules with no thresholds
Only Advisor cost recommendations emailed weekly
Node CPU and memory utilization thresholds, NotReady node counts, pod phase (Failed/Pending) counts, and node disk space
explain: Microsoft's recommended Container insights alert set covers node CPU/memory pressure, nodes in NotReady state, pod phase counts (Failed, Pending, Unknown), and node disk space — the core cluster-health signals. Activity Log alerts only catch control-plane operations, Prometheus rules without thresholds alert on nothing, and Advisor cost recommendations are optimization guidance, not health alerting.

q: From the Heartbeat table you need the most recent heartbeat row for each computer, including all its columns. Which summarize expression should you use?
options: latest = arg_max(TimeGenerated, *) by Computer
latest = max(TimeGenerated) by Computer
top 1 by TimeGenerated desc
distinct Computer
explain: arg_max(TimeGenerated, *) returns the full row carrying the maximum TimeGenerated per Computer — the latest heartbeat with all columns. max(TimeGenerated) returns only the timestamp, losing the other columns. top 1 gives the single latest row overall, not per computer, and distinct just lists computer names.

q: You need SigninLogs rows where the Location field is missing or empty (some records have null, others an empty string). Which filter catches both?
options: where Location == ''
where isempty(Location)
where isnull(Location)
where Location has ''
explain: isempty() returns true for both null and empty-string values — the only predicate catching both cases. Comparing to '' misses nulls, isnull() misses empty strings, and has performs a full-text term match rather than an emptiness test.

q: A single VM shows as unavailable in the portal. You need to determine whether Azure platform health or the guest OS is at fault. Which blade answers that?
options: Azure Service Health
The Azure status page
Resource Health for that VM
Log Analytics workspace health
explain: Resource Health gives the per-resource platform view (Available, Degraded, Unavailable, Unknown) plus platform events for that specific VM — distinguishing Azure-side issues from guest-OS problems. Service Health and the status page report service/region-wide events, not one VM's state. There is no 'workspace health' blade for this purpose.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: Your query returns 40 columns but the report only needs all columns except TenantId, MGMTGroup, and SourceSystem. What is the cleanest way to drop just those three?
options: List the other 37 columns in a project operator
Use summarize to rebuild the table
Use the drop operator
Pipe to project-away TenantId, MGMTGroup, SourceSystem
explain: project-away removes the named columns and keeps everything else — the cleanest way to drop a few columns from a wide result. project requires enumerating all 37 keepers, summarize reshapes the data rather than trimming columns, and drop is not a KQL operator.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: You deploy the Azure Monitor Agent to Windows VMs and need the Security event log collected into the Log Analytics workspace. Where do you define that collection?
options: In the data collection rule, as a Windows Event Logs data source
In the data collection rule, as a Syslog data source
In the Log Analytics agent's legacy configuration
In the VM's diagnostic boot settings
explain: AMA collects Windows Event Logs (including Security) through a Windows Event Logs data source defined in the data collection rule. Syslog is the Linux equivalent. The legacy Log Analytics agent (MMA) is deprecated for this path, and boot diagnostics capture serial console output, not event logs.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: You need Processor Time and Available Memory performance counters from Windows VMs in your Log Analytics workspace for a capacity workbook. How do you collect them with AMA?
options: Enable the IIS Logs data source in the DCR
Add a Performance Counters data source in the data collection rule
Query the InsightsMetrics table; counters flow automatically
Install the Dependency agent on each VM
explain: Performance counters are collected by AMA through a Performance Counters data source in the data collection rule, where you specify the counters and sampling interval. IIS Logs collect web logs, not perf counters. InsightsMetrics receives data only from configured sources — nothing flows automatically. The Dependency agent powers the Service Map, not counter collection.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: A custom table has a dynamic column AllowedIPs containing an array of addresses per row. You need one row per address for filtering. Which operator expands the array into rows?
options: parse
mv-expand AllowedIPs
split(AllowedIPs, ',')
extend
explain: mv-expand expands a dynamic array into one row per element — exactly the row-per-address transformation needed. parse extracts fields from strings, split() produces an array (still one row), and extend only adds computed columns.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: Your application logs are not appearing in the ContainerLog table for your AKS cluster, though Container insights is enabled and other telemetry flows. The app writes its logs to local files inside the container. What is the most likely cause?
options: The Log Analytics workspace needs the ContainerLog solution reinstalled
AMA only collects logs from Windows node pools
The cluster needs the legacy Log Analytics agent instead of AMA
Container insights collects container stdout and stderr streams — the app must log there instead of local files
explain: Container insights collects the container stdout/stderr streams into the ContainerLog table; logs written to local files inside the container are invisible to it. No solution reinstall is needed — collection is working for other telemetry. AMA collects from Linux and Windows nodes alike, and the legacy agent is deprecated, not the fix.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: You need sign-in rows where the request duration was between 1,000 and 5,000 milliseconds, inclusive. Which filter expresses this most directly?
options: where DurationMs between (1000 .. 5000)
where DurationMs in (1000, 5000)
where DurationMs has 1000
where DurationMs > 1000
explain: The between operator with (min .. max) is the inclusive range comparison — the most direct expression of the requirement. in() tests set membership (only the two endpoint values), has performs full-text matching rather than numeric comparison, and > 1000 alone misses the upper bound.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: Your team wants the VM CPU metric chart visible on the shared production dashboard, with access controlled by Azure RBAC. How do you publish it?
options: Take a screenshot of the chart and upload it as a dashboard tile
Pin the chart from Metrics explorer to the shared Azure dashboard
Create an action group that emails the chart image hourly
Export the metrics to a workbook template file and share the file
explain: Metrics explorer charts can be pinned directly to Azure dashboards, which are RBAC-controlled shared resources — the live, governed answer. Screenshots are static and instantly stale. Action groups send notifications, not dashboard tiles, and a workbook template file is a different artifact without the dashboard's RBAC sharing model.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: A help-desk technician issues Temporary Access Passes valid for 30 days with one-time use disabled, arguing it cuts down repeat calls from new hires registering FIDO2 keys. You are asked to review the practice. What is the correct guidance?
options: Shorten the lifetime and enable one-time use; a 30-day reusable TAP is effectively a long-lived password-equivalent credential, while the policy default maximum lifetime is 8 hours
The practice is fine; a TAP is single-use by design regardless of the policy setting
TAP lifetimes cannot exceed 8 hours, so the 30-day passes will fail at creation
Require a P2 license before any TAP can be issued
explain: TAP lifetimes are configurable from 10 minutes up to 30 days (43,200 minutes), with a default maximum of 8 hours — so the 30-day passes do work, which is exactly the risk. A long-lived reusable TAP defeats its purpose as a short bootstrap credential; best practice is a short lifetime with one-time use enabled. One-time use is a policy setting (default False), not inherent behavior, and TAP requires no P2 license.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: Your users approve Microsoft Authenticator push notifications without reading them, and number matching is already enforced. You want each approval prompt to also show which application is being accessed and from where, so users can spot attacker-triggered prompts. Where do you enable this?
options: In the Conditional Access policy, under Session controls
In the Microsoft Authenticator settings, enable 'Show application name' and 'Show geographic location' in push and passwordless notifications
In Identity Protection, under the sign-in risk policy
In the legacy per-user MFA service settings
explain: Additional context for Authenticator notifications — Show application name and Show geographic location — is configured on the Configure tab of the Microsoft Authenticator authentication method settings, and it gives approvers the context needed to reject fraudulent pushes. Conditional Access session controls govern session lifetime, Identity Protection evaluates risk, and the legacy per-user MFA settings manage an older method list; none of them change Authenticator notification content.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: You assign an Audit-effect Azure Policy at the subscription scope. An hour later the compliance dashboard still shows a known non-compliant storage account as compliant. No remediation has run. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Audit-effect policies never evaluate existing resources, only new deployments
Policy assignments take 7 days to become effective
The standard compliance evaluation cycle runs once every 24 hours; run an on-demand scan with Start-AzPolicyComplianceScan to force re-evaluation
The policy must be reassigned after every resource change
explain: Azure Policy re-evaluates assignments on a standard cycle once every 24 hours (plus triggers on resource create/update, assignment changes, and exemption changes), so a fresh assignment can lag behind reality. Start-AzPolicyComplianceScan triggers an on-demand evaluation scan for a subscription or resource group. Audit policies absolutely evaluate existing resources, assignments are effective immediately, and no reassignment is needed per change.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: Your organization standardizes on YubiKey 5 Series keys. In the Passkey (FIDO2) policy you set 'Enforce key restrictions' to Yes with an allow-list of the YubiKey AAGUIDs, but you leave 'Enforce attestation' set to No to reduce registration friction. What should you understand about this configuration?
options: The AAGUID allow-list is fully enforced regardless of attestation
Key restrictions only apply at registration time, so existing non-YubiKey registrations keep working for sign-in
Removing an AAGUID from the allow-list later has no effect on users who already registered that key model
Without attestation, the AAGUID list acts as a policy guide rather than a strict security control, because Microsoft Entra ID cannot cryptographically verify the authenticator model
explain: Microsoft documents that AAGUID key restrictions should be treated as a policy guide, not a strict security control, when Enforce attestation is No — without attestation there is no cryptographic proof of the authenticator make and model. Key restrictions govern both registration and authentication, and removing a previously allowed AAGUID blocks sign-in for users who registered that model, so the allow-list is not registration-only or consequence-free.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: You deploy Windows Hello for Business with cloud Kerberos trust so users sign in with FIDO2 keys and get SSO to an on-premises file server. A remote user on hotel Wi-Fi signs in fine but cannot reach the on-premises file server. What is the missing requirement?
options: The client must have line of sight to a domain controller to exchange the partial TGT for a full TGT for on-premises resources
The user must sign in with a password once before FIDO2 works with cloud Kerberos trust
Cloud Kerberos trust requires Active Directory Federation Services
The FIDO2 key must be re-registered on every new network
explain: With cloud Kerberos trust, Microsoft Entra ID issues only a partial TGT; the client must contact a real domain controller to exchange it for a full TGT carrying group memberships — so on-premises resource access still needs DC line of sight. The whole point of the model is key-based sign-in (password sign-in is not supported), and it removes the AD FS dependency rather than requiring it. Registration is network-independent.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: The finance team wants step-up authentication: normal sign-in is fine for the expense app, but approving payments over $10,000 must force phishing-resistant MFA even for users who already signed in with MFA. Which Conditional Access design implements this?
options: Create a separate Conditional Access policy per finance user with a stronger authentication strength
Define a Microsoft Entra authentication context for high-value approvals, publish it to the finance app, and require it as a grant control in the Conditional Access policy
Set the sign-in frequency session control to 1 hour on the expense app
Apply a Terms of Use grant control to the payment approval page
explain: Authentication contexts let an app signal that a sensitive action needs step-up: the app publishes the context value, and a Conditional Access policy requires it as a grant control with a phishing-resistant authentication strength, triggering re-authentication exactly at the sensitive action. Per-user policies do not scale and cannot trigger mid-session, sign-in frequency is time-based rather than action-based, and Terms of Use presents a consent document rather than demanding stronger authentication.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: Identity Protection flags a user at medium user risk after their credentials appeared in a breach dump. The user resets their password via SSPR. An administrator then opens the risky users report. What is the correct administrative action?
options: Delete the user account; medium risk always indicates compromise
Take no action; user risk clears automatically the moment SSPR completes
Dismiss the user risk or confirm the user as compromised based on investigation; the password reset lets the user self-remediate and close the risk
Block the user from all Conditional Access policies permanently
explain: A password reset enables user self-remediation, which closes the user risk, but the administrator should still review the risky users report and either dismiss the risk (legitimate activity) or confirm compromise (which revokes sessions and forces re-registration). Medium risk is a signal, not proof of compromise, so deletion is excessive; risk does not vanish the instant SSPR runs without the remediation flow, and policy exclusion is not a remediation step.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: You plan to roll out a custom banned-password list with the on-premises password protection DC agent. The help desk fears a flood of rejected password changes on day one. What is the recommended rollout approach?
options: Enable Enforced mode immediately; Audit mode also blocks weak passwords
Skip the DC agent; the banned list applies to on-premises AD automatically
Deploy in Audit mode permanently, since Enforced mode is not supported for custom lists
Deploy the DC agent in Audit mode first, review the event logs for passwords that would be rejected, then switch to Enforced mode
explain: The documented rollout is Audit mode first: the DC agent logs events for passwords that would fail validation without rejecting them, letting you measure impact before flipping to Enforced. Audit mode never blocks — that is its purpose. The DC agent and its proxy are required for on-premises enforcement; the cloud banned list does not reach domain controllers on its own. Enforced mode fully supports custom banned lists.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: You assign a DeployIfNotExists policy that deploys a Log Analytics agent extension. The assignment succeeds but remediation fails with an error about the managed identity. What is the most likely cause?
options: DeployIfNotExists assignments must specify a location, which is used to create the assignment's managed identity
DeployIfNotExists does not use a managed identity at all
The managed identity is created in the region of each non-compliant resource automatically
Only the Owner role at the tenant root can create the managed identity
explain: A DeployIfNotExists (or AuditIfNotExists) assignment that performs remediation needs a managed identity, and the assignment must include a location because the identity is created in that region. Without a location the identity cannot be provisioned and remediation fails. The identity is not per-resource-region, and assignment-scoped MI creation requires sufficient RBAC at the assignment scope, not tenant-root Owner.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: You apply a CanNotDelete resource lock to the production resource group, then run an ARM template deployment in Complete mode at that resource-group scope. The template omits an old test VM that still exists in the group. What happens to the deployment?
options: The deployment succeeds and deletes the test VM; Complete mode overrides resource locks
The deployment fails when it tries to delete the test VM, because Complete mode deletes out-of-template resources and the CanNotDelete lock blocks the delete
Complete mode skips resources protected by locks and the deployment succeeds
The lock is automatically removed during Complete mode deployments and reapplied afterward
explain: Complete mode deletes any resources in the scope that are not in the template — and the CanNotDelete lock blocks that delete, failing the deployment. Complete mode does not override or bypass locks, does not silently skip locked resources, and never removes locks on its own. The fix is to remove the test VM from the lock's protection intentionally (or delete it manually) before the Complete mode deployment.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: An administrator builds a dynamic membership rule for the 'All-London-Staff' group using the expression user.memberOf -eq 'London-Managers'. The rule fails validation. What is wrong?
options: Dynamic rules support nesting but only for security groups, not Microsoft 365 groups
The memberOf operator requires Microsoft Entra ID P2
Dynamic membership rules cannot reference other groups; they can only evaluate direct user or device attributes such as department or city
Dynamic group rules must be written in KQL, not the rule builder syntax
explain: Dynamic membership rules evaluate properties of the user or device object itself (department, city, jobTitle, userType) — they cannot query membership of another group, so memberOf-style nesting is invalid. There is no security-group-only nesting exception, no P2 requirement for the operator (dynamic groups are P1), and rules use the membership rule builder syntax, not KQL.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: The database team is eligible for membership in the 'DB-Admins' group through PIM for Groups, and that group holds the SQL DB Contributor role assignment. A team member activates their eligible group membership. What is the effect?
options: The member must separately activate each Azure role assigned to the group
Group activation is permanent and cannot expire
Only the group owner can activate membership; eligible members can only request
Activating the group membership activates the group's role assignments, so the member can exercise SQL DB Contributor after activation
explain: PIM for Groups is designed so that activating eligible membership in the group activates everything assigned to the group — the member inherits the group's role assignments for the activation duration without separate per-role activations. Activation honors the configured maximum duration and expiry; it is not permanent. Eligible members activate their own membership (subject to approval settings); ownership is not required.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: A security engineer asks you to create a deny assignment that blocks the networking team from deleting any virtual network in the subscription. How do you respond?
options: Deny assignments cannot be created directly by administrators; they are created by Azure on behalf of services such as Deployment Stacks and Azure Blueprints
Create the deny assignment in the portal under Access control (IAM) > Deny assignments
Assign the built-in Deny Administrator role to the networking team
Deny assignments can only be created with Azure PowerShell, not the portal
explain: Deny assignments are system-created — Azure creates them to protect resources managed by Deployment Stacks (denySettings) and Blueprints. There is no portal blade, cmdlet, or built-in role that lets an administrator author one directly; there is also no 'Deny Administrator' role. To block deletions for a team, use RBAC (withhold delete permissions) or resource locks, not deny assignments.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: Legal updates the Terms of Use document referenced by your Conditional Access grant control and uploads it as version 2. Users who accepted version 1 last quarter complain they are being prompted to accept again. Is this expected?
options: No; acceptance of any version covers all future versions permanently
Yes; Terms of Use documents are versioned, and publishing a new version requires users to re-accept before the grant control is satisfied
Yes, but only for guest users; members are exempt from re-acceptance
No; the Conditional Access policy must be recreated to reference the new version
explain: Terms of Use supports document versioning precisely so policy changes have legal effect — when you publish a new version, prior acceptances no longer satisfy the grant control and users must accept the new version at next sign-in. Acceptance is per-version, not perpetual, and it applies to all targeted users including members. The existing Conditional Access policy picks up the new version automatically; no recreation is needed.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: Finance buys a one-year reserved instance for 16 vCPUs and wants the discount to float across all subscriptions in the MCA billing scope rather than being pinned to one subscription. Which reservation scope should they select?
options: Single subscription scope
Single resource group scope
Shared scope
Management group scope without enrollment
explain: The Shared (billing scope) reservation scope applies the discount to usage across subscriptions under the billing account/profile, which is exactly the floating behavior finance wants. Single subscription scope pins the discount, single resource group scope is even narrower, and reservation scopes do not include a standalone management-group option outside the billing hierarchy.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: A DevOps engineer needs to rotate the connection strings stored as secrets in Key Vault and also manage key vault access policies and network rules. The engineer currently has Contributor on the resource group. Which additional role assignment follows least privilege?
options: Key Vault Secrets Officer, which grants data-plane secret read/write but not vault management
Owner on the key vault resource
No additional role; Contributor already includes secret data-plane access
Key Vault Administrator, which grants control-plane management of the vault including secrets management
explain: Key Vault Administrator is the control-plane role for managing the vault itself (access policies, network rules, settings) and includes secrets management. Secrets Officer is data-plane only and cannot manage the vault. Owner is broader than needed, and Contributor grants control-plane rights except it explicitly cannot read secret values — the classic trap that Contributor is insufficient for secret data access.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: Five VMs share one user-assigned managed identity for pulling images from ACR. You delete one of the VMs during cleanup. What happens to the managed identity and the remaining VMs?
options: The identity is unaffected; user-assigned managed identities have an independent lifecycle and deleting one associated resource does not delete the identity
The identity is deleted with the VM and must be recreated for the other four
The remaining VMs lose the identity assignment automatically
The identity is disabled for 30 days before it can be reused
explain: User-assigned managed identities are standalone Azure resources with their own lifecycle — deleting a VM that references one does not delete the identity, and the other four VMs keep working. The delete-with-resource behavior describes system-assigned identities. There is no automatic unassignment cascade and no 30-day disablement.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: In cross-tenant access settings, you want to control which external Microsoft Entra organizations your users can access through Teams shared channels and B2B collaboration. Which setting governs this?
options: Inbound trust settings for MFA claims
Outbound access settings, including the allow/deny lists for external organizations
The B2B guest invite redemption policy
Tenant restrictions on the corporate proxy
explain: Cross-tenant access outbound settings control what your users can do in external tenants — including B2B collaboration and Teams shared-channel access — with allow/deny lists for target organizations. Inbound settings govern what external users can do in your tenant (such as trusting their MFA claims). The redemption policy covers invitation acceptance mechanics, and tenant restrictions are a proxy feature, not the Entra control for this.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: Your tenant already synchronizes password hashes. You now enable pass-through authentication for a pilot group. During the pilot the on-premises agents go offline for an hour. What happens to sign-ins for synchronized users?
options: All sign-ins fail until the agents return, because PTA is now the only path
Only cloud-only users can sign in during the outage
Sign-ins continue via password hash synchronization, which acts as a fallback when PTA agents are unreachable
You must disable PTA before sign-ins resume
explain: When both methods are enabled, pass-through authentication takes precedence and password hash synchronization remains as an automatic fallback — if no agent responds, Microsoft Entra ID validates against the synced hashes. There is no need to disable PTA or wait for agents, and cloud-only users are unaffected either way since they never depended on PTA.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: A branch office still authenticates VPN users against an on-premises Azure MFA Server. The server OS is out of support and the team asks whether to upgrade the MFA Server. What do you tell them?
options: Upgrade to the latest MFA Server release; it remains the recommended on-premises MFA solution
Keep the current server; retired services continue to receive security patches
Replace it with the NPS extension only, which is a full MFA Server replacement for all scenarios
Plan a migration to cloud-based Microsoft Entra MFA; Azure MFA Server is retired and no longer the supported path
explain: Azure MFA Server was retired (September 30, 2024); Microsoft directs customers to migrate to cloud-based Microsoft Entra MFA, and there is no supported upgrade path. Staying on a retired service means no security updates. The NPS extension covers RADIUS scenarios such as VPN, but it is not a general MFA Server replacement — the strategic answer is the cloud migration.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: An application generates a service SAS at runtime and immediately uses it, but the first requests fail with authentication errors while retries a minute later succeed. The SAS start time is set to the current time. What is the most likely cause and fix?
options: Clock skew between the client and Azure; set the SAS start time 15 minutes in the past to tolerate skew
The storage account key was rotated; regenerate the SAS with the new key
Service SAS tokens require 5 minutes to propagate before first use
The SAS must be created with an access policy; ad-hoc SAS values are evaluated lazily
explain: Azure validates the SAS start time against its own clock, so a client clock running slightly ahead produces a SAS that is 'not yet valid' — the classic fix is to backdate the start time by about 15 minutes. Key rotation would break all SASs, not just the first minute; there is no 5-minute propagation delay for SAS; and ad-hoc SAS works fine without a stored access policy.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: A deployment pipeline runs AzCopy on a build agent using Microsoft Entra authentication (azcopy login) to copy build artifacts into a blob container. The copy fails with authorization errors, although the service principal can list the storage account in the portal. What role does the principal need?
options: Reader on the storage account
Storage Blob Data Contributor on the storage account or container
Storage Account Key Operator Service Role
No role; AzCopy with Microsoft Entra auth only needs the account name
explain: AzCopy data-plane operations with Microsoft Entra auth require a data-plane role such as Storage Blob Data Contributor — Reader grants only control-plane visibility (listing the account), which is why the principal sees the account but cannot write blobs. Storage Account Key Operator grants key access, not data access, and Microsoft Entra auth never bypasses RBAC.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: A lifecycle management rule deletes blobs older than 365 days. After the rule runs, the storage account's used capacity barely drops. Soft delete for blobs is enabled with a 30-day retention. What explains this?
options: Lifecycle delete only removes the blob index, not the data
Lifecycle policies cannot delete blobs; they can only change tiers
The deleted blobs enter a soft-deleted state and continue to occupy capacity until the 30-day soft-delete retention expires
The rule must also delete snapshots, otherwise base blobs are protected
explain: With blob soft delete enabled, a lifecycle delete moves blobs into a soft-deleted state where they are retained — and billed — for the configured retention period, so capacity does not drop immediately. Lifecycle delete absolutely removes data (the delete action is fully supported), and while snapshot handling matters for tiering rules, the capacity observation here is explained by soft-delete retention.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: A premium block blob storage account holds 20 TB of infrequently accessed image data. The team wants to tier it to Cool to save cost. What is the correct approach?
options: Apply a lifecycle management policy with a tierToCool action
Use Set Blob Tier to change the blobs to Cool
Enable hierarchical namespace, which unlocks tiering on premium block blobs
Copy the blobs to a standard GPv2 account's Cool tier using AzCopy or Put Block From URL; tiering is not supported inside a premium block blob account
explain: Tiering is not supported in a premium block blob storage account — neither Set Blob Tier nor lifecycle management can move the data; the documented path is a synchronous server-side copy (AzCopy or Put Block From URL) to the Hot tier of a different account, from where normal tiering applies. Hierarchical namespace does not change this limitation, and premium block blob accounts do not support HNS-based tiering either.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: Compliance requires guest-OS-level disk encryption on a VM that uses Ultra Disks for a database workload. The engineer tries to enable Azure Disk Encryption and it fails. What is the correct design?
options: Azure Disk Encryption is not supported on Ultra Disks or Premium SSD v2; use encryption at host or server-side encryption with customer-managed keys instead
Enable BitLocker manually inside the guest; ADE is optional for Ultra Disks
Convert the Ultra Disks to Premium SSD, enable ADE, then convert back
ADE works on Ultra Disks only when the VM is deallocated first
explain: Azure Disk Encryption explicitly does not support Ultra Disks or Premium SSD v2 disks — the supported alternatives are encryption at host (end-to-end including temp disk and caches) or server-side encryption with customer-managed keys via a Disk Encryption Set. Manual BitLocker inside the guest is not ADE and is not the managed answer, disk type conversion does not enable ADE, and deallocation changes nothing about the limitation.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: An engineer deploys a Premium SSD v2 data disk with host caching set to ReadOnly for a SQL Server VM, and the deployment is rejected. What is wrong?
options: ReadOnly caching is invalid for data disks; use ReadWrite
Premium SSD v2 does not support host caching; set caching to None
Host caching requires the disk and VM to be in different zones
Premium SSD v2 requires ReadWrite caching for all data disks
explain: Premium SSD v2 (like Ultra Disks) does not support host caching at all — caching must be None, and its sub-millisecond latency is designed to make the cache unnecessary. ReadOnly is the recommended setting for database data files on Premium SSD v1, but that guidance does not transfer to v2. Zone placement and ReadWrite requirements are unrelated to the rejection.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: A Microsoft Entra-joined laptop on a home network needs to open an Azure Files share secured with Microsoft Entra Kerberos for hybrid identities. There is no VPN to the corporate network. Will it work?
options: No; Entra Kerberos always requires line of sight to a domain controller
No; Azure Files requires Active Directory Domain Services identity, not Entra Kerberos
Yes; Microsoft Entra ID issues the Kerberos tickets for the cloud file share, so no line of sight to a domain controller is needed for this cloud resource
Yes, but only if the laptop is hybrid-joined rather than Entra-joined
explain: For cloud resources such as Azure Files, Microsoft Entra Kerberos lets Entra ID issue the needed Kerberos tickets without the client reaching a domain controller — the line-of-sight requirement applies to on-premises resources needing a partial-to-full TGT exchange. Entra Kerberos is a supported identity source for Azure Files SMB alongside AD DS, and Entra-joined devices are supported clients.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: You create an SFTP local user on a storage account with a home directory pointing at a container. The user connects successfully and can list files but uploads fail. What is the most likely misconfiguration?
options: The SSH key must be regenerated after the first connection
SFTP requires hierarchical namespace, which cannot be enabled on this account
Local users cannot write; only Microsoft Entra identities can upload via SFTP
The local user is missing write permission on the container; SFTP local users need explicit container-level permissions (read, write, list, delete, create)
explain: SFTP local users get no permissions by default — you grant container-scoped permissions (r/w/l/d/c) per container, so list-without-write is the signature of a missing write grant. SSH keys do not need regeneration, hierarchical namespace is a prerequisite for SFTP but the successful connection proves it is enabled, and local users fully support upload once permitted.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: You host a static website in the $web container and map a custom domain directly to the storage endpoint. Browsers show a certificate name mismatch over HTTPS. What is the correct fix?
options: Front the static website with Azure CDN or Azure Front Door and use its managed certificate for the custom domain; the storage static-website endpoint cannot serve your own TLS certificate
Upload a TLS certificate to the $web container
Enable secure transfer required on the storage account
Move the site out of $web into a custom container name
explain: The storage static-website endpoint serves HTTPS with Microsoft's certificate only; custom-domain TLS requires placing Azure CDN or Front Door in front and binding its managed certificate to the custom domain. Uploading a cert to $web does nothing, secure transfer only enforces HTTPS (not your hostname), and the $web container name is mandatory for static websites.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: An application overwrites the same configuration blob several times a day, and twice this month a bad overwrite caused an outage with no prior version to roll back to. What is the best fix?
options: Enable blob soft delete, which keeps overwritten versions
Enable blob versioning; every write or overwrite then automatically creates a restorable prior version
Take manual snapshots before each write
Enable the blob change feed to reconstruct prior versions
explain: Blob versioning automatically captures a new version on every create/overwrite, giving point-in-time rollback without application changes. Soft delete only restores deleted blobs, not overwritten content. Manual snapshots work but require the app to take them on every write — operationally fragile. The change feed records what changed (an audit trail), not the prior bytes, so it cannot restore content.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: A lifecycle management rule with a tierToArchive action never archives blobs in a container that has a default encryption scope configured. Other containers archive normally. Why?
options: Encryption scopes require premium block blob accounts, which do not support tiering
tierToArchive requires hierarchical namespace on the container
The Archive tier does not support blobs that use an encryption scope
The rule must include daysAfterLastTierChangeGreaterThan to archive scoped blobs
explain: Lifecycle management cannot move a blob that uses an encryption scope to the Archive tier — the archive action is explicitly unsupported for encryption-scope blobs, so those containers silently skip archiving while others proceed. Encryption scopes work on standard accounts, HNS is unrelated to the archive limitation, and daysAfterLastTierChangeGreaterThan guards against re-archiving rehydrated blobs rather than enabling scoped archiving.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: You design an Azure Table storage schema for customer orders queried by customer ID and order date. A colleague suggests adding a secondary index on order date for fast lookups. What do you tell them?
options: Secondary indexes are supported but limited to one per table
Add the index through the portal under Table > Indexes
Secondary indexes require the premium table tier
Table storage has no secondary indexes; design the PartitionKey/RowKey so point and range queries resolve via the key (for example PartitionKey = customer ID, RowKey = inverted date)
explain: Azure Table storage offers no secondary indexes — query performance comes from key design, since only PartitionKey/RowKey lookups are efficient and anything else scans. There is no portal index blade, no one-index limit to work around, and no premium tier that adds indexing; the fix is modeling the access pattern into the keys.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: A worker-role pattern needs strict first-in-first-out processing with duplicate detection across competing consumers. The team proposes Azure Storage Queues. What should you advise?
options: Use Azure Service Bus queues instead; Storage Queues offer best-effort ordering and at-least-once delivery without built-in duplicate detection or sessions, while Service Bus supports FIFO via sessions and duplicate detection
Storage Queues are the right choice; they guarantee FIFO ordering
Use Storage Queues with a 64 KB message limit to enforce ordering
Strict FIFO is impossible in Azure messaging; redesign the workflow
explain: Azure Storage Queues provide best-effort ordering and at-least-once delivery with no duplicate detection — the wrong tool for strict FIFO. Service Bus queues support ordered delivery through sessions and duplicate detection windows. The 64 KB limit is a size constraint, not an ordering mechanism, and strict FIFO is achievable with the right service rather than impossible.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: You must apply the same tag-based lifecycle operation across 50 storage accounts in three subscriptions — something lifecycle management policies cannot do natively. Which Azure capability fits?
options: A single lifecycle management policy assigned at the management group scope
A storage task in Azure Storage Actions, which runs serverless data operations at scale across many accounts and subscriptions
AzCopy with a wildcard account name
An Azure Policy DeployIfNotExists assignment that copies the lifecycle policy
explain: Storage tasks (Azure Storage Actions) are the serverless framework for running data operations across millions of objects and many storage accounts — the designed answer for cross-account scale. Lifecycle policies are per-account resources and cannot be assigned at management group scope. AzCopy has no multi-account orchestration, and a DeployIfNotExists policy could stamp out policies but not execute the data operation itself.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: A regional application needs zone-redundant managed disks for a file server, but Premium SSD ZRS exceeds the budget. Which disk option provides ZRS at a lower price point?
options: Standard HDD with ZRS
Premium SSD v2 with ZRS
Standard SSD with ZRS
Ultra Disk with ZRS
explain: Standard SSDs support zone-redundant storage (ZRS), giving zonal redundancy below Premium pricing. Standard HDDs are LRS-only. Premium SSD v2 and Ultra Disks are LRS-only as well — neither supports ZRS — so the budget-friendly zone-redundant choice is Standard SSD ZRS.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: You keep seven daily incremental snapshots of a 2 TB data disk for a week. Finance asks why snapshot storage costs are far lower than 14 TB. How do incremental snapshots bill?
options: Snapshots are free for the first 30 days
Each snapshot bills at 10% of the disk size regardless of change
Snapshot billing is capped at the size of one full disk
Incremental snapshots bill only for the changed blocks (deltas) since the previous snapshot, not for full copies each day
explain: Incremental snapshots store only the deltas between snapshots — the first is a full copy and each subsequent one stores changed blocks, so seven daily snapshots of a mostly static disk cost far less than seven full copies. There is no 30-day free window, no flat 10% rule, and no cap at one disk size; billing follows actual delta storage.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: Your Compute Gallery image definition publishes version 1.0.3 with a breaking change. The pipeline always deploys 'latest', and you need 1.0.2 to remain the default for existing consumers while 1.0.3 stays available for testing. What do you set on version 1.0.3?
options: Set excludeFromLatest on version 1.0.3 so 'latest' still resolves to 1.0.2
Delete version 1.0.3 after testing
Move version 1.0.3 to a different gallery
Image versions cannot be hidden from 'latest' once published
explain: The excludeFromLatest flag on an image version removes it from latest-version resolution while keeping it directly addressable — exactly the staged-rollout pattern. Deleting it removes the test artifact, a separate gallery fractures the definition, and latest-resolution is controllable, not immutable.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: You need to convert a Windows VM to Linux by swapping its OS disk. The VM is deallocated and you attempt the OS disk swap. What will happen?
options: The swap succeeds; the VM boots Linux from the new disk
The swap fails; an OS disk swap cannot change the operating system type (Windows to Linux or vice versa)
The swap succeeds but the VM keeps the Windows license billing
The swap requires the VM to be running, not deallocated
explain: OS disk swap replaces the disk but the VM retains its OS type — swapping a Windows VM to a Linux disk (or reverse) is explicitly unsupported and fails. The deallocated state is the correct prerequisite (the misconception is inverted), and billing follows the VM's OS type, which cannot be changed this way; conversion requires redeploying a new VM.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: You configure customer-managed keys for a storage account pointing at a Key Vault key. The configuration fails validation. The vault has soft delete enabled but purge protection is off. What is missing?
options: The key must be RSA 1024-bit for storage accounts
Customer-managed keys are not supported for storage accounts, only for managed disks
Purge protection must also be enabled on the Key Vault; storage CMK requires both soft delete and purge protection
The storage account must be premium block blobs
explain: Storage account customer-managed keys require the Key Vault to have both soft delete and purge protection enabled — purge protection guards against malicious or accidental permanent key deletion that would render data unrecoverable. Key size minimums are 2048-bit, CMK is fully supported for storage accounts, and it works on standard tiers including GPv2.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: You provision a 128 GiB premium page blob to use as a managed data disk. Which performance tier does it land in, and what determines that?
options: P20; all premium page blobs default to P20 regardless of size
P4; page blob tiers are fixed at creation and never change
P30; the tier follows the VM size, not the disk size
P10; premium page blob tiers are determined by provisioned disk size
explain: Premium page blob (Premium SSD v1) tiers map to provisioned size bands — 128 GiB falls in the P10 band (128 GiB), P20 is the 512 GiB band, and P4 is 32 GiB. The tier is a function of disk size (you move tiers by resizing the disk), not of VM size, and there is no fixed default tier.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: A developer installs the Hyper-V role inside an Azure VM sized Standard_D2_v2 to run nested test VMs, but virtualization fails to start. The VM is running Windows Server 2022. What is the fix?
options: Resize to a Dv3-series or later size; nested virtualization requires v3+ (or equivalent newer) sizes and is not available on Dv2
Enable nested virtualization in the guest OS settings; D2_v2 supports it
Nested virtualization requires a B-series burstable VM
Install the Hyper-V role on the host instead of the guest
explain: Nested virtualization in Azure requires sizes with virtualization extensions exposed — Dv3/Ev3 and later (plus Fsv2, M, and newer generations); Dv2-series sizes do not support it, so no guest setting can enable it. B-series does not support nested virtualization, and there is no access to the physical host — the resize is the fix.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: An architect designs an availability set spanning five fault domains for rack-level isolation. You must correct the design. What do you tell them?
options: Availability sets support up to 20 fault domains, so five is fine

Availability sets support a maximum of 3 fault domains per region (2 in some regions); fault domains represent racks with separate power and networking, while update domains (up to 20) handle planned maintenance
Fault domains are unlimited; the limit applies to update domains
Use five update domains instead; they provide rack isolation
explain: Fault domains cap at 3 per region (2 in regions without 3) — they model physical separation (racks, power, switches). The 'up to 20' figure belongs to update domains, which sequence planned-maintenance reboots. Five fault domains is invalid; if broader isolation is needed, availability zones are the answer, and update domains do not provide rack isolation.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: You enable Application Logging (Filesystem) on a production web app to chase an intermittent error. Two days later the logs stop appearing, although the app still runs. What happened?
options: The log quota was exceeded and logging is permanently disabled
Application logging requires Always On, which was turned off
Filesystem application logging automatically disables itself after 12 hours; it is intended for temporary debugging, while Blob storage logging persists
Filesystem logs are deleted after 12 hours but logging continues
explain: The Filesystem option for App Service application logging is a temporary debugging aid by design — Azure turns it off automatically after 12 hours. For continuous capture you point application logging at Blob storage (with configurable retention). It is the setting that disables, not deletion of files while continuing; Always On affects idle shutdown, not logging; and no quota permanently kills it.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: A function app on the Elastic Premium plan shows steady charges overnight even though no executions ran. The plan has two pre-warmed instances configured. What explains the cost?
options: Premium plan bills per execution like Consumption; the charges are a billing error
The function app scaled to zero, which incurs a parking fee
Charges come from the storage account, not the plan
Pre-warmed (always-ready) instances are billed for the whole time they are provisioned, regardless of executions
explain: Elastic Premium always-ready (pre-warmed) instances reserve capacity and are billed continuously whether or not functions execute — that is the price of eliminating cold starts. Per-execution billing is the Consumption model, Premium does not scale to zero (that is Flex Consumption), and while storage has its own cost it does not explain plan-sized overnight charges.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: A CI agent needs pull-only access to exactly one repository, 'payments/api', in your Azure Container Registry. The registry admin user is disabled per policy. What is the least-privilege approach?
options: Create a token with a scope map granting content/read and metadata/read on the payments/api repository only
Enable the admin user temporarily for the CI agent
Assign the built-in AcrPull role to the agent's identity
Give the agent Contributor on the registry resource
explain: ACR tokens with scope maps provide repository-scoped permissions — content/read plus metadata/read on payments/api gives exactly pull access to one repo. Re-enabling the admin user grants full registry admin, violating the policy and least privilege. AcrPull is registry-wide (all repositories), and Contributor is control-plane management, far broader than pulling one image.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: You design an AKS cluster and plan to run all workloads on user node pools, deleting the initial system node pool afterward to save cost. What is wrong with this plan?
options: Nothing; system node pools are optional once user pools exist
Every AKS cluster must retain at least one system node pool for core system pods; user node pools are for workloads but cannot replace the system pool
System node pools can only be deleted via support ticket
User node pools cannot run in the same virtual network as system pools
explain: AKS requires at least one system node pool at all times to host critical system pods (CoreDNS, metrics, etc.) — user node pools supplement it for application workloads but the system pool cannot be removed. Deletion is a normal API operation (just blocked for the last system pool), and pool types share networking without restriction.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: You set up Azure VM Image Builder to build golden images in a locked-down subscription. The build fails with authorization errors accessing the staging resource group. What identity requirement did you miss?
options: Image Builder only works with system-assigned identities
Image Builder needs no identity; it uses the portal user's credentials
Image Builder requires a user-assigned managed identity with permissions (for example Contributor) on the resource group, to create and manage build resources
The identity must be assigned at the tenant root
explain: VM Image Builder acts through a user-assigned managed identity that you create and grant (typically Contributor) on the build resource group — it provisions temporary build VMs, disks, and networking as that identity. System-assigned is not the model here, the service never borrows your portal credentials, and tenant-root assignment is unnecessary and excessive.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: A file server protected by the MARS agent needs backups every 6 hours to meet RPO. The backup admin schedules four backup times per day. What happens?
options: The schedule works; MARS supports up to 6 backups per day
MARS runs continuous backup, so schedules are unnecessary
The agent backs up hourly regardless of schedule
MARS supports a maximum of 3 scheduled backups per day; the fourth schedule cannot be created
explain: The Microsoft Azure Recovery Services agent supports at most three scheduled backups per day — a fourth daily schedule is rejected. MARS is schedule-based, not continuous, and it never invents an hourly cadence. For sub-6-hour RPO with Azure Backup, a different approach (such as Azure VM backup or more frequent alternative protection) is needed.
