domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: You are locked out of a Linux VM: the SSH key was replaced and the password is unknown. The VM agent is running. What is the fastest supported recovery?
options: Reset the SSH key or password with the VMAccess extension (az vm user update / Set-AzVMAccessExtension)
Use the serial console to log in as root without credentials
Restart the VM; Azure regenerates the SSH key on boot
Delete and recreate the VM from the OS disk
explain: The VMAccess extension resets SSH keys, passwords, and even SSH configuration on a running VM with a healthy agent — the designed lockout recovery. Serial console still requires credentials, restart does not regenerate keys, and recreating the VM is unnecessary destruction when the agent channel is available.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: You must protect an on-premises physical server with Azure Site Recovery. The server runs a custom application with no virtualization host. What must you deploy on-premises first?
options: Only the Mobility service agent on the physical server
The Azure Site Recovery replication appliance (OVA) plus the Mobility service agent on the server
The MARS agent on the physical server
An ExpressRoute circuit; ASR requires private connectivity
explain: Physical servers (and VMware VMs) replicate through the ASR replication appliance — a dedicated on-premises VM (deployed from OVA) that discovers servers and coordinates replication — with the Mobility service agent installed on each protected machine. The agent alone cannot replicate without the appliance, MARS is backup not disaster recovery, and ASR works over the internet with HTTPS; ExpressRoute is optional.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: A regulated workload needs an App Service Environment with zone redundancy and no cold starts. The team proposes ASE v3 on a Consumption-style plan that scales to zero. What do you correct?
options: ASE v3 does not support zone redundancy; use multiple ASEs instead
ASE requires no dedicated subnet, so the plan is fine
ASE v3 supports zone redundancy, but an ASE is dedicated infrastructure that cannot scale to zero; there is no Consumption plan for ASE
Cold starts are unavoidable on ASE v3
explain: ASE v3 does support zone redundancy, but it is an isolated, dedicated App Service footprint — it is always warm and billed for the provisioned workers, with no scale-to-zero or Consumption option. That is the design trade-off for isolation. Multiple ASEs are not needed for zonal redundancy, a dedicated (delegated) subnet is mandatory, and cold starts are precisely what dedicated workers avoid.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: Your team wants immutable function app deployments: every release should deploy a versioned zip and the app should run directly from the package without unpacking to wwwroot. Which app setting implements this?
options: Always On set to true
WEBSITE_NODE_DEFAULT_VERSION
Deployment slots with auto-swap
WEBSITE_RUN_FROM_PACKAGE set to 1 with the package URL
explain: WEBSITE_RUN_FROM_PACKAGE=1 makes the app run directly from the deployment package (zip in Blob storage or local), giving atomic, immutable releases with no wwwroot writes. Always On prevents idle shutdown, the Node version setting picks a runtime, and slots with auto-swap orchestrate traffic — none of them change how the bits are hosted.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: You resize a VM from Standard_D4s_v3 to Standard_E8s_v3 and the operation fails, suggesting deallocation first. The sizes are both available in the region. What is the most likely reason?
options: The target size is not available on the current host cluster; deallocating lets Azure place the VM on a cluster that supports the new size
Resizing between VM families is never supported
The VM must be resized through a new VM deployment; in-place resize is not supported
The OS disk must be detached before any resize
explain: In-place resize works only if the target size is offered on the physical cluster hosting the VM — when it is not, Azure requires stop (deallocate) so the VM can be re-placed on a suitable cluster. Cross-family resize is fully supported, in-place resize is the normal path, and the OS disk stays attached through a resize.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: An on-premises inventory app must reach an Azure web app over a private channel, but the security team will not allow any inbound firewall rules or VPN changes on-premises. Which App Service connectivity option fits?
options: Regional VNet integration
A Hybrid Connection, with the Hybrid Connection Manager installed on-premises initiating an outbound connection to Azure Relay
A private endpoint on the web app
Service endpoints on the on-premises network
explain: Hybrid Connections work through Azure Relay with the on-premises Hybrid Connection Manager making an outbound connection — no inbound firewall rules, no VPN, and no network changes required. Regional VNet integration gives the app outbound VNet access (the wrong direction here), a private endpoint secures inbound to the app from a VNet but still needs network path setup, and service endpoints are an Azure VNet feature, not an on-premises one.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: Your supply-chain policy requires container images to be digitally signed so clusters only run verified images. In Azure Container Registry, which feature provides image signing?
options: Repository-scoped tokens
ACR Tasks
Content trust (Notary), a Premium SKU feature that signs images at push time so consumers can verify signatures
Geo-replication
explain: ACR content trust integrates Notary to sign images on push; Docker clients with content trust enabled then verify signatures before pulling — the signing story. Tokens and scope maps handle authorization, not signatures. ACR Tasks build images, and geo-replication copies them; neither signs anything.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: A Windows VM running SQL Server needs application-consistent backups without stopping the database. Which Azure Backup mechanism provides this?
options: Crash-consistent snapshots only; application consistency requires pausing SQL Server
MARS agent file-level backup
Copy the database files to Blob storage manually before each backup
The Azure VM backup takes application-consistent snapshots using the Windows VSS framework (and pre/post scripts on Linux)
explain: Azure VM backup coordinates with the Windows Volume Shadow Copy Service to quiesce supported applications like SQL Server, producing application-consistent recovery points without downtime; on Linux it can run pre/post scripts. Crash-consistent alone is the fallback, not the design. MARS is file/folder backup without VM-level app consistency, and manual copies are operational toil the platform already automates.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: During an ARM deployment you need to run a custom PowerShell script that registers the new VM in an external CMDB, using a managed identity for credentials. Which template resource type runs arbitrary scripts as part of the deployment?
options: Microsoft.Resources/deploymentScripts, which executes scripts during deployment under a user-assigned managed identity
Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/extensions with CustomScript
Microsoft.Resources/templateSpecs
Microsoft.Automation/automationAccounts/runbooks
explain: The deploymentScripts resource type runs Azure CLI or PowerShell scripts inline as part of the ARM/Bicep deployment lifecycle, authenticating with a user-assigned managed identity — designed for exactly this post-provisioning integration. The Custom Script Extension runs on the VM guest (not the deployment), Template Specs store templates, and Automation runbooks live outside the deployment transaction.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: You run Spot VMs for a rendering farm and want the VMs to be evicted only when the Spot price exceeds your bid, paying no more than that bid per hour. How do you configure this?
options: Spot VMs always evict at the on-demand price; no configuration is possible
Set a maximum price (eviction when the Spot price exceeds it); without a max price you pay the current Spot price up to the on-demand rate
Enable automatic OS upgrades to lock the price
Spot pricing requires a reservation to cap the price
explain: Spot VMs support an optional maximum price: Azure evicts the VM when the Spot price exceeds your max, and you never pay above it. Without a max price you pay the fluctuating Spot price (capped at the on-demand rate). OS upgrades, reservations, and on-demand price eviction are unrelated to the max-price control.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: A multi-tenant SaaS app on App Service needs each customer to reach the app over TLS on the same IP address with their own certificate. Which TLS binding type supports this?
options: IP-based SSL, which assigns a dedicated public IP per certificate
A single wildcard certificate for all tenants
SNI SSL, which serves the correct certificate based on the hostname in the TLS handshake on a shared IP
App Service cannot serve multiple certificates on one IP
explain: SNI (Server Name Indication) SSL lets the app present the right certificate per hostname during the TLS handshake on a shared IP — the standard multi-tenant pattern. IP-based SSL burns a dedicated public IP per certificate and is the legacy approach. A single wildcard only works if all tenants share one domain, and multi-cert single-IP is exactly what SNI was built for.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: Your AKS cluster needs occasional burst capacity for month-end batch jobs, but you do not want to pay for idle node pools all month. Which Azure integration provides serverless burst nodes?
options: Cluster autoscaler with a zero minimum node count
Node auto-provisioning (NAP) with Spot priority
A second system node pool that you manually start and stop
Virtual nodes (ACI connector), which burst pods to Azure Container Instances without pre-provisioned nodes
explain: Virtual nodes via the ACI connector schedule burst pods onto Azure Container Instances — true serverless burst with per-second billing and no idle nodes. Cluster autoscaler still needs node pools (and VM startup latency), NAP provisions real nodes rather than serverless capacity, and manually toggling a node pool is operational toil compared to the built-in burst path.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: You associate an NSG with the GatewaySubnet hosting an ExpressRoute gateway, using a default-deny inbound posture. The gateway provisioning fails. What must the NSG allow?
options: Inbound from the GatewayManager service tag; the gateway control plane requires it
Inbound from the Internet service tag on all ports
Outbound to the storage service tag only
NSGs are not supported on GatewaySubnet at all
explain: Gateway subnets may carry an NSG, but it must permit inbound from the GatewayManager service tag — the Azure control plane manages the gateway through it, and default-deny breaks provisioning and health. Opening all Internet ports is excessive and unnecessary, storage-only outbound misses the control plane, and NSGs are supported on GatewaySubnet with these specific allowances.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: An Azure Firewall policy has a DNAT rule forwarding RDP to a VM, a network rule allowing the VM outbound on 443, and an application rule allowing the same FQDN the DNAT targets. In which order does the firewall evaluate these rule types?
options: Application rules, then network rules, then DNAT rules
DNAT rules first, then network rules, then application rules
Rules are evaluated alphabetically by rule collection name
Network rules first, then DNAT, then application
explain: Azure Firewall processes rule collections in a fixed order: DNAT first (inbound destination translation), then network rules, then application rules. Application-first or alphabetical ordering does not exist; knowing DNAT wins is essential because a DNAT match short-circuits the rest of the evaluation for that connection.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: Peak-hour RDP sessions through Azure Bastion are being throttled. You plan to scale the Bastion host. What are the scaling bounds and SKU requirement?
options: 1 to 10 instances on any SKU including Developer
Bastion cannot be scaled; deploy a second Bastion host instead
2 to 50 instances on the Standard SKU; scale units are configured on the Bastion host
Up to 100 instances on the Basic SKU
explain: Azure Bastion scales from 2 to 50 instances, and configurable scale units require the Standard SKU. Developer SKU is a fixed, low-capacity offering without scaling. A second Bastion host per VNet is unnecessary when scale units exist, and there is no Basic Bastion SKU with 100 instances.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: You need Traffic Manager to route users from the 10.20.0.0/16 corporate network to the on-premises endpoint and everyone else to Azure endpoints. Which routing method implements source-IP-based routing?
options: Geographic routing
Weighted routing
Multivalue routing
Subnet routing
explain: The Subnet routing method maps source IP ranges to specific endpoints — the designed answer for steering a corporate address block to a designated endpoint. Geographic routing maps by user geography (DNS resolver location), not arbitrary subnets. Weighted splits traffic by ratio, and multivalue returns multiple healthy endpoints rather than steering by source IP.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: You configure point-to-site VPN with certificate authentication. Users report they cannot connect, and you realize no certificates were uploaded to the gateway. What must you upload?
options: The public data (.cer) of the root certificate; clients present certificates chained to it
Each user's client certificate
The root certificate's private key
A wildcard TLS certificate for the gateway's public IP
explain: P2S certificate authentication requires uploading the root certificate's public data to the VPN gateway; clients authenticate with client certificates issued from that root. Uploading individual client certs does not scale and is not the mechanism, the private key must never leave your CA, and a TLS cert for the gateway IP is unrelated to client authentication.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: Compliance requires encrypted traffic over an ExpressRoute private peering connection. The circuit is already provisioned through a connectivity provider. How do you meet the requirement?
options: Enable MACsec on the provider-provisioned circuit
Run IPsec over the ExpressRoute private peering to encrypt traffic end to end
ExpressRoute private peering encrypts traffic by default; no action is needed
Move the traffic to Microsoft peering, which is encrypted
explain: ExpressRoute private peering is not encrypted by default — the supported pattern is IPsec tunnels over the private peering for encrypted transport. MACsec is available only on ExpressRoute Direct (provider-independent ports), not provider-provisioned circuits. Microsoft peering is also unencrypted by default; it carries public prefixes, not private traffic encryption.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: You manage 40 spoke VNets and want every spoke to reach every other spoke without configuring 780 individual peerings. Which Azure Virtual Network Manager capability builds this full mesh?
options: A security admin rule collection
A routing configuration with static routes
A connectivity configuration with a mesh topology
IPAM pools
explain: Virtual Network Manager connectivity configurations with mesh topology automatically create the full peering mesh across member VNets — the designed answer at this scale. Security admin rules enforce traffic policy, not connectivity. Routing configurations manage UDRs, and IPAM manages address allocation; neither creates the mesh.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: Your Front Door origin serves product images with URLs like /images?id=123&size=large. Cached responses are being served for the wrong size parameter. Which Front Door setting controls this?
options: The health probe interval on the origin group
The WAF managed rule set
Origin host header
Query string caching behavior on the route; caching every unique URL (query string included) versus ignoring query strings changes cache keys
explain: Front Door routes have a query string caching behavior: cache every unique URL treats each query-string variant as a separate cache key, while ignoring query strings serves one cached object for all variants — the misconfiguration behind wrong-size images. Health probes, WAF rules, and host headers do not affect cache-key construction.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: An application behind Application Gateway keeps losing user sessions because requests land on different backend VMs. The app cannot use a shared session store. What should you enable?
options: Cookie-based affinity, so the gateway pins a client to the same backend server
Connection draining
End-to-end TLS
A custom health probe
explain: Cookie-based affinity makes Application Gateway insert an affinity cookie so subsequent requests from the same client route to the same backend VM — the fix for in-memory session state. Connection draining controls how in-flight requests finish during backend removal, end-to-end TLS encrypts backend traffic, and health probes detect unhealthy backends; none of them provide session stickiness.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: On-premises servers must resolve a storage account's private endpoint to its private IP, but they use the on-premises DNS servers and resolve the public IP instead. What is the correct DNS design?
options: Add hosts-file entries on every on-premises server
Configure a conditional forwarder on the on-premises DNS for the privatelink zone (or deploy the Private DNS Resolver) so private endpoint names resolve to private IPs
Disable public network access on the storage account; DNS will follow
Private endpoints cannot be resolved from on-premises networks
explain: Private endpoint DNS names live in privatelink zones; on-premises resolvers need a conditional forwarder for those zones pointing at Azure DNS (168.63.129.16) or a Private DNS Resolver inbound endpoint. Hosts files do not scale, disabling public access changes connectivity but not name resolution, and on-premises resolution of private endpoints is a standard supported pattern.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: You tune a Standard Load Balancer health probe for fast failover of a web farm. What are the default probe interval and unhealthy threshold you are tuning from?
options: 15-second interval with an unhealthy threshold of 3
30-second interval with an unhealthy threshold of 1
5-second interval with an unhealthy threshold of 2 consecutive failures
60-second interval with an unhealthy threshold of 5
explain: The portal defaults for a load balancer health probe are a 5-second interval and an unhealthy threshold of 2 consecutive failures — roughly a 10-second detection window. The 15/3, 30/1, and 60/5 combinations are not the defaults; knowing the real baseline matters because aggressive tuning below it can flap healthy instances out of rotation.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: You place an NSG on the Application Gateway subnet with a default-deny inbound rule. The gateway becomes unhealthy. Which inbound traffic must the NSG allow?
options: Only HTTPS from the Internet on port 443
All traffic from the VirtualNetwork service tag
Inbound from the AzureLoadBalancer tag only
The GatewayManager service tag, plus ports 65200-65535 for backend health and control-plane communication
explain: Application Gateway subnets require inbound from the GatewayManager service tag and the 65200-65535 port range for control-plane and health signaling — default-deny breaks the gateway without them. Allowing only 443 misses the management plane, opening all VNet traffic is broader than required, and the AzureLoadBalancer tag governs a different resource's probes.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: You enable ExpressRoute Microsoft peering to reach Microsoft 365. The peering establishes but no routes are exchanged. What is missing?
options: A route filter; Microsoft peering requires route filters to advertise the public prefixes you are authorized for
BGP must be disabled on Microsoft peering
The circuit must be Premium SKU for any peering to exchange routes
Private peering must be enabled first as a prerequisite
explain: Microsoft peering exchanges routes only for prefixes listed in an attached route filter — without it, the peering is up but advertises nothing. BGP is required (not disabled) on all peerings, Standard SKU supports Microsoft peering (Premium is needed for Global Reach, not for peering itself), and peerings are independent of each other.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: You need a public IP for a zone-redundant NAT gateway in a region with availability zones. Which statement about Standard SKU public IPs is correct?
options: Standard public IPs are zonal by default and must be converted
Standard public IPs are zone-redundant by default in regions with availability zones
Only Basic SKU public IPs support zone redundancy
Zone redundancy requires a public IP prefix, not a single IP
explain: Standard SKU public IP addresses are zone-redundant by default in regions with availability zones — no extra configuration needed for the NAT gateway scenario. They are not zonal-by-default, Basic SKU is retired and was never zone-redundant, and while prefixes are also an option, a single Standard IP is already zone-redundant.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: You enable the WAF on Application Gateway and accept the default rule set. Which OWASP ModSecurity Core Rule Set version is applied by default, and what does that imply?
options: CRS 2.2.9; the oldest stable rule set
CRS 4.0; a preview-only rule set
CRS 3.2; the current default managed rule set protecting against OWASP Top 10 patterns like SQL injection and XSS
No default; the WAF blocks nothing until you import custom rules
explain: Application Gateway WAF applies OWASP CRS 3.2 by default — the managed rule set covering SQL injection, cross-site scripting, and other Top 10 patterns. CRS 2.2.9 is the legacy option, there is no CRS 4.0 default, and the WAF is protective out of the box rather than empty until customized.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: You enable NSG flow logs v2 on several subnets and want a visual map of allowed and denied traffic with drill-down by application and geography. Which Azure Monitor capability consumes the flow logs for this?
options: Connection Monitor
IP flow verify
The flow logs are visualized automatically in the storage account
Traffic Analytics, which processes NSG flow logs into a Log Analytics workspace for visualization and query
explain: Traffic Analytics is the Azure Monitor solution that ingests NSG (and VNet) flow logs into Log Analytics and renders traffic visualizations, top talkers, and geo-distribution. Connection Monitor measures connectivity and latency rather than analyzing flow logs, IP flow verify is a one-time packet simulation, and raw flow logs in storage are JSON blobs with no built-in visualization.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: A partner integration requires clients to present certificates to the Application Gateway before reaching the backend API. Which Application Gateway capability enforces client-certificate authentication?
options: Mutual authentication (mTLS) on the frontend listener using a trusted client CA certificate chain
End-to-end TLS to the backend pool
Cookie-based affinity
The WAF in detection mode
explain: Application Gateway v2 supports mutual TLS: you upload the trusted client CA certificate chain to the frontend listener and the gateway validates client certificates during the handshake. End-to-end TLS encrypts backend traffic but does not authenticate clients, cookie affinity provides stickiness, and WAF detection mode only logs rule matches.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: Your on-premises team asks for a DNS zone transfer (AXFR) of the privatelink blob zone so their BIND servers can serve it locally. How do you respond?
options: Enable zone transfers on the private DNS zone; they are disabled by default
Azure Private DNS zones do not support zone transfers; link the on-premises VNets' resolver via conditional forwarding or the Private DNS Resolver instead
Export the zone file from the portal and import it into BIND
Zone transfers work only for public Azure DNS zones
explain: Azure Private DNS has no zone-transfer mechanism — resolution is provided by linking VNets to the zone (with auto-registration optional), and on-premises networks reach it through conditional forwarders to Azure DNS or the Private DNS Resolver service. There is no AXFR toggle to enable and no zone-file export; the architecture is link-and-resolve, not transfer.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: Your application has endpoints in East US, West Europe, and Southeast Asia, and you want each user routed to the endpoint with the lowest network latency to them. Which Traffic Manager routing method implements this?
options: Geographic routing
Weighted routing
Performance routing
Priority routing
explain: The Performance routing method directs each user to the endpoint with the lowest measured latency from their location — the designed answer for latency-based steering. Geographic routing maps by user geography (not measured latency), weighted splits traffic by ratio regardless of latency, and priority is active-passive failover rather than latency optimization.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: You order an ExpressRoute circuit through a connectivity provider for private peering. The provider says the circuit is provisioned on their side, but the circuit shows 'NotProvisioned' in Azure. What is the missing step?
options: The provider must also create the Azure resource; customers cannot create circuits
NotProvisioned means the circuit is ready; it changes state on first use
ExpressRoute Direct must be ordered instead of provider circuits
You must create the ExpressRoute circuit resource in Azure with the matching service key/SKU, and the provider provisions against it — both sides create their objects
explain: Provider-provisioned ExpressRoute is a two-sided workflow: you create the circuit resource in Azure (SKU, peering location, bandwidth) and the provider provisions connectivity against your service key. Neither side alone completes it — the provider cannot create your Azure resource, NotProvisioned genuinely means incomplete, and ExpressRoute Direct is the alternative port-based model, not a fix for this state.
domain: Domain 4: Implement and manage virtual networking

q: You need to find every log entry mentioning a compromised service account across all tables in a Log Analytics workspace, without knowing which tables hold the data. Which KQL approach works?
options: Use the search operator, for example search 'svc-backup' , which scans all tables in scope
Use where, which automatically spans all tables
Query each table individually; cross-table text search is not supported
Use the union operator with a wildcard table name
explain: The KQL search operator performs a full-text search across all tables in the query scope when no table is specified — the tool for 'find this string everywhere'. The where operator filters rows within tables already in scope and cannot span tables by itself. Union requires explicit table names (no wildcards for this purpose), and per-table querying is the slow manual path search exists to replace.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: You create a log search alert that evaluates every 60 minutes over the last 5 minutes of data. The alert team says this configuration is invalid. What is the rule?
options: The time window cannot exceed 30 minutes for log alerts
The alert frequency cannot exceed the query time window; frequency must be less than or equal to the time window
Frequency and time window must be identical values
Log alerts cannot run more often than hourly
explain: A log search alert's evaluation frequency must be less than or equal to its query time window — evaluating every 60 minutes over only 5 minutes of data would silently skip 55 minutes of data each cycle, so Azure rejects it. Time windows support far more than 30 minutes, frequency and window need not match (a 5-minute frequency over a 60-minute window is valid), and frequencies down to 1 minute are supported.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: You connect a Log Analytics workspace to an Azure Monitor Private Link Scope and set the query access mode to Private Only, leaving ingestion on Open during migration. What is the effect?
options: Both ingestion and query share one access mode; the settings conflict and the scope fails validation
Private Only for queries also blocks ingestion regardless of its setting
Queries are restricted to private networks while ingestion still accepts public traffic; ingestion and query each have an independent Open or Private Only mode
Open ingestion prevents the Private Only query setting from taking effect
explain: AMPLS exposes separate access modes for ingestion and query, each independently Open or Private Only — the designed migration pattern is Private Only queries with Open ingestion, then tightening ingestion later. The modes do not conflict, query restrictions do not cascade to ingestion, and Open ingestion does not override the query setting. Note the caveat: Log Analytics ingestion uses resource-specific endpoints, so a workspace firewall is still needed to fully block public ingestion.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: Your Application Insights resource still uses URL ping availability tests. You receive a retirement notice. What is the migration path?
options: Migrate to multi-step web tests, which remain fully supported
URL ping tests are permanent; the notice is informational only
Replace them with custom TrackAvailability() calls, the recommended current approach
Migrate to Standard tests; URL ping tests retire on September 30, 2026, and multi-step web tests are already retired
explain: URL ping tests are deprecated and will be retired on September 30, 2026 — the migration target is Standard tests, which add TLS certificate validity checks, HTTP verbs, and custom headers. Multi-step web tests were retired earlier, the notice is a real retirement, and TrackAvailability() custom tests are archived classic guidance, not the recommended path.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: You build an Update Manager maintenance configuration with a dynamic scope filtering VMs by the tag PatchGroup=Prod across two subscriptions. A VM tagged after the schedule is created gets patched on the next run. Why?
options: Dynamic scopes are evaluated at schedule run time, so machines matching the criteria at that moment are included
The schedule rescans tags every 5 minutes continuously
Tag changes trigger an immediate out-of-band patch run
Dynamic scopes only evaluate at creation; the VM was included by coincidence
explain: Dynamic scope criteria (subscriptions, resource groups, locations, tags, OS type) are evaluated when the maintenance configuration runs — the machine list at run time is authoritative, so newly tagged VMs are picked up automatically. There is no continuous 5-minute rescan, tag changes do not trigger immediate runs, and creation-time evaluation is explicitly not the model (the portal even warns the preview list may differ at run time).
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: You must collect a custom application log file from Linux VMs into Log Analytics. The Monitoring Agent (AMA) is already deployed. What do you configure?
options: Install the legacy Log Analytics agent alongside AMA
Create a data collection rule with a custom text log data source pointing at the log file path
Custom text logs require Azure Monitor Agent in gateway mode
Copy the log file to Blob storage and query it with KQL
explain: AMA data collection rules support custom text log sources — you define the file path and delimiter/record parsing in the DCR and the agent ships the rows to the workspace. The legacy MMA agent is deprecated and should not be added, gateway mode is for proxied connectivity rather than a log-type requirement, and Blob storage is not queryable by Log Analytics KQL.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: You put a Log Analytics workspace behind an AMPLS with Private Only ingestion, but agents on the VNet still fail to ingest. The workspace firewall allows the VNet. What else is commonly required?
options: Nothing; AMPLS Private Only ingestion is sufficient on its own
Enable the daily cap to throttle ingestion
Link a storage account to the workspace, because Log Analytics ingestion uses resource-specific endpoints that do not adhere to AMPLS access modes
Move the workspace to the same region as the AMPLS
explain: Microsoft documents that Log Analytics ingestion uses resource-specific endpoints and does not adhere to AMPLS access modes — the documented complement is linking a storage account to the workspace for ingestion over the private path (plus workspace firewall rules blocking public endpoints). AMPLS alone does not complete the private-ingestion story, the daily cap is a cost control, and region alignment with the AMPLS is not the ingestion blocker.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: Your action group sends alerts to a webhook that parses the payload. After enabling the common alert schema, the webhook breaks. What should the webhook owner know?
options: The schema can only be enabled for the entire action group at once
Enabling the schema disables all email actions in the group
The common alert schema applies only to metric alerts, not log alerts
The common alert schema is enabled per action, standardizing the JSON payload shape; the webhook must parse the new schema
explain: The common alert schema is a per-action toggle that replaces each alert type's native payload with one standardized JSON shape — webhook receivers must be coded against it. It is not group-wide-or-nothing, it does not disable email actions, and it applies across alert types (metric, log, activity log) precisely to unify parsing.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: You need an availability test that also warns you before the site's TLS certificate expires. Which test type provides proactive certificate lifetime checking?
options: Standard test, which includes TLS/SSL certificate validity and proactive lifetime checks
URL ping test
Multi-step web test
A custom KQL-based log alert
explain: Standard availability tests natively validate TLS/SSL certificates and include proactive lifetime checks that warn before expiry — beyond the old URL ping's simple up/down. URL ping is deprecated, multi-step web tests are retired, and a KQL log alert cannot probe an external endpoint's certificate.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: You write a KQL query to show the 10 VMs with the highest average CPU over the last day. Which pattern is correct?
options: Perf | where CounterName == '% Processor Time' | top 10 by CounterValue
Perf | where CounterName == '% Processor Time' | summarize avg(CounterValue) by Computer | sort by avg_CounterValue desc | take 10
Perf | take 10 | sort by CounterValue
Perf | where CounterName == '% Processor Time' | limit 10
explain: The correct pattern aggregates first (summarize avg by Computer), then sorts descending and takes 10 — top-N by an aggregated value requires the aggregation step. top 10 by CounterValue ranks raw samples, not per-VM averages; take/limit before sorting returns arbitrary rows. The sort-then-take sequence is the canonical KQL top-N idiom.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: You must stream the Azure activity log to Event Hubs for a SIEM, covering the entire subscription including control-plane writes. Where do you configure this?
options: A diagnostic setting on each resource group individually
An action group with an Event Hubs action
A diagnostic setting at the subscription scope targeting Event Hubs
Activity log export is only available per resource, not per subscription
explain: The activity log is a subscription-level log, and its diagnostic setting is created at the subscription scope with Event Hubs (or Log Analytics, or storage) as the destination — one setting covers the whole subscription. Per-resource-group settings would miss subscription-level operations, action groups route alert notifications rather than log streams, and per-resource export is the wrong scope for the activity log.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: You create an Update Manager maintenance configuration with a 6-hour maintenance window for weekend patching. The creation fails. What is the constraint?
options: Maintenance windows must be exactly 4 hours
Weekend schedules are not supported; use weekday windows
The window must match the VM's time zone exactly
The maximum maintenance window is 3 hours 55 minutes
explain: Update Manager maintenance configurations cap the maintenance window at 3 hours 55 minutes — a 6-hour window is rejected. There is no exact-4-hour rule, weekend recurrence is fully supported, and the window is configured in the schedule's time context rather than being forced to match each VM's time zone.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: A manager asks what kinds of guidance Azure Advisor provides beyond cost savings. Which categories does Advisor cover?
options: Cost, security, reliability, operational excellence, and performance
Cost only; other guidance comes from Defender for Cloud
Security only, and only with Defender for Cloud enabled
Reliability only, focused on availability zones
explain: Azure Advisor recommendations span five categories: cost, security, reliability, operational excellence, and performance. Cost is just one pillar. Defender for Cloud enriches the security pillar but Advisor's security recommendations exist independently, and reliability covers more than zone placement (backups, redundancy, failover readiness).
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: A dashboard charts VM CPU but the team wants the chart split per VM instance instead of one aggregate line. In Azure Metrics, what enables this?
options: Changing the aggregation from Average to Maximum
Splitting (applying) by a dimension such as the VM resource ID
Increasing the time grain to 1 hour
Pinning the chart to a shared dashboard
explain: Metric splitting (dimension application) breaks one metric chart into per-dimension series — here one line per VM. Aggregation changes the math (avg vs max) but not the series count, time grain changes resolution, and pinning only relocates the chart. Splitting by dimension is the standard multi-instance visualization technique.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: During an Azure outage your VM shows 'Unavailable' in Resource Health, but Service Health shows no active events for the region. A colleague says the dashboards contradict each other. How do you explain it?
options: Resource Health is delayed by 24 hours; trust Service Health
Service Health only tracks planned maintenance, not outages

They measure different scopes: Resource Health reports the health of your specific resource, while Service Health reports service-wide events; a host-level failure can affect your VM without a regional service event
One of the two blades is misconfigured
explain: Resource Health is per-resource (your VM's host may have failed), while Service Health tracks broader service/region incidents — a single-host failure shows in Resource Health with no corresponding Service Health event, and that is expected rather than contradictory. Resource Health is near-real-time, Service Health covers outages plus planned maintenance and advisories, and neither blade needs 'configuration' to report.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: You onboard 200 VMs to VM insights. A colleague proposes creating one data collection rule per VM for isolation. What is the better design?
options: One DCR per VM is required for VM insights
DCRs cannot be shared; each VM needs its own workspace instead
VM insights does not use data collection rules
A single DCR can target many VMs (via associations or the VM insights data collection rule), centralizing syslog, performance counters, and event configuration
explain: Data collection rules are designed for many-to-one: one DCR defines the data sources (performance counters, Windows events, syslog) and destinations, and many VMs associate to it — the standard at-scale VM insights pattern. Per-VM DCRs create unmanageable sprawl, workspaces are not per-VM either, and VM insights onboarding is DCR-based (the policy initiative deploys the association).
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: You set a 100 GB daily cap on a Log Analytics workspace to control cost. Ingestion hits the cap at 6 PM. What happens to data ingested after that?
options: Ingestion stops until the cap resets the next day; data sent over the cap is dropped
Older data is deleted to make room for new data
Ingestion continues and the overage is billed at commitment-tier rates
The workspace automatically upgrades to a commitment tier
explain: The daily cap halts ingestion once reached — data sent afterward is dropped until the cap resets at midnight UTC (with a warning state as it approaches). It never deletes existing data to make room, overage is not billed (that is the point of the cap), and no automatic tier upgrade occurs. Commitment tiers are a separate opt-in pricing choice.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: The on-call team wants critical alerts to page at night but only send email during business hours, without editing each alert rule. Which Azure Monitor feature implements time-based notification routing?
options: A second action group with quiet hours configured on each alert
Alert processing rules with a schedule scope, which can add or suppress action groups on matching alerts during defined times
Diagnostic settings with time filters
Azure Policy with a time-based effect
explain: Alert processing rules apply at fire time across alert rules: a scheduled suppression or action-group-adding rule routes notifications by time without touching individual alert definitions. Quiet hours are not an action-group feature, diagnostic settings route logs not alert notifications, and Policy governs resource compliance rather than alert delivery.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: A network engineer wants a one-time check of whether a VM can reach a database on port 1433 right now, including hop-by-hop path analysis. Which Network Watcher tool fits, and how does it differ from Connection Monitor?
options: Connection Monitor; it is the one-time diagnostic tool
IP flow verify; it monitors continuously
Connection troubleshoot; it is a one-time on-demand connectivity check, whereas Connection Monitor runs continuous scheduled monitoring with latency trends
Next hop; it runs on a schedule
explain: Connection troubleshoot performs an on-demand, one-time connectivity check with detailed hop analysis — the right tool for 'can it reach right now'. Connection Monitor is the continuous counterpart: scheduled probes over time with latency and loss trends. The distractors invert the two, and IP flow verify / next hop are single-packet simulations, not monitoring solutions.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: You write KQL to chart failed sign-ins per hour: SigninLogs | where ResultType != 0 | summarize count() by bin(TimeGenerated, 1h) | render timechart. A colleague removes the summarize line and keeps render timechart. What breaks?
options: Nothing; render timechart aggregates automatically
The query fails because bin() requires summarize
render timechart only works on the Perf table
The chart breaks or renders meaningless output; timechart needs aggregated series (one row per time bucket), which summarize produces — raw rows have no bucketed values to plot
explain: render timechart expects aggregated data — typically one row per time bucket per series. Without summarize, the query returns raw rows and the visualization has no bucketed values to plot (or plots noise). The operator does not auto-aggregate, bin() is valid without summarize (it just adds a column), and timechart works on any table with suitable aggregated output.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: Your company allows personal devices to access corporate apps, but after a malware incident, security mandates that Android devices be blocked while iOS, Windows, and macOS devices remain allowed. You need to enforce this in Conditional Access. Which condition do you configure?
options: The Device platforms condition, selecting Android as blocked while leaving iOS, Windows, and macOS allowed
The Grant control "Require device to be marked as compliant", because non-compliant Android devices are blocked automatically
The Locations condition with named locations, because device type is derived from the network
The Client apps condition, because Android only uses mobile apps
explain: The Device platforms condition filters by OS (Android, iOS, Windows, macOS, Linux), so it is the direct way to block Android while allowing the others. The compliant-device grant controls on Intune compliance state, not OS type. Named locations filter by network, not device, and client apps filter by app type (browser vs mobile client), not by platform.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: Engineers from a partner organization access your Azure resources as B2B guests using accounts from their own Microsoft Entra tenant. Several forget their passwords and your help desk tries to reset them in your tenant, but the resets fail. What is the correct guidance?
options: Have the guests use your tenant self-service password reset page; it works for all B2B guests
The guests reset their passwords in their home tenant, so the partner must have SSPR enabled there; you cannot reset passwords for accounts homed in another directory
Convert the guests to member userType so your SSPR policy applies to them
Disable SSPR in your tenant and let the partner tenant handle all resets
explain: For B2B guests whose accounts are managed by another Microsoft Entra directory, password reset happens in the home tenant — only the guest or a home-tenant admin can reset it, and the home tenant needs SSPR enabled. Your tenant cannot reset passwords for accounts it does not home. Converting userType does not change where the account is homed, and disabling your own SSPR helps nobody.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: You maintain two emergency-access (break-glass) accounts excluded from Conditional Access. The CISO wants an alert any time either account signs in, so misuse is caught immediately. What is the right implementation?
options: Create a Conditional Access policy that requires MFA for the break-glass accounts and alerts on failure
Assign the accounts to Privileged Identity Management so activations generate alerts
Stream Microsoft Entra sign-in logs to Log Analytics with diagnostic settings and build a log search alert rule that fires on sign-ins by those two accounts
Enable the Identity Protection user risk policy for the break-glass accounts
explain: Sign-in logs contain every authentication event, so routing them to Log Analytics and alerting on the break-glass account names gives immediate detection of any use. A Conditional Access policy cannot alert, and putting break-glass accounts under CA or PIM defeats their purpose as policy-independent recovery accounts. The user risk policy remediates risky sign-ins, it does not page on a specific account signing in.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: You enable password writeback in the Microsoft Entra Connect wizard and confirm the tenant has P1 licenses, but users still get an error when SSPR tries to write passwords back on-premises. The Connect server is the active (non-staging) server. What did you most likely miss?
options: Password hash synchronization must also be enabled for writeback to function
The domain controllers must be upgraded to the latest Windows Server version
Restarting the ADSync service, which applies the wizard change automatically
Enabling writeback in the Microsoft Entra admin center under Password reset > On-premises integration, because writeback requires both the Connect wizard switch and the portal switch
explain: Password writeback has two switches: the Connect wizard optional feature and "Write back passwords to your on-premises directory" in the Entra admin center — both must be on. Writeback works with PHS, pass-through, or federation, so PHS is not mandatory. Domain controller version is irrelevant to the missing switch, and no service restart substitutes for the portal setting.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: Your access package grants contractors access to a project. Compliance requires that every time a request is approved, a ticket is opened automatically in ServiceNow with the request details. What should you configure?
options: A custom extension on the access package catalog that triggers a Logic App at the approval stage of the assignment request workflow
An access review on the access package that opens tickets for denied requests
A Conditional Access policy with a Terms of Use control referencing ServiceNow
An Azure Automation runbook scheduled hourly to poll for new assignments
explain: Entitlement management custom extensions let you attach a Logic App to stages of the access package assignment workflow (request, approval, assignment), which is exactly how you fire an external ticket on approval. Access reviews govern continued need, not provisioning side effects. Conditional Access cannot call external systems, and a polling runbook is a fragile substitute for the native workflow hook.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: A user taps "Report" on an unexpected Microsoft Authenticator push prompt they did not initiate. The next morning the help desk sees the user flagged as high risk in Identity Protection with a "User reported suspicious activity" detection. What caused this?
options: Smart lockout automatically escalated the account after the report
The "Report suspicious activity" setting: when a user reports a prompt, Microsoft sets the user to high user risk and records the detection, so risk-based policies can then block or remediate
The legacy fraud alert feature, which still auto-blocks the account
A Conditional Access policy that blocks all Authenticator push notifications
explain: Report suspicious activity (the current name for the old fraud alert, which Microsoft retired in March 2025) marks the reporting user as high risk with a "User reported suspicious activity" detection in Identity Protection; risk-based Conditional Access or manual remediation then handles the account. Smart lockout throttles brute-force attempts, it does not react to user reports. The legacy fraud alert auto-block no longer exists, and no CA policy blocks push prompts themselves.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: You assign the built-in "Allowed locations" policy with a Deny effect to a subscription, permitting only East US and West Europe. A developer points out several existing VMs running in Southeast Asia and asks whether the policy will stop or delete them. What do you tell them?
options: The policy deletes the non-compliant VMs at the next evaluation cycle
The policy stops the VMs but keeps their disks so they can be moved
The Deny effect only blocks new deployments outside the allowed regions; existing resources are flagged non-compliant but keep running
The policy automatically moves the VMs to an allowed region
explain: Deny prevents non-compliant write operations going forward — it never deletes, stops, or moves resources that already exist. Those VMs simply show as non-compliant until remediated (for example by moving them). Options A, B, and D describe remediation behaviors the Deny effect does not perform.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: You need a custom RBAC role ("VM Operator") that administrators can assign in any of the five subscriptions under the "Production" management group, but nowhere else. How should you scope the custom role definition?
options: Set assignableScopes to each subscription individually and copy the role five times
Set assignableScopes to the tenant root so it is available everywhere, then restrict with policy
Use NotActions to exclude the other management groups
Set assignableScopes to the "Production" management group; the role can then be assigned at the management group or any child subscription or resource group scope
explain: assignableScopes controls where a custom role may be assigned — scoping it to the management group makes it assignable at that level and everywhere beneath it, covering all five subscriptions in one definition. Copying the role per subscription is unnecessary duplication. Tenant-root scoping overexposes it, and NotActions limits permissions within the role, not where the role can be assigned.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: After a reorganization you rename a subscription from "IT-Dev" to "Platform-Dev" and add a "CostCenter" tag to the subscription. A junior admin worries that renaming will change resource IDs and break billing history, and asks whether resources now inherit the tag. What is accurate?
options: Renaming changes only the subscription display name; the subscription ID, resource IDs, and billing history are unaffected, and subscription tags are not inherited by resources
Renaming generates a new subscription ID, so all role assignments must be recreated
Tags on a subscription propagate to every resource group and resource within it
Renaming a subscription requires moving it to a new management group
explain: A subscription rename is a display-name-only change: IDs, resource IDs, role assignments, and billing continuity are untouched. Tags do not inherit downward in Azure — a tag on the subscription applies only to the subscription object itself, just as resource group tags do not flow to resources. No re-creation of assignments or management group move is involved.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: Finance wants automatic detection of unexpected cost spikes without setting fixed budget thresholds, plus email notification to the FinOps team. Which native capability fits, and what is its key limitation?
options: Budget alerts with forecasted thresholds, which detect spikes at any scope including resource groups
Cost anomaly alerts, which use ML on the subscription\u2019s spend pattern and email recipients, but they work at subscription scope only and the sensitivity cannot be tuned
Azure Policy with a cost effect, which blocks the spending that causes the spike
Advisor cost recommendations, which email the team whenever spend deviates
explain: Cost anomaly alerts are the ML-based spike detector: they learn the subscription\u2019s normal spend and email recipients on anomalies, with no threshold to configure. Their limits are real — subscription scope only, no sensitivity tuning, and they need some history before they are reliable. Budget alerts need explicit thresholds, Azure Policy has no cost effect, and Advisor recommendations do not send spike emails.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: Users keep requesting access to third-party SaaS apps that require admin consent, and IT wants a self-service flow: users request, designated reviewers approve or deny, and decisions are audited. Where do you configure this?
options: In each app registration\u2019s manifest, by adding the reviewers as owners
In Conditional Access, with an app-enforced restrictions session control
In Microsoft Entra ID under Enterprise apps > User settings, by enabling the admin consent workflow and designating reviewers
In Privileged Identity Management, by making the app\u2019s admin role eligible
explain: The admin consent workflow (Enterprise apps > User settings) gives users a "request approval" path for apps needing admin consent, routes requests to designated reviewers, and logs decisions. App registration ownership does not create a request flow. Conditional Access cannot grant consent, and PIM governs role activation, not application consent.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: An auditor requires 12 months of Microsoft Entra sign-in and audit logs for the tenant. The tenant has P1 licenses. What do you explain about native retention, and how do you meet the requirement?
options: Sign-in and audit logs are retained 90 days natively; extend retention in the Entra admin center
Logs are kept indefinitely in the portal once P1 is licensed
Retention is unlimited if you enable the logs in Microsoft Defender for Cloud

Microsoft Entra retains sign-in and audit logs for 30 days by default; for 12 months, route them with diagnostic settings to a Log Analytics workspace or storage account where retention is configurable
explain: The Entra portal/API keeps sign-in and audit logs for 30 days (with P1/P2); there is no native 12-month retention. The supported path is diagnostic settings streaming the logs to Log Analytics or storage, where you control retention. 90 days is the Activity Log retention, not Entra sign-in logs, and Defender for Cloud does not extend Entra log retention.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: HR stores a cost-center code in each user\u2019s on-premises extensionAttribute1. You want a dynamic Microsoft Entra group that automatically contains all users whose cost center is "CC-4400". How do you build the rule?
options: Create a dynamic membership rule such as user.extensionAttribute1 -eq "CC-4400", because directory extension attributes synced from on-premises are usable in dynamic group rules
Manually add the users, because custom attributes cannot be referenced in dynamic rules
Use an administrative unit, because extension attributes only work for scoping roles
Build the rule on user.department, because extension attributes are never synchronized to Microsoft Entra ID
explain: On-premises extension attributes (extensionAttribute1–15) synchronize to Microsoft Entra ID and are directly referenceable in dynamic membership rules as user.extensionAttribute1. Manual membership defeats the purpose of a dynamic group, administrative units scope administration rather than express membership, and the claim that the attributes never sync is false.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: The company wants every new Microsoft 365 group to start with "GRP-" and to block names containing "CEO" or "Payroll". Where do you enforce this, and what is its scope?
options: In a Conditional Access policy targeting group creation
In the group\u2019s naming policy in Microsoft Entra ID (Groups > Naming policy): it applies a prefix/suffix and blocked words, but only to Microsoft 365 groups, not security groups
In an Azure Policy assigned to the tenant root
In the Exchange admin center transport rules
explain: The Microsoft 365 group naming policy enforces prefixes/suffixes and a blocked-words list at creation time, and it applies specifically to Microsoft 365 groups — security groups are unaffected. Conditional Access governs sign-in, not group naming; Azure Policy governs Azure resources, not Entra group names; transport rules govern mail flow.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: Identity Protection raises a "risky workload identity" alert: a service principal\u2019s credential appears in a public code repository. The service principal runs a production automation. What is the right response?
options: Delete the service principal immediately to stop the exposure
Ignore it; Identity Protection only evaluates user accounts, so this must be a false positive
Treat it like a compromised credential: investigate recent sign-ins, rotate the service principal\u2019s credential, then dismiss or confirm the risk in Identity Protection
Block the service principal with a Conditional Access user-risk policy
explain: Identity Protection (P2) does detect risky workload identities such as leaked service-principal credentials; the correct handling is investigate, rotate the credential, and then dismiss or confirm-compromised the risk. Deleting the service principal would break the production automation. The user-risk CA policy targets users, not workload identities, and ignoring a leaked credential is never correct.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: Remote employees need browser access to an internal HR web app that lives on-premises. Security forbids opening inbound firewall ports or deploying VPN for this. Which solution publishes the app with Microsoft Entra pre-authentication?
options: Azure Bastion, which publishes web apps through the Azure portal
Azure Front Door with a private origin
A site-to-site VPN with forced tunneling
Microsoft Entra application proxy: install a lightweight connector on the corporate network (outbound-only) and publish the app, so users authenticate at Microsoft Entra before reaching it
explain: Application proxy publishes on-premises web apps through an outbound-only connector — no inbound firewall rules, no VPN — and enforces Microsoft Entra pre-authentication (with Conditional Access) before traffic reaches the app. Bastion is for VM RDP/SSH, not web apps. Front Door front-ends public or private-link origins but does not broker on-premises apps this way, and a VPN violates the stated constraint.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: HR wants new hires automatically provisioned into ServiceNow (accounts created, updated, and deprovisioned from Microsoft Entra ID) without custom code. The app supports SCIM 2.0. What do you configure?
options: Automatic user provisioning in the ServiceNow enterprise app, which uses SCIM 2.0 to create, update, and remove accounts on a schedule
Microsoft Entra Connect sync with an OU filter for ServiceNow users
A Conditional Access policy that provisions users on first sign-in
An access package that emails the ServiceNow admin on each hire
explain: The enterprise app\u2019s automatic (SCIM-based) provisioning syncs identities on a schedule — creating, updating, and deprovisioning accounts with no custom code. Entra Connect syncs to Microsoft Entra ID, not out to SaaS apps. Conditional Access authorizes sign-ins; it does not provision accounts. An access package can gate access but does not write accounts into ServiceNow.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: A Microsoft partner will administer a customer\u2019s Microsoft 365 tenant for a migration project. The customer wants the partner to have only the Exchange Administrator and Teams Administrator roles, approved explicitly, expiring automatically after one year. Which model delivers this?
options: Delegated admin privileges (DAP), which grants the partner Global Administrator automatically
Granular delegated admin privileges (GDAP): the partner requests specific Microsoft Entra roles, the customer approves, and the relationship is time-bound up to two years
A B2B guest invitation for each partner engineer with the required roles
Azure Lighthouse, which delegates Microsoft Entra roles in the customer tenant
explain: GDAP replaced DAP for partner administration: partners request only the Entra roles they need, the customer explicitly approves, and access expires automatically (max two years) — exactly the least-privilege, time-bound ask. DAP granted broad Global Admin and is deprecated for new relationships. B2B guests do not confer delegated admin roles, and Lighthouse delegates Azure (resource) management, not Entra directory roles.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: A warehouse runs shared tablets across three shifts. Workers must sign in quickly without passwords, and a lost or stolen tablet must not yield a reusable credential. Which authentication approach fits?
options: Issue every worker a FIDO2 security key to share between shifts
Use one shared password for all tablets and rotate it monthly
Issue Temporary Access Passes with short lifetimes and one-time use for sign-in on the shared devices
Enable passwordless phone sign-in on each worker\u2019s personal phone
explain: Temporary Access Passes are designed for exactly this: short-lived, optionally one-time credentials for bootstrapping sign-in on shared or frontline devices, so a compromised pass quickly becomes useless. Sharing FIDO2 keys destroys non-repudiation, a shared password is a standing credential on every device, and phone sign-in ties authentication to personal devices the shift model does not guarantee.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: After enabling Microsoft Entra Connect sync, several new hires never appear in Microsoft Entra ID. Synchronization Service Manager shows export errors mentioning duplicate proxy addresses for those objects. What is happening and how do you fix it?
options: The sync scheduler is paused; run Start-ADSyncSyncCycle to resume
The users are in an OU excluded by filtering; move them to a synced OU
Password hash sync is disabled, which blocks user object creation
The objects are quarantined by duplicate-attribute resiliency; resolve the duplicate proxy addresses on-premises and the objects will sync on the next cycle
explain: Duplicate attribute resiliency quarantines objects whose UPN or proxy addresses collide with existing ones instead of failing the whole sync — fixing the duplicates on-premises lets them flow on the next cycle. A paused scheduler or OU filtering would affect all objects, not specific ones with attribute errors, and password hash sync has no bearing on whether user objects are created.
domain: Domain 1: Manage identities and governance in Azure

q: Compliance requires a point-in-time copy of an Azure file share every night at 2 AM, restorable file-by-file. There is no built-in schedule for this in the portal. How do you implement it?
options: Schedule an Azure Automation runbook (or Logic App) to take a share snapshot nightly; each snapshot is a read-only point-in-time copy you can copy individual files back from
Enable soft delete on the share, which automatically captures nightly snapshots
Configure a lifecycle management policy on the storage account with a daily snapshot rule
Use Azure Backup\u2019s file share backup, which only supports manual on-demand snapshots
explain: Share snapshots are manual point-in-time, read-only copies with no native scheduler, so a scheduled runbook or Logic App taking nightly snapshots is the standard pattern — individual files are restored by copying from the snapshot. Soft delete protects against deletion but does not take scheduled copies. Lifecycle management applies to blob storage, not file shares, and Azure Backup for Files supports scheduled backups, not "manual only".
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: A premium (SSD) file share holds a production database\u2019s backup files. Ransomware protection requires an off-site, vaulted copy with multi-year retention, not just local snapshots. What is supported?
options: Only snapshot-tier backup, because vaulted backup does not support premium file shares
Azure Backup vaulted (vault-standard) backup for premium file shares, storing recovery points in a Backup vault with retention up to 10 years
File share soft delete with a 10-year retention setting
AzCopy the share to a cool blob container nightly
explain: Azure Backup supports vaulted backup for premium (SSD) file shares in FileStorage accounts, keeping recovery points in a Backup vault for up to 10 years — the off-site ransomware-protection story. Snapshot-tier-only is wrong; vaulted tier is supported. Soft delete retention maxes out far below multi-year needs and is not an off-site copy. AzCopy is a DIY copy with no backup catalog, retention policy, or centralized restore.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: Linux clients in a hybrid environment need to mount an Azure Files NFS 4.1 share with Kerberos authentication. The users are hybrid identities synced from on-premises AD DS. Which identity source should the share use?
options: Microsoft Entra ID OAuth, because NFS 4.1 uses bearer tokens
Anonymous access with firewall IP rules, because NFS cannot do Kerberos
AD DS Kerberos (krb5p), which fits hybrid identities; Microsoft Entra Kerberos is the alternative for environments without AD DS line-of-sight needs
SMB identity settings, because NFS inherits the SMB authentication configuration
explain: NFS 4.1 shares authenticate with Kerberos: AD DS Kerberos (krb5p) is the natural choice for synced hybrid identities, while Microsoft Entra Kerberos serves cloud-centric setups. NFS does not use Entra ID OAuth bearer tokens, anonymous-plus-firewall provides no user authentication, and NFS and SMB each have their own identity configuration on the share.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: You must move 600 TB of archival data from on-premises to Azure over a slow WAN link, in a single shipment. Which Data Box option fits, and what is its usable capacity?
options: Data Box Disk, 40 TB per order — order fifteen sets
Data Box, 100 TB per order — order six devices
Data Box Gateway, which ships as a physical appliance with 500 TB usable
Data Box Heavy, about 1 PB raw / 770 TB usable per order — one order covers 600 TB
explain: Data Box Heavy provides roughly 1 PB raw (770 TB usable) per order, so a single Heavy covers 600 TB. Standard Data Box is 100 TB per order (80 TB usable) and Data Box Disk is 40 TB per order — both would need many shipments. Data Box Gateway is a virtual (software) appliance, not a shippable device.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: After a storage account failover from the primary to the secondary region, the DR team asks what redundancy now protects the data and how to restore the original posture. What do you tell them?
options: The account keeps its original GRS replication; nothing changes after failover
Failover converts the account to read-access geo-redundant automatically
The account is now locally redundant (LRS) in the new primary region; reconfigure the replication setting (for example back to GRS) to re-establish geo-redundancy
Replication is disabled after failover and the account must be recreated to get redundancy back
explain: A completed failover leaves the account as LRS in the new primary region — the secondary copy became the only copy. To restore geo-redundancy you change the replication type back (e.g., to GRS/GZRS), which re-establishes the paired secondary. The account does not retain GRS through the failover, does not become RA-GRS on its own, and certainly does not need recreating.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: A worker role pulls messages from an Azure Storage queue; some messages take 20 minutes to process, but the visibility timeout is 5 minutes, so messages reappear and get processed twice. What should the worker do?
options: Call UpdateMessage to extend the visibility timeout while processing long-running messages, so the message stays invisible until work completes
Delete the message immediately after reading it and re-add it when done
Increase the queue\u2019s time-to-live setting, which controls visibility
Switch to a Service Bus queue, because Storage queues cannot change visibility
explain: UpdateMessage lets you extend a message\u2019s visibility timeout (and optionally update its content) while it is being processed — the standard fix for long-running work. Deleting up front risks data loss if the worker crashes. Time-to-live governs how long a message lives in the queue, not invisibility, and Storage queues fully support visibility management without switching services.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: You need anonymous users to be able to read blobs via direct URLs, but they must NOT be able to list the container\u2019s contents. Which public access level do you set on the container?
options: Private (no anonymous access), and share SAS URLs instead
Blob: anonymous read access for blobs only, without container listing
Container: anonymous read access for blobs and container listing
Disable "Allow Blob public access" on the storage account and use a CDN
explain: The Blob public-access level grants anonymous reads of individual blobs but not listing of the container — exactly the requirement. Container level would additionally allow anonymous listing. Private blocks all anonymous access (SAS is a different mechanism), and disabling blob public access at the account level removes anonymous access entirely rather than scoping it.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: A storage account firewall is set to default-deny with "Allow trusted Microsoft services" enabled. An Azure Function with a system-assigned managed identity still gets 403s accessing blobs, while Azure Backup works fine. What is the explanation and fix?
options: The Function needs the Storage Blob Data Contributor role; the firewall is irrelevant
Disable the firewall entirely, because trusted services bypass does not work with managed identities

The trusted-services bypass covers only specific listed services (like Azure Backup), not arbitrary Azure services; give the Function network access via a VNet integration plus a VNet firewall rule, or a private endpoint
Enable shared key access, which the trusted-services setting requires
explain: Allow trusted Microsoft services is an allowlist of specific services — Azure Backup is on it, a general Azure Function is not — so the Function is still denied at the network layer despite its RBAC role. The fix is a network path: VNet integration with a VNet rule, or a private endpoint. RBAC alone never passes a firewall, disabling the firewall is overkill, and shared key access is an authorization setting unrelated to the network rule.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: For DR you copy a 2 TB incremental snapshot of a data disk to a storage account in another region every month with AzCopy. Finance asks how this is billed. What do you tell them?
options: Incremental copies stay incremental across regions, so only changed blocks are billed with no egress
There is no charge because snapshot copies within Azure are free
Use object replication instead, which is free for snapshots
Each cross-region copy materializes a full copy in the target region: you pay egress for the data transferred plus storage for the full copy
explain: Copying a snapshot across regions (or accounts) creates a full blob copy — the incremental chain does not transfer — so every monthly copy moves the full 2 TB (egress) and stores a full 2 TB copy. "Incremental across regions" and "free copies" are both false. Object replication applies to block blobs, not managed disk snapshots.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: On an ADLS Gen2 filesystem you set a default ACL on a directory granting the analytics group read/execute. New files created afterwards inherit it correctly, but files created before the change do not. A junior admin calls this a bug. What do you explain?
options: This is by design: default ACLs are inherited only by child items created after the default ACL is set; to change existing items you must update their access ACLs, recursively if needed
The default ACL was set on the wrong scope; default ACLs apply retroactively when set at the filesystem root
POSIX ACLs are evaluated after RBAC, so the RBAC assignment is overriding the default ACL
Default ACLs only apply to directories, never to files
explain: Default ACLs are a creation-time inheritance template: they stamp the access ACL of new children, but never retroactively modify existing items — updating old files requires an explicit (recursive) ACL change. Filesystem-root placement does not make them retroactive. RBAC-before-ACL evaluation order is real but unrelated, and default ACLs absolutely do propagate to newly created files.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: A database needs 40,000 IOPS on a 100 GiB data disk. With Premium SSD v1 you would need a huge disk to reach that tier. What does Premium SSD v2 let you do instead?
options: Nothing; v2 uses the same size-band tiers, so you must provision a multi-terabyte disk
Provision IOPS and throughput independently of disk size: a 100 GiB v2 disk supports up to 3000 + 500 per GiB (50,000 IOPS max), so 40,000 IOPS is configurable on the 100 GiB disk
Use bursting credits, which v2 accrues faster than v1
Attach the disk as an Ultra disk instead, because v2 cannot exceed 20,000 IOPS
explain: Premium SSD v2 decouples performance from capacity: baseline 3,000 IOPS / 125 MB/s free, then up to 500 additional IOPS per GiB to a max of 80,000 IOPS — so a 100 GiB disk can be set to 40,000 IOPS without growing the disk. Size-band tiering is the v1 model. Bursting is a v1 concept, and v2\u2019s ceiling is 80,000 IOPS, not 20,000.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: A latency-sensitive workload needs 60,000 IOPS on a 500 GiB data disk, and the team asks whether to use Premium SSD v1 or Ultra Disk. What is the key Ultra Disk characteristic that decides this?
options: Ultra Disks use the same P-tier size bands as Premium SSD v1
Ultra Disks require host caching to be set to ReadOnly
Ultra Disks let you provision IOPS and throughput (up to 400,000 IOPS) at disk creation, independent of disk size, and are LRS-only and data-disk-only
Ultra Disks are zone-redundant by default
explain: Ultra Disks take provisioned IOPS/MBps at creation time (up to 400,000 IOPS), independent of capacity — the way to get 60,000 IOPS on a 500 GiB disk — with the constraints that they are LRS-only, data-disk-only, and need zonal co-location with the VM. They do not use v1 P-tier bands, host caching is not supported on Ultra, and they are zonal, not zone-redundant.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: Two teams share a region but must keep their data in separate storage accounts for chargeback. Team A wants its container asynchronously copied into Team B\u2019s account in the SAME region for analytics. Can object replication do this?
