options: No; object replication requires the destination to be in a different region
No; object replication only works with hierarchical namespace accounts
Yes, but only by first converting both accounts to GRS

Yes: source and destination accounts may be in the same region or different regions (and different subscriptions); it replicates block blobs asynchronously, requires versioning and change feed on the source, and does not support HNS accounts
explain: Object replication explicitly supports same-region source/destination pairs — it is about account-to-account copying, not necessarily cross-region. It needs blob versioning and change feed enabled on the source, and it does not work with hierarchical namespace (ADLS Gen2) accounts. No GRS conversion is involved.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: A Linux VM fails to mount an Azure Files NFS 4.1 share with "mount.nfs: access denied by server". The share exists, the VNet service endpoint is configured, and "Secure transfer required" is enabled on the storage account. What is the fix?
options: Disable "Secure transfer required" on the storage account (or mount with the AZNFS mount helper with encryption in transit), because a standard NFS client cannot mount while the setting is enabled
Enable SMB 3.0 on the share, because NFS mounts require SMB to be enabled first
Add a private endpoint, because NFS shares cannot use service endpoints
Switch the share to the Hot tier, because NFS requires Hot
explain: A standard NFS client mount is denied when "Secure transfer required" is enabled; the documented fixes are disabling the setting or using the AZNFS mount helper with encryption in transit for NFS. SMB settings are irrelevant to NFS, service endpoints are a supported path for NFS shares, and access tier has no bearing on the mount failure.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: An application must encrypt each blob with a key the application supplies per request, and the key must never be stored in Azure. Customer-managed keys in Key Vault do not satisfy the "never stored" requirement. Which mechanism fits?
options: Infrastructure encryption, which uses Microsoft-managed keys per request
Customer-provided keys (CPK): the app passes the key in the REST request headers and Azure never stores it
Encryption scopes, which store one key per container in Key Vault
Storage Service Encryption with Microsoft-managed keys plus a Key Vault firewall
explain: Customer-provided keys let the client supply the encryption key in the request headers (REST only); Azure uses it for the operation and never persists it — matching the "never stored" requirement. CMK and encryption scopes both persist keys in Key Vault. Infrastructure encryption is a creation-time double-encryption option using Microsoft-managed keys, not per-request client keys.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: You plan premium (SSD) file shares for a latency-sensitive application and need to choose replication. Which redundancy options are available for premium file shares?
options: GRS and GZRS, because premium shares need geo-protection
RA-GRS for read access in the secondary region
LRS and ZRS only; premium file shares do not support GRS/GZRS, so cross-region protection must be built with AzCopy, File Sync, or similar
Any redundancy option, the same as standard file shares
explain: Premium file shares (FileStorage accounts) support only LRS and ZRS — geo-redundant options are not available for them, so cross-region DR needs a custom replication approach. Standard shares get the full LRS/ZRS/GRS/GZRS set. RA-GRS and GZRS are not offered on premium shares.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: After a ransomware scare, you must protect blob data against both accidental and malicious deletion, including the ability to restore the account to a point in time. Which combination do you enable?
options: Blob soft delete alone, which covers every deletion scenario
Azure Backup vaulted backup only, which replaces the need for soft delete
Version-level immutability with a legal hold on every blob
Layered data protection: blob versioning plus blob soft delete plus container soft delete, with point-in-time restore enabled for the account
explain: No single toggle covers everything: versioning preserves overwritten blobs, blob soft delete retains deleted blobs, container soft delete retains deleted containers, and point-in-time restore rolls the whole account back — together they form the ransomware/malicious-deletion defense. Soft delete alone does not restore containers or roll back en masse, vaulted backup is a separate (also valid) strategy but not the asked-for combination, and legal holds on everything would freeze normal operations.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: A data disk\u2019s filesystem is corrupted. You have an incremental snapshot of the disk from last night. What is the correct restore sequence?
options: Create a new managed disk from the snapshot, then attach or swap it in for the corrupted disk; snapshots cannot be restored in place onto the existing disk
Copy the snapshot\u2019s blocks directly onto the corrupted disk with AzCopy
Restore the snapshot in place from the Snapshots blade, which overwrites the disk
Detach the disk, wait for the snapshot to merge, then reattach
explain: Managed disk snapshots restore by creating a new disk from the snapshot and then attaching it (or swapping it for an OS disk) — there is no in-place snapshot restore onto an existing disk. AzCopy cannot write snapshot blocks onto a live disk, the portal has no in-place restore, and snapshots never "merge" back automatically.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: An admin enabled the "Large file shares" option (up to 100 TiB) on a storage account for a one-off migration. The migration is done and they want to disable the option to simplify the account. What do you tell them?
options: Disable it in the portal; the setting is reversible once all shares are under 5 TiB
The large-file-shares capability is a one-way, account-level opt-in: once enabled it cannot be disabled
It disables automatically after 30 days of no share exceeding 5 TiB
Open a support ticket; only Microsoft can disable it
explain: Enabling large file shares is an irreversible, account-level decision — the portal warns it cannot be undone, so it should only be enabled when genuinely needed. There is no auto-expiry, no size-based reversion, and support cannot reverse it either.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: An application requires a 99.9% read availability SLA and millisecond first-byte latency for data accessed a few times per year. The architect proposes the Cool tier. What is wrong with this choice?
options: Cool tier latency is measured in hours, not milliseconds
Cool tier does not support millisecond latency for reads
Cool (and Cold) tiers carry a 99% availability SLA versus 99.9% for Hot, so the SLA requirement fails even though first-byte latency is still milliseconds
Cool tier cannot be read without rehydration
explain: Hot, Cool, and Cold all offer millisecond first-byte latency — Cool fails here only on availability: 99% versus Hot\u2019s 99.9%. Hours-long retrieval and offline data are Archive-tier characteristics, not Cool. The tier choice is fine for infrequent access but wrong against a 99.9% SLA.
domain: Domain 2: Implement and manage storage

q: A VMSS runs a platform image pinned to version 2024.01.15. You enable automatic OS image upgrades so instances stay patched, but no upgrades ever occur. What is the cause?
options: Automatic OS upgrades work with pinned versions; the health probe must be misconfigured
Automatic OS upgrades require the upgrade policy to be set to Manual
Data disks are preserved during upgrade, which blocks the OS disk replacement
Automatic OS image upgrades require the image reference version to be "latest" — with a pinned version there is nothing new to roll out, so set the version to latest
explain: Automatic OS upgrades roll instances to the newest published image in batches, which is only possible when the image reference uses "latest"; a pinned version means the scale set never sees a newer image. The upgrade policy must be Rolling (not Manual), health monitoring is a prerequisite but not the root cause here, and data-disk preservation is expected behavior, not a blocker.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: A compliance audit requires all App Service web apps to negotiate TLS 1.2 or higher. Where do you enforce this per app?
options: In the app\u2019s TLS/SSL settings, set "Minimum TLS version" to 1.2; this is enforced at the front end regardless of application code
In the application code, by rejecting older TLS handshakes
On the App Service plan, because TLS settings are plan-wide
In Azure Front Door, because App Service cannot control TLS versions
explain: Each App Service app has a "Minimum TLS version" setting (1.0/1.1/1.2) enforced by the platform front end — no code change needed. It is per-app, not plan-wide, and Front Door only governs its own edge, not the app\u2019s direct endpoint.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: You build a Durable Functions order workflow that needs a durable counter shared across many orchestrations (e.g., total orders today). Which Durable Functions concept provides addressable, stateful instances you signal from orchestrators?
options: Activity functions, which hold shared state between orchestrations
Durable entities: stateful instances with an identity that you read and update via signals (SignalEntityAsync) from orchestrators or clients
Sub-orchestrators, which share memory with the parent
External events, which persist counters in table storage automatically
explain: Durable entities are the stateful primitive: each entity has an identity and state, and orchestrators/clients interact with it through signals and calls. Activity functions are stateless units of work, sub-orchestrators do not share memory, and external events deliver one-off inputs rather than addressable state.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: You deploy an app plus a logging sidecar as an Azure Container Instances container group. The team asks about lifecycle and billing: what happens when one container exits, and how is the group billed?
options: Each container has an independent lifecycle and is billed per container per hour
Sidecars are not supported; each container needs its own group

The group is billed per second of execution, and all containers in the group share fate: they start together, share localhost networking and volumes, and the group\u2019s restart policy governs the whole group
Billing is per vCPU reserved per month regardless of runtime
explain: A container group is the atomic unit: containers share lifecycle, localhost, and storage volumes, the restart policy (Always/Never/OnFailure) applies to the group, and billing is per-second for actual execution. Per-container independent lifecycles and monthly vCPU reservations describe other services, and sidecars are precisely what container groups are for.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: Security requires AKS nodes to receive OS security patches automatically, but the team does not want full node-image upgrades changing the OS version unexpectedly. Which node OS upgrade channel meets this?
options: The cluster auto-upgrade channel, set to "stable"
Disable all upgrades and patch nodes manually
NodeImage, which upgrades to the newest node image weekly
The node OS upgrade channel set to "SecurityPatch", which applies OS security patches without moving to a new node image version
explain: The node OS upgrade channel is separate from the Kubernetes version auto-upgrader: "SecurityPatch" applies OS security patches only, "NodeImage" moves to newer node images, and "None" disables it. The cluster auto-upgrade channel governs Kubernetes versions, not OS patches. Manual patching defeats the automation requirement.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: A developer tries to create a function app without specifying a storage account, arguing that HTTP-triggered functions do not need one. What do you tell them?
options: They are right for HTTP triggers; storage is only required for queue and blob triggers
A storage account (AzureWebJobsStorage) is required for every function app on all hosting plans — the Functions runtime uses it for keys, triggers state, and leases
Storage is only required on the Consumption plan; Premium and Dedicated manage state internally
A storage account is required only when deployment slots are used
explain: The Functions host requires AzureWebJobsStorage on every plan (Consumption, Premium, Dedicated, Flex) for internal state: keys, trigger bookkeeping, and leases. HTTP triggers do not exempt the app, Premium/Dedicated do not remove the requirement, and slots are unrelated to the storage dependency.
domain: Domain 3: Deploy and manage Azure compute resources

q: A Recovery Services vault was created with the default GRS replication and already protects 40 VMs. Finance now wants LRS to cut costs. What are the options?
options: Change the replication type in vault Properties; it applies to existing recovery points
Storage replication type must be chosen before the first backup is configured — once items are protected the setting is locked, so you need a new LRS vault and re-register the workloads
Switch to ZRS, which is cheaper than LRS and can be changed in place
Disable backup, change the setting, then re-enable backup on the same vault
explain: The vault\u2019s storage replication type (GRS/LRS/ZRS, default GRS) can only be set before any backup is configured; afterwards the option is disabled. Changing it requires a new vault with the desired replication and re-registering workloads. In-place changes are not possible, ZRS is not cheaper than LRS, and disable/re-enable does not unlock the setting.

q: An Azure-to-Azure Site Recovery recovery plan must update DNS records and run a health check after the application tier VMs start during failover. How do you automate these steps inside the plan?
options: Add a Custom Script extension to each VM that runs on boot
Use Azure Policy to deploy the DNS update at failover time
Add script actions to the recovery plan (pre- or post-steps per group) that invoke Azure Automation runbooks; Azure-to-Azure supports runbooks for both failover and failback
Schedule an Azure Automation runbook on a timer and hope it coincides with the failover
explain: Recovery plans support inserting script or manual actions as pre-steps/post-steps per group, and for Azure-to-Azure replication those scripts are Azure Automation runbooks — supported for both failover and failback. Custom Script extensions run at VM provisioning, not orchestrated failover time. Azure Policy does not execute failover workflows, and a timer-based runbook cannot coordinate with the plan\u2019s sequencing.

q: You publish a gallery image version and select East US 2 and West Europe as target replication regions, while the gallery itself lives in East US. In which regions will the image version be available?

Only East US, because replication follows the gallery location
All Azure regions, because gallery images replicate globally by default
East US, East US 2, and West Europe — the source region is always included as a replica region automatically
explain: The region where the image version is created (source region) is always implicitly a replica target — you get East US plus your two selected regions. Selecting targets does not exclude the source, replication is not limited to the gallery\u2019s region, and it certainly does not go global by default.

q: A rendering farm runs on a Spot VMSS. During a busy afternoon several instances are evicted and renders fail. The architect asks whether Spot was the wrong choice. What is the accurate guidance?
options: Spot VMs are never evicted once allocated; the failures must come from another cause
Azure gives a 30-day notice before Spot evictions, so the farm should have drained
Spot is unsuitable for any production workload under any circumstances

Spot VMs can be evicted at any time when Azure needs capacity; they suit fault-tolerant, interruptible batch work only if the application handles evictions (e.g., via the scheduled-events termination notice), not stateful or deadline-critical renders without checkpointing
explain: Spot VMs trade deep discounts for preemptibility: Azure can evict them whenever capacity is needed, with only a short termination notice via scheduled events — there is no 30-day warning and no eviction immunity. Spot fits batch workloads designed for interruption (checkpointing, retries); blaming Spot entirely or claiming immunity both misstate the model.

q: A team needs two different disk protections: a 30-day retained, policy-driven backup for compliance, and a quick rollback point before a risky OS upgrade this weekend. Which tools map to which need?

Snapshots for both, because Azure Backup cannot retain recovery points for 30 days
Azure Backup for both, because snapshots cannot be taken manually
RAID via Storage Spaces for both requirements
explain: Azure Backup is the policy engine: scheduled, retention-managed, app-consistent recovery points for compliance. A managed snapshot is the ad-hoc point-in-time copy for a pre-change rollback. Snapshots have no retention policy engine (wrong for the 30-day need), Azure Backup absolutely supports 30-day retention, and Storage Spaces RAID is availability, not backup.

q: An HTTP-triggered function processes uploaded videos, routinely taking 20 minutes per invocation. The team deploys it to a Consumption plan and executions are killed. What is the fix?

Move the function app to a Premium or Dedicated (App Service) plan, where executions are not subject to the Consumption 5-minute default / 10-minute maximum timeout
Split the function into four 5-minute functions chained by queues
Enable Always On, which removes the Consumption timeout

Premium and Dedicated plans have effectively unbounded execution time. Chaining is a workaround, not the fix, and Always On is a different setting (keeping the app warm) that does not lift the Consumption timeout.

q: You design a Durable Functions expense-approval workflow: submit, wait for a manager\u2019s approval (up to 48 hours), then reimburse or reject on timeout. Which Durable Functions pattern is this?

Async HTTP APIs, because the manager calls back over HTTP
The human interaction pattern: the orchestrator waits on an external event (the approval) with a durable timer for the timeout
The monitor pattern, because it polls the manager\u2019s inbox
explain: Human interaction is the pattern for workflows that pause for a person: the orchestrator waits for an external event and uses a durable timer to handle the no-response timeout. Fan-out/fan-in parallelizes work, async HTTP is for long-running API calls, and the monitor pattern polls on a schedule rather than waiting on an event.

q: A legacy web app moved to Azure Container Apps keeps session state in memory. With multiple replicas, users randomly lose their sessions. The team cannot refactor to external state this quarter. What is the immediate mitigation?

Switch the ingress to TCP mode, which is inherently sticky
Increase the minimum replica count, which pins users to replicas
Set the ingress stickySessions affinity to "sticky" so a client is routed to the same replica (cookie-based), while planning to externalize session state
explain: Container Apps ingress supports session affinity (stickySessions.affinity = sticky), which pins a client to one replica via cookie — the standard stopgap for in-memory session state. Scale-to-zero does not guarantee a single replica under load, TCP ingress has no HTTP cookie affinity, and replica count does not control routing. Externalizing state remains the durable fix.

q: A stateless API on App Service scales out to 10 instances, but traffic is uneven: a few instances are saturated while others sit idle. The app sets no affinity cookie itself. What is the likely cause and fix?

Always On is disabled, causing cold starts on idle instances
The App Service plan is not zone-redundant, causing the imbalance
Autoscale is using a schedule profile instead of a metric rule
explain: ARR affinity adds an affinity cookie that sticks each client to one instance — great for stateful apps, harmful for stateless scale-out where it defeats even distribution. Disabling it lets the front ends spread load. Always On affects cold starts, not distribution; zone redundancy is about availability; and the autoscale trigger does not cause per-instance stickiness.

q: Security mandates that administrators SSH to Linux VMs and RDP to Windows VMs using their Microsoft Entra identities — no local VM accounts. What do you deploy and which RBAC roles grant access?

The AADSSHLoginForLinux / AADLoginForWindows VM extensions, with the "Virtual Machine Administrator Login" or "Virtual Machine User Login" RBAC roles assigned on the VMs
Azure Bastion with Kerberos passthrough, plus the Reader role
Just-in-time VM access in Defender for Cloud, which replaces local accounts
explain: Microsoft Entra login for Azure VMs uses the AADLoginForWindows / AADSSHLoginForLinux extensions, and access is granted via the purpose-built "Virtual Machine Administrator Login" / "Virtual Machine User Login" roles. The Custom Script extension does not provide Entra auth, Bastion is a connectivity path (not an identity), and JIT controls network access timing rather than the login identity.

q: You need every new Linux VM to run a bootstrap script exactly once at first boot (install agents, write config), with no agent dependency beyond the platform. Which mechanism fits, and how does it differ from the Custom Script Extension?
options: Run Command, which runs at first boot without an agent
The Desired State Configuration extension, which only runs at first boot
Custom data (cloud-init on Linux): passed at provisioning time and consumed once at first boot, whereas the Custom Script Extension runs post-provisioning and can be re-run or updated at any time
A scheduled task deployed by Azure Policy guest configuration
explain: Custom data / cloud-init is the first-boot mechanism: supplied with the VM model, executed once during initial provisioning. The Custom Script Extension is a post-provisioning agent-based extension that can run, update, and re-run scripts throughout the VM\u2019s life. Run Command needs the agent and is on-demand, DSC is ongoing configuration management, and guest configuration is policy-driven drift control.

q: You must stand up an identical copy of a production web app in another region for a DR drill — same configuration and content — without rebuilding the deployment pipeline. The app runs on a Standard plan. What is the fastest supported path?

Use deployment slots, which replicate the app across regions
Export the ARM template and redeploy, which copies the content automatically

Clone the app (supported on Standard and higher, same backup limitations): it creates a full copy in the same or a different region, though some settings like autoscale and Easy Auth need manual reconfiguration
explain: App cloning is built for this: a full copy of the app (config plus content) into the same or another region, available on Standard tier and above with the same limitations as App Service backup. Backup/restore works but is a two-step process aimed at recovery, not cloning. Slots live in the same plan/region, and an ARM template redeploys configuration — not the site content.

q: An architect asks for a "zone-redundant" single virtual machine so it survives a datacenter failure. What do you tell them?
options: A single VM is always zonal — it lives in one availability zone (or no zone); zone redundancy for compute requires a Virtual Machine Scale Set spread across zones (or paired services), not a single VM
Enable zone redundancy in the VM\u2019s availability options blade
Attach the VM\u2019s disks as zone-redundant storage to make the VM zone-redundant
Deploy the VM to the region\u2019s paired region instead
explain: Zone redundancy is a property of a fleet, not an instance: one VM occupies one zone, so surviving a zone failure needs multiple instances across zones (VMSS) with a load balancer. There is no per-VM "zone-redundant" toggle, zone-redundant disks protect data (not the compute instance), and the paired region is for DR, not zonal resilience.

q: A monitoring VM averages 8% CPU with brief daily spikes to 70%. The team wants the cheapest suitable size. Why is a B-series VM the right call?
options: B-series VMs are the only sizes that support burstable workloads
B-series VMs bank CPU credits while running below their baseline and spend them during spikes, so a mostly-idle VM with bursts costs far less than a full-performance size
B-series VMs never throttle, so the 70% spikes are guaranteed
B-series VMs include free premium storage
explain: B-series (burstable) VMs accrue CPU credits when under their baseline and consume them when bursting above it — ideal for low-average, spiky workloads at low cost. They absolutely do throttle when credits run out (no guaranteed bursting), other series also handle bursts (at full price), and storage is unrelated to the CPU credit model.

q: An Azure Firewall protecting a large virtual desktop deployment hits SNAT port exhaustion during morning logon storms. The firewall currently has one public IP. What are the two supported ways to scale SNAT ports?
options: Enable accelerated networking on the firewall, which multiplies SNAT ports
Switch the firewall to the Basic SKU, which has no SNAT limit

Associate additional public IP addresses with the firewall (2,496 SNAT ports per IP per instance, up to 250 IPs), or integrate a NAT gateway on the firewall subnet for dynamic SNAT allocation (64,512 ports per IP)
Add more firewall instances manually in the portal
explain: Azure Firewall scales SNAT two ways: more public IPs (2,496 ports per PIP per backend instance, up to 250 PIPs) or a NAT gateway on AzureFirewallSubnet (64,512 ports per IP, dynamically allocated). Accelerated networking does not change SNAT math, there is no Basic firewall SKU without limits, and firewall scaling is managed by the platform, not manual instance adds.

q: Remote users on macOS and Windows need point-to-site VPN with Microsoft Entra authentication (no certificates to distribute). Which VPN protocol should you configure on the gateway?
options: SSTP, because it is the only protocol supporting Entra authentication
IKEv2, because OpenVPN cannot use Entra authentication
Point-to-site does not support Entra authentication at all
OpenVPN, which supports Microsoft Entra authentication and works cross-platform; SSTP is Windows-only and IKEv2 suits native OS clients without Entra auth
explain: OpenVPN is the P2S protocol that supports Microsoft Entra ID authentication and has clients for macOS and Windows — the no-certificate ask. SSTP is Windows-only, and while IKEv2 works natively on many OSes, Entra-authenticated P2S is the OpenVPN scenario. Claiming P2S cannot do Entra auth is simply wrong.

q: A branch office connects over ExpressRoute. For resilience you add a second path using a VPN gateway, but the gateway in place is policy-based and the coexistence configuration will not establish. What must you do to the gateway?
options: ExpressRoute and VPN cannot coexist; remove ExpressRoute first
The VPN gateway must be route-based: ExpressRoute/VPN coexistence (and BGP) requires a route-based gateway, so the policy-based gateway must be deleted and recreated as route-based
Enable BGP on the policy-based gateway, which is sufficient
Add a second policy-based gateway for the failover path
explain: Coexistence of ExpressRoute with a site-to-site VPN requires a route-based VPN gateway (BGP-capable); policy-based gateways support neither coexistence nor BGP. The fix is delete-and-recreate as route-based — there is no in-place SKU/family conversion. Removing ExpressRoute defeats the purpose, and BGP cannot be bolted onto a policy-based gateway.

q: An Application Gateway fronts two backend web apps. App1 expects Host: app1.contoso.com but the gateway\u2019s public listener uses www.contoso.com. Requests fail host-header validation on App1. How do you fix it without changing the app?
options: Create a second gateway, because one gateway cannot serve two host names
In the backend HTTP settings, override the host name (or pick host name from the backend target) so the gateway sends the expected Host header to App1
Enable cookie-based affinity, which rewrites the Host header
Add a rewrite rule that changes the backend\u2019s certificate
explain: Backend HTTP settings control the Host header sent upstream: you can override it with a specific value or pick it from the backend target\u2019s FQDN — the direct fix for host-header validation failures. A second gateway is unnecessary, cookie affinity affects session routing not headers, and rewrite rules manipulate paths/headers but the host-name setting is the purpose-built control.

q: A NAT gateway with one public IP supports about 64,512 SNAT ports. An application needs roughly 200,000 concurrent outbound connections. What is the correct scaling math?
options: Enable TCP reset on idle, which multiplies the port count
One NAT gateway cannot exceed 64,512 ports under any configuration
Associate additional public IPs with the NAT gateway (up to 16): each adds about 64,512 SNAT ports, so four IPs yield roughly 258,000 ports
Switch to a Basic SKU public IP, which doubles the ports per IP
explain: NAT gateway scales SNAT linearly with public IPs: ~64,512 ports per IP, up to 16 IPs per gateway — four IPs give about 258,000 ports. TCP reset on idle reclaims ports faster but does not raise the ceiling. A single IP is indeed capped, and SKU has no bearing on the per-IP port count.

q: Long-lived SSH sessions through a public IP to a jump host drop after exactly 4 minutes of inactivity. The SSH server\u2019s keepalive is disabled by policy. What should you adjust?
options: The network security group, because NSGs enforce a 4-minute idle timeout
The virtual network\u2019s DNS settings, which control session lifetime
Enable accelerated networking, which extends idle timeouts
The public IP\u2019s TCP idle timeout: it defaults to 4 minutes and is configurable from 4 to 30 minutes
explain: The 4-minute drop is the public IP / load balancer TCP idle timeout default; raising it (4–30 minutes) keeps idle flows alive without touching SSH config. NSGs do not impose idle timeouts, DNS settings are unrelated to TCP flows, and accelerated networking improves throughput, not timeout behavior.

q: A legacy client holds database connections open through an Azure Load Balancer for hours. When the LB\u2019s idle timeout expires, connections hang instead of failing fast, and the app cannot detect the dead connection. Which two settings address this?
options: Increase the backend pool size and enable floating IP
Raise the LB rule\u2019s idle timeout (4–30 minutes, default 4) and enable "TCP reset on idle" so both ends get a RST when the timeout expires
Switch the LB SKU to Basic, which never times out idle flows
Enable SNAT on the backend pool, which keeps connections alive indefinitely
explain: The LB rule idle timeout (default 4 minutes, tunable 4–30) controls how long an idle flow is kept; enabling TCP reset on idle sends a reset packet at expiry so the app fails fast instead of hanging on a black-holed connection. Floating IP/DSR changes routing, not timeouts; Basic SKU has the same timeout model; and SNAT does not keep idle flows alive.

q: An Application Gateway returns 502 errors for a backend report endpoint that takes 60 seconds to generate. The backend is healthy and responds when called directly. What is the likely cause and fix?
options: The backend\u2019s TLS certificate is invalid, causing the 502
The gateway\u2019s request timeout (default 20 seconds) is exceeded; increase it in the backend HTTP settings (up to 86,400 seconds)
The health probe is misconfigured, so the backend is marked unhealthy
WAF is blocking the long-running request as an anomaly
explain: Application Gateway aborts backend requests exceeding its request timeout (20s default) with a 502 — a 60-second report needs the timeout raised in the backend HTTP settings. A bad certificate or unhealthy probe would fail all requests, not just slow ones, and WAF does not police request duration.

q: An e-commerce site behind Azure Front Door stores shopping carts in server memory. Users report items disappearing from carts as requests land on different origins. What should you enable?
options: Front Door caching, which will pin users to origins
Anycast routing, which guarantees origin stickiness
Session affinity on the Front Door: cookie-based affinity routes a client to the same origin while the cookie lives
WAF rate limiting, which reduces origin switching
explain: Front Door session affinity uses a cookie to keep a client on the same origin — the fix for in-memory session state. Caching stores responses, it does not route clients; anycast gets the client to the nearest edge, not to a specific origin; and WAF rate limiting throttles requests rather than pinning them.

q: You create an application security group and try to add VM NICs from two peered VNets (hub and spoke). The portal rejects the spoke NICs. Why?
options: ASGs require the VMs to be in the same availability zone
The NSG referencing the ASG is in the wrong region
ASGs only support NICs with accelerated networking enabled
Application security groups are scoped to a single virtual network; all member NICs must belong to the same VNet, so peered-VNet NICs cannot join
explain: An ASG\u2019s membership is limited to network interfaces in the same virtual network as the ASG — peering does not extend it. Create one ASG per VNet (or restructure the NSG rules). Availability zones, NSG region, and accelerated networking have nothing to do with ASG membership scope.

q: Deploying Azure Firewall fails when you attach an existing Basic SKU public IP. What is the requirement?
options: Azure Firewall requires Standard SKU public IP addresses; Basic is not supported
The public IP must be in a different region than the firewall
The public IP must be zone-redundant, which Basic cannot provide
Firewall public IPs must come from a public IP prefix, never a standalone IP
explain: Azure Firewall only accepts Standard SKU public IPs — Basic SKU addresses are rejected at deployment. Region pairing is not the issue (same region is correct), zone redundancy is recommended but the SKU itself is the gate, and standalone Standard IPs are fine (prefixes are optional).

q: An Application Gateway WAF policy blocks a legitimate admin path (/admin/health) that the rest of the site needs protected. You want the exclusion to apply only to that path. How do you scope it?
options: Create a second WAF policy and attach it to the same listener
Associate the WAF policy at the listener and override it per path-based rule, so /admin/health gets its own policy (or exclusion) while the rest keeps the strict policy
Disable the WAF policy and rely on NSG rules instead
Edit the managed rule set, which automatically scopes to paths
explain: WAF policies attach to listeners, but path-based (URL path map) rules can each reference their own policy — letting /admin/health run under a tuned policy while the rest stays strict. Two policies cannot attach to one listener, NSGs cannot do WAF exclusions, and managed rule sets are global to the policy, not path-aware by themselves.

q: A compliance review requires the existing Azure Firewall to be zone-redundant. The firewall was deployed without availability zones selected. What are the options?
options: Select the zones in the firewall\u2019s configuration blade; the firewall redeploys automatically
Enable zone redundancy through the firewall policy
Availability zones are chosen at firewall creation and cannot be changed afterwards — you must deploy a new zone-redundant firewall and migrate
Zones apply automatically once the region supports them
explain: Zone selection for Azure Firewall is a creation-time decision and immutable afterwards; making an existing firewall zone-redundant means redeploying and migrating (IP, rules via policy, routes). There is no in-place toggle, firewall policy does not control zone placement, and nothing happens automatically.

q: A hub VNet in East US has a VPN gateway to on-premises. A spoke VNet in West Europe is peered to the hub, and you enable "Use remote gateways" on the spoke side — but the option is unavailable. Why?
options: Gateway transit requires the spoke to have its own gateway first
The spoke\u2019s address space overlaps the hub\u2019s
"Allow gateway transit" was not enabled on the hub side
Gateway transit / remote gateways only work when both VNets are in the same region; global (cross-region) peering does not support gateway transit
explain: Gateway transit is a same-region peering feature — over global (cross-region) peering the remote-gateway options are unavailable by design. The fix is a regional hub (or VWAN) in West Europe. The spoke must NOT have its own gateway (that is what "use remote" is for), overlap would break peering itself, and hub-side transit is necessary but not the blocker here.

q: You configure BGP on a site-to-site VPN. The on-premises router uses ASN 65001. What ASN does the Azure VPN gateway use by default, and what must you ensure?
options: Azure uses ASN 65515 by default; ensure the on-premises ASN differs from Azure\u2019s (and from any ExpressRoute ASN in use)
Azure uses ASN 65001 by default to match on-premises
Azure assigns a random ASN per gateway that you must read from the portal
BGP requires both sides to use the same ASN
explain: Azure VPN gateways default to BGP ASN 65515; you can customize it, but it must differ from the on-premises ASN (65001 here) and from any ExpressRoute gateway ASN — BGP peers must have distinct ASNs. Azure does not mirror your ASN, does not randomize it, and same-ASN peering would not establish.

q: A hybrid application must fail over between an Azure web app and an on-premises datacenter endpoint during a regional outage. Which Traffic Manager endpoint type supports the on-premises target?
options: External endpoints: Traffic Manager can target any internet-resolvable FQDN, including on-premises, for hybrid failover routing
Azure endpoints only; on-premises targets are not supported
Nested profiles only, which require both endpoints to be Traffic Manager profiles
Private endpoints, which extend Traffic Manager into the datacenter
explain: Traffic Manager supports external (non-Azure) endpoints addressed by FQDN — exactly the hybrid failover case. "Azure only" is false, nested profiles chain profiles rather than enabling on-premises targets, and private endpoints are an Azure resource-networking concept, not a Traffic Manager endpoint type.

q: A developer in your tenant creates a private endpoint to a partner\u2019s Azure SQL server in another tenant. The connection sits in "Pending" state. Who must act, and where?
options: Your tenant\u2019s network admin, in the private endpoint\u2019s network settings

The owner of the SQL server (or someone with approval permission on it) must approve the private endpoint connection — in cross-tenant cases this is a manual approval in Private Link Center / the resource\u2019s Private endpoint connections blade
The Azure platform approves it automatically after 24 hours
The developer, by deleting and recreating the endpoint until it auto-approves
explain: Private endpoint connections auto-approve only when the requestor has approval rights on the target (typically same-tenant owner); cross-tenant requests go to Pending and the resource owner must approve them manually. Your network admin cannot approve someone else\u2019s resource, there is no 24-hour auto-approval, and recreating does not change the approval requirement.

q: A site-to-site VPN shows "Connected" but no traffic passes: on-premises uses 10.0.0.0/16 and the Azure VNet also uses 10.0.0.0/16. What is the problem?
options: The VPN gateway SKU is too small for the traffic volume
BGP is required for any traffic to flow
The overlapping address space: Azure cannot route between identical prefixes, so the VNet or on-premises range must be re-addressed to non-overlapping space
The GatewaySubnet is missing a route table
explain: Identical address ranges on both sides of the VPN make routing ambiguous — packets cannot be directed correctly, so the address space must be changed on one side. Gateway SKU affects throughput, not routability; BGP is optional for S2S; and GatewaySubnet must not have a conflicting route table, but that is not the cause of overlap-induced blackholing.

q: Outbound emails from a VM are rejected by recipient servers with "reverse DNS validation failed". The VM uses a Standard SKU public IP. How do you fix it?
options: Add an SPF record to the VM\u2019s hostname
Enable DDoS Protection on the public IP, which adds reverse DNS automatically
Switch to a Basic SKU public IP, which includes reverse DNS by default
Set the reverse FQDN (PTR record) on the public IP to the mail server\u2019s forward hostname
explain: Recipient servers validate that the sending IP\u2019s PTR record resolves forward — you configure this with the public IP\u2019s ReverseFqdn property. SPF is a TXT record for the domain, not reverse DNS. DDoS Protection does not create PTR records, and Basic vs Standard SKU is irrelevant to reverse DNS support.

q: A junior admin assumes a new subnet\u2019s NSG blocks all outbound internet traffic by default. What is the actual default, and how do you properly restrict egress?
options: Outbound internet is allowed by default (AllowInternetOutBound); to restrict egress you add explicit Deny rules with lower priority numbers than the default allow
Outbound is denied by default; no action is needed
Outbound is allowed by default and cannot be changed on an NSG
The default depends on the subnet\u2019s address prefix
explain: NSGs ship with default allow rules for outbound internet (AllowInternetOutBound, priority 65001) — you override them with your own Deny rules at lower priority numbers. "Denied by default" is wrong for outbound (inbound from internet is the denied-by-default direction), the defaults are absolutely changeable, and address prefixes do not alter default rules.

q: A KQL query computes an expensive list of faulty devices in a subquery, then references that result twice (once to count, once to join). How do you avoid computing it twice?
options: Use the join operator twice, which caches automatically
Wrap the subquery with materialize() so it is evaluated once and the cached result is reused
Split it into two separate queries and merge the results manually
Use the take operator, which memoizes subqueries
explain: materialize() evaluates its subquery once and caches the result for reuse within the query — the purpose-built fix for repeated expensive subqueries. Joins do not cache inputs, splitting queries doubles the work rather than halving it, and take only limits rows.

q: A log search alert fires a webhook to ServiceNow, but the ticket lacks the affected resource ID and the alert\u2019s custom dimensions. How do you include them in the payload?
options: Switch to an email action, which always includes dimensions
The webhook payload is fixed and cannot be changed
Configure a custom JSON payload on the webhook action, referencing the alert\u2019s dimensions and fields (e.g., resource ID) so the ticket system receives them
Enable the common alert schema, which automatically adds custom dimensions
explain: Webhook actions support a custom JSON payload where you embed dimensions and alert fields (like the affected resource ID) — the way to feed ticketing systems structured data. Email does not guarantee dimensions, the payload is not fixed, and the common alert schema standardizes the schema but does not inject your custom dimensions by itself.

q: During a major incident, dozens of alerts fire and the on-call engineer\u2019s phone receives only a few SMS messages; the rest never arrive. What is happening, and what is the robust fix?

SMS is throttled by the carrier; switch to a different phone number
Use the Azure mobile app push instead, which has no limits

SMS and voice actions are rate-limited to one notification per phone number every five minutes (excess dropped); for high-volume paging use a non-rate-limited action such as webhook, Logic App, function, or runbook feeding the paging system
explain: Azure Monitor rate-limits SMS/voice to one per number per five minutes and drops the excess — exactly the silent loss seen in an alert storm. Webhook, Logic App, function, and runbook actions are not rate-limited, so routing those into the paging system is the robust design. The action group is not broken, the carrier is not the limiter, and push notifications have their own limits.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: Application Insights adaptive sampling is dropping most telemetry, but the team must keep 100% of /login requests while discarding noisy /healthz checks entirely. How do you achieve both?
options: Configure sampling overrides: keep the default adaptive percentage but override /login to 100% and /healthz to 0% based on telemetry attributes
Set the sampling percentage to 100, which keeps /login but also the health checks
Use ingestion sampling, which can filter by URL path
Disable sampling completely, which keeps everything including the noise
explain: Sampling overrides let you set per-telemetry-type/attribute percentages on top of the default — 100% for the critical /login requests, 0% for the noisy health checks. Disabling sampling or setting 100% globally keeps the noise too. Ingestion sampling applies at the service endpoint only when no SDK sampling is in effect and cannot do per-path overrides.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: An operator "acknowledges" a fired metric alert in the Azure portal. A colleague worries this stops the alert rule from evaluating. What is the actual effect?
options: Acknowledging deletes the alert rule so it never fires again
Alert state (New → Acknowledged → Closed) is the operator\u2019s workflow tracking; the monitor condition (Fired/Resolved) is separate and the rule keeps evaluating regardless of state
Acknowledging pauses the rule for 24 hours
The alert is resolved, which clears the underlying metric condition
explain: Azure Monitor separates the operator workflow (alert state: New, Acknowledged, Closed) from the signal (monitor condition: Fired/Resolved) — acknowledging records that a human owns it but the rule continues evaluating and can fire again. It does not delete, pause, or resolve anything.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: In Azure Advisor, which of these recommendations belongs to the Operational Excellence category?
options: Right-size underutilized virtual machines to reduce cost
Enable multifactor authentication for subscription owners
Create Azure Service Health alerts so the team is notified of platform issues affecting their resources
Migrate to Premium SSD for higher disk throughput
explain: Operational Excellence covers process and manageability best practices — Service Health alerts are a textbook example. Rightsizing is Cost, MFA for owners is Security, and Premium SSD migration is Performance. Matching the recommendation to its category is how you prioritize Advisor output.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: In Metrics Explorer you cannot find the "Percentage CPU" metric for a virtual machine, though the VM exists. What should you check first?
options: The metric\u2019s aggregation type, because Percentage CPU requires the Max aggregation
The Log Analytics workspace, because metrics are stored there
The alert rule, because metrics only appear once an alert references them
The metric namespace: select the correct namespace (e.g., Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines) for the resource type, since metrics are organized by namespace
explain: Metrics are grouped under namespaces per resource provider (Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines for VM platform metrics) — the wrong namespace is the classic reason a metric seems missing. Aggregation does not hide metrics, platform metrics are not in Log Analytics, and metrics exist independently of alert rules.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: During an Azure platform incident, management asks exactly which of your resources are affected. Where do you find the authoritative impacted-resource list?
options: In Service Health: open the service issue event to see the impacted resources (and their resource-health states) for that event
In Resource Health, which lists every resource in the subscription
In the Activity Log, filtered to the incident timeframe
In Azure Advisor, under High Availability recommendations
explain: Service Health events carry the impacted-resources view for that specific platform issue — the authoritative per-event list. Resource Health shows per-resource current state but not the event-scoped impact list, the Activity Log records control-plane operations (not platform health), and Advisor gives proactive recommendations, not incident impact.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: You need a Network Watcher packet capture on a VM that records only SQL traffic (TCP 1433) to a storage account. What do you configure, and what storage prerequisite applies?
options: Start the capture with no filters and search the file afterwards; no storage prerequisite exists

Enable packet filtering on the 5-tuple (protocol, local/remote IP, local/remote port) — e.g., TCP with remote port 1433 — and ensure storage account key access is enabled, because captures use SAS tokens (premium storage accounts are not supported)
Use Connection Monitor instead, which filters by port natively
Enable NSG flow logs, which capture full packet payloads
explain: Packet capture filters on the 5-tuple, so TCP/1433 isolates the SQL traffic at capture time. Captures authenticate to storage with SAS tokens, requiring key access on the account, and premium storage accounts cannot be capture targets. Unfiltered captures waste space, Connection Monitor measures connectivity rather than capturing packets, and flow logs record flow metadata — not payloads.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: You built a standard monitoring workbook that must be deployed identically to 20 subscriptions via your IaC pipeline. How do you deploy workbooks programmatically?
options: Workbooks can only be created in the portal; export and import them manually per subscription
Use Azure Policy to generate workbooks from compliance data
Deploy them with an ARM template (or Bicep): workbooks are Azure resources (Microsoft.Insights/workbooks) and support template deployment
Copy the workbook\u2019s JSON into each subscription\u2019s Log Analytics workspace as a saved query
explain: Workbooks are first-class ARM resources, so an ARM/Bicep template deploys the identical workbook to any number of subscriptions in a pipeline. Portal-only creation is false, Azure Policy does not author workbooks, and a saved KQL query is not a workbook (no visualizations, parameters, or layout).
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: You need a timechart of failed requests per 5 minutes over the last day, including intervals with zero failures. Which KQL approach guarantees the empty buckets appear?
options: summarize count() by bin(timestamp, 5m) | render timechart, which always includes empty bins
Use the top operator, which fills gaps automatically
Query with | take 288, which returns one row per 5-minute interval
Use make-series to build the time series (it emits a value — zero — for every bin in the range), then render the series
explain: make-series generates a complete series with an entry per bin (defaulting missing bins to zero), which is exactly what a gap-free timechart needs. summarize-by-bin only emits bins that have data, top limits rows rather than filling gaps, and take just caps row count.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: You manage 50 VMs and want one log search alert rule that fires a separate alert per VM when its CPU exceeds 90%, without creating 50 rules. How do you configure the rule?
options: Enable "Split by dimensions" on the alert rule (e.g., by ResourceId or Computer) so each dimension value produces its own alert
Create one action group per VM and assign them all to the rule
Use a metric alert instead, which splits automatically
Set the alert frequency to 5 minutes, which creates per-VM alerts
explain: Splitting by dimensions turns one log alert rule into per-dimension alerts — one per VM when split by ResourceId/Computer. Multiple action groups do not split alerts, metric alerts have their own multi-resource model (a different feature), and frequency only controls evaluation cadence.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: An Application Insights resource ingests far more telemetry than expected and the bill spikes. What native cost control caps daily ingestion?
options: The Log Analytics daily cap, which automatically applies to linked Application Insights
The Application Insights daily data volume cap: ingestion stops (with notifications at thresholds) once the cap is reached
Sampling overrides, which cap billing directly
The commitment tier, which refunds overage
explain: Application Insights has its own daily data volume cap that throttles ingestion at the limit (with warning emails as it approaches) — the direct cost guardrail. The Log Analytics daily cap governs the workspace, not the classic/App Insights ingestion path. Sampling reduces volume but is not a cap, and commitment tiers discount volume rather than capping or refunding it.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: A query unions data across many Log Analytics workspaces with workspace(). At what scale does Microsoft document this pattern breaking down?
options: Cross-workspace queries are limited to 2 workspaces
The limit is 10 workspaces per query
Performance degrades and the pattern cannot scale above 100 workspaces; beyond a few dozen, centralize or use a dedicated cluster
There is no limit; unions scale to any number of workspaces
explain: Microsoft documents that querying across workspaces gets slow and cannot scale above 100 workspaces — for large estates, centralize ingestion or co-locate workspaces on a dedicated cluster instead of fanning out. Two workspaces is well within limits, "no limit" ignores the documented guidance, and 10 is not the documented threshold.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: You want KQL itself to flag anomalous spikes in a web app\u2019s response-time series without a prebuilt alert rule. Which function performs time-series anomaly detection inline?
options: dcount(), which counts anomalies automatically
arg_max(), which returns the most anomalous point
materialize(), which detects outliers during caching
series_decompose_anomalies(): decomposes the series and scores each point\u2019s anomaly level, which you can filter on
explain: series_decompose_anomalies() is the built-in time-series anomaly detector: it decomposes trend/seasonality and emits an anomaly score per point for filtering. dcount counts distinct values, arg_max returns the row with the maximum of an expression, and materialize only caches — none detect anomalies.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: After a security incident, you must determine which Azure Firewall rule allowed a suspicious outbound connection. Which diagnostic log categories do you enable on the firewall?
options: AzureFirewallApplicationRule, AzureFirewallNetworkRule, and AzureFirewallDnsProxy: the application, network, and DNS-proxy rule logs record allow/deny decisions per rule
AzureActivity, which logs firewall rule evaluations
SigninLogs, which record the connection\u2019s user identity
Firewall logs are not available; use NSG flow logs on the firewall subnet instead
explain: The firewall\u2019s resource-specific log categories — application rule, network rule, and DNS proxy — record each rule evaluation, which is how you trace an allowed connection to its rule. AzureActivity logs control-plane operations, SigninLogs cover Entra authentications (not firewall flows), and NSG flow logs on AzureFirewallSubnet do not capture the firewall\u2019s own rule decisions.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: A Metrics Explorer chart of VM CPU over the last hour shows chunky 5-minute averages, but you need 1-minute granularity to spot a brief spike. What do you change?
options: The metric namespace, which controls granularity
The chart type, because only line charts support 1-minute data
The time grain: select a finer grain (e.g., 1 minute) — granularity depends on the metric\u2019s supported grains and the selected time range
The aggregation, because Average always uses 5-minute bins
explain: Time grain controls the bin size of the plotted series; choosing 1 minute (where the metric and time range support it) reveals the spike. Namespace selects which metrics exist, chart type only changes rendering, and aggregation (Average vs Maximum) is independent of grain.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: Leadership wants a formal root-cause report for last week\u2019s Azure storage outage that affected your region. Where do you obtain Microsoft\u2019s post-incident analysis?
options: In Resource Health, which archives RCAs per resource
Open a support ticket; RCAs are only delivered on request
In Service Health history: select the past event to read its summary, updates, and the published root cause analysis (RCA)
In the Activity Log, which contains the RCA as an event
explain: Service Health keeps a history of past service issues, each with its communications and the published root cause analysis — the formal record leadership is asking for. Resource Health shows current per-resource state, the Activity Log records your control-plane actions, and while support can help, the RCA is published in Service Health without needing a ticket.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: Data residency rules now require all monitoring data in a new region. The Log Analytics workspace is in the old region. Can you move the workspace to the new region?
options: Yes, change the region in the workspace\u2019s settings; data migrates automatically
Use Azure Resource Mover, which moves workspaces across regions with data
Yes, but only if the workspace uses the Analytics table plan

No: a workspace\u2019s region is fixed — cross-region relocation means creating a new workspace in the target region and reconfiguring data sources (same-region subscription/resource-group moves are supported)
explain: Log Analytics does not support in-place cross-region moves: the documented relocation is a new workspace in the target region plus re-pointing agents, DCRs, and diagnostic settings (historical data stays behind under retention). Same-region moves across subscriptions/resource groups are supported. Resource Mover does not handle workspaces, and table plan is irrelevant.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources

q: An auditor asks who deleted a production virtual machine last Tuesday. In the Activity Log, which category do you filter on to find the deletion operation?
options: Security, because deletions are security events
ServiceHealth, because the VM is now unhealthy
Administrative: control-plane operations like VM create/update/delete are logged under the Administrative category
Alert, because the deletion triggered a resource health alert
explain: The Administrative category records control-plane (ARM) operations — including who deleted the VM and when. Security covers policy/role events, ServiceHealth covers platform incidents, and Alert covers fired alert rules; none of them is where resource-management operations live.
domain: Domain 5: Monitor and maintain Azure resources
